translations.an10.13:1: “These ten, monks, are fetters. Which ten? Five lower fetters, five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, attachment to precepts and practices, sensual desire, ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: “Monks, whatever beings there are—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, with form, formless, percipient, non-percipient, neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them, the arahant, perfectly enlightened; even so, monks, whatever skillful qualities there are, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their resort. Heedfulness is declared their foremost.
translations.an10.15:2: “Just as, monks, whatever tracks there are of forest creatures, all of them converge on the elephant’s footprint, and the elephant’s footprint is declared their foremost, in terms of size; even so, monks, whatever skillful qualities there are, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their resort. Heedfulness is declared their foremost.
translations.an10.15:3: “Just as, monks, whatever rafters there are of a peaked house, all of them slope toward the peak, incline toward the peak, have the peak as their resort, the peak is declared their foremost; even so, monks, whatever skillful qualities there are, all of them have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their resort. Heedfulness is declared their foremost.
translations.an10.15:7: “Just as, monks, whatever petty kings there are, all of them follow behind King Wheel-turning, King Wheel-turning is declared their foremost; even so, monks …
translations.an10.15:8: “Just as, monks, whatever light there is of the star constellations, all of it is not worth one sixteenth part of the moon’s light, the moon’s light is declared their foremost; even so, monks …
translations.an10.15:9: “Just as, monks, when the sun has risen piercing the sky, free of clouds, it illuminates, dispels, and shines upon all that is in space and has come to be there; even so, monks …
translations.an10.17:1: “Monks, dwell with a protector, do not dwell without a protector. Suffering, monks, is dwelling without a protector. These ten, monks, are qualities that make one a protector. Which ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the monastic code, perfect in conduct and livelihood, seeing danger in the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains in the training rules. And that, monks, a monk is virtuous … undertaking he trains in the training rules—this too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.17:2: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is very learned, a keeper of what he has learned, a storehouse of what he has learned, those qualities that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, meaningful, well-phrased, complete and pure, a supreme way of life, a holy life—they are very learned by him, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated by wisdom. And that, monks, a monk is very learned … penetrated by wisdom—this too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.17:3: “Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, good comrades. And that, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, good comrades—this too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:10: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness, one who remembers and recalls even what was done or said long ago. ‘This monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness, one who remembers and recalls even what was done or said long ago’—even senior monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … and novice monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed. For one pitied by seniors, pitied by middles, pitied by novices, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:11: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise, endowed with wisdom leading to the arising and ending, noble penetrating wisdom, right wisdom leading to the complete ending of suffering. ‘This monk is wise, endowed with wisdom leading to the arising and ending, noble penetrating wisdom, right wisdom leading to the complete ending of suffering’—even senior monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … and novice monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed. For one pitied by seniors … not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:2: “Monks, dwell with a protector, do not dwell without a protector. Suffering, monks, is dwelling without a protector. These ten, monks, are qualities that make one a protector. Which ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous … undertaking he trains in the training rules. ‘This monk is virtuous, dwells restrained by the monastic code, perfect in conduct and livelihood, seeing danger in the slightest faults, undertaking he trains in the training rules’—even senior monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … and novice monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed. For one pitied by seniors, pitied by middles, pitied by novices, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:4: “Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, good comrades. ‘This monk has good friends, good companions, good comrades’—even senior monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … and novice monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed. For one pitied by seniors, pitied by middles, pitied by novices, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:5: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to admonish, endowed with qualities that make one easy to admonish, patient, one who accepts advice. ‘This monk is easy to admonish, endowed with qualities that make one easy to admonish, patient, one who accepts advice’—even senior monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed, middle monks … and novice monks regard him as one to be spoken to and instructed. For one pitied by seniors, pitied by middles, pitied by novices, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk is capable and energetic regarding those high and low duties for his fellow monks, endowed with investigation of the proper method, capable of doing and arranging. ‘This monk is capable and energetic regarding those high and low duties for his fellow monks, endowed with investigation of the proper method, capable of doing and arranging’—even the senior monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed, the middle monks … the novice monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is pitied by the seniors, pitied by the middle ones, pitied by the novices, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This quality too makes one a guardian.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, monks, a monk delights in the Teaching, welcomes it gladly, has great joy regarding the Teaching and Discipline. ‘This monk delights in the Teaching, welcomes it gladly, has great joy regarding the Teaching and Discipline’—even the senior monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed, the middle monks … the novice monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is pitied by the seniors, pitied by the middle ones, pitied by the novices, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This quality too makes one a guardian.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells energetic, for the abandoning of unskillful qualities, for the undertaking of skillful qualities, strong in effort, firm in exertion, not casting off the burden regarding skillful qualities. ‘This monk dwells energetic, for the abandoning of unskillful qualities, for the undertaking of skillful qualities, strong in effort, firm in exertion, not casting off the burden regarding skillful qualities’—even the senior monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed, the middle monks … the novice monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is pitied by the seniors, pitied by the middle ones, pitied by the novices, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This quality too makes one a guardian.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicines and requisites for curing the sick. ‘This monk is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicines and requisites for curing the sick’—even the senior monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed, the middle monks … the novice monks regard him as one who should be spoken to and instructed. For one who is pitied by the seniors, pitied by the middle ones, pitied by the novices, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This quality too makes one a guardian.
translations.an10.20:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks …pe….
translations.an10.20:10: And how, monks, is a monk tranquil in bodily formation? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant equanimity and mindfulness, purity of equanimity. That is how, monks, a monk is tranquil in bodily formation.
translations.an10.20:11: And how, monks, is a monk supremely freed in mind? Here, monks, a monk’s mind is freed from lust, freed from hatred, freed from delusion. That is how, monks, a monk is supremely freed in mind.
translations.an10.20:2: ‘These ten, monks, are noble dwellings that the nobles dwelt in, dwell in, or will dwell in. Which ten? Here, monks, a monk is one who has abandoned the five factors, possessed of the six factors, guarded by one, armed with four, has set aside partial truths, delights in what accords with the age, has unclouded intentions, tranquil in bodily formation, supremely freed in mind, supremely freed in wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how, monks, is a monk one who has abandoned the five factors? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned sensual desire, has abandoned ill will, sloth and torpor have been abandoned, restlessness and remorse have been abandoned, doubt has been abandoned. That is how, monks, a monk is one who has abandoned the five factors.
translations.an10.20:4: And how, monks, is a monk possessed of the six factors? Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is neither pleased nor displeased, dwells equanimous, mindful, clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear … Having smelled an odor with the nose … Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … Having felt a tangible object with the body … Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither pleased nor displeased, dwells equanimous, mindful, clearly comprehending. That is how, monks, a monk is possessed of the six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk guarded by one? Here, monks, a monk possesses a mind guarded by mindfulness. That is how, monks, a monk is guarded by one.
translations.an10.20:6: And how, monks, is a monk armed with four? Here, monks, a monk uses one thing after reflection, endures one thing after reflection, avoids one thing after reflection, removes one thing after reflection. That is how, monks, a monk is armed with four.
translations.an10.20:7: And how, monks, is a monk one who has set aside partial truths? Here, monks, those partial truths of ordinary recluses and brahmins, namely: ‘The world is eternal’ or ‘The world is not eternal’ or ‘The world is finite’ or ‘The world is infinite’ or ‘The soul is the same as the body’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body another’ or ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all these are put aside, rejected, discarded, released from, relinquished. That is how, monks, a monk is one who has set aside partial truths.
translations.an10.20:8: And how, monks, is a monk one who delights in what accords with the age? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned sensual desire, has abandoned desire for existence, sensual desire is subsided. That is how, monks, a monk is one who delights in what accords with the age.
translations.an10.20:9: And how, monks, is a monk one who has unclouded intentions? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned sensual intention, has abandoned intention of ill will, has abandoned intention of harm. That is how, monks, a monk is one who has unclouded intentions.
translations.an10.24:1: On one occasion Venerable Mahācunda was dwelling among the Cetis at Sahajātiya. There Venerable Mahācunda addressed the monks: ‘Friends, monks.’ And those monks replied to Venerable Mahācunda: ‘Friend.’ Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: Just as, friends, a man who is wealthy would speak of being wealthy, one who has wealth would speak of having wealth, one who has property would speak of having property. When some opportunity for acquiring wealth arises, he would be able to bring in wealth or grain or silver or gold. People would know him thus: ‘This venerable one who is wealthy speaks of being wealthy, this venerable one who has wealth speaks of having wealth, this venerable one who has property speaks of having property. Why is that? Because this venerable one, when some opportunity for acquiring wealth arises, is able to bring in wealth or grain or silver or gold.’
translations.an10.24:2: A monk who speaks a talk on knowledge, friends: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching.’ If, friends, that monk is overcome by greed and it stands, by hatred … by delusion … by anger … by hostility … by dissimulation … by obstinacy … by envy … by stinginess … by evil jealousy … by evil desire and it stands, he should be regarded thus: ‘This venerable one does not know in such a way that when one knows greed does not arise, yet greed overcomes this venerable one and stands; this venerable one does not know in such a way that when one knows hatred does not arise … delusion … anger … hostility … dissimulation … obstinacy … envy … evil jealousy … evil desire does not arise, yet evil desire overcomes this venerable one and stands.’
translations.an10.24:3: A monk who speaks a talk on development, friends: ‘I have developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, developed wisdom.’ If, friends, that monk is overcome by greed and it stands, by hatred … by delusion … by anger … by hostility … by dissimulation … by obstinacy … by envy … by stinginess … by evil jealousy … by evil desire and it stands, he should be regarded thus: ‘This venerable one does not know in such a way that when one knows greed does not arise, yet greed overcomes this venerable one and stands; this venerable one does not know in such a way that when one knows hatred does not arise … delusion … anger … hostility … dissimulation … obstinacy … envy … evil jealousy … evil desire does not arise, yet evil desire overcomes this venerable one and stands.’
translations.an10.24:5: Just as, friends, a man who is poor would speak of being wealthy, one who has no wealth would speak of having wealth, one who has no property would speak of having property. When some opportunity for acquiring wealth arises, he would not be able to bring in wealth or grain or silver or gold. People would know him thus: ‘This venerable one who is poor speaks of being wealthy, this venerable one who has no wealth speaks of having wealth, this venerable one who has no property speaks of having property. Why is that? Because this venerable one, when some opportunity for acquiring wealth arises, is not able to bring in wealth or grain or silver or gold.’
translations.an10.24:9: And, friends, a monk who speaks a talk on knowledge and a talk on development: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching, I have developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, developed wisdom.’ If, friends, that monk is not overcome by greed and it does not stand, by hatred … by delusion … by anger … by hostility … by dissimulation … by obstinacy … by envy … by stinginess … by evil jealousy … by evil desire and it does not stand, he should be regarded thus: ‘This venerable one knows in such a way that when one knows greed does not arise, and greed does not overcome this venerable one and stand; this venerable one knows in such a way that when one knows hatred does not arise … delusion … anger … hostility … dissimulation … obstinacy … envy … evil jealousy … evil desire does not arise, and evil desire does not overcome this venerable one and stand.’
translations.an10.29:1: ‘As far as Kāsi and Kosala extend, as far as king Pasenadi of Kosala’s realm reaches, there king Pasenadi of Kosala is supreme. Yet even for king Pasenadi of Kosala there is alteration, change, in what exists for him.’ Seeing thus, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple is disillusioned even with supremacy. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards it, how much more with inferiority.
translations.an10.29:10: One who has internal perception of no-form, one kind, sees external forms, blue, blue-colored, blue-showing, blue-lustrous. Just as a blue lotus flower is blue, blue-colored, blue-showing, blue-lustrous, or a Bārāṇasī cloth, smoothed on both sides, is blue, blue-colored, blue-showing, blue-lustrous; even so, one who has internal perception of no-form, one kind, sees external forms, blue, blue-colored, blue-showing, blue-lustrous; ‘having overcome them, I know, I see,’ thus one has such perception. This is the fifth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: One who has internal perception of no-form, one kind, sees external forms, yellow, yellow-colored, yellow-showing, yellow-lustrous. Just as a kaṇikāra flower is yellow, yellow-colored, yellow-showing, yellow-lustrous, or a Bārāṇasī cloth, smoothed on both sides, is yellow, yellow-colored, yellow-showing, yellow-lustrous; even so, one who has internal perception of no-form, one kind, sees external forms, yellow, yellow-colored, yellow-showing, yellow-lustrous; ‘having overcome them, I know, I see,’ thus one has such perception. This is the sixth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: One who has internal perception of no-form sees external forms that are red, red in color, with a red appearance, with a red luster. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, red in color, with a red appearance, with a red luster; or just as that Bārāṇasī cloth washed on both sides is red, red in color, with a red appearance, with a red luster; in the same way, one who has internal perception of no-form sees external forms that are red, red in color, with a red appearance, with a red luster; ‘having overcome them, I know, I see,’ thus he has such perception. This is the seventh abhibhāyatana.
translations.an10.29:13: One who has internal perception of no-form sees external forms that are white, white in color, with a white appearance, with a white luster. Just as an osadhitāraka star is white, white in color, with a white appearance, with a white luster; or just as that Bārāṇasī cloth washed on both sides is white, white in color, with a white appearance, with a white luster; in the same way, one who has internal perception of no-form sees external forms that are white, white in color, with a white appearance, with a white luster; ‘having overcome them, I know, I see,’ thus he has such perception. This is the eighth abhibhāyatana. These, monks, are the eight abhibhāyatanāni.
translations.an10.29:14: The foremost of these eight abhibhāyatanāni, monks, is this: one who has internal perception of no-form sees external forms that are white, white in color, with a white appearance, with a white luster; ‘having overcome them, I know, I see,’ thus he has such perception. There are beings, monks, who have such perception. And there is change and alteration even for beings who have such perception. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned even with that. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: These four, monks, are ways of practice. Which four? A painful way of practice with slow direct knowledge, a painful way of practice with quick direct knowledge, a pleasant way of practice with slow direct knowledge, a pleasant way of practice with quick direct knowledge—these, monks, are the four ways of practice.
translations.an10.29:16: The foremost of these four ways of practice, monks, is the pleasant way of practice with quick direct knowledge. There are beings, monks, who practice thus. And there is change and alteration even for beings who practice thus. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned even with that. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: These four, monks, are perceptions. Which four? One perceives limited, one perceives exalted, one perceives measureless, one perceives ‘there is nothing’ at the sphere of nothingness—these, monks, are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The foremost of these four perceptions, monks, is this: one perceives ‘there is nothing’ at the sphere of nothingness. There are beings, monks, who have such perception. And there is change and alteration even for beings who have such perception. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned even with that. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: As far, monks, as the moon and sun revolve, shining, illuminating the quarters, to that extent the world is a thousandfold. In that thousandfold world there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru king-mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurūs, a thousand Pubbavidehas, a thousand four great oceans, a thousand four great kings, a thousand cātumahārājikas, a thousand Tāvatiṁsas, a thousand Yāmas, a thousand Tusitas, a thousand Nimmānaratis, a thousand Paranimmitavasavattīs, a thousand brahmalokas. As far, monks, as the thousandfold world-sphere, therein Great Brahmā is declared foremost. And there is change and alteration even for Great Brahmā. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned even with that. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim the purification of ultimate reality. The foremost of those who proclaim the purification of ultimate reality, monks, is this: having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. They teach the teaching for the direct realization of that by superknowledge. There are beings, monks, who speak thus. And there is change and alteration even for beings who speak thus. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned even with that. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, monks, when this world contracts. When the world is contracting, monks, beings for the most part become bound for the Ābhassara. There they are mind-made, feeding on joy, self-luminous, moving through the air, glorious, and they remain for a long, very long period of time. When the world is contracting, monks, the Ābhassara gods are declared foremost. And there is change and alteration even for the Ābhassara gods. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned even with that. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: These ten, monks, are kasiṇa bases. Which ten? One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, across, boundless, measureless; one perceives the water kasiṇa … one perceives the fire kasiṇa … one perceives the air kasiṇa … one perceives the blue kasiṇa … one perceives the yellow kasiṇa … one perceives the red kasiṇa … one perceives the white kasiṇa … one perceives the space kasiṇa … one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, boundless, measureless. These, monks, are the ten kasiṇa bases.
translations.an10.29:5: This is the foremost, monks, among these ten kasiṇa bases, namely the consciousness kasiṇa: one perceives it above, below, across, unlimited, measureless. Even among those with such perception, monks, there are beings. Even among beings with such perception, monks, there is change and alteration. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned with that, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:6: There are eight abhibhāyatana, monks. Which eight? One who has an internal perception of forms sees external forms, limited, with beautiful and ugly colors; ‘I know and see those that overcome them’, thus one has such perception. This is the first abhibhāyatana.
translations.an10.29:7: One who has an internal perception of forms sees external forms, measureless, with beautiful and ugly colors; ‘I know and see those that overcome them’, thus one has such perception. This is the second abhibhāyatana.
translations.an10.29:8: One who has no internal perception of forms sees external forms, limited, with beautiful and ugly colors; ‘I know and see those that overcome them’, thus one has such perception. This is the third abhibhāyatana.
translations.an10.29:9: One who has no internal perception of forms sees external forms, measureless, with beautiful and ugly colors; ‘I know and see those that overcome them’, thus one has such perception. This is the fourth abhibhāyatana.
translations.an10.51:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks.’ ‘Venerable sir’, those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.an10.51:3: And how, monks, is a monk skilled in reviewing his own mind? Just as, monks, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, reviewing the sign of his own face in a mirror or in a clear well-polished bright bowl of water, if he sees there any dirt or blemish, makes effort to remove that very dirt or blemish. But if he does not see there any dirt or blemish, he is pleased and satisfied: ‘Good indeed, mine is clean.’ In the same way, monks, reviewing is very beneficial for a monk with regard to skillful qualities: ‘Do I frequently dwell with covetousness, or do I frequently dwell without covetousness, do I frequently dwell with ill will, or do I frequently dwell without ill will, do I frequently dwell overcome by sloth and torpor, or do I frequently dwell free from sloth and torpor, do I frequently dwell agitated, or do I frequently dwell unagitated, do I frequently dwell doubting, or do I frequently dwell without doubt, do I frequently dwell angry, or do I frequently dwell without anger, do I frequently dwell with a defiled mind, or do I frequently dwell with an undefiled mind, do I frequently dwell with a tense body, or do I frequently dwell without a tense body, do I frequently dwell lazy, or do I frequently dwell with aroused energy, do I frequently dwell unconcentrated, or do I frequently dwell concentrated?’
translations.an10.51:4: If, monks, a monk reviewing thus knows: ‘I frequently dwell with covetousness, I frequently dwell with ill will, I frequently dwell overcome by sloth and torpor, I frequently dwell agitated, I frequently dwell doubting, I frequently dwell angry, I frequently dwell with a defiled mind, I frequently dwell with a tense body, I frequently dwell lazy, I frequently dwell unconcentrated’, then, monks, that monk should make intense desire, effort, energy, exertion, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very unskillful qualities. Just as, monks, if one’s clothes or head were on fire, one would make intense desire, effort, energy, exertion, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the extinguishing of that very clothes or head. In the same way, monks, that monk should make intense desire, effort, energy, exertion, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very unskillful qualities.
translations.an10.54:2: And how, monks, is a monk skilled in reviewing his own mind? Just as, monks, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, reviewing the sign of his own face in a mirror or in a clear well-polished bright bowl of water, if he sees there any dirt or blemish, makes effort to remove that very dirt or blemish. But if he does not see there any dirt or blemish, he is pleased and satisfied: ‘Good indeed, mine is clean.’ In the same way, monks, reviewing is very beneficial for a monk with regard to skillful qualities: ‘Am I a gainer internally of the calming of mind, or am I not a gainer internally of the calming of mind, am I a gainer of insight into qualities by higher wisdom, or am I not a gainer of insight into qualities by higher wisdom?’
translations.an10.54:5: But if, monks, a monk reviewing thus knows: ‘I am not a gainer internally of the calming of mind, I am not a gainer of insight into qualities by higher wisdom’, then, monks, that monk should make intense desire, effort, energy, exertion, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the attainment of those very skillful qualities. Just as, monks, if one’s clothes or head were on fire, one would make intense desire, effort, energy, exertion, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the extinguishing of that very clothes or head. In the same way, monks, that monk should make intense desire, effort, energy, exertion, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the attainment of those very skillful qualities. Before long he becomes a gainer internally of the calming of mind and a gainer of insight into qualities by higher wisdom.
translations.an10.54:6: But if, monks, a monk reviewing thus knows: ‘I am a gainer internally of the calming of mind, I am a gainer of insight into qualities by higher wisdom’, then, monks, that monk, established in those very skillful qualities, should make effort for the destruction of the āsavas.
translations.an10.58:1: “Suppose, monks, wanderers of other sects were to ask you: ‘What is the root of all things, from what do all things originate, on what do all things converge, what is the resort of all things, what is the leader of all things, what is the lord of all things, what is the highest of all things, what is the essence of all things, what is the swamp of all things, what is the culmination of all things?’ Being asked thus, monks, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?” “Things have the Blessed One as root, as guide, as resort. Good, sir, may the Blessed One himself clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it.”
translations.an10.58:2: “Well then, monks, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.an10.59:1: “Therefore, monks, you should train like this: ‘Our mind will be developed in the way of going forth, and arisen evil unskillful qualities will not take possession and remain in the mind; our mind will be developed in impermanence perception, our mind will be developed in not-self perception, our mind will be developed in unattractiveness perception, our mind will be developed in danger perception, having known the even and uneven of the world, our mind will be developed in that perception, having known existence and non-existence of the world, our mind will be developed in that perception, having known the arising and passing away of the world, our mind will be developed in that perception, our mind will be developed in relinquishment perception, our mind will be developed in dispassion perception, our mind will be developed in cessation perception’—you should train like this, monks.
translations.an10.60:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. At that time venerable Girimānanda was sick, afflicted, gravely ill. Then venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ānanda, is cessation perception? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, cessation, nibbāna.’ This is called cessation perception, Ānanda.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ānanda, is perception of non-delight in the entire world? Here, Ānanda, a monk dwells with the clinging, obsessions, attachments, and underlying tendencies of the mind regarding the world abandoned, not taking them up. This is called perception of non-delight in the entire world, Ānanda.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ānanda, is perception of disenchantment with all formations? Here, Ānanda, a monk is disenchanted, repelled, and disgusted with all formations. This is called perception of disenchantment with all formations, Ānanda.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front. Mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he knows: ‘I breathe in long.’ Breathing out long, he knows: ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, he knows: ‘I breathe in short.’ Breathing out short, he knows: ‘I breathe out short.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the whole body.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the whole body.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in calming the bodily formation.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out calming the bodily formation.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to rapture.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to rapture.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to pleasure.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to pleasure.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the mental formation.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the mental formation.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in calming the mental formation.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out calming the mental formation.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the mind.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the mind.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in gladdening the mind …’ … ‘I will breathe in concentrating the mind …’ … ‘I will breathe in liberating the mind …’ … ‘I will breathe in contemplating impermanence …’ … ‘I will breathe in contemplating dispassion …’ … ‘I will breathe in contemplating cessation …’ … He trains: ‘I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment.’ This is called mindfulness of breathing, Ānanda.
translations.an10.60:14: If you, Ānanda, were to speak these ten perceptions to monk Girimānanda, it is possible that his illness would abate.
translations.an10.60:2: “Venerable Girimānanda, sir, is sick, afflicted, gravely ill. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would go to venerable Girimānanda out of compassion.” “If you, Ānanda, were to speak ten perceptions to monk Girimānanda, it is possible that his illness would abate.
translations.an10.60:3: What ten? Impermanence perception, not-self perception, unattractiveness perception, danger perception, relinquishment perception, dispassion perception, cessation perception, perception of non-delight in the entire world, perception of disenchantment with all formations, mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ānanda, is impermanence perception? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.’ Thus he abides contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates subject to clinging. This is called impermanence perception, Ānanda.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of not-self? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: ‘The eye is not-self, forms are not-self, the ear is not-self, sounds are not-self, the nose is not-self, odors are not-self, the tongue is not-self, flavors are not-self, the body is not-self, tangibles are not-self, the mind is not-self, dhammas are not-self.’ Thus he abides contemplating not-self in these six internal and external bases. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of not-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of the foul? Here, Ānanda, a monk reviews this very body from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, full of many kinds of impurity: ‘There are in this body hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, contents of the stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine.’ Thus he abides contemplating the foul in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of the foul.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a monk who has gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects: ‘This body is much suffering, full of many dangers. In this body various diseases arise, such as: eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, lip disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, old age, stomach disease, fainting, dysentery, colic, gripes, skin disease, scrofula, leprosy, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, herpes, rash, tetter, blood disease, bile disease, diabetes, boils, abscesses, fistula, diseases originating from bile, diseases originating from phlegm, diseases originating from wind, diseases from the three humors, diseases due to change of climate, diseases due to irregular diet, epidemic diseases, diseases due to karma, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.’ Thus he abides contemplating danger in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of relinquishment? Here, Ānanda, a monk does not dwell upon a thought of sensual desire that has arisen, he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, annihilates it. He does not dwell upon a thought of ill will that has arisen, he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, annihilates it. He does not dwell upon a thought of cruelty that has arisen, he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, annihilates it. He does not dwell upon any evil unskillful dhammas that have arisen, he abandons them, dispels them, destroys them, annihilates them. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of relinquishment.
translations.an10.61:1: ‘The former limit of ignorance cannot be discerned: “Before this there was no ignorance, then afterwards it came into being.”’ Though this is said, bhikkhus, it is nevertheless discerned: ‘With this as condition, ignorance [comes to be].’
translations.an10.61:2: Bhikkhus, I say that ignorance has nutriment, it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? ‘The five hindrances’ should be the answer. Bhikkhus, I say that the five hindrances have nutriment, they are not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? ‘The three kinds of misconduct’ should be the answer. Bhikkhus, I say that the three kinds of misconduct have nutriment, they are not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three kinds of misconduct? ‘Lack of sense restraint’ should be the answer. Bhikkhus, I say that sense restraint has nutriment, it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for sense restraint? ‘Mindfulness and clear comprehension when not eating’ should be the answer. Bhikkhus, I say that mindfulness and clear comprehension when not eating has nutriment, it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for mindfulness and clear comprehension when not eating? ‘Wrong attention’ should be the answer. Bhikkhus, I say that wrong attention has nutriment, it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for wrong attention? ‘Disbelief’ should be the answer. Bhikkhus, I say that disbelief has nutriment, it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for disbelief? ‘Listening to wrong dhamma’ should be the answer. Bhikkhus, I say that listening to wrong dhamma has nutriment, it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for listening to wrong dhamma? ‘Association with bad persons’ should be the answer.
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, bhikkhus, association with bad persons completes listening to wrong dhamma, listening to wrong dhamma completed completes disbelief, disbelief completed completes wrong attention, wrong attention completed completes mindfulness and clear comprehension when not eating, mindfulness and clear comprehension when not eating completed completes sense restraint, sense restraint completed completes the three kinds of misconduct, the three kinds of misconduct completed complete the five hindrances, the five hindrances completed complete ignorance; thus ignorance has nutriment, and thus it is completed.
translations.an10.61:4: Just as, bhikkhus, when it is raining heavily on the upper mountain covered with thick forest (…) that water, flowing along its natural course, completes the mountain clefts, gullies, and ravines; the mountain clefts, gullies, and ravines completed complete the little streams; the little streams completed complete the large streams; the large streams completed complete the great rivers; the great rivers completed complete the great ocean, the sea; thus the great ocean, the sea has nutriment, and thus it is completed.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, bhikkhus, association with good persons completes listening to true dhamma, listening to true dhamma completed completes faith, faith completed completes right attention, right attention completed completes mindfulness and clear comprehension, mindfulness and clear comprehension completed completes sense restraint, sense restraint completed completes the three kinds of good conduct, the three kinds of good conduct completed complete the four establishments of mindfulness, the four establishments of mindfulness completed complete the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven factors of enlightenment completed complete knowledge and freedom; thus knowledge and freedom has nutriment, and thus it is completed.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the Venerable Sāriputta; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having exchanged greetings and polite talk, he sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an10.7:2: “Could there be, friend Sāriputta, such an attainment of concentration for a monk by which he would not perceive earth as earth, not perceive water as water, not perceive fire as fire, not perceive wind as wind, not perceive the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, not perceive the base of consciousness as the base of consciousness, not perceive the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, not perceive the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not perceive this world as this world, not perceive the other world as the other world; and yet he would be percipient?”
translations.an10.7:4: “But how, friend Sāriputta, could there be such an attainment of concentration for a monk by which he would not perceive earth as earth … and yet he would be percipient?” “Once, friend Ānanda, I was staying right here in Sāvatthī in the Andhavana. There I entered such a concentration by which I was not percipient of earth as earth, not percipient of water as water, not percipient of fire as fire, not percipient of wind as wind, not percipient of the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, not percipient of the base of consciousness as the base of consciousness, not percipient of the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, not percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not percipient of this world as this world, not percipient of the other world as the other world; and yet I was percipient.”
translations.an3.10:1: “Bhikkhus, endowed with three qualities, having not abandoned three stains, one is cast down as it were where it has fallen, right into hell. Which three? He is unethical, and the stain of unethicality is not abandoned; he is envious, and the stain of envy is not abandoned; he is stingy, and the stain of stinginess is not abandoned. Endowed with these three qualities, bhikkhus, having not abandoned these three stains, one is cast down as it were where it has fallen, right into hell.
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, bhikkhus, in whatever place a monk truly understands ‘this is suffering’ as it really is, truly understands ‘this is the origin of suffering’ as it really is, truly understands ‘this is the cessation of suffering’ as it really is, truly understands ‘this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’ as it really is. This, bhikkhus, is the second thing that is desirable for a monk as long as life lasts.
translations.an3.15:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: ‘Bhikkhus!’ ‘Venerable sir!’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.an3.15:2: “Once upon a time, bhikkhus, there was a king named Saceta. Then, bhikkhus, king Saceta addressed the chariot-maker: ‘Friend chariot-maker, a battle will take place for me after six months from now. Can you make a new chariot for me?’ ‘I can, sire,’ bhikkhus, the chariot-maker replied to king Saceta. Then, bhikkhus, the chariot-maker finished one wheel in six months and four nights. Then, bhikkhus, king Saceta addressed the chariot-maker: ‘Friend chariot-maker, a battle will take place for me after six days from now. Is the new chariot ready?’ ‘Sire, with these six months and four nights one wheel is finished.’ ‘Can you then, friend chariot-maker, finish the second wheel in these six days?’ ‘I can, sire,’ bhikkhus, the chariot-maker replied. In six days he finished the second wheel, took up the new chariot, and went to king Saceta; having gone, he said to king Saceta: ‘Sire, here is your new chariot finished.’ ‘Friend chariot-maker, what is the difference between this wheel finished in six months and this wheel finished in six days? I see no difference.’ ‘There is a difference, sire. May the king see the difference.’
translations.an3.15:3: Then, bhikkhus, the chariot-maker rolled the wheel that had been finished in six days. When rolled, it went as far as the momentum of the fabrication carried it, then wobbling it fell to the ground. But he rolled the wheel that had been finished in six months and four nights. When rolled, it went as far as the momentum of the fabrication carried it, and it stood as if pegged.
translations.an3.15:5: Perhaps, bhikkhus, it occurs to you: ‘Surely someone else was that chariot-maker at that time.’ No, bhikkhus, it should not be seen like this. I was that chariot-maker at that time. Then, bhikkhus, I was skilled in axle-wood, axle-flaws, axle-diseases. But now, bhikkhus, I am fully enlightened, skilled in body-axles, body-flaws, body-diseases, skilled in speech-axles, speech-flaws, speech-diseases, skilled in mind-axles, mind-flaws, mind-diseases. For whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī has unabandoned body-axle, body-flaw, body-disease, unabandoned speech-axle, speech-flaw, speech-disease, unabandoned mind-axle, mind-flaw, mind-disease, such ones fall from this Dhamma and Vinaya, bhikkhus, like that wheel finished in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: For whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī has abandoned body-axle, body-flaw, body-disease, abandoned speech-axle, speech-flaw, speech-disease, abandoned mind-axle, mind-flaw, mind-disease, such ones stand firm in this Dhamma and Vinaya, bhikkhus, like that wheel finished in six months and four nights.
translations.an3.1:3: Thus, bhikkhus, the fool is fearful, the wise man is fearless. The fool is troubled, the wise man is untroubled. The fool is affected, the wise man is unaffected. Bhikkhus, for the wise man there is no fear, no trouble, no affectation.
translations.an3.20:1: “Bhikkhus, endowed with three qualities, a merchant quickly attains greatness and abundance in wealth. Which three? Here, bhikkhus, a merchant has vision and is unburdened and well-supported. And how, bhikkhus, does a merchant have vision? Here, bhikkhus, a merchant knows about goods: ‘This merchandise, bought in such a way, sold in such a way, will have such a cost price, such a profit.’ In this way, bhikkhus, a merchant has vision.
translations.an3.20:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a merchant unburdened? Here, bhikkhus, a merchant is skilled in buying goods and selling them. In this way, bhikkhus, a merchant is unburdened.
translations.an3.20:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a merchant well-supported? Here, bhikkhus, those householders or householders’ sons who are wealthy, with great wealth, great possessions, know about this merchant: ‘This merchant has vision, is unburdened, and is capable of supporting a family and giving us support from time to time.’ They provide him with wealth: ‘Sir merchant, having made wealth here, support a family and give us support from time to time.’ In this way, bhikkhus, a merchant is well-supported. Bhikkhus, endowed with these three qualities, a merchant quickly attains greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: Just so, bhikkhus, endowed with three qualities, a bhikkhu quickly attains greatness and abundance in wholesome qualities. Which three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has vision and is unburdened and well-supported. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu have vision? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu truly understands: ‘This is suffering,’ truly understands: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ truly understands: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ truly understands: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has vision.
translations.an3.20:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu unburdened? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu lives with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the undertaking of wholesome qualities, strong in effort, firm in exertion, unburdened in wholesome qualities. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is unburdened.
translations.an3.22:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of sick people existing and found in the world. Which three? Here, bhikkhus, some sick person, whether receiving or not receiving suitable food, whether receiving or not receiving suitable medicines, whether receiving or not receiving a suitable attendant, does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some sick person, receiving suitable food, not not receiving, receiving suitable medicines, not not receiving, receiving a suitable attendant, not not receiving, recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: Bhikkhus, among them, that sick person who, receiving suitable food, not not receiving, receiving suitable medicines, not not receiving, receiving a suitable attendant, not not receiving, recovers from that illness—because of this sick person, food for the sick has been allowed, medicines for the sick have been allowed, an attendant for the sick has been allowed. And, bhikkhus, because of this sick person, other sick people should also be attended. Bhikkhus, these three kinds of sick people exist and are found in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: Just so, bhikkhus, there are these three simile sick people existing and found in the world. Which three? Here, bhikkhus, some person, whether getting or not getting to see the Tathāgata, whether getting or not getting to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, does not enter upon and abide in the fixed course of rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.22:6: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some person, whether getting or not getting to see the Tathāgata, whether getting or not getting to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, enters upon and abides in the fixed course of rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.24:1: “Bhikkhus, these three persons are of great help to a person. Which three? Bhikkhus, depending on that person, a person goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dhamma, goes for refuge to the Saṅgha; this person, bhikkhus, is of great help to this person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, depending on that person, a person truly understands: ‘This is suffering,’ truly understands: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ truly understands: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ truly understands: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’; this person, bhikkhus, is of great help to this person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, depending on that person, a person, with the destruction of the taints, abides having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taint-free deliverance of mind, deliverance through wisdom; this person, bhikkhus, is of great help to this person. Bhikkhus, these three persons are of great help to a person.
translations.an3.2:1: “The fool is marked by action, bhikkhus, the wise person is marked by action, wisdom shines by living on. A fool should be understood as endowed with three qualities. Which three? Body misconduct, speech misconduct, mind misconduct. Bhikkhus, endowed with these three qualities, a fool should be understood.
translations.an3.2:2: A wise person should be understood as endowed with three qualities. Which three? Body good conduct, speech good conduct, mind good conduct. Bhikkhus, endowed with these three qualities, a wise person should be understood.
translations.an3.30:4: A man of inverted wisdom, stupid, without insight; Even if he goes frequently to the presence of bhikkhus.
translations.an3.30:5: The beginning of the talk, the middle, and the end are just like that; He cannot grasp it, for he lacks wisdom.
translations.an3.30:6: A man of eminent wisdom, he is said to be better than that; Even if he goes frequently to the presence of bhikkhus.
translations.an3.30:8: A man of broad wisdom, he is said to be better than those; Even if he goes frequently to the presence of bhikkhus.
translations.an3.32:4: “Here, Ānanda, a monk has this thought: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nibbāna.’ Such, Ānanda, is the attainment of concentration for a monk when there are no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit regarding this body with consciousness, and no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit regarding anything external in all signs; and when entering and dwelling in mental liberation and wisdom liberation, there are no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit, and he enters and dwells in that mental liberation and wisdom liberation.”
translations.an3.33:1: Then the Venerable Sāriputta went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, I could teach the Dhamma in brief, or in detail, or in both brief and detail, but knowers are hard to find.” “Blessed One, this is the time, Well-Gone One, this is the time for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma in brief, or in detail, or in both brief and detail. Knowers of the Dhamma will arise.”
translations.an3.33:2: “Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train like this: ‘There will be no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit regarding this body with consciousness, and no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit regarding anything external in all signs, and when entering and dwelling in mental liberation and wisdom liberation, there are no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit—we will enter and dwell in that mental liberation and wisdom liberation.’ That’s how, Sāriputta, you should train.
translations.an3.33:3: “And when, Sāriputta, a monk has no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit regarding this body with consciousness, and no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit regarding anything external in all signs, and when entering and dwelling in mental liberation and wisdom liberation, there are no latent tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit, and he enters and dwells in that mental liberation and wisdom liberation: this one, Sāriputta, is called ‘a monk who has cut off craving, has broken the fetters, has completely understood conceit through proper comprehension, has made an end of suffering.’ And this, Sāriputta, was said in the Pārāyana on the question about arising:
translations.an3.33:4: ‘The giving up of perceptions of sensuality,  and of both kinds of displeasure;  The dispelling of sloth-and-torpor,  The warding off of remorse.
translations.an3.34:1: “These three, monks, are the sources for the arising of kamma. Which three? Greed is a source for the arising of kamma, hatred is a source for the arising of kamma, delusion is a source for the arising of kamma.
translations.an3.34:10: Monks, that kamma made by non-delusion, born of non-delusion, originating from non-delusion, arisen from non-delusion, when delusion has ceased, such kamma is abandoned, its root destroyed, like a palm stump, made like a non-thing, not to arise in the future.
translations.an3.34:11: Just as, monks, seeds that are unbroken, unrotten, unaffected by wind and heat, full of life, well-placed, if a person were to burn them with fire, and having burned them with fire, make them into ash, and having made them into ash, scatter them in a strong wind or carry them away by a swift-flowing river: those seeds, monks, would be without root, like a palm stump, made like a non-thing, not to arise in the future. In the same way, monks, that kamma made by non-greed, born of non-greed, originating from non-greed, arisen from non-greed, when greed has ceased, such kamma is abandoned, its root destroyed, like a palm stump, made like a non-thing, not to arise in the future.
translations.an3.34:13: Whatever kamma is made by greed, hatred,  or delusion, whether little or much;  It is to be experienced right here,  No other basis is found.
translations.an3.34:2: Monks, that kamma made by greed, born of greed, originating from greed, arisen from greed, where a being’s selfhood arises, there that kamma ripens. Where that kamma ripens, there one experiences the result of that kamma, either in the present life, or in a later life, or in some subsequent period.
translations.an3.34:5: Just as, monks, seeds that are unbroken, unrotten, unaffected by wind and heat, full of life, well-placed, placed in well-prepared ground, and if the sky god were to send suitable rain: those seeds, monks, would grow, increase, and prosper. In the same way, monks, that kamma made by greed, born of greed, originating from greed, arisen from greed, where a being’s selfhood arises, there that kamma ripens. Where that kamma ripens, there one experiences the result of that kamma, either in the present life, or in a later life, or in some subsequent period.
translations.an3.34:6: That kamma made by hatred …pe… that kamma made by delusion, born of delusion, originating from delusion, arisen from delusion, where a being’s selfhood arises, there that kamma ripens. Where that kamma ripens, there one experiences the result of that kamma, either in the present life, or in a later life, or in some subsequent period. These three, monks, are the sources for the arising of kamma.
translations.an3.34:9: Monks, that kamma made by non-hatred, born of non-hatred, originating from non-hatred, arisen from non-hatred, when hatred has ceased, such kamma is abandoned, its root destroyed, like a palm stump, made like a non-thing, not to arise in the future.
translations.an3.35:3: “Well then, young man, I will ask you about this matter. Answer as you think fit. What do you think, young man, here a householder or householder’s son has a dwelling that is well-plastered inside and out, draught-free, with close-fitting doors, a couch with legs of cattle wood, or rosewood, or figs wood, spread with woolen coverlets, with a scarlet woolen blanket on both sides; a lamp is burning there; and four serving-women are standing by, charming and appealing. What do you think, young man, would he lie down comfortably or not? Or how do you see it?” “He would lie down comfortably, sir. And among those in the world who experience pleasure, he would be one of them.”
translations.an3.35:4: “What do you think, young man, would feelings of burning born of lust—bodily or mental—arise for that householder or householder’s son, by which, burning with those feelings of burning born of lust, he would lie in pain?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.an3.35:8: He always sleeps in happiness, the brahmin who is fully cooled; He does not cling to sensual pleasures, cooled down, without substrata.
translations.an3.39:10: While dwelling thus, knowing the Dhamma without substrata; The intoxications of health, youth, and life.
translations.an3.39:2: I had three palaces, monks—one for the winter season, one for the hot season, one for the rainy season. During the four months of the rainy season in the rainy-season palace, I was entertained by female musicians and did not descend from the palace below. Just as in the dwellings of others slave women and men are given coarse food with scraps, even so, monks, in my father’s dwelling slave women and men were given rice and meat.
translations.an3.39:3: When I possessed such majesty and such subtle happiness, this thought arose: ‘The unlearned ordinary person, being himself subject to aging, not gone beyond aging, seeing another who is aged, is disgusted, distressed, and repelled, after having surpassed himself. I too am subject to aging, not gone beyond aging. If I, being subject to aging, not gone beyond aging, seeing another who is aged, were to be disgusted, distressed, and repelled, that would not be fitting for me.’ When I reflected thus, the intoxication of youth was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:4: The unlearned ordinary person, being himself subject to illness, not gone beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, is disgusted, distressed, and repelled, after having surpassed himself: ‘I too am subject to illness, not gone beyond illness. If I, being subject to illness, not gone beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, were to be disgusted, distressed, and repelled, that would not be fitting for me.’ When I reflected thus, the intoxication of health was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:5: The unlearned ordinary person, being himself subject to death, not gone beyond death, seeing another who is dead, is disgusted, distressed, and repelled, after having surpassed himself: ‘I too am subject to death, not gone beyond death. If I, being subject to death, not gone beyond death, seeing another who is dead, were to be disgusted, distressed, and repelled, that would not be fitting for me.’ When I reflected thus, the intoxication of life was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:7: Monks, a monk intoxicated with the intoxication of youth gives up the training and returns to a lower way of life. Intoxicated with the intoxication of health … Intoxicated with the intoxication of life, a monk gives up the training and returns to a lower way of life.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to aging, and subject to death; Being such, existing thus, ordinary people are disgusted.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to be disgusted by these living beings subject to such things; That would not be fitting for me, dwelling thus.
translations.an3.40:1: “These three sovereignties, monks. What three? Self-sovereignty, world-sovereignty, Dhamma-sovereignty. And what is self-sovereignty? Here, monks, a monk dwelling in the forest, at the root of a tree, or in an empty hut reflects thus: ‘I did not go forth from the household life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Nor for the sake of almsfood, nor for the sake of lodging, nor for the sake of existence or non-existence did I go forth from the household life into homelessness. But I went forth because I was overcome by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, overcome by suffering, overpowered by suffering. Perhaps the complete ending of this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’ If, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and discipline, I were to dwell indolent and heedless, that would not be fitting for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be exerted, unremitting; my mindfulness shall be established, not confused; my body shall be calm, not tense; my mind shall be concentrated, one-pointed.’ Making himself sovereign, he abandons unskillful qualities, develops skillful qualities, abandons blameworthy qualities, develops blameless qualities, and keeps himself pure. This is called self-sovereignty, monks.
translations.an3.40:3: And what is Dhamma-sovereignty? Here, monks, a monk dwelling in the forest, at the root of a tree, or in an empty hut reflects thus: ‘I did not go forth from the household life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Nor for the sake of almsfood, nor for the sake of lodging, nor for the sake of existence or non-existence did I go forth from the household life into homelessness. But I went forth because I was overcome by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, overcome by suffering, overpowered by suffering. Perhaps the complete ending of this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’ The Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be personally experienced by the wise. There are fellow monastics of mine who dwell knowing and seeing. If, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and discipline, I were to dwell indolent and heedless, that would not be fitting for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be exerted, unremitting; my mindfulness shall be established, not confused; my body shall be calm, not tense; my mind shall be concentrated, one-pointed.’ Making the Dhamma sovereign, he abandons unskillful qualities, develops skillful qualities, abandons blameworthy qualities, develops blameless qualities, and keeps himself pure. This is called Dhamma-sovereignty, monks. These are the three sovereignties, monks.
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secret in the world when doing evil deeds; One’s own self knows the man, whether truth or lie.
translations.an3.40:5: It’s good, witness, you overrate yourself; You who conceal evil existing in yourself.
translations.an3.40:6: Devas and Tathāgatas see the fool acting crookedly in the world; Therefore the sage who is self-sovereign, world-sovereign, wise, and a meditator; Dhamma-sovereign and follower of the Dhamma, the sage striving in truth does not decline.
translations.an3.48:1: “Monks, relying on the Himalayan mountain king, great crops grow by three kinds of growth. Which three? They grow by branches, leaves, and bark; by skin and rind; by soft core. Monks, relying on the Himalayan mountain king, great crops grow by these three kinds of growth.”
translations.an3.48:2: “Just so, monks, relying on a householder of faith, people in the town grow by three kinds of growth. Which three? They grow by faith, by virtue, by wisdom. Monks, relying on a householder of faith, people in the town grow by these three kinds of growth.”
translations.an3.48:3: “Just as a rocky mountain,  in a wilderness, in a wild place;  Trees rely on it,  and those forest growths grow.”
translations.an3.51:1: Then two aged, elderly, senior brahmins who were advanced in years and had reached the age of two hundred years by birth went to the Blessed One. Having gone to him, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After the exchange of greetings and polite conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: “We, good Gotama, are brahmins—aged, elderly, senior, advanced in years, having reached the age of two hundred years by birth. But we have not done what is wholesome, not done what is skillful, not done protection. May the good Gotama instruct us, may he teach us, for our long-term welfare and happiness.”
translations.an3.51:2: “Indeed, brahmins, you are aged, elderly, senior, advanced in years, having reached the age of two hundred years by birth. But you have not done what is wholesome, not done what is skillful, not done protection. This world, brahmins, is swept away by old age, sickness, and death. When the world is being swept away by old age, sickness, and death, restraint of body, restraint of speech, restraint of mind is protection, shelter, lamp, refuge, and final resort for that being.”
translations.an3.51:3: “Life is swept away, short in span;  For one swept away by old age there are no shelters.  Seeing fear in death,  Make merit that brings happiness.”
translations.an3.52:4: “Thus the world is burning,  with old age and death;  Get it out with giving,  what is given is well gathered.”
translations.an3.57:2: “Vaccha, those who said: ‘The ascetic Gotama said this: “Gifts are to be given to me alone … what is given to others’ disciples has great fruit”’—they are not speaking my words. They misrepresent me with what is untrue and false. Vaccha, one who prevents others from giving a gift is an obstacle maker to three, a obstructer to three. Which three? He is an obstacle to the merit of the giver, an obstacle to the gain of the recipients, and moreover, he himself is ruined and injured beforehand. Vaccha, one who prevents others from giving a gift is an obstacle maker to these three, an obstructer to three.”
translations.an3.5:1: “Monks, a fool should be understood as endowed with three qualities. Which three? He asks an unskillful question, he answers an unskillful question, and when another has answered a skillful question with coherent, eloquent words and phrases that are polished, smooth, and circumspect, he does not approve. Monks, a fool should be understood as endowed with these three qualities.”
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Sangarava went to the Blessed One. Having gone to him, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After the exchange of greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Sangarava said to the Blessed One: “We, good Gotama, are called brahmins. We offer sacrifices and have sacrifices offered. There, good Gotama, both one who sacrifices and one who has a sacrifice offered, all of them undertake a multi-based path of merit, namely, the sacrificial action. But this one, good Gotama, who goes forth from the house life into homelessness from this or that family, restrains himself alone, composes himself alone, and makes an end of himself alone—this one undertakes a single-based path of merit, namely, the going forth action.”
translations.an3.60:10: “And again, brahmin, suppose someone does not divine by a sign, but he divines after hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or gods: ‘This is your mind, this is your mind, this is your thought.’ If he divines much, it is just so, not otherwise.”
translations.an3.60:11: “And again, brahmin, suppose someone does not divine by a sign nor after hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or gods, but after thinking and reflecting, he hears the sound of the expansion of thought and divines: ‘This is your mind, this is your mind, this is your thought.’ If he divines much, it is just so, not otherwise.”
translations.an3.60:12: “And again, brahmin, suppose someone does not divine by a sign, nor after hearing the sound of humans, non-humans, or gods, nor after hearing the sound of the expansion of thought while thinking and reflecting, but with mind he knows mind, having encompassed the mind of one who has entered concentration without placing the mind and without sustained attention: ‘Just as the mental formations of this gentleman are directed, he will think such and such a thought next.’ If he divines much, it is just so, not otherwise. This is called, brahmin, the miracle of demonstration.”
translations.an3.60:13: “And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, someone instructs: ‘Think thus, do not think that; attend thus, do not attend that; abandon this, live having undertaken that.’ This is called, brahmin, the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Brahmin, of these three miracles, which miracle seems to you more excellent and sublime?”
translations.an3.60:14: “There, good Gotama, that miracle where someone experiences various psychic powers … even as far as the brahma world he wields mastery with the body—this miracle, good Gotama, whoever makes it experiences it himself, whoever makes it, it is for him alone. This miracle, good Gotama, seems to me like an illusory, magical display.”}
translations.an3.60:16: And this miracle, sir Gotama, when someone here instructs in this way: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that; attend like this, don’t attend like that; abandon this, live having entered and dwelling in that.’ This miracle alone, sir Gotama, seems to me more splendid and sublime than these three miracles.
translations.an3.60:17: Amazing, sir Gotama, marvelous, sir Gotama. How well-spoken this is by you, sir Gotama. We hold you, sir Gotama, endowed with these three miracles. For you, sir Gotama, experience various psychic powers …pe… even as far as the brahma world you wield bodily power. You, sir Gotama, with mind encompassing mind, understand the mind of one who has entered first-jhāna samādhi without thought and without examination: ‘Just as the mental factors of this venerable one are directed, next he will think such-and-such a thought.’ You, sir Gotama, instruct in this way: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that; attend like this, don’t attend like that; abandon this, live having entered and dwelling in that.’
translations.an3.60:18: “Indeed, brahmin, those words of yours were brought forward; but I will reply to them. For I, brahmin, experience various psychic powers …pe… even as far as the brahma world I wield bodily power. For I, brahmin, with mind encompassing mind, understand the mind of one who has entered first-jhāna samādhi without thought and without examination: ‘Just as the mental factors of this venerable one are directed, next he will think such-and-such a thought.’ For I, brahmin, instruct in this way: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that; attend like this, don’t attend like that; abandon this, live having entered and dwelling in that.’
translations.an3.60:19: “But is there, sir Gotama, any other monk endowed with these three miracles apart from you, sir Gotama?” “Not just one, brahmin, nor two, nor three, nor four, nor five hundred, but far more monks endowed with these three miracles.” “But where, sir Gotama, are those monks dwelling right now?” “Right here in this Saṅgha, brahmin.”
translations.an3.60:2: “Well then, brahmin, I will ask you a counter-question. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, brahmin: Suppose the Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant perfectly awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, sublime, knower of worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed. He says: ‘This is the path, this is the practice: having practiced like this, I have directly known and realized for myself the unsurpassed goal of the holy life and proclaimed it. You too should practice like this, and having practiced like this, you too will directly know and realize for yourselves the unsurpassed goal of the holy life and live having entered and dwelling in it.’ When the teacher teaches Dhamma like this, and others practice for that purpose, then there are not just hundreds, not just thousands, not just hundreds of thousands.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin, in that case, is the meritorious practice single-based or multi-based, namely, the basis of going forth?” “In that case, sir Gotama, the meritorious practice is multi-based, namely, the basis of going forth.”
translations.an3.60:4: When this was said, venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “Of these two practices, brahmin, which one seems to you easier to practice, requiring less effort, more fruitful, and more beneficial?” When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to venerable Ānanda: “Just as sir Gotama regards sir Ānanda. These are my venerables, these are my praises.”
translations.an3.60:5: For a second time venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “I’m not asking you, brahmin, ‘Who are your venerables? Who are your praises?’ Rather, I’m asking you, brahmin: ‘Of these two practices, which one seems to you easier to practice, requiring less effort, more fruitful, and more beneficial?’” For a second time the brahmin Saṅgārava said to venerable Ānanda: “Just as sir Gotama regards sir Ānanda. These are my venerables, these are my praises.”
translations.an3.60:7: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “Even for a third time the brahmin Saṅgārava, when questioned by Ānanda on a legitimate question, approves but does not answer. Why don’t I release him?” Then the Blessed One said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “What’s the matter, brahmin? What conversation arose among the royal retainers while they were sitting together in the king’s inner palace?” “This is what happened, sir Gotama, among the royal retainers while they were sitting together in the king’s inner palace: ‘In the past there were fewer monks but more who demonstrated superhuman psychic miracles; but now there are more monks but fewer who demonstrate superhuman psychic miracles.’ This is what happened, sir Gotama, among the royal retainers while they were sitting together in the king’s inner palace.”
