translations.an3.60:8: “There are these three miracles, brahmin. What three? The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of demonstration, the miracle of instruction. And what is the miracle of psychic power? Here, brahmin, someone experiences various psychic powers: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, ramparts, and mountains as if through space; he walks in on water without sinking as if on earth; he sits cross-legged in space as if in the sky; he touches and strokes with his hand the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; even as far as the brahma world he wields bodily power. This is called the miracle of psychic power, brahmin.
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of demonstration? Here, brahmin, some person demonstrates by means of a sign: ‘Your mind is in this way, your mind is in that way, your mind is thus.’ And even if he demonstrates much, it is just so for that person, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: ‘These are the four noble truths,’ bhikkhus—this Dhamma has been taught by me untaken, untainted, blameless, irreproachable by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. So it was said. And with reference to what was this said? Bhikkhus, dependent on the six elements there is descent into the womb; with descent there is name-and-form, dependent on name-and-form is the sixfold base, dependent on the sixfold base is contact, dependent on contact is feeling. And what is felt, bhikkhus, that I declare to be suffering; this I declare to be the origin of suffering; this I declare to be the cessation of suffering; this I declare to be the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:14: And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, … death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering, association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base; with the sixfold base as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the sixfold base; with the cessation of the sixfold base, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: Bhikkhus, for those who return to past deeds in terms of their essence, there is no desire, effort, or ‘this should be done, this should not be done.’ Thus, when what should be done and what should not be done is not found in truth and reality, for those who dwell forgetful and unvigilant there is no personal valid teaching of a contemplative. Bhikkhus, this is the first valid refutation with regard to those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views.
translations.an3.61:8: Bhikkhus, these three tirthas, when examined, grasped, and questioned by the wise, stand firm even when going to others, in inaction.
translations.an3.61:9: Bhikkhus, this Dhamma has been taught by me untaken, untainted, blameless, irreproachable by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. And what, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma taught by me untaken, untainted, blameless, irreproachable by ascetics and brahmins who are wise? ‘These six elements,’ bhikkhus—this Dhamma has been taught by me untaken, untainted, blameless, irreproachable by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. ‘These six bases for contact,’ bhikkhus—this Dhamma has been taught by me untaken, untainted, blameless, irreproachable by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. ‘These eighteen mental investigations,’ bhikkhus—this Dhamma has been taught by me untaken, untainted, blameless, irreproachable by ascetics and brahmins who are wise. ‘These four noble truths,’ bhikkhus—this Dhamma has been taught by me untaken, untainted, blameless, irreproachable by ascetics and brahmins who are wise.
translations.an3.62:1: ‘There are these three mother-and-son-less fears,’ says the unlearned ordinary person. Which three? There comes a time, bhikkhus, when a great blaze arises. When a great blaze has arisen, bhikkhus, villages are burnt, towns are burnt, cities are burnt. When villages are burning, towns are burning, cities are burning, there a mother does not find her son, a son does not find his mother. This, bhikkhus, the unlearned ordinary person speaks of as the first mother-and-son-less fear.
translations.an3.62:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, there comes a time when a great cloud arises. When a great cloud has arisen, bhikkhus, a great flood is produced. When a great flood is produced, bhikkhus, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. When villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there a mother does not find her son, a son does not find his mother. This, bhikkhus, the unlearned ordinary person speaks of as the second mother-and-son-less fear.
translations.an3.62:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, there comes a time when there is fear of banditry in the wilderness, and mounted bandits roam the countryside. When there is fear, bhikkhus, and banditry in the wilderness, and mounted bandits roam the countryside, there a mother does not find her son, a son does not find his mother. This, bhikkhus, the unlearned ordinary person speaks of as the third mother-and-son-less fear. These are the three mother-and-son-less fears, bhikkhus, the unlearned ordinary person speaks of.
translations.an3.62:4: These three fears, monks, the unlearned ordinary person speaks of as fears that are with mother and child, but they are fears without mother and child. Which three? There comes a time, monks, when a great blaze arises. When a great blaze has arisen, monks, villages burn, towns burn, cities burn. When villages are burning, towns are burning, cities are burning, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her child, a child finds his mother. This, monks, is the first fear that is with mother and child, but the unlearned ordinary person speaks of it as a fear without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:5: And again, monks, there comes a time when a great cloud arises. When a great cloud has arisen, monks, a great flood is produced. When a great flood has been produced, monks, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. When villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her child, a child finds his mother. This, monks, is the second fear that is with mother and child, but the unlearned ordinary person speaks of it as a fear without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:6: And again, monks, there comes a time when there is fear of bandits, when mounted on chariots the countryfolk travel around. When there is fear, monks, of bandits, when countryfolk mounted on chariots are traveling around, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her child, a child finds his mother. This, monks, is the third fear that is with mother and child, but the unlearned ordinary person speaks of it as a fear without mother and child. These three fears, monks, the unlearned ordinary person speaks of as fears that are with mother and child, but they are fears without mother and child.
translations.an3.62:7: These three, monks, are fears without mother and child. Which three? The fear of aging, the fear of illness, the fear of death. A mother does not find her child aging like this: ‘I am aging, may my child not age’; and a child does not find his mother aging like this: ‘I am aging, may my mother not age.
translations.an3.62:8: A mother does not find her child falling ill like this: ‘I am falling ill, may my child not fall ill’; and a child does not find his mother falling ill like this: ‘I am falling ill, may my mother not fall ill.
translations.an3.62:9: A mother does not find her child dying like this: ‘I am dying, may my child not die’; and a child does not find his mother dying like this: ‘I am dying, may my mother not die.’ These three, monks, are fears without mother and child.
translations.an3.63:1: On one occasion the Blessed One, while wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Saṅgha of monks, arrived at Venāgapura, a village of Kosalan brahmins. The brahmin householders of Venāgapura heard: ‘The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans, from a Sakyan family, gone forth, has reached Venāgapura. And of that Blessed Gotama this fine report has spread: “This Blessed One is accomplished, fully awakened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of worlds, unsurpassed trainer of tamable people, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.” He by himself directly knowing and realizing has proclaimed this world with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, its recluses and brahmins, its demons and humans. He sets forth a teaching that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, meaningful, well-phrased, complete and pure in every aspect, disclosing a spiritual life that is utterly perfect. It is good indeed to see such arahants.’
translations.an3.63:11: ‘It is amazing, Gotama, it is astounding, Gotama. Who else will gain unimpeded, effortless, untroublesome attainment of such noble lofty exalted states, apart from Gotama?’
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmin householders of Venāgapura went to the Blessed One. Having gone to the Blessed One, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and when this courteous talk was finished, sat down to one side; some, having raised their hands in homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some, having announced their name and clan, sat down to one side; some sat down to one side silently. When the Venāgapura brahmin Vacchagotta had sat down to one side, he said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an3.63:5: ‘There are these three lofty exalted states, brahmin, which I now gain unimpeded, effortless, untroublesome. Which three? The divine lofty exalted state, the Brahmā lofty exalted state, the noble lofty exalted state. These three, brahmin, are the lofty exalted states which I now gain unimpeded, effortless, untroublesome.’
translations.an4.10:10: Beings go to saṁsāra,  going to birth and death;  Those who fully understand sensual pleasures,  and existence-yoke entirely.
translations.an4.10:9: Tied up with the yoke of sensual pleasures,  and both with the yoke of existence;  Tied up with the yoke of views,  led by ignorance.
translations.an4.18:1: ‘These four, monks, are ways of non-going. Which four? One does not go by desire, does not go by hatred, does not go by delusion, does not go by fear— These, monks, are the four ways of non-going.’
translations.an4.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjis at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks.’ ‘Venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.an4.1:4: ‘Virtue, concentration, wisdom,  and unsurpassed liberation;  These principles were realized  by Gotama, the glorious one.
translations.an4.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāketa in Kāḷakārāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks.’ ‘Venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said—
translations.an4.24:2: ‘Monks, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or considered by the mind by any ascetic or brahmin—by gods, humans, or demons—in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and commoners—that I know.’
translations.an4.24:5: Bhikkhus, whatever … I would say I know and do not know, that would be just so for him.
translations.an4.24:7: Bhikkhus, so the Tathāgata, having seen what is to be seen, does not conceive the seen, does not conceive the unseen, does not conceive what is to be seen, does not conceive one who sees; having heard what is to be heard, does not conceive the heard, does not conceive the unheard, does not conceive what is to be heard, does not conceive one who hears; having sensed what is to be sensed, does not conceive the sensed, does not conceive the unsensed, does not conceive what is to be sensed, does not conceive one who senses; having known what is to be known, does not conceive the known, does not conceive the unknown, does not conceive what is to be known, does not conceive one who knows. Bhikkhus, so the Tathāgata is just so regarding phenomena that are to be seen, heard, sensed, and known. He says: ‘There is no one else who is just so, superior, or more sublime than that one who is just so.’
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed, adhered to as true by others; among those who are self-conceited, he would not declare that as true or false.
translations.an4.28:1: Bhikkhus, there are these four noble families that are supreme, cherished, renowned, ancient, untainted, untainted from the beginning, not being tainted, not becoming tainted, unblameworthy by ascetics, brahmins, and wise people. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is content with whatever robe, speaks praise of contentment with whatever robe, does not engage in unseemly search for robe, does not worry when robe is not obtained, and uses the obtained robe without attachment, without greed, without miserliness, seeing danger, understanding relinquishment; and by that contentment with whatever robe he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. For one who is capable, unlazy, clearly comprehending, mindful there, they say, ‘Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu stands in the ancient, supreme noble family.’
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu delights in development, is devoted to development, delights in relinquishment, is devoted to relinquishment; and by that delight in development, devotion to development, delight in relinquishment, devotion to relinquishment he does not exalt himself nor disparage others. For one who is capable, unlazy, clearly comprehending, mindful there, they say, ‘Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu stands in the ancient, supreme noble family.’ These, bhikkhus, are the four noble families that are supreme, cherished, renowned, ancient, untainted, untainted from the beginning, not being tainted, not becoming tainted, unblameworthy by ascetics, brahmins, and wise people.
translations.an4.28:5: Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these four noble families, if he dwells in the east, that very disenchantment bears him up, that disenchantment does not bear him up; if he dwells in the west, that very disenchantment bears him up, that disenchantment does not bear him up; if he dwells in the north, that very disenchantment bears him up, that disenchantment does not bear him up; if he dwells in the south, that very disenchantment bears him up, that disenchantment does not bear him up. Why is that? For a wise person disenchantment is the bearer of disenchantment.
translations.an4.28:6: Disenchantment does not bear up the wise, the wise does not bear up disenchantment; the wise bears up disenchantment, for the wise is the bearer of disenchantment.
translations.an4.31:1: Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels by which, for those endowed with them, the four-wheeled chariot turns for gods and humans, by which gods and humans attain greatness and abundance in enjoyments without great difficulty. What four? Dwelling in a suitable location, reliance on good people, right intention regarding oneself, and former deeds of merit—these, bhikkhus, are the four wheels by which, for those endowed with them, the four-wheeled chariot turns for gods and humans, by which gods and humans attain greatness and abundance in enjoyments.
translations.an4.32:1: Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of sympathy. What four? Giving, kind speech, doing welfare, equality—these, bhikkhus, are the four bases of sympathy.
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kind speech here, doing welfare; equality regarding qualities, in each case as appropriate; these are the sympathies in the world, like the axle-pin of a cart’s wheel.
translations.an4.32:3: If there were no sympathies, not on account of a child would a mother do for her child; nor would a father do for his child.
translations.an4.33:1: Bhikkhus, the lion, king of beasts, in the evening emerges from his lair. Having emerged from his lair, he stretches. Having stretched, he looks around in all four directions. Having looked around in all four directions, he roars a lion’s roar three times. Having roared a lion’s roar three times, he sets out for food. Now those animals of the wild that hear the sound of the lion, king of beasts, roaring, for the most part fall into fear, terror, and fright. They enter a hole, enter a lair, enter a forest, birds take to the sky. Even those elephants of the king in village, town, and royal city, bound with strong leather straps, even they break and burst those bonds in fear and, excreting and urinating, flee here and there. Such is the power, bhikkhus, of the lion, king of beasts, such is his majesty, such his might.
translations.an4.33:2: Just so, bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata arises in the world, an perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, world-knowing, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed, he teaches Dhamma thus: ‘This is embodiment, this is the origin of embodiment, this is the cessation of embodiment, this is the practice that leads to the cessation of embodiment.’ Those gods, bhikkhus, who are long-lived, good-looking, much happy, abiding long in lofty palaces, even they, on hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of Dhamma, for the most part fall into fear, terror, and fright: ‘It turns out, sirs, that we who thought we were permanent have come to impermanence; it turns out, sirs, that we who thought we were stable have come to instability; it turns out, sirs, that we who thought we were eternal have come to non-eternal. It turns out, sirs, that we are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, included within embodiment.’ Such is the power, bhikkhus, of the Tathāgata in the world with its gods, such his majesty, such his might.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, by higher knowledge, set rolling the Dhamma wheel, the teacher unequalled of the world with its gods.
translations.an4.33:4: Embodiment and its cessation, and the origin of embodiment; the noble eightfold path leading to the calming of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: “These four highest confidences, monks. Which four? As far as there are beings—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, with form or formless, percipient or non-percipient or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared the highest of them, the arahant, perfectly enlightened. Those who have confidence in the Buddhas have confidence in what is highest. And for those who have confidence in what is highest, the result is highest.”
translations.an4.34:2: “As far as there are conditioned dhammas, monks, the noble eightfold path is declared the highest of them. Those who have confidence in the noble eightfold path have confidence in what is highest. And for those who have confidence in what is highest, the result is highest.”
translations.an4.34:3: “As far as there are dhammas, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the highest of them, that is, the dispassion free from intoxication, the destruction of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the breaking of the cycle, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Those who have confidence in the dharmas of dispassion have confidence in what is highest. And for those who have confidence in what is highest, the result is highest.”
translations.an4.34:4: “As far as there are communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the highest of them, namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals; this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of añjali, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in what is highest. And for those who have confidence in what is highest, the result is highest. These, monks, are the four highest confidences.”
translations.an4.34:5: “Having confidence in the highest, knowing the highest dhamma; having confidence in the highest Buddha, the unsurpassed recipient of offerings.”
translations.an4.34:6: “Having confidence in the highest dhamma, the bliss of dispassion and peace; having confidence in the highest Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.”
translations.an4.34:7: “Giving a gift to the highest, the highest merit increases; highest lifespan, beauty, fame, glory, happiness, strength.”
translations.an4.35:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, said to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: “We love a man of great wisdom endowed with four dhammas, Gotama. Which four? Here, Gotama, he is very learned, and of what he has learned there, of what has been said, he knows the meaning: ‘This is the meaning of this statement, this is the meaning of this statement.’ And he is mindful, able to recollect and remember even what was said and done long ago. And as for those duties of a householder’s servant, he is capable and diligent, possessed of investigative skill, able to accomplish and arrange. With these four dhammas, Gotama, we love a man of great wisdom. If it should be approved, Gotama, may the venerable Gotama approve; if it should be rejected, may the venerable Gotama reject.”
translations.an4.35:6: “He who knows all beings, the release from death’s domain; beneficial to gods and humans, he proclaims the true dhamma; seeing and hearing whom, many people are at peace.”
translations.an4.36:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Ukkatthā and Setabya. And Doṇa the brahmin too was traveling along the road between Ukkatthā and Setabya. Doṇa the brahmin saw on the Blessed One’s feet thousand-spoked wheel marks, with rims and hubs, complete in every detail; seeing them, he thought: ‘It’s wonderful, sir, it’s marvelous. Surely these cannot be the feet of a human being.’ Then the Blessed One left the road, sat down cross-legged at the root of a certain tree, having straightened his body, established mindfulness in front. Then Doṇa the brahmin, following the Blessed One’s footprints, saw the Blessed One sitting at the root of a certain tree, serene, inspiring serenity, with calm faculties, calm mind, attained to the supreme taming and calming, tamed, guarded, with restrained faculties, a nāga. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.36:2: “‘Will the venerable one be a god?’ ‘No, brahmin, I will not be a god.’ ‘Will the venerable one be a gandhabba?’ ‘No, brahmin, I will not be a gandhabba.’ ‘Will the venerable one be a yakkha?’ ‘No, brahmin, I will not be a yakkha.’ ‘Will the venerable one be a human?’ ‘No, brahmin, I will not be a human.’”
translations.an4.36:4: “Brahmin, if I were to be a god because of not abandoning those taints, those taints of mine are abandoned, their root destroyed, like a palm tree made a stump, made non-existent, not subject to future arising. If I were to be a gandhabba … a yakkha … a human because of not abandoning those taints, those taints of mine are abandoned, their root destroyed, like a palm tree made a stump, made non-existent, not subject to future arising. Just as, brahmin, a lotus or water lily born in water, grown in water, stands reaching beyond the water, unsoiled by water; even so, brahmin, born in the world, grown in the world, having overcome the world, I dwell unsoiled by the world. ‘A Buddha,’ brahmin, is what you should understand me to be.”
translations.an4.37:1: “A monk endowed with four dhammas is incapable of decline, dwelling near Nibbāna. Which four? Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue, a guard of the sense doors, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: “And how, monks, is a monk accomplished in virtue? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of proper conduct and livelihood, seeing danger in the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains in the training rules. Thus, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue.”}
translations.an4.37:3: And how, monks, is a monk a guardian of the sense doors? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not one who grasps at signs, nor one who grasps at details. That the eye faculty would be unprotected for him, and because of that unprotectiveness bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure might flow in, for that he practices restraint; he guards the eye faculty; he arrives at restraint regarding the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear … smelled an odor with the nose … tasted a flavor with the tongue … touched a tangible object with the body … cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not one who grasps at signs, nor one who grasps at details. That the mind faculty would be unprotected for him, and because of that unprotectiveness bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure might flow in, for that he practices restraint; he guards the mind faculty; he arrives at restraint regarding the mind faculty. Thus, monks, a monk is a guardian of the sense doors.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, monks, is a monk moderate in eating? Here, monks, a monk eats food reflecting properly: ‘Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification; only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, for supporting the holy life. Thus I will put an end to old feeling and not produce new feeling, and I will be healthy and blameless and stay comfortable.’ Thus, monks, a monk is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, monks, is a monk devoted to vigilance? Here, monks, a monk during the day purifies his mind of obstructive qualities by walking and sitting; in the first watch of the night purifies his mind of obstructive qualities by walking and sitting; in the middle watch of the night lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, legs drawn up one on the other, mindful and aware, having the perception of rising in mind; in the last watch of the night rises, purifies his mind of obstructive qualities by walking and sitting. Thus, monks, a monk is devoted to vigilance. Endowed with these four qualities, monks, a monk is incapable of decline; he has nibbāna right there.
translations.an4.37:6: Established in virtue, restrained in the senses;  Moderate in eating, devoted to vigilance.
translations.an4.37:7: Thus dwelling, ardent,  Untiring by day and night;  Developing skillful qualities,  For arrival at security from yoke.
translations.an4.38:1: ‘A monk with refined partial truths is called “one who seeks according to age-mates, with pacified bodily formations, retracted”.’ And how, monks, is a monk with refined partial truths? Here, monks, those partial truths of ordinary recluses and brahmins, namely: ‘The world is eternal’ or ‘The world is not eternal’ or ‘The world is finite’ or ‘The world is infinite’ or ‘The soul is the same as the body’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body another’ or ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’; all those are refined, refined away, spat out, eliminated, relinquished, let go. Thus, monks, a monk is with refined partial truths.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, monks, is a monk retracted? Here, monks, a monk’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, its root destroyed like a palm tree stump, made like a hollow, unable to rise up in the future. Thus, monks, a monk is retracted. ‘A monk with refined partial truths is called “one who seeks according to age-mates, with pacified bodily formations, retracted”.’
translations.an4.38:5: Sensual desire, becoming-desire,  Together with holy-life-desire;  Thus the clinging to truths,  Accumulations in viewpoints.
translations.an4.38:6: For one detached from all lust,  Freed by the destruction of craving;  Desires are relinquished,  Viewpoints are eradicated.
translations.an4.52:1: ‘Monks, there are these four meritorious intentions, skillful intentions, productive of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading upwards to heaven, agreeable, pleasant, delightful, beneficial, leading to happiness. Which four? Here, monks, a noble disciple has unwavering confidence in the Buddha: “That Blessed One is accomplished, fully awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.” This, monks, is the first meritorious intention … leading to happiness.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has unwavering confidence in the teaching: “The teaching is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be personally experienced by the wise.” This, monks, is the second meritorious intention … leading to happiness.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of good conduct; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of upright conduct; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of true conduct; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of proper conduct; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals; this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of añjali, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” This, monks, is the third meritorious intention … leading to happiness.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with noble ethics that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, spotless, freeing, praised by the wise, not grasped, conducive to samādhi. This, monks, is the fourth meritorious intention … leading to happiness. These, monks, are the four meritorious intentions … leading to happiness.
translations.an4.52:5: He whose confidence in the Tathāgata  Is unshakable, well-established;  Whose virtue is good,  Noble, praised.
translations.an4.52:6: One who has faith in the Saṅgha, and has straight view; They call him not poor, his life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Madhura and Veranja. Several householders and householder’s wives were also traveling along the road between Madhura and Veranja. Then the Blessed One, having left the road, sat down at the root of a certain tree (…) . The householders and householder’s wives saw the Blessed One sitting at the root of a certain tree. Seeing him, they went to the Blessed One; going to him, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. When they were sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to those householders and householder’s wives:
translations.an4.53:10: Both have faith and are grateful, restrained, living by the Dhamma; They are loving parents, speaking kindly to each other.
translations.an4.53:11: They have abundant meaning, happiness arises; Enemies are miserable, toward those of like conduct.
translations.an4.53:2: “There are these four kinds of cohabitation, householders. What four? A wretch lives together with a wretch, a wretch lives together with a goddess, a god lives together with a wretch, a god lives together with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a wretch live together with a wretch? Here, householders, the husband is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, indulges in wines, liquors, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness; he is immoral, of evil character, with a mind overcome by stinginess and miserliness, dwelling in a house, abusive and abusive toward ascetics and brahmins; and his wife is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, indulges in wines, liquors, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness; she is immoral, of evil character, with a mind overcome by stinginess and miserliness, dwelling in a house, abusive and abusive toward ascetics and brahmins. Thus, householders, a wretch lives together with a wretch.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is immoral, stingy, abusive; The wife is virtuous, grateful, free from stinginess; She too, the goddess, lives together with the wretch husband.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, grateful, free from stinginess; The wife is immoral, stingy, abusive; She too, the wretch, lives together with the god husband.
translations.an4.5:1: “There are these four persons existing and found in the world, bhikkhus. What four? The person who goes with the stream, the person who goes against the stream, the person who stands firm, the brahmin who has crossed over and stands on the further shore. And what, bhikkhus, is the person who goes with the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and does evil deeds. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who goes with the stream.
translations.an4.5:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who goes against the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures, does not do evil deeds, and—with pain and displeasure, weeping and wailing—practices the complete and pure holy life. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who stands firm? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is one who, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is due to be reborn [spontaneously], and there attains final cessation; he is not subject to return to this world. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who stands firm.
translations.an4.5:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who has crossed over and stands on the further shore, the brahmin? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, with the destruction of the taints, abides having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless deliverance of mind, deliverance through wisdom. This, bhikkhus, is called the person who has crossed over and stands on the further shore, the brahmin. These, bhikkhus, are the four persons existing and found in the world.”
translations.an4.5:5: Those people who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, not free from lust, sensual pleasure seekers here; They go from birth to aging and death again and again, overcome by craving, going with the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore the wise one, established in mindfulness here, not indulging in sensual pleasures and evil; Even with pain, he would abandon sensual pleasures, They call that person one who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:7: He who has abandoned the five defilements, the trainee complete, not subject to decline; Master of mind, with faculties controlled, That man is called one who stands firm.
translations.an4.62:2: “There are these four kinds of happiness to be obtained by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures, at the right time, occasionally. What four? The happiness of alms, the happiness of wealth, the happiness of debtlessness, the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of alms? Here, householder, a clansman has wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, obtained by lawful means. He experiences happiness, he experiences joy: ‘I have wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of my arms, earned by sweat, obtained by lawful means.’ This is called, householder, the happiness of alms.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of debtlessness? Here, householder, a clansman does not owe anyone anything, great or small. He experiences happiness, he experiences joy: ‘I do not owe anyone anything, great or small.’ This is called, householder, the happiness of debtlessness.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, householder, a noble disciple is endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, endowed with blameless mental action. He experiences happiness, he experiences joy: ‘I am endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, endowed with blameless mental action.’ This is called, householder, the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness to be obtained by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures, at the right time, occasionally.”
translations.an4.62:7: Having known the happiness of debtlessness, and then the happiness of alms; The person enjoys the happiness of wealth, thereafter wisdom discerns.
translations.an5.23:1: “These five are impurities of gold, monks, by which the gold that is impure does not become malleable or workable or lustrous or workable for crafting. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, silver—these are the five impurities of gold, by which the gold that is impure does not become malleable or workable or lustrous or workable for crafting. But when gold is freed from these five impurities, monks, then the gold becomes malleable and workable and lustrous and not brittle, and it is properly workable for crafting. Whatever kind of ornament he wishes to make—whether a crown or earrings or a necklace or a gold chain—he obtains his purpose thereby.
translations.an5.23:2: Just so, monks, there are these five impurities of mind, by which the mind that is impure does not become malleable or workable or lustrous or concentrated properly for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt—these are the five impurities of mind by which the mind that is impure does not become malleable or workable or lustrous or concentrated properly for the destruction of the taints. But when the mind is freed from these five impurities, monks, then the mind becomes malleable and workable and lustrous and not brittle, and it concentrates properly for the destruction of the taints. It inclines and directs itself to whatever superhuman state of knowledge and vision is to be realized by direct knowledge, and there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, it gains the capacity.
translations.an5.23:3: He, if he wishes: ‘With various psychic powers I would experience manifold supernormal powers: having been one, I would become many; having been many, I would become one; I would appear and vanish; I would pass through barriers without obstruction, as if in space; I would plunge in and out of the earth as if it were water; I would walk on water without sinking as if it were earth; seated cross-legged I would travel in space as if on a bird’s wing; even with my hand I would touch and stroke the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; I would wield bodily power even up to the world of Brahmā,’ there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, he gains the capacity.
translations.an5.23:4: He, if he wishes: ‘With clear, surpassing human divine ear element I would hear both sounds, divine and human, whether far or near,’ there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, he gains the capacity.
translations.an5.23:5: He, if he wishes: ‘With mind I would know the minds of other beings and persons: a mind with sensual desire as “a mind with sensual desire,” or a mind without sensual desire as “a mind without sensual desire”; a mind with ill will as “a mind with ill will,” or a mind without ill will as “a mind without ill will”; a mind with delusion as “a mind with delusion,” or a mind without delusion as “a mind without delusion”; a contracted mind as “a contracted mind,” or a distracted mind as “a distracted mind”; an exalted mind as “an exalted mind,” or an unexalted mind as “an unexalted mind”; a surpassed mind as “a surpassed mind,” or an unsurpassed mind as “an unsurpassed mind”; a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind,” or an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind”; a liberated mind as “a liberated mind,” or an unliberated mind as “an unliberated mind,’ there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, he gains the capacity.
translations.an5.25:1: “Monks, right view supported by five factors bears the fruit of liberation of mind and the result of liberation of mind, and bears the fruit of liberation by wisdom and the result of liberation by wisdom.
translations.an5.26:1: “Monks, there are these five bases of liberation where, when a monk dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his mind that is unliberated becomes liberated, his taints that are not eliminated go to their elimination, and he arrives at the supreme security from bondage that he has not yet arrived at.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, monks, it is not only that the teacher teaches the Dhamma, or some fellow monk in the holy life who is a senior companion, but he teaches the Dhamma to others in detail, as he has learned and memorized it. Monks, however much a monk teaches the Dhamma to others in detail, as he has learned and memorized it, just so much he is one who understands the meaning and the Dhamma in that Dhamma. For one who understands the meaning and the Dhamma, joy is born. For one joyful, rapture is born. With a rapturous mind, the body is pacified. With pacified body, he experiences pleasure. With mind pleased, the mind concentrates. This, monks, is the second base of liberation where, when a monk dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his mind that is unliberated becomes liberated, his taints that are not eliminated go to their elimination, and he arrives at the supreme security from bondage that he has not yet arrived at.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, monks, it is not only that the teacher teaches the Dhamma, or some fellow monk in the holy life who is a senior companion, nor does he teach the Dhamma to others in detail, as he has learned and memorized it, but he recites the Dhamma in detail, as he has learned and memorized it. Monks, however much a monk recites the Dhamma in detail, as he has learned and memorized it, just so much he is one who understands the meaning and the Dhamma in that Dhamma. For one who understands the meaning and the Dhamma, joy is born. For one joyful, rapture is born. With a rapturous mind, the body is pacified. With pacified body, he experiences pleasure. With mind pleased, the mind concentrates. This, monks, is the third base of liberation where, when a monk dwells diligent, ardent … he arrives at the supreme security from bondage.
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk’s teacher does not teach him the Dhamma, nor does any fellow spiritual practitioner held in esteem, nor does he teach others the Dhamma in detail as he has learned and memorized it, nor does he recite the Dhamma in detail as he has learned and memorized it, nor does he mentally apply himself, reflect, and contemplate the Dhamma as he has learned and memorized it; but he has well grasped some meditation sign, well attended to it, well retained it, thoroughly penetrated it with wisdom. Monks, just as a monk has well grasped some meditation sign, well attended to it, well retained it, thoroughly penetrated it with wisdom, just so he directly realizes the meaning and the Dhamma in that Dhamma. For one who directly realizes the meaning and the Dhamma, rapture is born. For one who is rapturous, joy is born. For one with a joyful mind, the body is pacified. The body of one whose body is pacified experiences bliss. The mind of one who is blissful is concentrated. Monks, this is the fifth liberation base in dependence on which, when a monk dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his mind, if not yet freed, is freed, or if his defilements are not yet ended, they go to their end, or if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it.
translations.an5.27:1: ‘Develop boundless concentration, monks, with wisdom and mindfulness. Monks, for those who develop boundless concentration with wisdom and mindfulness, five kinds of knowledge arise personally for them. Which five? “This concentration is pleasant in the present and ripens in future pleasure”—knowledge arises personally for them; “this concentration is noble and free from taints”—knowledge arises personally for them; “this concentration is practiced by worthy persons”—knowledge arises personally for them; “this concentration is peaceful, sublime, gained by calming, attained by singleness, not attained by suppression of thought-formations”—knowledge arises personally for them; “I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully”—knowledge arises personally for them.
translations.an5.28:1: ‘I will teach you the development of the fivefold noble right concentration of the noble one. Listen to it, pay close attention, I will speak.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.an5.28:10: Just as, monks, a skilled trainer of thoroughbred horses harnesses a thoroughbred colt chariot to a four-way crossroads on level ground, holding the goad in his right hand and the reins in his left, and drives it and turns it back wherever he wishes, just so, monks, a monk who has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, who has frequently practiced it, directs his mind to whichever superknowledge to be realized by direct knowledge, and there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, he attains the ability to realize it.
translations.an5.28:15: If he wishes: ‘With the divine eye, purified, surpassing that of humans, … I would know beings by their karmic destination,’ there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, he attains the ability to realize it.
translations.an5.28:7: Monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, who has frequently practiced it, directs his mind to whichever superknowledge to be realized by direct knowledge, and there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, he attains the ability to realize it.
translations.an5.28:8: ‘Just as, monks, a water jar placed on a support is full of water up to the brim, so that a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to tilt it wherever he wished, would water come out?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ ‘Just so, monks, a monk who has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, who has frequently practiced it, directs his mind to whichever superknowledge to be realized by direct knowledge, and there and then, whenever there is an opportunity, he attains the ability to realize it.’
translations.an5.28:9: ‘Just as, monks, on level ground there is a pond four inches deep, walled in, full of water up to the brim, so that a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to break the wall wherever he wished, would water come out?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ ‘Just so, monks, a monk who has developed and cultivated the noble fivefold right concentration, who has frequently practiced it, directs his mind to whichever superknowledge to be realized by direct knowledge … whenever there is an opportunity.’
translations.an5.2:1: ‘These five are powers of training, monks. Which five? The power of faith, the power of shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: ‘And what, monks, is the power of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple has faith, he places faith in the awakening of the Tathāgata: “That Blessed One is accomplished, fully awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.” This, monks, is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: ‘And what, monks, is the power of shame? Here, monks, a noble disciple is shameful, he is ashamed of body misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, he is ashamed of the attainment of evil unwholesome dhammas. This, monks, is called the power of shame.
translations.an5.2:4: ‘And what, monks, is the power of moral dread? Here, monks, a noble disciple is apprehensive, he apprehends body misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, he apprehends the attainment of evil unwholesome dhammas. This, monks, is called the power of moral dread.
translations.an5.2:5: ‘And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome dhammas, for the undertaking of wholesome dhammas, strong in effort, firm in exertion, not turning back from wholesome dhammas. This, monks, is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: ‘And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise, endowed with wisdom leading to the arising of the destruction of suffering, noble penetrating wisdom leading to the right destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers of training.’
translations.an5.30:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the lands of the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at Icchānaṅgala, a village of Kosalan brahmins. There the Blessed One stayed at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. The Icchānaṅgala brahmin householders heard: “The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans from the Sakyan clan who went forth, has reached Icchānaṅgala; he is staying at Icchānaṅgala in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. And of that Blessed Gotama such a beautiful voice of praise has spread: ‘That Blessed One is accomplished, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed’. He has realized by direct knowledge and proclaims this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans. He teaches Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, meaningful, well-phrased, complete and pure, and reveals the holy life. It is good indeed to see such Arahants.” Then the Icchānaṅgala brahmin householders, having spent that night, took much hard and soft food and went to the Icchānaṅgala forest grove; having gone, they stood outside the gatehouse making a loud noise.
translations.an5.30:3: “May the Blessed One consent, venerable sir, may the Sublime One consent; this is now the time for the Blessed One’s consent, venerable sir. Wherever the Blessed One goes from here, the brahmin householders from the town and countryside will go in that direction. Just as, venerable sir, when the thullaphusitaka devas are raining, the water flows in the direction it inclines; even so, venerable sir, wherever the Blessed One goes from here, the brahmin householders from the town and countryside will go in that direction. Why is that? Because, venerable sir, of the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.”
translations.an5.31:1: On one occasion …pe… in the park of Anāthapiṇḍika. Then princess Sumanā, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, went to the Blessed One; having gone, she paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, princess Sumanā said to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: Endowed with virtue just so,  faithful among persons;  All misers in the world,  he outshines with generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud thundering,  with lightning flashes a hundred times;  Fills the lowlands,  raining down on the earth.
translations.an5.31:12: Even so, endowed with vision,  disciple of the perfectly enlightened one;  The wise one overcomes the miser,  in five ways.
translations.an5.31:2: “Venerable sir, here the Blessed One has two disciples of equal faith, equal virtue, equal wisdom—one a giver, the other a non-giver. After the breakup of the body, after death, would they be reborn in a good bourn, the heavenly world? But among those who have become deities, venerable sir, would there be a distinction for them, would there be a reason for difference?”
translations.an5.31:3: “There would, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said: “Sumanā, the giver, when he has become a deity, overcomes that non-giver deity in five ways—with divine life span, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, divine lordship. Sumanā, the giver overcomes that non-giver deity in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:4: “But if from there they pass away and are reborn elsewhere, would there be a distinction for them as human beings, venerable sir, would there be a reason for difference?” “There would, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said: “Sumanā, the giver, when he has become a human being, overcomes that non-giver human being in five ways—with human life span, human beauty, human happiness, human fame, human lordship. Sumanā, the giver overcomes that non-giver human being in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:5: “But if both go forth from the household life into homelessness, would there be a distinction for them as gone forth, venerable sir, would there be a reason for difference?” “There would, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said: “Sumanā, the giver overcomes that non-giver gone forth in five ways—he enjoys much requisite of robes when asked, little when unasked; much almsfood when asked, little when unasked; much lodging when asked, little when unasked; much medicinal requisites when asked, little when unasked. Those fellow monastics with whom he stays mostly treat him with pleasing bodily deeds, little with displeasing; mostly with pleasing verbal deeds, little with displeasing; mostly with pleasing mental deeds, little with displeasing; they mostly offer him pleasing gifts, little displeasing. Sumanā, the giver overcomes that non-giver gone forth in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:6: “But if both attain arahantship, would there be a distinction for them as arahants, venerable sir, would there be a reason for difference?” “Here, Sumanā, I say there is no distinction, that is, liberation by liberation.”
translations.an5.31:9: “Just as the moon pure,  travels in the space realm;  All star groups in the world,  it outshines with light.
translations.an5.34:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Forest in the hall with the peaked roof. Then the general Sīha went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the general Sīha said to the Blessed One: “Can the Blessed One, venerable sir, point out the visible fruit of giving?”
translations.an5.34:2: “One can, Sīha,” the Blessed One said: “Sīha, a giver, a patron of giving, is dear and agreeable to many people. That a giver, a patron of giving, is dear and agreeable to many people—this too is a visible fruit of giving.
translations.an5.34:8: The giver is dear, many resort to him,  He obtains fame, and glory increases;  Unafraid, he enters the assembly,  The man without stingency becomes confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore wise ones give gifts,  Having abandoned the stain of stinginess, the happy ones;  Established long in the heaven realm,  They rejoice, arrived among the gods.
translations.an5.36:1: “These five, monks, are timely gifts. Which five? One gives a gift to a guest; one gives a gift to a traveler; one gives a gift to the sick; one gives a gift during famine; one first establishes those nine-fruited trees in those endowed with virtue. These, monks, are the five timely gifts.”
translations.an5.36:2: Those who give at the right time, wise, grateful, without stinginess; The gift given at the right time to the noble ones, to such upright ones.
translations.an5.36:3: With a serene mind, his offering is abundant; Those who rejoice in it there, or perform services; That offering is not diminished by that, they too share in the merit.
translations.an5.37:1: “Monks, giving food, the giver gives five things to the recipients. Which five? One gives life, one gives beauty, one gives happiness, one gives strength, one gives intelligence. Having given life, one shares in life, whether divine or human; having given beauty, one shares in beauty, whether divine or human; having given happiness, one shares in happiness, whether divine or human; having given strength, one shares in strength, whether divine or human; having given intelligence, one shares in intelligence, whether divine or human. Monks, giving food, the giver gives these five things to the recipients.”
translations.an5.37:2: The wise one gives life and strength, gives beauty and intelligence; The giver of happiness, intelligent, attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: “Just as, monks, on good ground at a four-way crossroads a great banyan tree becomes a refuge for birds all around; even so, monks, a faithful clansman becomes a refuge for many people, for monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers.”
translations.an5.38:3: Endowed with branches, leaves, and fruit, like a great cloud with thunder; With roots, endowed with fruit, it becomes a refuge for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: In a delightful location, birds resort to it; Those seeking shade go for shade, those seeking fruit for fruit.
translations.an5.38:5: Just so, endowed with virtue, faithful, a person of noble character; Of humble conduct, firm, learned, charming, gentle.
translations.an5.38:6: Free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, without taints; In the world, fields of merit, they resort to such a man.
translations.an5.41:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika: ‘There are these five ways of using wealth, householder. Which five? Here, householder, a noble disciple with wealth acquired through energy and exertion, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, obtained by lawful means, enjoys it himself, makes his mother and father enjoy it, makes his children, wife, servants, and workers enjoy it, he keeps himself in true happiness. This is the first way of using wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple with wealth acquired through energy and exertion, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, obtained by lawful means, makes the fivefold offering. The offering to relatives, the offering to guests, the offering to the departed, the offering to the king, the offering to devas—this is the fourth way of using wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple with wealth acquired through energy and exertion, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by sweat, obtained by lawful means, establishes an uplifting offering to those ascetics and brahmins who abstain from intoxication and heedlessness, who are devoted to patience and gentleness, who tame themselves, pacify themselves, and attain nirvana for themselves; an offering that is heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading to heaven. This is the fifth way of using wealth. These, householder, are the five ways of using wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If, householder, for that noble disciple, when these five ways of using wealth are used, his wealth diminishes, he thinks: ‘The ways of using wealth—those I have used, and my wealth is diminishing.’ He has no remorse. If, householder, for that noble disciple, when these five ways of using wealth are used, his wealth increases, he thinks: ‘The ways of using wealth—those I have used, and my wealth is increasing.’ He has no remorse in either way.
translations.an5.41:7: Wealth enjoyed and well-used, dangers overcome; Uplifting offerings given, and the five offerings made; Virtuous ones supported, continent in the holy life.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever purpose wealth is wished for by the wise householder; That purpose has been reached by me, nothing blameworthy has been done.
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
translations.an5.43:4: ‘Householder, a noble disciple who desires life should not beg for life or delight in it or seek a cause for life. Householder, a noble disciple who desires life should practice the path leading to life. When practiced, that path leads to the attainment of life. He becomes one who obtains life, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: ‘Householder, a noble disciple who desires beauty should not beg for beauty or delight in it or seek a cause for beauty. Householder, a noble disciple who desires beauty should practice the path leading to beauty. When practiced, that path leads to the attainment of beauty. He becomes one who obtains beauty, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: ‘Householder, a noble disciple who desires happiness should not beg for happiness or delight in it or seek a cause for happiness. Householder, a noble disciple who desires happiness should practice the path leading to happiness. When practiced, that path leads to the attainment of happiness. He becomes one who obtains happiness, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:7: Indeed, householder, a noble disciple who desires fame ought not to seek fame or delight in it or make any cause for fame. Householder, a noble disciple who desires fame should practice the path leading to fame. When he practices that path leading to fame, it leads to obtaining fame. He becomes one who obtains fame, whether celestial or human.
translations.an5.43:9: Long life, beauty, fame, and glory, Heaven, and noble birth; Pleasures, desired one after another, Sublime, one after another.
translations.an5.49:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then king Pasenadi of Kosala went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now on that occasion queen Mallikā had died. Then a certain man went to king Pasenadi of Kosala, and after approaching, he announced it to king Pasenadi of Kosala’s attendant: ‘Queen Mallikā has died, sire.’ When this was said, king Pasenadi of Kosala sat sorrowful, distressed, with his body hunched over, with face downcast, brooding, uncommunicative.
translations.an5.51:3: Monks, it is impossible for a monk who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstacles to the mind, weakeners of wisdom, with unweakened wisdom, weak wisdom, to know his own benefit, or another’s benefit, or both his own and another’s benefit, or to realize that superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Just as, monks, a river originating in the mountains, far-flowing, swift-currented, carrying along obstacles—for it a man would open the irrigation outlets on both sides. Thus, monks, the stream of that river in the middle would be broken, scattered, spread out, and it would neither flow far, nor have a swift current, nor carry along obstacles. In the same way, monks, it is impossible for a monk who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstacles to the mind, weakeners of wisdom, with unweakened wisdom, weak wisdom, to know his own benefit, or another’s benefit, or both his own and another’s benefit, or to realize that superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain monk went to his preceptor, and after approaching, he said to his preceptor: ‘Venerable sir, now my body is light and pleasant, the directions do not appear to me, the teachings do not appear to me, sloth and torpor has taken hold of my mind and stands possessing it, I practice the holy life without delight, and I have doubt about the teachings.’
translations.an5.56:3: ‘It is just so, monk, for one who has unguarded sense doors, is not moderate in eating, is not devoted to wakefulness, does not gain insight into beneficial teachings, and dwells without being devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment night and morning: his body becomes light and pleasant, the directions do not appear to him, the teachings do not appear to him, sloth and torpor takes hold of his mind and stands possessing it, he practices the holy life without delight, and he has doubt about the teachings. Therefore, monk, you should train like this: “I will be one with guarded sense doors, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, one who gains insight into beneficial teachings, and I will dwell devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment night and morning.” That’s how you should train, monk.’
translations.an5.56:4: Then that monk, advised by the Blessed One with this admonition, rising from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him on his right, and departed. Then that monk, dwelling alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute, in no long time— for that for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, the supreme consummation of the holy life— realizing it for himself with direct knowledge here and now entered upon and dwelt in. ‘My birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being,’ he understood. That monk became one of the arahants.
translations.an5.57:10: ‘It is not just me alone who is separated and parted from all that is dear and agreeable, but all beings who come, go, pass away, and are reborn, all beings are separated and parted from what is dear and agreeable.’ When he frequently reflects on that fact, the path arises in him. He cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it. When he cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it, the fetters are utterly abandoned, the latent tendencies are ended.
translations.an5.57:11: ‘It is not just me alone who is heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, bound by my actions, supported by my actions—whatever action I do, good or bad, of that I will be the heir; but all beings who come, go, pass away, and are reborn, all beings are heirs to their actions, born of their actions, related through their actions, bound by their actions, supported by their actions—whatever action they do, good or bad, of that they will be the heirs.’ When he frequently reflects on that fact, the path arises in him. He cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it. When he cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it, the fetters are utterly abandoned, the latent tendencies are ended.
translations.an5.57:15: I conquered all intoxication, Seeing renunciation as security; Thereby I had the effort, Aiming at Nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: Indeed, monks, that noble disciple reflects thus: ‘It is not just me alone who is subject to aging, not passed over by aging, but all beings who come, go, pass away, and are reborn, all beings are subject to aging, not passed over by aging.’ When he frequently reflects on that fact, the path arises in him. He cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it. When he cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it, the fetters are utterly abandoned, the latent tendencies are ended.
translations.an5.57:8: ‘It is not just me alone who is subject to illness, not passed over by illness, but all beings who come, go, pass away, and are reborn, all beings are subject to illness, not passed over by illness.’ When he frequently reflects on that fact, the path arises in him. He cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it. When he cultivates that path, develops it, repeatedly practices it, the fetters are utterly abandoned, the latent tendencies are ended.
translations.an8.13:1: “Bhikkhus, endowed with eight qualities, a king’s fine thoroughbred royal horse is worthy of a king, enjoys royal provisions, and goes to the king’s stable. Which eight? Here, bhikkhus, a king’s fine thoroughbred is well-born on both sides—from mother and from father. He is born in the same direction where other fine thoroughbreds are born. Whatever food they give him—whether soft or dry—he eats it carefully without scattering. He is not agitated for defecating, urinating, lying down, or sitting down. He is content and easy to live with, and does not disturb other horses. Whatever deceits, crookednesses, cunning, and deceptions he has, he discloses them to the charioteer as they really are. He strives for the charioteer’s trampling. He has the mentality: ‘Whether these horses pull or not, I will pull here.’ When going, he goes by a straight path. He is strong as long as he lives until his life’s end. Bhikkhus, endowed with these eight qualities, a king’s fine thoroughbred royal horse is worthy of a king, enjoys royal provisions, and goes to the king’s stable.”
translations.an8.14:1: “Bhikkhus, I will teach eight defects of horses, eight faults of horses, eight defects of men, and eight faults of men. Listen to it, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.an8.14:2: “And what, bhikkhus, are the eight defects of horses and eight faults of horses? Here, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, turns back and pulls the chariot from behind. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the first fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, bucks behind, hits the yoke-bar, and breaks the cross-pole. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the second fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, throws off the chariot pole and crushes the chariot box itself. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the third fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:5: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, takes a side road and uproots the chariot. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:6: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, bucks and lifts his forelegs onto the previous team. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:7: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, without neighing, without neighing at the charioteer, grinds the goad-stick between his teeth and departs wherever he wants. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:8: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, neither advances nor retreats, but stands there rooted to the spot. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:9: Furthermore, bhikkhus, some horse, when ordered ‘giddy-up,’ though goaded and urged by the charioteer, draws in his forelegs and hind legs and sits down right there on all four legs. Such a one, bhikkhus, there is here a defective horse. This, bhikkhus, is the eighth fault of a horse. These, bhikkhus, are the eight defects of horses and eight faults of horses.
translations.an8.19:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Veranja at the foot of Naḷeru puppha tree. Then Pahārāda the asura king approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One said this to Pahārāda the asura king:
translations.an8.22:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjis at Hatthigāma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, maintain Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: But if, venerable sir, I were to pass away before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to declare about me: ‘There is no fetter by which Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma is bound such that he would return to this world.’ This, venerable sir, is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality that is found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These, venerable sir, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that are found in me. But I do not know: ‘By which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities has the Blessed One declared me endowed?’”
translations.an8.22:12: Then that bhikkhu, having obtained almsfood at the residence of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then that bhikkhu, having returned from the alms round after his meal, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu reported to the Blessed One all the conversation he had had with Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went to the residence of Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma; having gone, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma, went to that monk; having gone, he paid respects to the monk and sat down to one side. To Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma, seated to one side, that monk said this: “You, householder, have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. Which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities are those by which you have been declared by the Blessed One?”
translations.an8.22:3: “I do not know, sir: ‘By which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities have I been declared by the Blessed One.’ But those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that exist for me, listen to them, pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, householder,” that monk replied to Ugga, the householder of Hatthigāma. Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma said: “When, sir, I was attending in the elephant grove, I first saw the Blessed One from afar; with the very sight of him, sir, my mind was pleased with the Blessed One, and my passion for drink was abandoned. This, sir, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality that exists for me.
translations.an8.22:4: Then, with a mind full of faith, I approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave me progressive talk, namely: talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation. When the Blessed One knew my mind was ready, soft, without hindrance, elated, and full of faith, then he revealed the teaching spoken by the Tathāgata: suffering, its origin, its cessation, the path. Just as a clean cloth, free from stains, would properly take dye; even so, right there in that seat, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose for me: ‘Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.’ Then, sir, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma, without doubt, without uncertainty, attained confidence, independent of others in the Teacher’s teaching, right there I went for refuge to the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, and undertook the five training precepts of the holy life. This, sir, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality that exists for me.
translations.an8.22:5: I had four young daughters, sir, who were married. Then, sir, I went to those married daughters; having gone, I said this to those married daughters: ‘I have undertaken the five training precepts of the holy life, sisters. Whichever of you wishes may enjoy wealth here and make merit, or go to her own family. Or perhaps there is a man she wishes to be given to?’ When this was said, sir, the eldest married daughter said this to me: ‘Give me, dear son, to such-and-such a man.’ Then, sir, I had that man summoned, took the married daughter by the left hand, took the dowry with the right hand, and gave her away to that man. But, sir, in giving away the young girl as a wife, I do not perceive any change of mind. This, sir, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality that exists for me.
translations.an8.22:6: And, sir, wealth exists in my family. And it has not been improperly used on those endowed with virtue and good qualities. This, sir, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality that exists for me.
translations.an8.22:7: And, sir, whichever monk I attend upon, I attend upon him diligently, not carelessly. If that venerable one teaches Dhamma to me, I listen diligently, not carelessly. If that venerable one does not teach Dhamma to me, I teach Dhamma to him. This, sir, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality that exists for me.
