translations.an8.22:8: It is not extraordinary, sir, that when the Saṅgha is invited, deities come and announce: ‘Such-and-such a householder’s monk is freed both ways, such-and-such is liberated by wisdom, such-and-such is a body-witness, such-and-such has attained view, such-and-such is faith-freed, such-and-such follows the Dhamma, such-and-such follows faith, such-and-such is virtuous, endowed with good qualities, such-and-such is unvirtuous, endowed with evil qualities.’ But, sir, when I am serving the Saṅgha, I do not perceive a mind arising thus: ‘I give a little to this one, a lot to that one.’ Rather, sir, I give with an equal mind. This, sir, is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality that exists for me.
translations.an8.22:9: It is not extraordinary, sir, that deities come to me and announce: ‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, householder.’ When this was said, sir, I say to those deities: ‘Whether you deities would say it or not, still the Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.’ But, sir, I do not perceive any exaltation of mind on account of that: ‘Those deities come to me, I converse with deities.’ This, sir, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality that exists for me.
translations.an8.23:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, regard Hatthaka the Āḷavaka as endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. Which seven? Hatthaka the Āḷavaka is faithful, monks; virtuous, monks; has shame, monks; has moral dread, monks; is learned, monks; is a giver, monks; is wise, monks—these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities, monks, regard Hatthaka the Āḷavaka as endowed with.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went to the residence of Hatthaka the Āḷavaka; having gone, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Hatthaka the Āḷavaka went to that monk; having gone, he paid respects to the monk and sat down to one side. To Hatthaka the Āḷavaka, seated to one side, that monk said this:
translations.an8.23:3: “You, friend, are endowed with seven marvelous and astonishing qualities declared by the Blessed One. Which seven? ‘Faithful, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī; virtuous … having shame … having moral dread … very learned … a giver … wise, monks, is Hatthaka of Āḷavī.’ With these seven marvelous and astonishing qualities, friend, you are endowed, declared by the Blessed One.” “Was there no layperson there dressed in white?” “No layperson dressed in white was there, friend.” “Good, sir, that no layperson dressed in white was there.”
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having received almsfood at Hatthaka Āḷavaka’s dwelling, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, having returned from almsround after the meal, went to the Blessed One, and having approached, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava shrine. Then Hatthaka Āḷavaka, surrounded by five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to Hatthaka Āḷavaka: “This is a large assembly, Hatthaka. How do you bring together this large assembly?” “These four means of gathering taught by the Blessed One, sir—I bring together this large assembly with them. I, sir, know: ‘This one should be gathered with a gift,’ and I gather him with a gift; I know: ‘This one should be gathered with kind words,’ and I gather him with kind words; I know: ‘This one should be gathered with helpful deeds,’ and I gather him with helpful deeds; I know: ‘This one should be gathered with impartiality,’ and I gather him with impartiality. And there are abundant possessions in my family, sir. They think: ‘We should hear the teaching from one who is not poor.’” “Good, good, Hatthaka. You have a wise way of gathering this large assembly, Hatthaka. Whoever in the past, Hatthaka, gathered a large assembly, all gathered it with these same four means of gathering. Whoever in the future, Hatthaka, will gather a large assembly, all will gather it with these same four means of gathering. Whoever at present, Hatthaka, gathers a large assembly, all gather it with these same four means of gathering.”
translations.an8.26:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka the prince’s son approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Jīvaka the prince’s son said to the Blessed One: “How, sir, is one a lay follower?” “When, Jīvaka, one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—to that extent, Jīvaka, one is a lay follower.”
translations.an8.26:2: “And how, sir, is a lay follower virtuous?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower abstains from killing living beings … abstains from the bases of intoxicants—to that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous.”
translations.an8.26:3: “And how, sir, is a lay follower practicing for his own benefit, not for another’s?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower is accomplished in faith himself, but does not encourage another to accomplishment in faith … having understood benefit and Dhamma himself, he practices in accordance with Dhamma, but does not encourage another to practice in accordance with Dhamma. To that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for his own benefit, not for another’s.”
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, sir, a monk with taints destroyed has developed and well developed the four establishments of mindfulness. That the four establishments of mindfulness have been developed and well developed in a monk with taints destroyed—this too, sir, is a strength of a monk with taints destroyed by relying on which he declares the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, sir, a monk with taints destroyed has developed and well developed the four bases of psychic power … the five faculties … the seven awakening factors … the noble eightfold path. That the noble eightfold path has been developed and well developed in a monk with taints destroyed—this too, sir, is a strength of a monk with taints destroyed by relying on which he declares the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.2:1: “There are eight causes, eight conditions that lead to the obtaining of the initial higher mind that has not been obtained, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment when obtained. Which eight? Here, monks, a monk lives depending on the teacher or on some fellow monk who is worthy of esteem, such that there is sharp shame and moral dread established in him, and affection and respect. This, monks, is the first cause, the first condition that leads to the obtaining of the initial higher mind that has not been obtained, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment when obtained.
translations.an8.2:11: ‘This venerable one, having heard the Dhamma, makes it clear with the twofold seclusion—bodily seclusion and mental seclusion. Surely this venerable one knows, seeing.’ This quality too leads to affection, respect, development, monkhood, and unity.
translations.an8.2:15: ‘This venerable one, having gone to the Saṅgha, is not a speaker of worldly topics, not a speaker of animal topics. He himself speaks on the Dhamma or requests another or approves of noble silence. Surely this venerable one knows, seeing.’ This quality too leads to affection, respect, development, monkhood, and unity.
translations.an8.2:2: Dwelling dependent on that teacher, he approaches a certain respected fellow monk who inspires him with intense shame and moral dread, affection and respect, and from time to time he goes to him and asks and questions: ‘How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerables explain what has not been explained to him, make plain what has not been made plain, and dispel his doubts concerning the many doubtful teachings. This, monks, is the second reason, the second condition that leads to the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life for one who has not attained it, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment for one who has attained it.
translations.an8.2:4: He is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the monastic code, perfect in conduct and livelihood, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and he undertakes and trains in the training rules. This, monks, is the fourth reason, the fourth condition that leads to the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life for one who has not attained it, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment for one who has attained it.
translations.an8.2:5: He has heard much, is a bearer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, meaningful, well-phrased, complete, pure, and that proclaim the holy life—such teachings are much heard by him, borne in mind, recited by speech, examined in mind, and well penetrated by view. This, monks, is the fifth reason, the fifth condition that leads to the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life for one who has not attained it, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment for one who has attained it.
translations.an8.2:6: He dwells with aroused energy, for the abandoning of unskillful qualities and the undertaking of skillful qualities, energetic, firm in exertion, with unwavering effort regarding skillful qualities. This, monks, is the sixth reason, the sixth condition that leads to the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life for one who has not attained it, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment for one who has attained it.
translations.an8.2:7: When in the community, he is not one to talk much on worldly topics. He either speaks the Teaching himself, or asks someone else to do so, or he does not disparage noble silence. This, monks, is the seventh reason, the seventh condition that leads to the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life for one who has not attained it, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment for one who has attained it.
translations.an8.2:8: He dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates of clinging: ‘Thus form, thus the arising of form, thus the passing away of form; thus feeling … thus the arising of feeling, thus the passing away of feeling; thus perception … thus volitional formations … thus consciousness, thus the arising of consciousness, thus the passing away of consciousness.’ This, monks, is the eighth reason, the eighth condition that leads to the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life for one who has not attained it, and to its increase, development, and fulfillment for one who has attained it.
translations.an8.2:9: His fellow monks speak of him thus: ‘This venerable one dwells dependent on the teacher or on a certain respected fellow monk who inspires him with intense shame and moral dread, affection and respect. Surely this venerable one knows, surely he sees.’ This quality also leads to affection, respect, development, monkhood, and unity.
translations.an8.30:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhagga at Sumsumaragiri in the Bhesakala Grove in the Deer Park. At that time the venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Cetis in the Pacinavamsadaya. Then, while the venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: ‘This Teaching is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires; this Teaching is for the contented, not for the discontented; this Teaching is for the secluded, not for one who delights in company; this Teaching is for the energetic, not for the lazy; this Teaching is for the mindful, not for the unmindful; this Teaching is for one who is concentrated, not for the unconcentrated; this Teaching is for the wise, not for the unwise.’
translations.an8.30:10: Anuruddha, when you think these eight thoughts of a great man and become a facile attainer of these four jhanas that are of mental absorption, pleasant dwellings in the here and now, effortless and easy to attain, then your tree-root dwelling will seem to you like a householder’s or householder’s son’s lofty chamber with well-plastered walls and roof, draught-free, with close-fitting doors, as you dwell contented, with delight, free from anxiety, in pleasant abiding for entering nibbana.
translations.an8.30:11: Anuruddha, when you think these eight thoughts of a great man and become a facile attainer of these four jhanas that are of mental absorption, pleasant dwellings in the here and now, effortless and easy to attain, then your grass-mat bed will seem to you like a householder’s or householder’s son’s couch with supports at the head and feet, spread with wool, with a fine-spreader, covered with a blanket, with an upper coverlet of crimson woolen cloth, as you dwell contented, with delight, free from anxiety, in pleasant abiding for entering nibbana.
translations.an8.30:12: Anuruddha, when you think these eight thoughts of a great man and become a facile attainer of these four jhanas that are of mental absorption, pleasant dwellings in the here and now, effortless and easy to attain, then your putrid urine medicine will seem to you like a householder’s or householder’s son’s various medicines, such as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses, as you dwell contented, with delight, free from anxiety, in pleasant abiding for entering nibbana. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should stay here among the Cetis in the Pacinavamsadaya even for the late rainy season.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the venerable Anuruddha replied to the Blessed One.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Blessed One, having advised Venerable Anuruddha with this admonition—just as a strong man might stretch out a flexed arm or flex an extended arm; in the same way—disappeared among the Cetī in the Eastern Pacīnavaṁsadāya and reappeared in the deer park in Bhesakaḷā forest on Susumāragira among the Bhaggas. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, I will teach eight thoughts of a great man, listen to that …pe… What are the eight thoughts of a great man? Monks, this teaching is for one of few desires, this teaching is not for one of many desires; monks, this teaching is for one who is content, this teaching is not for one who is discontent; monks, this teaching is for one who delights in seclusion, this teaching is not for one who delights in company; monks, this teaching is for one of roused energy, this teaching is not for the lazy one; monks, this teaching is for one with established mindfulness, this teaching is not for one with muddled mindfulness; monks, this teaching is for one who is concentrated, this teaching is not for one who is unconcentrated; monks, this teaching is for one endowed with wisdom, this teaching is not for one without wisdom; monks, this teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation and is a non-proliferator, this teaching is not for one who delights in proliferation and is a proliferator.
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Blessed One, having known with his mind the mind of Venerable Anuruddha—just as a strong man might stretch out a flexed arm or flex an extended arm; in the same way—disappeared among the Bhaggas on Susumāragira in Bhesakaḷā forest in the deer park and reappeared right in front of Venerable Anuruddha among the Cetī in the Eastern Pacīnavaṁsadāya. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Venerable Anuruddha also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said this to Venerable Anuruddha, who was sitting to one side:
translations.an8.30:22: Then Venerable Anuruddha also spent the rainy season retreat there among the Cetī in the Eastern Pacīnavaṁsadāya. Then Venerable Anuruddha, dwelling alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute, in no long time—by that for which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, the supreme culmination of the spiritual life—realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered upon and dwelled in. ‘My birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being,’ he understood. And Venerable Anuruddha became one of the arahants. Then Venerable Anuruddha, having attained arahantship at that time, spoke these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: “Knowing my intention,  the Teacher, unexcelled in the world;  with a mind-made body,  he approached with his power.
translations.an8.30:24: As was my intention,  he taught even more than that;  the Buddha delights in non-proliferation,  he taught non-proliferation.
translations.an8.30:3: “Good, good, Anuruddha. Well done, Anuruddha, that you thought the thought of a great man: ‘This teaching is for one of few desires, this teaching is not for one of many desires; this teaching is for one who is content, this teaching is not for one who is discontent; this teaching is for one who delights in seclusion, this teaching is not for one who delights in company; this teaching is for one of roused energy, this teaching is not for the lazy one; this teaching is for one with established mindfulness, this teaching is not for one with muddled mindfulness; this teaching is for one who is concentrated, this teaching is not for one who is unconcentrated; this teaching is for one endowed with wisdom, this teaching is not for one without wisdom.’ Come then, Anuruddha, think also this eighth thought of a great man: ‘This teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation and is a non-proliferator, this teaching is not for one who delights in proliferation and is a proliferator.’
translations.an8.30:4: Anuruddha, when you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, whenever you wish, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful qualities, you will enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which has thought and applied thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.an8.30:5: Anuruddha, when you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, whenever you wish, with the subsiding of thought and applied thought, with internal clarity and unification of mind, without thought and applied thought, you will enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
translations.an8.30:6: Anuruddha, when you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, whenever you wish, with the fading away of rapture you will enter and dwell in the third jhāna, abiding in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiencing pleasure with the body, on account of which the nobles say: ‘He has equanimity and mindfulness, abiding in pleasure.’
translations.an8.30:7: Anuruddha, when you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, whenever you wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, you will enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-painful-nor-pleasurable equanimity and mindfulness, completely pure.
translations.an8.39:1: “Monks, there are these eight streams of merit, streams of good karma, nourishing happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, leading upwards to heaven, pleasant, pleasing, charming, beneficial, leading to happiness. Which eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha. Monks, this is the first stream of merit, stream of good karma, nourishing happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, leading upwards to heaven, pleasant, pleasing, charming, beneficial, leading to happiness.
translations.an8.39:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Dhamma. Monks, this is the second stream of merit …pe… leading to happiness.
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. This, monks, is the third meritorious recourse, skillful recourse, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading upwards to heaven, leading to what is lovely, agreeable, pleasing, profitable, happiness. These five, monks, are gifts, great gifts, foremost gifts, cherished gifts, ancestral gifts, ancient gifts, unmeasured gifts, unmeasured before, not measured, not to be measured, unblameworthy by ascetics, brahmins, and the wise. Which five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned killing living beings, abstains from killing living beings. Abstaining from killing living beings, monks, the noble disciple gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings, gives non-hostility, gives non-harm. Having given fearlessness to immeasurable beings, having given non-hostility, having given non-harm, he becomes a sharer in immeasurable fearlessness, non-hostility, non-harm. This, monks, is the first gift, great gift, foremost gift, cherished gift, ancestral gift, ancient gift, unmeasured gift, unmeasured before, not measured, not to be measured, unblameworthy by ascetics, brahmins, and the wise. This, monks, is the fourth meritorious recourse, skillful recourse, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading upwards to heaven, leading to what is lovely, agreeable, pleasing, profitable, happiness.
translations.an8.39:7: having abandoned fermented liquor, distilled liquor, intoxicants that are grounds for heedlessness, he abstains from fermented liquor, distilled liquor, intoxicants that are grounds for heedlessness. Abstaining from fermented liquor, distilled liquor, intoxicants that are grounds for heedlessness, monks, the noble disciple gives fearlessness to immeasurable beings, gives non-hostility, gives non-harm. Having given fearlessness to immeasurable beings, having given non-hostility, having given non-harm, he becomes a sharer in immeasurable fearlessness, non-hostility, non-harm. This, monks, is the fifth gift, great gift, foremost gift, cherished gift, ancestral gift, ancient gift, unmeasured gift, unmeasured before, not measured, not to be measured, unblameworthy by ascetics, brahmins, and the wise. This, monks, is the eighth meritorious recourse, skillful recourse, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, ripening in happiness, leading upwards to heaven, leading to what is lovely, agreeable, pleasing, profitable, happiness.
translations.an8.40:1: Killing living beings, monks, when cultivated and developed, leads to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm. Its complete result, for one reborn as a human being, leads to short life.
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, monks, when cultivated and developed, leads to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm. Its complete result, for one reborn as a human being, leads to loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Wrong conduct in sensual pleasures, monks, when cultivated and developed, leads to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm. Its complete result, for one reborn as a human being, leads to having many rivals.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, monks, when cultivated and developed, leads to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm. Its complete result, for one reborn as a human being, leads to being reviled with untrue speech.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, monks, when cultivated and developed, leads to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm. Its complete result, for one reborn as a human being, leads to separation from friends.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, monks, when cultivated and developed, leads to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm. Its complete result, for one reborn as a human being, leads to hearing displeasing speech.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, monks, when cultivated and developed, leads to hell, to the animal realm, to the ghost realm. Its complete result, for one reborn as a human being, leads to not being listened to.
translations.an8.6:2: For an unlearned ordinary person, monks, there arises gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. For a learned noble disciple, monks, there also arises gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. What is the difference, monks, what is the distinction, what is the reason for difference between a learned noble disciple and an unlearned ordinary person?' 'Our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, their guide, their refuge. May the Blessed One please clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.'
translations.an8.6:4: Gain seizes his mind and remains, loss seizes his mind and remains, fame seizes his mind and remains, disrepute seizes his mind and remains, blame seizes his mind and remains, praise seizes his mind and remains, pleasure seizes his mind and remains, pain seizes his mind and remains. He is pleased with arisen gain, displeased with loss; pleased with arisen fame, displeased with disrepute; pleased with arisen praise, displeased with blame; pleased with arisen pleasure, displeased with pain. Involved in this adherence and opposition, he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. 'He is not freed from suffering,' I say.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disrepute,  blame and praise, pleasure and pain;  These dhammas among humans are impermanent,  not eternal, subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Knowing these, the mindful one of good wisdom,  sees the dhammas subject to change;  Lovely dhammas do not agitate his mind,  he does not resent the unlovely.
translations.an8.7:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One, regarding Devadatta, addressed the monks: “Monks, it is good for a monk to periodically reflect on his own misfortune. Monks, it is good for a monk to periodically reflect on others’ misfortune. Monks, it is good for a monk to periodically reflect on his own good fortune. Monks, it is good for a monk to periodically reflect on others’ good fortune. Monks, Devadatta, overcome and mastered in mind by eight unrighteous things, is bound for the underworld, bound for hell, bound for many aeons, incurable.”
translations.an8.7:2: “By which eight? Monks, Devadatta, overcome and mastered in mind by gain, is bound for the underworld, bound for hell, bound for many aeons, incurable. By loss … by fame … by disrepute … by honor … by dishonor … by evil desire … by evil friendship, monks, overcome and mastered in mind, Devadatta is bound for the underworld, bound for hell, bound for many aeons, incurable. Monks, overcome and mastered in mind by these eight unrighteous things, Devadatta is bound for the underworld, bound for hell, bound for many aeons, incurable.”
translations.an8.7:3: “Monks, a monk should dwell having repeatedly overcome arisen gain, arisen loss … arisen fame … arisen disrepute … arisen honor … arisen dishonor … arisen evil desire … arisen evil friendship.”
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of gods, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his stretched-out arm, in the same way vanished among the gods of the Thirty-Three and reappeared on the Black Rock Mountain at Mahisavatthu, in front of Venerable Uttara, on a rocky plateau. Then Sakka, lord of gods, approached Venerable Uttara; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Uttara and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of gods, said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: “Is it true, sir, that Venerable Uttara taught the monks this teaching: ‘Good, friends, a monk periodically reflects on his own misfortune, good, friends, a monk periodically reflects on others’ misfortune … his own good fortune … others’ good fortune’? ‘Yes, lord of gods.’ ‘But sir, is this Venerable Uttara’s own inspiration, or is it the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One?’ ‘In that case, lord of gods, I will give you a simile. For by a simile some wise people understand the meaning of what is spoken.’
translations.an8.8:6: ‘Just as, lord of gods, not far from a village or town there is a great heap of grain. A great crowd of people might bring grain from there—with baskets, pots, baskets on carrying poles, and with their hands clasped together. Now, lord of gods, if someone approached that great crowd of people and asked: “Where are you bringing this grain from?”, how would that great crowd, rightly explaining, rightly answer?’ ‘“We are bringing it from that great heap of grain,” sir, that great crowd, rightly explaining, would answer.’ ‘In the same way, lord of gods, whatever is well-spoken, all of it is the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One. Taking hold of that, we and others speak.’
translations.an8.8:7: ‘Amazing, sir, marvelous. How well-spoken by Venerable Uttara: “Whatever is well-spoken, all of it is the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One. Taking hold of that, we and others speak.” On one occasion, Venerable Uttara, the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One, regarding Devadatta, addressed the monks:
translations.mn108:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, Kalandaka’s Park, not long after the Blessed One had passed away.
translations.mn108:13: “Brāhmaṇa, that Blessed One, the knower, the seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One, has taught ten inspiring teachings. In whomever these teachings are found, we at present honor, respect, esteem, and revere him; having honored, respected, esteemed, and revered, we dwell in dependence on him. Which ten?
translations.mn108:14: Here, brāhmaṇa, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the monastic code, perfect in conduct and livelihood, seeing danger in the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains in the training rules.
translations.mn108:15: He is very learned, a keeper of what he has learned, a storehouse of what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, meaningful, well-phrased, complete and pure, explaining the holy life—these teachings he has very learned, retained, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated by wisdom.
translations.mn108:17: He attains and dwells in the four absorptions, mental pleasures herein and now, without exertion, without strain.
translations.mn108:18: With supernormal power he experiences many kinds of supernormal power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, ramparts, and mountains as if through space; he walks on water without sinking as if on earth; he travels sitting cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird; he extends his hand and touches, strokes the moon and sun with their great power and great majesty; even as far as the Brahmā-world he wields bodily power.
translations.mn108:19: With clear, purified divine ear surpassing that of humans, he hears both divine sounds and human sounds, whether far or near.
translations.mn108:2: Now on that occasion King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was fortifying Rājagaha, fearing King Pajjota.
translations.mn108:20: He understands the minds of other beings, other persons with his own mind. A mind with lust, ‘a mind with lust,’ he understands; a mind without lust, ‘a mind without lust,’ he understands; a mind with hate, ‘a mind with hate,’ he understands; a mind without hate, ‘a mind without hate,’ he understands; a mind with delusion, ‘a mind with delusion,’ he understands; a mind without delusion, ‘a mind without delusion,’ he understands; a sluggish mind, ‘a sluggish mind,’ he understands; a distracted mind, ‘a distracted mind,’ he understands; an exalted mind, ‘an exalted mind,’ he understands; an unexalted mind, ‘an unexalted mind,’ he understands; a mediocre mind, ‘a mediocre mind,’ he understands; an unexcelled mind, ‘an unexcelled mind,’ he understands; a concentrated mind, ‘a concentrated mind,’ he understands; an unconcentrated mind, ‘an unconcentrated mind,’ he understands; a liberated mind, ‘a liberated mind,’ he understands; an unliberated mind, ‘an unliberated mind,’ he understands.
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having directly realized and entered upon and attained the taint-free deliverance of mind, deliverance through wisdom, in this very life, by himself through direct knowledge. Indeed, brahmin, these ten inspiring dhammas have been declared by that Blessed One, the knower, the seer, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one. In whomever these dhammas are found, we now honor, revere, esteem, and worship him; dwelling supported, having honored and revered.
translations.mn108:25: Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, said to the venerable Ānanda: ‘But where, reverend Ānanda, do you now dwell?’ ‘At Vulture Peak, brahmin, is where I now dwell.’ ‘Is Vulture Peak, reverend Ānanda, pleasant, quiet, free from noise, secluded, a place for sleeping in privacy, suitable for retreat?’ ‘Indeed, brahmin, Vulture Peak is pleasant, quiet, free from noise, secluded, a place for sleeping in privacy, suitable for retreat, as it is protected by keepers and guardians such as you.’ ‘Indeed, reverend Ānanda, Vulture Peak is pleasant, quiet, free from noise, secluded, a place for sleeping in privacy, suitable for retreat, as it is for recluses who resort to jhāna and are devoted to jhāna. The reverends are jhāna-practitioners and devoted to jhāna. Once, reverend Ānanda, on one occasion the reverend Gotama was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Forest in the assembly hall with peaked roof. Then I, reverend Ānanda, went to the Great Forest, to the assembly hall with peaked roof, to the reverend Gotama. There the reverend Gotama spoke on jhāna in many ways. That reverend Gotama was a jhāna-practitioner and devoted to jhāna. And that reverend Gotama praised jhāna entirely.’
translations.mn108:28: ‘Apparently, reverend Ānanda, that reverend Gotama criticized jhāna and praised it. But now, reverend Ānanda, we will go; we have much to do and much to attend to.’ ‘Now is the time, brahmin, whenever you think it fit.’ Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the Magadhan chief minister, having rejoiced in and approved of what the venerable Ānanda had said, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then the venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the venerable Ānanda: ‘It is too late today to go almsrounding in Rājagaha. What if I were to go to the work-place of the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna, to the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna?’
translations.mn108:4: Then the venerable Ānanda went to the work-place of the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna, to the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna. The brahmin Gopakamoggallāna saw the venerable Ānanda coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the venerable Ānanda: ‘Come, reverend Ānanda. Welcome to reverend Ānanda. It has been long since reverend Ānanda took the opportunity of coming here. Sit, reverend Ānanda, this seat has been prepared.’ The venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. The brahmin Gopakamoggallāna took a low seat and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Gopakamoggallāna said to the venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: ‘Is there, reverend Ānanda, even a single monk endowed with all those qualities in every way with which that reverend Gotama—the arahant, perfectly enlightened one—was endowed?’ ‘There is not, brahmin, even a single monk endowed with all those qualities in every way with which that Blessed One—the arahant, perfectly enlightened one—was endowed. For that Blessed One, brahmin, brought forth the unarisen path, produced the unproduced path, made known the unknown path, became a knower of the path, an expert in the path, a skilled one in the path. And now his disciples dwell following the path, endowed with it afterwards.’
translations.mn108:7: ‘Is there, reverend Ānanda, even a single monk whom that reverend Gotama established: “This one will be a refuge for you after my passing,” whom you now practice accordingly?’ ‘There is not, brahmin, even a single monk whom that Blessed One—the knower, the seer, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one—established: “This one will be a refuge for you after my passing,” whom we now practice accordingly.’
translations.mn108:9: ‘But in the absence of a refuge, reverend Ānanda, what is the cause of concord?’ ‘We are not without a refuge, brahmin; we have a refuge, brahmin; we have the Dhamma as a refuge.’
translations.mn117:10: There, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? He understands wrong intention as ‘wrong intention,’ understands right intention as ‘right intention.’ That is his right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, monks, is wrong intention? Intention of sensuality, intention of ill will, intention of harmfulness—this, monks, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, monks, is right intention? Right intention, monks, I say is of two kinds—there is, monks, right intention that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth; there is, monks, right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, monks, is right intention that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-harmfulness: this, monks, is right intention that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth.
translations.mn117:14: And what, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Here, monks, when a noble one’s mind, taintless mind, one who possesses the noble path, develops the noble path, the thought, directed thought, intention, application of mind, deployment of mind, mental formation of speech—this, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: He strives for the abandoning of wrong intention for the attainment of right intention, that becomes his right effort. Mindful, he abandons wrong intention, mindful he dwells having attained right intention; that becomes his right mindfulness. Thus these three things run around and circle around right intention, namely—right view, right effort, right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: Therein, monks, right view is the forerunner. And how, monks, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong speech as ‘wrong speech’, he understands right speech as ‘right speech’; that becomes his right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, monks, is right speech? Right speech, monks, I say is of two kinds—there is, monks, right speech that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth; there is, monks, right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, monks, is right speech that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth? Abstinence from false speech, abstinence from malicious speech, abstinence from harsh speech, abstinence from frivolous talk—this, monks, is right speech that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth.
translations.mn117:2: ‘I will teach you, monks, noble right concentration with its supports and with its requisites. Listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Here, monks, when a noble one’s mind, taintless mind, one who possesses the noble path, develops the noble path, the abstaining, refraining, abstention through aversion from the four kinds of verbal misconduct—this, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: Therein, monks, right view is the forerunner. And how, monks, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong action as ‘wrong action’, he understands right action as ‘right action’; that becomes his right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, monks, is right action? Right action, monks, I say is of two kinds—there is, monks, right action that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth; there is, monks, right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what, monks, is right action that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth? Abstinence from killing living beings, abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from sexual misconduct—this, monks, is right action that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth.
translations.mn117:28: Therein, monks, right view is the forerunner. And how, monks, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong livelihood as ‘wrong livelihood’, he understands right livelihood as ‘right livelihood’; that becomes his right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, monks, is wrong livelihood? Deceiving, flattering, hinting, belittling, pursuing gain with gain—this, monks, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, monks, is right livelihood? Right livelihood, monks, I say is of two kinds—there is, monks, right livelihood that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth; there is, monks, right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what, monks, is right livelihood that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns his living by right livelihood—this, monks, is right livelihood that is with taint, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth.
translations.mn117:34: Therein, monks, right view is the forerunner. And how, monks, is right view the forerunner? For one with right view, monks, right intention is possible, for one with right intention right speech is possible, for one with right speech right action is possible, for one with right action right livelihood is possible, for one with right livelihood right effort is possible, for one with right effort right mindfulness is possible, for one with right mindfulness right concentration is possible, for one with right concentration right knowledge is possible, for one with right knowledge right freedom is possible. Thus, monks, the trainee is endowed with eight factors, the arahant with ten factors. There too, with right knowledge many evil unskillful qualities are abandoned, they reach fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:35: Therein, monks, right view is the forerunner. And how, monks, is right view the forerunner? For one with right view, monks, wrong view is worn out. And those many evil unskillful qualities that arise due to wrong view are worn out for him. Due to right view many skillful qualities reach fulfillment by development. For one with right intention, monks, wrong intention is worn out …pe… for one with right speech, monks, wrong speech is worn out … for one with right action, monks, wrong action is worn out … for one with right livelihood, monks, wrong livelihood is worn out … for one with right effort, monks, wrong effort is worn out … for one with right mindfulness, monks, wrong mindfulness is worn out … for one with right concentration, monks, wrong concentration is worn out … for one with right knowledge, monks, wrong knowledge is worn out … for one with right freedom, monks, wrong freedom is worn out. And those many evil unskillful qualities that arise due to wrong freedom are worn out for him. And due to right freedom many skillful qualities reach fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:36: Thus, monks, there are twenty aspects of wholesome, twenty aspects of unwholesome—the great forty is a discourse on phenomena that cannot be overturned by a monk or a brahmin or a god or Māra or a brahmā or anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: There, monks, right view is the forerunner. And how, monks, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong view as ‘wrong view,’ he understands right view as ‘right view’—that is his right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, monks, is wrong view? ‘There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are no in the world monks or brahmins who are perfectly enlightened, who have perfectly practiced, who directly know and realize this world and the other world for themselves’—this, monks, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, monks, is right view? Right view, monks, I say, is of two kinds: there is, monks, right view that is with taints, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth; there is, monks, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, monks, is right view that is with taints, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth? ‘There is giving, there is offering, there is sacrifice; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is an other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world monks or brahmins who are perfectly enlightened, who have perfectly practiced, who directly know and realize this world and the other world for themselves’—this, monks, is right view that is with taints, conducive to merit, resulting in rebirth.
translations.mn117:8: And what, monks, is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? That wisdom, monks, wisdom faculty, wisdom power, investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, right view path factor, which is developed and cultivated in the noble one’s mind that is taintless, in one developing and cultivating the noble path— this is called, monks, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: He makes effort for the abandoning of wrong view, for the undertaking of right view—that is his right effort. Mindful, he abandons wrong view, mindful, he enters upon and dwells in right view—that is his right mindfulness. These three phenomena revolve around and turn around right view, namely—right view, right effort, right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in Migāra’s Mother’s mansion, together with many well-known elder disciples—together with the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, the Venerable Mahākappina, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ānanda, and other well-known elder disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, monks, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit, of great benefit. Mindfulness of breathing, monks, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness. The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. The seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, monks, a monk, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, establishing mindfulness in front. Mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, he knows: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he knows: ‘I breathe out long’; or breathing in short, he knows: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he knows: ‘I breathe out short.’ He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the whole body,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the whole body’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in calming the bodily formation,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out calming the bodily formation.
translations.mn118:19: He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to rapture,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to rapture’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to pleasure,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to pleasure’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to mental formations,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to mental formations’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in calming the mental formations,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out calming the mental formations.
translations.mn118:2: At that time the elder monks were advising and instructing the new monks. Some elder monks were advising and instructing ten monks, some elder monks twenty monks, some elder monks thirty monks, some elder monks forty monks. And these new monks, being advised and instructed by the elder monks, realized a superior distinction to what they had realized before.
translations.mn118:20: He trains: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the mind,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the mind’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in gladdening the mind,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out gladdening the mind’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in concentrating the mind,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out concentrating the mind’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in liberating the mind,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out liberating the mind.
translations.mn118:21: He trains: ‘I will breathe in contemplating impermanence,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out contemplating impermanence’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in contemplating fading away,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out contemplating fading away’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in contemplating cessation,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out contemplating cessation’; he trains: ‘I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment,’ he trains: ‘I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment.
translations.mn118:23: And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: When a monk, breathing in long, knows: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, knows: ‘I breathe out long’; breathing in short, knows: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, knows: ‘I breathe out short’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the whole body’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the whole body’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in calming the bodily formation’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out calming the bodily formation’—at that time, monks, a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. ‘One thing in the body I say, monks, namely, in-breathings and out-breathings.’ Therefore, monks, at that time a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:25: When a monk trains himself: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to rapture’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to rapture’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to pleasure’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to pleasure’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to mental formations’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to mental formations’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in calming the mental formations’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out calming the mental formations’—at that time, monks, a monk abides contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. ‘One thing in feelings I say, monks, namely, close attention to in-breathings and out-breathings.’ Therefore, monks, at that time a monk abides contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:26: When a monk trains himself: ‘I will breathe in sensitive to the mind’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out sensitive to the mind’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in gladdening the mind’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out gladdening the mind’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in concentrating the mind’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out concentrating the mind’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out liberating the mind’—at that time, monks, a monk abides contemplating the mind as mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. ‘I do not say mindfulness of breathing for one who is forgetful and not clearly comprehending.’ Therefore, monks, at that time a monk abides contemplating the mind as mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:27: When a monk trains himself: ‘I will breathe in contemplating impermanence’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out contemplating impermanence’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in contemplating fading away’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out contemplating fading away’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in contemplating cessation’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out contemplating cessation’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains himself: ‘I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment’—at that time, monks, a monk abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. He, having seen with wisdom the abandoning of covetousness and displeasure, closely watches. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:28: Thus developed and much practiced, monks, mindfulness of breathing fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: And how developed and much practiced, monks, do the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
translations.mn118:3: At that time the Blessed One was seated in the open air, surrounded by the monastic community, on the night of the fifteenth day of the fortnight with the moon at the full on the invitation day of the posatha. Then the Blessed One, having looked around at the silent monastic community, addressed the monks:
translations.mn118:30: When a monk abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world, at that time his mindfulness is established and not confused. When a monk’s mindfulness is established and not confused, at that time his mindfulness enlightenment factor is stirred up. At that time he develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor, and the mindfulness enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:31: Dwelling thus mindful, he properly investigates that dhamma with wisdom, scrutinizes it, makes a thorough examination. When a monk dwelling thus mindful properly investigates that dhamma with wisdom, scrutinizes it, makes a thorough examination, at that time his investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor is stirred up. At that time he develops the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor, and the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:33: When energy is stirred up, rapture free from taints arises. When rapture free from taints arises for a monk with aroused energy, at that time his rapture enlightenment factor is stirred up. At that time he develops the rapture enlightenment factor, and the rapture enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:34: When one is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil. When for a monk who is rapturous the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil, at that time his tranquility enlightenment factor is stirred up. At that time he develops the tranquility enlightenment factor, and the tranquility enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:35: For one whose body is tranquil and who feels pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated. When for a monk whose body is tranquil and who feels pleasure the mind becomes concentrated, at that time his concentration enlightenment factor is stirred up. At that time he develops the concentration enlightenment factor, and the concentration enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:36: His mind, thus concentrated, is well equanimous. Bhikkhus, whenever a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated and well equanimous, at that time the equanimity enlightenment factor is stirred up in him, at that time he develops the equanimity enlightenment factor, at that time the equanimity enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment for him by development.
translations.mn118:4: ‘Bhikkhus, I have made an effort in this practice; bhikkhus, my mind is devoted to this practice. Therefore, bhikkhus, make even more effort for the attainment of the unattained, the realization of the unrealized, the realization by direct knowledge of the un-realized-by-direct-knowledge. Right here in Sāvatthī I will enter a four-month rains residence of delighting.’
translations.mn118:40: Bhikkhus, when the four establishments of mindfulness are developed in this way and cultivated in this way, they fulfill the seven enlightenment factors.
translations.mn118:41: And how, bhikkhus, when the seven enlightenment factors are developed and cultivated, do they fulfill true knowledge and release?
translations.mn118:6: And those elder bhikkhus instruct and advise the new bhikkhus even more. Some elder bhikkhus instruct and advise ten bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus instruct and advise twenty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus instruct and advise thirty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus instruct and advise forty bhikkhus. And those new bhikkhus, being instructed and advised by the elder bhikkhus, realize a superior distinction after what was previously realized.
translations.mn118:9: Bhikkhus, there are in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus arahants whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetter of rebirth, and who are rightly freed with perfect gnosis—such bhikkhus exist in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
translations.mn11:13: Bhikkhus, in such a teaching and discipline, confidence in the Teacher is not declared to be well-placed; confidence in the teaching is not declared to be well-placed; fulfillment of ethics is not declared to be well-placed; affection for one’s co-religionists is not declared to be well-placed. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, it is just so in a teaching and discipline that is poorly proclaimed, poorly expounded, not leading onwards, not conducive to peace, not leading to Nibbāna, not proclaimed by one supremely enlightened.
translations.mn11:14: Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata— the arahant, perfectly enlightened one—declaring himself as one who proclaims the full understanding of all clinging, rightly proclaims the full understanding of all clinging: he proclaims the full understanding of sense-pleasure clinging, the full understanding of view clinging, the full understanding of rule-and-rite clinging, the full understanding of self-doctrine clinging.
translations.mn11:15: Bhikkhus, in such a teaching and discipline, confidence in the Teacher is declared to be well-placed; confidence in the teaching is declared to be well-placed; fulfillment of ethics is declared to be well-placed; affection for one’s co-religionists is declared to be well-placed. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, it is just so in a teaching and discipline that is well proclaimed, well expounded, leading onwards, conducive to peace, leading to Nibbāna, proclaimed by one supremely enlightened.
translations.mn11:2: ‘Here, bhikkhus, a contemplative, here a second contemplative, here a third contemplative, here a fourth contemplative; empty are the rejections of others by contemplatives.’ Bhikkhus, roar this lion’s roar rightly in that way.
translations.mn11:6: Bhikkhus, there are these two views: the view of being and the view of non-being. Bhikkhus, any contemplatives or brahmins who are devoted to the view of being, who have taken up that view, who are committed to that view, are opposed to the view of non-being. Bhikkhus, any contemplatives or brahmins who are devoted to the view of non-being, who have taken up that view, who are committed to that view, are opposed to the view of being.
translations.mn11:7: Bhikkhus, any contemplatives or brahmins who do not truly understand, as they really are, the origin and the passing away, the gratification and the danger, and the escape in the case of these two views, they are lustful, they are hateful, they are deluded, they have thirst, they have clinging, they are unseeing, they are devoted to opposing views, they delight in proliferation, they are proliferators; they do not escape from birth, from old age, from death, from sorrow, from lamentation, from pain, from grief, from despair; they do not escape from suffering, I say.
translations.mn11:9: Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clinging. What four? Sense-pleasure clinging, view clinging, rule-and-rite clinging, self-doctrine clinging.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Vesālī in the Great Forest, in the hall with the peaked roof.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as they really are what is possible and what is impossible. And that the Tathāgata understands as they really are what is possible and what is impossible—this too is a Tathāgata’s power by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the bull’s position, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:19: Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the destruction of the taints the Tathāgata lives having realized in this very life, by his own direct knowledge, the taintless freedom of mind, freedom through wisdom. And that the Tathāgata lives having realized in this very life, by his own direct knowledge, the taintless freedom of mind, freedom through wisdom—this too is a Tathāgata’s power by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the bull’s position, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:2: Now on that occasion Sunakkhatta, the Licchavi son, had recently left this teaching and discipline. In an assembly at Vesālī he was speaking this statement: ‘There is nothing in the ascetic Gotama’s doctrine and discipline that is a superhuman state, a state of superior knowledge and vision. The ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hemmed in by reasoning, trifling, and witty, and he has thought it up himself. And for whatever purpose he has taught the doctrine, that purpose is not realized by reasoning rightly for the complete destruction of suffering.’
translations.mn12:20: Sāriputta, these ten powers of a Tathāgata, with which the Tathāgata is endowed, by virtue of which he claims the bull’s position, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:22: Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata, with which the Tathāgata is endowed, by virtue of which he claims the bull’s position, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the holy wheel. What are the four?
translations.mn12:23: ‘These phenomena are not fully awakened to for one who claims to be a perfectly enlightened Buddha.’ Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for thinking that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could reasonably reproach me on this account. Sāriputta, not seeing any ground for reproach, I abide having attained safety, security, and fearlessness.
translations.mn12:24: ‘These taints are not extinguished for one who claims to have destroyed the taints.’ Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for thinking that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could reasonably reproach me on this account. Sāriputta, not seeing any ground for reproach, I abide having attained safety, security, and fearlessness.
translations.mn12:25: ‘Those obstructive phenomena that were spoken of are not sufficient for obstruction when practiced.’ Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for thinking that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could reasonably reproach me on this account. Sāriputta, not seeing any ground for reproach, I abide having attained safety, security, and fearlessness.
translations.mn12:26: ‘That for which the teaching was taught by you does not lead out, for one who practices it, to complete extinguishing of suffering.’ Sāriputta, I do not see any ground for thinking that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could reasonably reproach me on this account. Sāriputta, not seeing any ground for reproach, I abide having attained safety, security, and fearlessness.
translations.mn12:32: Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of birth. What four? Egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneous.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born? Sāriputta, those beings born by breaking open an egg-shell—this is called egg-born. And what, Sāriputta, is womb-born? Sāriputta, those beings born by breaking open a womb-shell—this is called womb-born. And what, Sāriputta, is moisture-born? Sāriputta, those beings born in putrid fish, or in putrid corpses, or in putrid dough, or in a midden—this is called moisture-born. And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous? Gods, denizens of hell, some humans, and some in the lower realms—this is called spontaneous. Sāriputta, these are the four kinds of birth.
translations.mn12:35: Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the domain of ghosts, humanity, gods.
translations.mn12:36: Sāriputta, I know hell, the path leading to hell, the practice leading to hell; and how one who practices thus, at the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of woe, in an inferior realm, a hell—this too I know. Sāriputta, I know the animal realm, the path leading to the animal realm, the practice leading to the animal realm; and how one who practices thus, at the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the animal realm—this too I know. Sāriputta, I know the domain of ghosts, the path leading to the domain of ghosts, the practice leading to the domain of ghosts; and how one who practices thus, at the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the domain of ghosts—this too I know. Sāriputta, I know humanity, the path leading to the human world, the practice leading to the human world; and how one who practices thus, at the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn among humans—this too I know. Sāriputta, I know the gods, the path leading to the divine world, the practice leading to the divine world; and how one who practices thus, at the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a fortunate destiny, in the heavenly world—this too I know. Sāriputta, I know Nibbāna, the path leading to Nibbāna, the practice leading to Nibbāna; and how one who practices thus, with the destruction of the taints, attains the taintless freedom of mind, freedom through wisdom, in this very life, by direct knowledge, realizing it for himself—this too I know.
translations.mn12:4: “Sāriputta, this Sunakkhatta the Licchāvin is an angry man, a worthless man. And this speech of his was spoken in anger. Sāriputta, this Sunakkhatta the worthless man, thinking ‘I will speak dispraise,’ speaks only praise of the Tathāgata. Sāriputta, this is praise of the Tathāgata, who would say: ‘That for which the teaching was taught by him leads out, for one who practices it, to complete extinguishing of suffering.’
translations.mn12:43: Sāriputta, whoever would say of me, knowing thus, seeing thus: ‘There is nothing beyond human states for the ascetic Gotama, no superhuman distinction of knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches a teaching hammered out by reasoning, following investigation, following his own fancy’—Sāriputta, not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that thought, not relinquishing that view, just as thrown there, he is thrown into hell. Sāriputta, just as a monk endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, endowed with wisdom would realize the unconditioned in this very life—so too, Sāriputta, I say, not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that thought, not relinquishing that view, just as thrown there, he is thrown into hell.
translations.mn12:44: Sāriputta, I recall living the holy life endowed with four factors—I was one who practiced asceticism, indeed extreme asceticism; lean, indeed extremely lean; one who eats little, indeed an extreme eater of little; withdrawn, indeed extremely withdrawn.
translations.mn12:46: Sāriputta, this is what emaciation was for me—dirt and dust accumulated on the body for less than a week, naturally formed. Sāriputta, just as the dust on a plasterer's trowel accumulates for less than a week, naturally formed—so too, Sāriputta, dirt and dust accumulated on my body for less than a week, naturally formed. Sāriputta, it did not occur to me: ‘Oh, may I rub this dirt and dust with my hand, or may others rub this dirt and dust on my body with their hands.’ Sāriputta, it did not even occur to me thus. Sāriputta, this is what emaciation was for me.
translations.mn12:47: Sāriputta, this is what eating little was for me—I walked mindfully forward, mindfully back, even compassion arose for a drop of water: ‘May I not cause harm to a tiny creature on uneven ground.’ Sāriputta, this is what eating little was for me.
translations.mn12:49: Just so, Sāriputta, those herds of cattle that were established but without a cowherd, there I approached as a quadruped and ate the dung of those young calves, suckling cows. And as long as my own dung and urine were undigested, Sāriputta, I ate just my own dung and urine. This, Sāriputta, was my great feasting.
translations.mn12:5: For this Sunakkhatta, the foolish man, will not have any regard for me with the thought: ‘That Blessed One is accomplished, a fully awakened one, consummate in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed trainer of tamable people, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’
translations.mn12:50: Just so, Sāriputta, I dwelt having entered a certain terrifying forest thicket. And there, Sāriputta, of that terrifying forest thicket it was terrifying—for anyone with lust who enters that forest thicket, their hair usually stands on end. Just so, Sāriputta, on those cold winter nights with snowfall, on such nights I dwelt in the open air at night, in the forest thicket by day; in the last months of summer, by day in the open air, at night in the forest thicket. And this verse, previously unheard by me, occurred to me unawares, Sāriputta: ‘Soaked with sweat, parched too, alone in a terrifying forest; naked, not eating fire, a sage free from craving.’
translations.mn12:51: Just so, Sāriputta, I made my bed in a charnel ground, supporting myself on my elbows. And villagers approached me, Sāriputta, some throwing sticks, some throwing cow dung, some throwing dirt, even inserting a stick into my ears. But I do not recall, Sāriputta, generating any evil intention toward them. This, Sāriputta, was my abiding in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Purification is by food.’ They say: ‘We will subsist on beans.’ They eat beans, bean powder, drink bean water—they consume various bean preparations. But I recall, Sāriputta, having subsisted on a single bean. And it might occur to you, Sāriputta: ‘Surely at that time there was a great bean.’ But, Sāriputta, it should not be seen like this. Even then there was just this much bean as there is now. While I subsisted on a single bean for my food, Sāriputta, my body reached an extreme emaciation. Just as the bones of an eighty-year-old or black bamboo; so were my limbs in every regard due to that food. Just as an antelope’s hoof; so was my hip due to that food. Just as a coiled rope; so was my backbone protruding due to that food. Just as the eaves of a roof with holes and gaps; so were my ribs due to that food. Just as the trunk of a young palm tree appears deep-set and hollow in a deep water jar; so did my eye sockets appear deep-set and hollow due to that food. Just as a ripe bitter gourd, cut open, shriveled by wind and sun, withered; so was my scalp shriveled and withered due to that food. Just so, Sāriputta, thinking ‘I will rub my belly skin,’ I just grasped my backbone; thinking ‘I will rub my backbone,’ I just grasped my belly skin—as long as, Sāriputta, my belly skin clung to my backbone due to that food. Just so, Sāriputta, thinking ‘I will defecate or urinate,’ I just fell down right there due to that food. Just so, Sāriputta, massaging that body with my hand, I stroked my limbs. While I stroked my limbs with my hand, Sāriputta, the hair roots, rotten, fell out from my body due to that food.
translations.mn12:56: Yet even by that behavior, that practice, that superhuman austerity, I did not attain any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why is that? Because it was unachieved by this noble wisdom by which the noble ones have achieved noble wisdom that leads out, leading one who acts in accordance with it to the complete end of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Purification is by wandering on in saṁsāra.’ But, Sāriputta, that saṁsāra is not easy, which I had not previously wandered on for this long time, except among the gods of the pure abodes. And if I were to wander on among the gods of the pure abodes, Sāriputta, I would not return to this world.
translations.mn12:6: For this Sunakkhatta, the foolish man, will not have any regard for me with the thought: ‘That Blessed One wields various kinds of psychic power: having been one he becomes many, having been many he becomes one; he is visible and invisible; he goes unhindered through walls, ramparts, and mountains as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without sinking as if it were earth; seated cross-legged he travels in space like a winged bird; even this moon and sun, so powerful, so mighty, he touches and strokes with his hand; even as far as the brahmā world he wields power with his body.’
translations.mn12:60: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Purification is by sacrifice.’ But, Sāriputta, that sacrifice is not easy, which I had not previously offered for this long time, and that by a king or a wealthy noble with oiled hair, or by a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:61: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Purification is by attending to fire.’ But, Sāriputta, that fire is not easy, which I had not previously attended for this long time, and that by a king or a wealthy noble with oiled hair, or by a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:62: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who have such a doctrine, such a view: ‘As long as this man is young, a youth with black hair, endowed with beauty and the prime of life, in the first stage of life, for so long he is endowed with the highest wisdom and ingenuity. But when this man has become old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, reached the age of decline, eighty years or ninety years or a hundred years of age, then that wisdom and ingenuity declines.’ This should not be seen like this, Sāriputta. Now I, Sāriputta, am old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, reached the age of decline; my age is eighty. Suppose, Sāriputta, I had four pupils with a lifespan of a hundred years, living a hundred years, endowed with supreme mindfulness, movement, and resolution, and with the highest wisdom and ingenuity. Just as, Sāriputta, a trained archer, an expert bowman, skilled in hand, an expert marksman, would shoot an arrow across through the crown of a palm tree with a light arrow and little effort, so too these endowed with supreme mindfulness, supreme movement, supreme resolution, and the highest wisdom and ingenuity. They would question me depending on and taking hold of the four establishments of mindfulness, and when questioned, I would answer them; and they would retain what I had explained after it was explained, and they would not question me a second time or beyond. Apart from what has been eaten, drunk, consumed, tasted, apart from excrement and urine, apart from spitting and vomiting, the Tathāgata’s teaching would not be burdensome, Sāriputta; the Tathāgata’s words and syllables would not be burdensome; the Tathāgata’s response to questions would not be burdensome. Then those four pupils with a lifespan of a hundred years, living a hundred years, would pass away after a hundred years. Even if you were to carry me around on a bier, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata’s wisdom and ingenuity would not become otherwise.
translations.mn12:7: For this too, Sāriputta, regarding me the foolish man Sunakkhatta will have no true comprehension of the Dhamma: ‘The Blessed One also hears sounds with the divine ear-element, purified, transcending the human, both divine and human sounds, whether far or near.’
translations.mn12:8: For this too, Sāriputta, regarding me the foolish man Sunakkhatta will have no true comprehension of the Dhamma: ‘The Blessed One also knows the minds of other beings, other persons with his own mind thus: a mind with lust as “a mind with lust,” or a mind without lust as “a mind without lust”; a mind with hatred as “a mind with hatred,” or a mind without hatred as “a mind without hatred”; a mind with delusion as “a mind with delusion,” or a mind without delusion as “a mind without delusion”; a contracted mind as “a contracted mind,” or a distracted mind as “a distracted mind”; an expanded mind as “an expanded mind,” or an unexpanded mind as “an unexpanded mind”; an inferior mind as “an inferior mind,” or an unequaled mind as “an unequaled mind”; a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind,” or an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind”; a liberated mind as “a liberated mind,” or an unliberated mind as “an unliberated mind.”’
translations.mn12:9: These ten, Sāriputta, are the Tathāgata’s powers with which the Tathāgata is endowed; with these powers the Tathāgata claims the bull’s position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, sets in motion the wheel of the teaching. Which ten?
