translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, young man, a certain woman or man is a non-giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes and creams, beddings, dwellings, lights. By that deed, completed in that way, undertaken in that way, after the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. If he does not, after the breakup of the body, after death, get reborn in a plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell, and if he comes to humanity, wherever he is reborn, he is of few enjoyments. This is a path leading to few enjoyments, young man, that is, not being a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes and creams, beddings, dwellings, lights.
translations.mn135:2: Then the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, went to the Blessed One; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their deeds, young man, heirs of their deeds, born of their deeds, related through their deeds, have their deeds as their refuge. It is their deeds that divide beings in terms of inferiority and superiority.
translations.mn135:3: “Now what is the cause, what is the reason, good Gotama, by which among human beings who are human beings, there is seen inferiority and superiority? For human beings are seen with short lifespans, good Gotama, human beings are seen with long lifespans; human beings are seen afflicted with many diseases, human beings are seen unafflicted with diseases; human beings are seen ugly, human beings are seen beautiful; human beings are seen of low birth, human beings are seen of high birth; human beings are seen with few enjoyments, human beings are seen with great enjoyments; human beings are seen born in low families, human beings are seen born in high families; human beings are seen stupid, human beings are seen wise. Now what is the cause, what is the reason, good Gotama, by which among human beings who are human beings, there is seen inferiority and superiority?”
translations.mn135:4: “Beings are owners of their deeds, young man, heirs of their deeds, born of their deeds, related through their deeds, have their deeds as their refuge. It is their deeds that divide beings in terms of inferiority and superiority.” “I do not understand in detail the meaning of this brief statement of the good Gotama which has not been elaborated. It would be good if the good Gotama would teach the Dhamma to me in such a way that I would understand in detail the meaning of this brief statement of the good Gotama which has not been elaborated.” “Very well then, young man, listen, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn135:5: “Here, young man, some woman or man is one who kills living beings, a hunter, blood-handed, devoted to killing and slaying, merciless toward living beings. By that deed, so made, so undertaken, after the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, downfall. If not, after the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, downfall, but if they come to humanity, wherever they are reborn, they have a short life. This, young man, is the course of action that leads to a short life: they are one who kills living beings, a hunter, blood-handed, devoted to killing and slaying, merciless toward living beings.
translations.mn135:6: But here, young man, some woman or man, having abstained from killing living beings, abstains from killing living beings, one who has laid down the rod, laid down the weapon, is ashamed, merciful, compassionate toward the welfare of all living beings, dwells thus. By that deed, so made, so undertaken, after the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. If not, after the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, but if they come to humanity, wherever they are reborn, they have a long life. This, young man, is the course of action that leads to a long life: having abstained from killing living beings, abstains from killing living beings, one who has laid down the rod, laid down the weapon, is ashamed, merciful, compassionate toward the welfare of all living beings, dwells thus.
translations.mn13:10: If those possessions arise for that clansman as he strives and makes effort, he experiences suffering and displeasure due to guarding and protecting those possessions: ‘How could kings or rulers take away my possessions, thieves take them, fire burn them, water carry them away, unloved heirs take them?’ When guarded and protected in this way, those possessions are taken by kings or rulers, or by thieves, or fire burns them, or water carries them away, or unloved heirs take them. He grieves, laments, beats his breast, weeps with arms waving, falls into bewilderment: ‘What I had is no more.’ This too, monks, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:11: Furthermore, monks, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, even kings quarrel with kings, khattiyas with khattiyas, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders, a mother quarrels with her son, a son with his mother, a father with his son, a son with his father, a brother with a brother, a brother with a sister, a sister with a brother, a friend with a friend. Involved in disputes, quarrels, and strife there, they attack each other with fists, clods, sticks, and weapons. There they go to death, and death itself is suffering. This too, monks, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:12: Furthermore, monks, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, taking up sword and shield, stringing the quiver, they enter battle fully armed, where arrows are swiftly shot, spears are swiftly thrown, swords flash. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, heads cut off by swords. There they go to death, and death itself is suffering. This too, monks, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:13: Furthermore, monks, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, taking up sword and shield, stringing the quiver, as mercenaries smeared with fresh blood, they enter where arrows are swiftly shot, spears are swiftly thrown, swords flash. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, drenched with molten metal, trampled under elephants’ feet, heads cut off by swords. There they go to death, and death itself is suffering. This too, monks, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:15: Furthermore, monks, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, they engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, misconduct by mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, misconduct by mind, after the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, downfall. This too, monks, is a danger in sensual pleasures in the future life, a mass of suffering, originating from sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, due to sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:16: And what, monks, is the escape from sensual pleasures? The removal of desire and lust for sensual pleasures, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: For those monks, ascetics or brahmins who do not truly understand as they are the pleasure in sensual pleasures and the danger and the escape from them, could they understand sensual pleasures themselves or exhort another to that understanding so that one practicing thus would understand sensual pleasures?—no, that is not possible. But for those monks, ascetics or brahmins who truly understand as they are the pleasure in sensual pleasures and the danger and the escape from them, they could understand sensual pleasures themselves or exhort another to that understanding so that one practicing thus would understand sensual pleasures—that is possible.
translations.mn13:18: And what, monks, is the pleasure in forms? Just as, monks, a noble maiden, or a brahmin maiden, or a householder maiden, around fifteen or sixteen years old, not too tall, not too short, not too thin, not too fat, not too dark, not too fair—at that time, monks, what is the finest complexion? ‘It is the beautiful complexion, venerable sir.’ That pleasure and joy that arises dependent on that beautiful complexion—this is the pleasure in forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, monks, is the danger in forms? Here, monks, he might see that same sister at a later time, eighty years old or ninety or a hundred years old by birth, aged, bent like a roof bracket, leaning on a stick, tottering as she goes, afflicted, past her prime, with broken teeth, gray-haired, with wrinkled skin, blotchy, her body mottled with spots. What do you think, monks, that former beautiful appearance has vanished, danger has appeared, hasn’t it? ‘Yes, lord.’ This too, monks, is a danger in forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then many monks, having dressed in the morning, taking their bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then those monks thought: ‘It’s too late now to go for alms in Sāvatthī. Why don’t we go to the park of wanderers of other sects?’ Then those monks went to the park of wanderers of other sects. Having gone, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. Having exchanged greetings consisting of polite conversation, they sat down to one side. As they sat to one side, those wanderers of other sects said this to those monks:
translations.mn13:20: Furthermore, monks, he might see that same sister afflicted with disease, suffering, gravely ill, smeared with her own urine and excrement, being lifted up by some, being laid down by others. What do you think, monks, that former beautiful appearance has vanished, danger has appeared, hasn’t it? ‘Yes, lord.’ This too, monks, is a danger in forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Furthermore, monks, he might see that same sister’s body discarded in a charnel ground— a skeleton with flesh and blood held together by sinews; a skeleton smeared with flesh and blood held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh and blood held together by sinews; bones disconnected in different directions— one hand bone here, one foot bone there, one shin bone here, one thigh bone there, one hip bone here, one backbone there, one rib bone here, one breast bone there, one shoulder bone here, one neck bone there, one jaw bone here, one tooth bone there, one skull here. What do you think, monks, that former beautiful appearance has vanished, danger has appeared, hasn’t it? ‘Yes, lord.’ This too, monks, is a danger in forms.
translations.mn13:29: Furthermore, monks, he might see that same sister’s body discarded in a charnel ground— bones bleached white like the color of a conch shell; bones heaped up, more than a year old; bones rotted and crumbled to powder. What do you think, monks, that former beautiful appearance has vanished, danger has appeared, hasn’t it? ‘Yes, lord.’ This too, monks, is a danger in forms.
translations.mn13:3: ‘The ascetic Gotama declares the full understanding of sensual pleasures, let us too declare the full understanding of sensual pleasures; the ascetic Gotama declares the full understanding of forms, let us too declare the full understanding of forms; the ascetic Gotama declares the full understanding of feelings, let us too declare the full understanding of feelings. So what is the difference, what is the distinction, what is the reason for diversity between the ascetic Gotama on the one hand and us on the other—namely, in teaching the Dhamma or in instructing?’
translations.mn13:30: And what, monks, is the escape from forms? The removal of lust and desire for forms, the abandoning of lust and desire—this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, monks, is the gratification in feelings? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. At the time, monks, a monk enters and remains in the first jhāna, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, at that time he does not intend harm for himself, nor for others, nor for both; he feels only feelings that are without harm. The highest gratification in feelings, monks, I declare to be without harm.
translations.mn13:36: And what, monks, is the danger in feelings? That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, monks, is the escape from feelings? The removal of lust and desire for feelings, the abandoning of lust and desire—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those monks neither approved nor rejected what those wanderers of other sects had said. Without approving or rejecting, they got up from their seats and left: ‘We will understand the meaning of this statement in the Blessed One’s presence.’
translations.mn13:6: ‘Monks, those wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed as follows: “But what, friends, is the gratification in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in forms, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in feelings, what is the danger, what is the escape?”’ When thus questioned, monks, the wanderers of other sects will not succeed and will meet with vexation beyond. Why is that? Because it is outside their domain, monks. I do not see anyone in this world with its gods, māras, and brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them here.
translations.mn13:8: And what, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures? Here, monks, a clansman earns a living by some craft—whether by basket-weaving, or accountancy, or computation, or farming, or trade, or cattle-herding, or archery, or as a royal officer, or by some other craft—exposed to cold, exposed to heat, exposed to the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and reptiles, tormented by hunger and thirst. This too, monks, is a danger in sensual pleasures visible here and now, a mass of suffering caused and originated by sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, a danger rooted in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:9: If those possessions do not come to fruition for that clansman as he strives and exerts himself in this way, he sorrows and grieves and laments, weeps beating his breast, and falls into bewilderment: ‘My striving was in vain, my effort was fruitless.’ This too, monks, is a danger in sensual pleasures visible here and now, a mass of suffering caused and originated by sensual pleasures, grounded in sensual pleasures, a danger rooted in sensual pleasures.
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadhan country and eventually arrived at Rājagaha. He went to the potter Bhaggava and said to him:
translations.mn140:12: ‘One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve the truth, should be devoted to relinquishment, should train in peace’—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, monk, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal earth element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is solid and clung to—this is called the internal earth element: head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, contents of the stomach, feces, or whatever other internally, belonging to oneself, is solid and clung to. This is called the internal earth element. Now both the internal earth element and the external earth element are just the earth element. One should see it thus as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, monk, is the water element? The water element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal water element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water and clung to—such as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil, urine, or whatever other internally, belonging to oneself, is water and clung to. This is called the internal water element. Now both the internal water element and the external water element are just the water element. One should see it thus as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, monk, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal fire element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire and clung to—by which one is warmed, by which one ages, by which one burns, by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted properly digests, or whatever other internally, belonging to oneself, is fire and clung to. This is called the internal fire element. Now both the internal fire element and the external fire element are just the fire element. One should see it thus as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, monk, is the wind element? The wind element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal wind element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is wind and clung to—such as up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-and-out breath, or whatever other internally, belonging to oneself, is wind and clung to. This is called the internal wind element. Now both the internal wind element and the external wind element are just the wind element. One should see it thus as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the wind element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the wind element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, monk, is the space element? The space element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal space element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is space and clung to—such as the hole of the ear, the hole of the nose, the hole of the mouth, by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted passes in, where what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted remains, by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted passes out below, or whatever other internally, belonging to oneself, is space, space-pervaded, cavity, cavity-pervaded, open, open-pervaded, unobstructed by flesh and blood, and clung to. This is called the internal space element. Now both the internal space element and the external space element are just the space element. One should see it thus as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the space element.
translations.mn140:2: ‘If you don’t mind, Bhaggava, let us stay in your workshop just one night.’ ‘I don’t mind, venerable sir. But there is a monk who arrived here first for lodging. If he gives permission, venerable sir, stay as you like.’
translations.mn140:20: And then only equanimity remains, pure, thoroughly purified, malleable, workable, and radiant. Just as, monk, a skilled goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice would take up a crucible, having taken up the crucible he would heat the crucible mouth, having heated the crucible mouth he would take pure gold with tongs and put it into the crucible mouth, he would blow on it from time to time, sprinkle it with water from time to time, and watch over it from time to time; that pure gold becomes thoroughly worked, well-worked, fully worked, malleable, workable, and radiant, and whatever ornament he wishes to make with it—whether a foil-ornament, earrings, a necklace, or a gold chain—he obtains his purpose thereby. In the same way, monk, and then only equanimity remains, pure, thoroughly purified, malleable, workable, and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: When he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to,’ he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ When he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to,’ he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ When he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to,’ he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’
translations.mn140:29: ‘One should not neglect wisdom, one should preserve the truth, one should speak in praise of relinquishment, one should train in peace’—whatever is stated, that is stated on account of this.
translations.mn140:3: At that time a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the house-life into homelessness out of faith in the Blessed One. He had first arrived at that potter’s hut for residence. Then the Blessed One approached the venerable Pukkusāti; having approached, he said to the venerable Pukkusāti: ‘Monk, if you have no objection, let us stay the night in this potter’s hut.’ ‘The potter’s hut is wide open, friend. Venerable sir, stay as is comfortable for you.’
translations.mn140:30: ‘Where it stands, conceiving does not proceed, and when conceiving does not proceed, the sage is called peaceful’—thus it is said. On account of what is this stated?
translations.mn140:31: ‘I am,’ monk, this is a conceiving; ‘This I am,’ this is a conceiving; ‘I will be,’ this is a conceiving; ‘I will not be,’ this is a conceiving; ‘I will be with form,’ this is a conceiving; ‘I will be formless,’ this is a conceiving; ‘I will be with perception,’ this is a conceiving; ‘I will be without perception,’ this is a conceiving; ‘I will be neither-with-perception-nor-without-perception,’ this is a conceiving. Conceiving, monk, is a disease; conceiving is a boil; conceiving is a dart. But by overcoming all conceivings, monk, the sage is called peaceful. And the peaceful sage, monk, is not born, does not age, does not die, is not shaken, does not yearn. For him, monk, there is nothing on account of which he would be born; not being born, how will he age? Not aging, how will he die? Not dying, how will he be shaken? Not being shaken, for what will he yearn?
translations.mn140:32: ‘Where it stands, conceiving does not proceed, and when conceiving does not proceed, the sage is called peaceful’—whatever is stated, that is stated on account of this. ‘You should bear in mind, monk, this brief analysis of the six elements that I have given you.’
translations.mn140:33: Then the venerable Pukkusāti thought: ‘My teacher has arrived, the Auspicious One has arrived, the Perfectly Enlightened One has arrived.’ Rising from his seat, arranging his robe over one shoulder, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said to the Blessed One: ‘A transgression has overcome me, venerable sir, as a fool, as one bewildered, as an unskilled person, in that I supposed that the Blessed One should be addressed with “friend.” May the Blessed One forgive me that transgression for the sake of restraint in the future.’ ‘Indeed, monk, a transgression has overcome you as a fool, as one bewildered, as an unskilled person, in that you supposed that I should be addressed with “friend.” And since you, monk, see the transgression as a transgression and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we forgive you. This, monk, is the way of growth in the noble discipline: seeing a transgression as a transgression, making amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and coming to restraint in the future.’
translations.mn140:34: ‘May I receive the upasampada ordination in the presence of the Blessed One, venerable sir.’ ‘But is your bowl and robe complete, monk?’ ‘My bowl and robe are not complete, venerable sir.’ ‘Tathāgatas do not give the upasampada ordination to one with incomplete bowl and robe.’
translations.mn140:35: Then the venerable Pukkusāti, having rejoiced in and approved of the Blessed One’s words, rising from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, walked around him keeping him to his right, and set out in search of bowl and robe. Then while the venerable Pukkusāti was searching for bowl and robe, a cow with a calf killed him.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Blessed One entered the potter’s hut, set out a grass mat on one side, sat down folding his legs crosswise, holding his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then the Blessed One spent much of the night sitting in meditation. The venerable Pukkusāti also spent much of the night sitting in meditation. Then this thought arose in the Blessed One: ‘This clansman conducts himself in a pleasing manner. What if I were to question him?’ Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: ‘For whom did you go forth, monk? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve?’ ‘There is, friend, the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans, gone forth from the Sakyan clan. And of that Blessed One Gotama this fine report has spread: “This Blessed One is an Arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, incomparable trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.” I went forth on account of that Blessed One. He is my teacher, and I approve of that Blessed One’s Dhamma.’ ‘But where, monk, does that Blessed One, the Arahant, perfectly enlightened, now dwell?’ ‘There is, friend, a city in the northern country called Sāvatthī. There that Blessed One now dwells, the Arahant, perfectly enlightened.’ ‘But have you seen that Blessed One before, monk? And if you saw him, would you know him?’ ‘I have not seen that Blessed One before, friend, and if I saw him I would not know him.’
translations.mn140:6: Then the Blessed One thought: “This clansman has gone forth in dependence on me. What if I were to teach him the Dhamma?” Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Pukkusāti: “Bhikkhu, I will teach you the Dhamma. Listen to it, pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” Venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn140:7: ‘This man, bhikkhu, is six elements, six spheres of contact, eighteen explorations of mind, four stations; standing therein, conceivings do not proliferate, and when conceivings do not proliferate, the monk is called serene. He should not neglect wisdom, he should preserve the truth, he should develop relinquishment, he should train in serenity’—this is the summary of the analysis of the elements.
translations.mn146:12: Sisters, this is a simile made by me for the explanation of the meaning. Sisters, this is the meaning here: ‘the inner flesh-body’ is a term for the six internal sense bases; ‘the outer skin-body’ is a term for the six external sense bases; ‘inner sinews, inner tendons, inner bonds’ is a term for sensual pleasure and lust; ‘a razor-pointed goad’ is a term used by noble ones for wisdom; that noble wisdom which cuts through defilement, cuts through fetters, cuts through bonds, cuts off, cuts away, cuts out.
translations.mn146:13: Now, sisters, there are seven factors of enlightenment, which, when developed and cultivated by a bhikkhu, lead to the destruction of the taints, to the realization of the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, even in the present life, personally known and realized by him, entered upon and dwelt in. Which seven? Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He develops the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor … the energy enlightenment factor … the rapture enlightenment factor … the tranquillity enlightenment factor … the concentration enlightenment factor … he develops the equanimity enlightenment factor relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. These, sisters, are the seven factors of enlightenment, which, when developed and cultivated by a bhikkhu, lead to the destruction of the taints, to the realization of the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, even in the present life, personally known and realized by him, entered upon and dwelt in.”
translations.mn146:14: Then Venerable Nandaka, having instructed and advised those bhikkhunīs with this exhortation, dismissed them: “Go, sisters; it is time.” Then those bhikkhunīs, delighting in and approving of Venerable Nandaka’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to Venerable Nandaka, circumambulated him keeping him on their right, and went to the Blessed One. Having gone to the Blessed One, they paid homage to him and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhunīs: “Go, bhikkhunīs; it is time.” Then those bhikkhunīs paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him on their right, and departed.
translations.mn146:3: At that time the elder bhikkhus were instructing the bhikkhunīs in due order. Venerable Nandaka did not wish to instruct the bhikkhunīs in due order. Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, whose turn is it today to instruct the bhikkhunīs in due order?” “Venerable sir, all have taken their turns to instruct the bhikkhunīs in due order. Venerable Nandaka, venerable sir, does not wish to instruct the bhikkhunīs in due order.”
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Nandaka: “Nandaka, instruct the bhikkhunīs; advise them, Nandaka; brahmin, give a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhunīs.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. Then, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, he entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after his meal, on returning from almsround, accompanied by one attendant, he went to the royal park. Those bhikkhunīs saw Venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat and washed his feet. Those bhikkhunīs paid homage to Venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Nandaka said to those bhikkhunīs:
translations.mn146:5: “Sisters, this will be a talk by way of question and answer. When you know something, you should say ‘We know’; when you do not know, you should say ‘We do not know.’ And if you have any doubt or uncertainty, you yourself should ask about it: ‘Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’” “Venerable sir, even by this much we are delighted and pleased with Venerable Nandaka, that Venerable Nandaka deigns to invite us.”
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in retreat, the following reflection arose in his mind: “The Dhammas that lead to the full ripening of liberation have become fully ripened in Rāhula. What if I were to lead Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints?” Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after his meal, on returning from almsround, he addressed Venerable Rāhula: “Take up a sitting mat, Rāhula; we will go to the Andhavana for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One, took up a sitting mat, and followed close behind the Blessed One.
translations.mn147:2: At that time many thousands of deities were following the Blessed One, thinking: "Today the Blessed One will guide the venerable Rāhula to the destruction of the āsavas beyond training." Then the Blessed One, having entered the Andhavana and sat down at the seat prepared at the foot of a certain tree, the venerable Rāhula paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. To the venerable Rāhula sitting to one side, the Blessed One said: "What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, Bhante." "And what is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, Bhante." "And what is impermanent, suffering, a dharma subject to change, is it fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, Bhante."
translations.mn148:16: And bhikkhus, this is the path leading to the arising of identity view—one regards the eye thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self';
translations.mn148:2: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you dhamma that is beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, beautiful in the end, with meaning, with details, complete in every way, perfectly pure, the holy life—I will make it clear, namely, the six sense spheres. Listen to it, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn148:22: And bhikkhus, this is the path leading to the cessation of identity view—one regards the eye thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.mn148:3: "Six internal sense spheres are to be known, six external sense spheres are to be known, six bodies of consciousness are to be known, six bodies of contact are to be known, six bodies of feeling are to be known, six bodies of craving are to be known."
translations.mn148:34: Bhikkhus, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Being touched by a pleasant feeling, he does not delight in it, approve of it, or dwell in attachment. His underlying tendency to lust does not become manifest. Being touched by a painful feeling, he does not sorrow, does not lament, does not beat his breast, does not weep with tearful face, does not fall into bewilderment. His underlying tendency to aversion does not become manifest. Being touched by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands as it really is its arising, its passing away, its allure, its danger, its escape. His underlying tendency to ignorance does not become manifest. Bhikkhus, it is possible that, having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust regarding pleasant feeling, removed the underlying tendency to aversion regarding painful feeling, eradicated the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, having abandoned ignorance and generated knowledge, one will be an end-maker of suffering here and now—it is possible.
translations.mn148:40: Bhikkhus, seeing thus, the instructed noble disciple is disillusioned with the eye, disillusioned with forms, disillusioned with eye-consciousness, disillusioned with eye-contact, disillusioned with feeling, disillusioned with craving.
translations.mn149:11: And what bhikkhus, are the dhammas to be directly known by higher knowledge? 'The five aggregates of clinging' is the term—it is this: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, the aggregate of clinging to consciousness. These dhammas are to be directly known by higher knowledge. And what bhikkhus, are the dhammas to be abandoned by higher knowledge? Ignorance and becoming-craving—these dhammas are to be abandoned by higher knowledge. And what bhikkhus, are the dhammas to be developed by higher knowledge? Calm and insight—these dhammas are to be developed by higher knowledge. And what bhikkhus, are the dhammas to be realized by higher knowledge? Knowledge and freedom—these dhammas are to be realized by higher knowledge.
translations.mn149:2: "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the great discourse on the six sense spheres. Listen to it, pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, Bhante," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn149:3: "Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and not seeing forms as they really are, not knowing and not seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, not knowing and not seeing eye-contact as it really is, not knowing and not seeing that feeling—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which arises with eye-contact as condition, as it really is, he is attached to the eye, attached to forms, attached to eye-consciousness, attached to eye-contact, attached to that feeling—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—which arises with eye-contact as condition. For one who dwells attached, entangled, confused, dwelling with regard to allurement, in the future the five aggregates of clinging increase. And craving—which brings renewal, is accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—increases for him. And his bodily stresses increase, his mental stresses increase; his bodily burnings increase, his mental burnings increase; his bodily fevers increase, his mental fevers increase. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:8: For one who dwells attached, entangled, confused, dwelling with regard to allurement, in the future the five aggregates of clinging increase. And craving—which brings renewal, is accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—increases for him. And his bodily stresses increase, his mental stresses increase; his bodily burnings increase, his mental burnings increase; his bodily fevers increase, his mental fevers increase. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: And, monks, knowing and seeing the eye as it really is, knowing and seeing forms as they really are, knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, knowing and seeing eye-contact as it really is, and that feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact, knowing and seeing that too as it really is, he is not attached to the eye, not attached to forms, not attached to eye-consciousness, not attached to eye-contact, not attached to that feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact. For one who lives unattached, un-clinging, undeluded, contemplating the drawbacks, in the future the five aggregates of clinging diminish. And craving—which brings renewal, is accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—that too is abandoned. His bodily distresses are abandoned, his mental distresses are abandoned; his bodily fevers are abandoned, his mental fevers are abandoned; his bodily burnings are abandoned, his mental burnings are abandoned. He experiences bodily pleasure and mental pleasure.
translations.mn19:11: Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks about and reflects on, that is the inclination his mind will have. If a monk, monks, frequently thinks about and reflects on renunciation-thoughts, he has abandoned sensual-thoughts, has made renunciation-thoughts predominant, then his mind inclines to that renunciation-thought. If with ill-will-thoughts, monks …pe… If a monk, monks, frequently thinks about and reflects on non-harm-thoughts, he has abandoned harm-thoughts, has made non-harm-thoughts predominant, then his mind inclines to that non-harm-thought.
translations.mn19:12: Just as, monks, in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops in the village fields have been harvested, a cowherd would watch over cows, and for him who is at the root of a tree or in an open space, there is just the need for mindfulness: ‘these cows.’ Even so, monks, there was just the need for mindfulness for me: ‘these qualities.’
translations.mn19:13: But, monks, my energy was exerted, not sluggish; mindfulness was established, not confused; the body was calm, not tense; the mind was concentrated, one-pointed.
translations.mn19:14: Then I, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn19:24: This, monks, was the third true knowledge gained by me in the last watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arisen; darkness was destroyed, light arisen—just as for one who is heedful, ardent, and resolute in dwelling thus.
translations.mn19:25: Just as, monks, in a forest, in a jungle, there was a large low-lying waterless pool. A large herd of deer would live depending on it. Then a certain man would arise, desiring harm, desiring ill, desiring no safety from bondage for the deer. He would close off the safe, beneficial, pleasant path, would open a bad path, would ruin the good range, would set up one who ranges in the bad. Thus that large herd of deer would in no long time come to harm and ruin. But for that same large herd of deer, monks, a certain man would arise, desiring welfare, desiring good, desiring safety from bondage for the deer. He would open the safe, beneficial, pleasant path, would close off the bad path, would remove the bad range, would destroy one who ranges in the bad. Thus that large herd of deer would in no long time prosper and flourish.
translations.mn19:26: This simile, monks, was made by me with reference to this meaning. And this is the meaning here: ‘a large low-lying waterless pool’ is a designation for sensual pleasures. ‘A large herd of deer’ is a designation for beings. ‘A man desiring harm, desiring ill, desiring no safety from bondage’ is a designation for Māra the Evil One. ‘Bad path’ is a designation for the wrong eightfold path, namely: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration. ‘Bad range’ is a designation for delight and lust. ‘One who ranges in the bad’ is a designation for ignorance. ‘A man desiring welfare, desiring good, desiring safety from bondage’ is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘Safe path, beneficial, pleasant’ is a designation for the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Thus, monks, I have opened the safe path, beneficial, pleasant; have closed the bad path; have removed the bad range; have destroyed one who ranges in the bad.
translations.mn19:3: While I dwelt heedful, ardent, and resolute thus, monks, there arose sensual-thoughts in me. I understood thus: ‘This sensual-thought has arisen in me. And it leads to self-affliction, leads to others’ affliction, leads to affliction of both; it is an obstacle to wisdom, inclines to agitation, leads to rebirth.’ ‘It leads to self-affliction’—when I reflected thus, monks, it led to harm; ‘leads to others’ affliction’—when I reflected thus, monks, it led to harm; ‘leads to affliction of both’—when I reflected thus, monks, it led to harm; ‘an obstacle to wisdom, inclines to agitation, leads to rebirth’—when I reflected thus, monks, it led to harm. Then I, monks, abandoned, dispelled, and made to cease arisen sensual-thoughts.
translations.mn19:6: Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks about and reflects on, that is the inclination his mind will have. If a monk, monks, frequently thinks about and reflects on sensual-thoughts, he has abandoned renunciation-thoughts, has made sensual-thoughts predominant, then his mind inclines to that sensual-thought. If with ill-will-thoughts, monks …pe… If a monk, monks, frequently thinks about and reflects on harm-thoughts, he has abandoned non-harm-thoughts, has made harm-thoughts predominant, then his mind inclines to that harm-thought.
translations.mn19:7: Just as, monks, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn time, a cowherd would guard cows in a crowded, overgrown area. He would drive them here and there with a stick, prod them, restrain them, and hold them back. For what reason? Because that cowherd sees that from that cause there would be killing or binding or fines or blame. Even so, monks, I saw the danger, degradation, and defilement in unwholesome dhammas, and the renunciation, benefit, and purity-aspect in wholesome dhammas.
translations.mn19:8: When I dwelt diligent, ardent, and resolute in this way, there arose in me thought of renunciation. I understood it thus: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. And it leads neither to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both. It is an increase of wisdom, on the side of non-torment, and leads to Nibbāna.’ If, monks, I were to dwell mentally engaging and reflecting on it at night, I do not see fear arising from that cause. If, monks, I were to dwell mentally engaging and reflecting on it during the day, I do not see fear arising from that cause. If, monks, I were to dwell mentally engaging and reflecting on it both at night and during the day, I do not see fear arising from that cause. But after a long time of mentally engaging and reflecting, my body would become fatigued. When the body is fatigued, the mind would waver. When the mind wavers, the mind becomes distant from concentration. So I, monks, steady the mind internally, quiet it, make it one-pointed, and concentrate it. For what reason? ‘Lest my mind waver.’
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Grove, at the foot of a sāla tree. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks.’ ‘Venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:10: He perceives Brahmā as Brahmā; having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, he fancies Brahmā, fancies ‘I am Brahmā,’ fancies ‘I am from Brahmā,’ fancies ‘Brahmā is mine,’ and delights in Brahmā. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:11: He perceives the Radiant as Radiant; having perceived the Radiant as Radiant, he fancies the Radiant, fancies ‘I am the Radiant,’ fancies ‘I am from the Radiant,’ fancies ‘the Radiant is mine,’ and delights in the Radiant. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:123: And that monk, monks, who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetter of being, and is rightly freed through perfect knowledge— he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not fancy earth, does not fancy ‘I am earth,’ does not fancy ‘I am from earth,’ does not fancy ‘earth is mine,’ and does not delight in earth. For what reason? Because of the destruction of delusion, he is free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: He perceives the Glorious as Glorious; having perceived the Glorious as Glorious, he fancies the Glorious, fancies ‘I am the Glorious,’ fancies ‘I am from the Glorious,’ fancies ‘the Glorious is mine,’ and delights in the Glorious. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:14: He perceives the Mighty One as Mighty One; having perceived the Mighty One as Mighty One, he fancies the Mighty One, fancies ‘I am the Mighty One,’ fancies ‘I am from the Mighty One,’ fancies ‘the Mighty One is mine,’ and delights in the Mighty One. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:147: The Tathāgata too, monks, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not fancy earth, does not fancy ‘I am earth,’ does not fancy ‘I am from earth,’ does not fancy ‘earth is mine,’ and does not delight in earth. For what reason? ‘It has been fully known by the Tathāgata,’ I say.
translations.mn1:171: The Tathāgata too, monks, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not fancy earth, does not fancy ‘I am earth,’ does not fancy ‘I am from earth,’ does not fancy ‘earth is mine,’ and does not delight in earth. For what reason? ‘Delight is the root of suffering’— having understood this, ‘becoming is birth for one who has come to be, and from birth there is aging and death.’ Therefore, monks, I say: ‘The Tathāgata, by utterly destroying, relinquishing, letting go, and giving up all craving, has awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment.’
translations.mn1:19: He perceives the seen as the seen; having perceived the seen as the seen, he fancies the seen, fancies ‘I am the seen,’ fancies ‘I am from the seen,’ fancies ‘the seen is mine,’ and delights in the seen. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:2: ‘Monks, I will teach you the root of all dhammas discourse. Listen to it, pay close attention, I will speak.’ ‘Yes, Bhante,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:20: He perceives the heard as the heard; having perceived the heard as the heard, he fancies the heard, fancies ‘I am the heard,’ fancies ‘I am from the heard,’ fancies ‘the heard is mine,’ and delights in the heard. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:22: He perceives the cognized as the cognized; having perceived the cognized as the cognized, he fancies the cognized, fancies ‘I am the cognized,’ fancies ‘I am from the cognized,’ fancies ‘the cognized is mine,’ and delights in the cognized. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:23: He perceives unity as unity; having perceived unity as unity, he fancies unity, fancies ‘I am unity,’ fancies ‘I am from unity,’ fancies ‘unity is mine,’ and delights in unity. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:24: He perceives diversity as diversity; having perceived diversity as diversity, he fancies diversity, fancies ‘I am diversity,’ fancies ‘I am from diversity,’ fancies ‘diversity is mine,’ and delights in diversity. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:25: He perceives all as all; having perceived all as all, he fancies all, fancies ‘I am all,’ fancies ‘I am from all,’ fancies ‘all is mine,’ and delights in all. For what reason? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:27: And that monk, monks, who is a trainee, whose mind is not yet reached, dwelling aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage, he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, ‘do not fancy earth, do not fancy “I am earth,” do not fancy “I am from earth,” do not fancy “earth is mine,” do not delight in earth.’ For what reason? ‘It should be fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:3: “Here, monks, the unlearned ordinary person, who has not seen noble ones, is unskilled and undisciplined in the noble teaching, who has not seen good men, is unskilled and undisciplined in the teaching of good men—perceives earth as earth. Having perceived earth as earth, he conceives earth, conceives of earth, conceives from earth, conceives ‘earth is mine,’ delights in earth. Why is that? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:4: He perceives water as water. Having perceived water as water, he conceives water, conceives of water, conceives from water, conceives ‘water is mine,’ delights in water. Why is that? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:5: He perceives fire as fire. Having perceived fire as fire, he conceives fire, conceives of fire, conceives from fire, conceives ‘fire is mine,’ delights in fire. Why is that? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:51: And that monk, monks, who is an arahant, whose effluents are ended, who has reached fulfillment, done the task, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, fully destroyed the fetter of being, and is rightly released through perfect gnosis, he too directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, does not conceive of earth, does not conceive from earth, does not conceive ‘earth is mine,’ does not delight in earth. Why is that? ‘It has been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:7: He perceives beings as beings. Having perceived beings as beings, he conceives beings, conceives of beings, conceives from beings, conceives ‘beings are mine,’ delights in beings. Why is that? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:8: He perceives gods as gods. Having perceived gods as gods, he conceives gods, conceives of gods, conceives from gods, conceives ‘gods are mine,’ delights in gods. Why is that? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn1:9: He perceives Brahmā as Brahmā. Having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, he conceives Brahmā, conceives of Brahmā, conceives from Brahmā, conceives ‘Brahmā is mine,’ delights in Brahmā. Why is that? ‘It has not been fully known by him,’ I say.
translations.mn20:2: “Monks, when a monk is devoted to higher mind, there are five signs that should be occasionally attended to. Which five?
translations.mn22:12: “Therefore, monks, if you understand the meaning of what I have said, you should remember it that way. And if you do not understand the meaning of what I have said, you should question me about it, or those monks who are learned.
translations.mn22:14: “Monks, I have taught the Dhamma by means of the raft simile. Even the Dhamma should be abandoned by those who understand, let alone what is not Dhamma.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: “‘Might there be anxiety due to something external when it is absent?’ ‘There might, monk,’ the Blessed One said. ‘Here, for some monk it occurs thus: “Oh, I had that, now it is not mine; oh, I might have had that, but now I do not get it.” He sorrows and grieves and laments, weeps beating his breast, and falls into confusion. Thus, monk, there is anxiety due to something external when it is absent.’
translations.mn22:19: “‘Might there be non-anxiety due to something external when it is absent?’ ‘There might, monk,’ the Blessed One said. ‘Here, for some monk it does not occur thus: “Oh, I had that, now it is not mine; oh, I might have had that, but now I do not get it.” He does not sorrow, does not grieve, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, does not fall into confusion. Thus, monk, there is non-anxiety due to something external when it is absent.’
translations.mn22:20: “‘Might there be anxiety due to something internal when it is absent?’ ‘There might, monk,’ the Blessed One said. ‘Here, monk, for some person there is such a view: “That world, that self, after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and I shall remain as I am eternally.” He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all standpoints, determinations, adherences, obsessions, and latent tendencies, for the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Then it occurs to him: “I will be annihilated, I will perish, I will not exist.” He sorrows and grieves and laments, weeps beating his breast, and falls into confusion. Thus, monk, there is anxiety due to something internal when it is absent.’
translations.mn22:23: “Monks, suppose one were to cling to that clinging to the self-view such that sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise. Do you see that clinging to the self-view such that sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise?” “No, sir.” “Good, monks. I too do not see that clinging to the self-view such that sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise.
translations.mn22:24: “Monks, suppose one were to resort to that reliance on view such that sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise. Do you see that reliance on view such that sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise?” “No, sir.” “Good, monks. I too do not see that reliance on view such that sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise.
translations.mn22:25: “Monks, when there is a self, would it be suitable to say ‘what is mine is in the self’?” “Yes, sir.” “When there is what belongs to self, would it be suitable to say ‘self is mine’?” “Yes, sir.” “Monks, when neither self nor what belongs to self is found as a real and true existent, that standpoint of view: ‘That world, that self, after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and I shall remain as I am eternally’—is it not completely and utterly a fool’s Dhamma?” “How could it not be, sir? It is completely and utterly a fool’s Dhamma.”}
translations.mn22:27: “Therefore, monks, any form whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one should see all form as ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’ with right understanding as it really is. Any feeling whatsoever … any perception whatsoever … any volitional formations whatsoever … any consciousness whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one should see all consciousness as ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’ with right understanding as it really is.
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, monks, the instructed noble disciple is disillusioned with form, disillusioned with feeling, disillusioned with perception, disillusioned with volitional formations, disillusioned with consciousness.
translations.mn22:29: Through disillusionment he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.mn22:30: He is called, monks, a monk who has lifted the bar, who has broken through the enclosure, who has escaped the roof, who has unbolted the door, a noble one with banner laid down, burden put down, unbound from the poison.
translations.mn22:31: And how, monks, is a monk one who has lifted the bar? Here, monks, a monk’s ignorance is abandoned, its root destroyed like a palm tree stump, made like a hollow, unable to grow in the future. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has lifted the bar.
translations.mn22:32: And how, monks, is a monk one who has broken through the enclosure? Here, monks, a monk’s rebirth into states of existence is abandoned, its root destroyed like a palm tree stump, made like a hollow, unable to grow in the future. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has broken through the enclosure.
translations.mn22:33: And how, monks, is a monk one who has escaped the roof? Here, monks, a monk’s craving is abandoned, its root destroyed like a palm tree stump, made like a hollow, unable to grow in the future. Thus, monks, a monk is one who has escaped the roof.
translations.mn22:34: And how, monks, is a monk unbolted? Here, monks, a monk’s five lower fetters are abandoned, their roots destroyed like palm tree stumps, made like hollows, unable to grow in the future. Thus, monks, a monk is unbolted.
translations.mn22:35: And how, monks, is a monk a noble one with banner laid down, burden put down, unbound from the poison? Here, monks, a monk’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, its root destroyed like a palm tree stump, made like a hollow, unable to grow in the future. Thus, monks, a monk is a noble one with banner laid down, burden put down, unbound from the poison.
translations.mn22:38: If others, monks, honor, respect, esteem, and worship the Tathāgata thus, then, monks, the Tathāgata has no delight, no joy, no mental exhilaration therein. If others, monks, honor, respect, esteem, and worship the Tathāgata thus, then, monks, the Tathāgata thinks thus: ‘This action is being done to me in this place where formerly there was full understanding.’
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, monks, even if others should abuse, revile, be angry with, and harass you, there should be no animosity, no resentment, no mental unsteadiness in you. Therefore, monks, even if others should honor, respect, esteem, and worship you, there should be no delight, no joy, no mental exhilaration in you. Therefore, monks, even if others should honor, respect, esteem, and worship you, you should think: ‘This action is being done to me in this place where formerly there was full understanding.’
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, monks, abandon what is not yours; that being abandoned will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.
translations.mn22:42: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork. In this well-expounded Dhamma, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork, those monks who are arahants, with taints destroyed, the holy life lived, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of being, and are rightly liberated through perfect knowledge—for them there is no state of being that can be pointed out.
translations.mn22:43: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork. In this well-expounded Dhamma, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork, those monks who have abandoned the five lower fetters—all of them attain rebirth in higher realms and are non-returners there, not liable to return to this world.
translations.mn22:44: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork. In this well-expounded Dhamma, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork, those monks who have abandoned three fetters and have attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion—all of them are once-returners: they come back only one more time to this world and then make an end to suffering.
translations.mn22:45: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork. In this well-expounded Dhamma, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork, those monks who have abandoned three fetters—all of them are stream-enterers, not liable to downfall, assured, bound for full awakening.
translations.mn22:46: Thus, monks, the Dhamma has been well-expounded by me, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork. In this well-expounded Dhamma, upright, open, proclaimed, free of patchwork, those monks who are followers by faith, followers by Dhamma—all of them are bound for full awakening.
translations.mn22:6: “Whose teaching on the Dhamma taught by me do you understand in this way, you foolish man? Haven’t I, you foolish man, spoken of obstructive things in many ways as obstructive? And yet by indulging in them you are heading for obstruction. I have said that sensual pleasures are of little gratification, very painful, very much distressful, and the danger in them is greater. I have said that sensual pleasures are like bones thrown away … like pieces of meat … like pieces of grass … like a pit of glowing charcoal … like dream-born … like borrowed … like fruit on a tree … like a meat hook … like a sword’s point … like a snake’s head, very painful, very much distressful, and the danger in them is greater. And yet you, you foolish man, with your own bad grasp, misrepresent me, dig your own grave, and create much demerit. That will be for your long-term harm and suffering.”
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “What do you think, monks, is this Ariṭṭha, the former charioteer, even more deluded than a donkey in this Dhamma and discipline?” “How could it be otherwise, Bhante? No, Bhante.” When this was said, Ariṭṭha the former charioteer sat silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping, downcast eyes, dejected, and without response. Then the Blessed One, having seen Ariṭṭha the former charioteer sitting silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping, downcast eyes, dejected, and without response, said to him: “You will be known by this own evil view, you foolish man. Here I will question the monks.”
translations.mn22:9: Monks, it is not possible to indulge in sensual pleasures while apart from sensual pleasures, apart from perceptions of sensual pleasures, apart from sensual thoughts.
translations.mn26:10: And what, monks, do you call a grief thing? Wife and children, monks, are a grief thing; slaves, servants, a grief thing; goats and sheep, a grief thing; fowl and pigs, a grief thing; elephants, cattle, horses, mares, a grief thing. These, monks, are fuel for grief. Bound, deluded, stupefied by these, being himself a grief thing, he seeks only a grief thing.
translations.mn26:11: And what, monks, do you call a defilement thing? Wife and children, monks, are a defilement thing; slaves, servants, a defilement thing; goats and sheep, a defilement thing; fowl and pigs, a defilement thing; elephants, cattle, horses, mares, a defilement thing; gold and silver, a defilement thing. These, monks, are fuel for defilement. Bound, deluded, stupefied by these, being himself a defilement thing, he seeks only a defilement thing. This, monks, is an ignoble search.
translations.mn26:13: I myself, monks, before enlightenment, while still a bodhisatta not fully awakened, being subject to birth, sought only birth; being subject to aging, sought only aging; being subject to sickness, sought only sickness; being subject to death, sought only death; being subject to grief, sought only grief; being subject to defilement, sought only defilement. Then, monks, this occurred to me: ‘Why am I, being subject to birth, seeking only birth; being subject to aging … sickness … death … grief … being subject to defilement, seeking only defilement? Why don’t I, being subject to birth, having understood the danger in birth, seek the unborn supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to aging, having understood the danger in aging, seek the unaging supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to sickness, having understood the danger in sickness, seek the unailing supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to death, having understood the danger in death, seek the deathless supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to grief, having understood the danger in grief, seek the ungrieving supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to defilement, having understood the danger in defilement, seek the undefiled supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna?’
translations.mn26:14: Then I, monks, after some time, while still young, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, no desire on the part of my unwilling mother and father with tearful faces weeping, having cut off my hair and donned ochre robes, went forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: Then I, monks, seeking the unexcelled peace from bondage, while wandering in stages through Magadha, arrived at Uruvelā, near Senānigama. There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a delightful grove of trees, a river flowing with clear, pleasant water, good for bathing, and nearby villages for alms. Then, monks, this occurred to me: ‘How delightful is this stretch of land, delightful the grove, the river flowing with clear, pleasant water, good for bathing, and nearby villages for alms. This is sufficient for a clansman with energy to strive.’ Then I, monks, sat down there—‘This is sufficient for striving.’
translations.mn26:21: Then I, monks, having understood the request of that Brahmā and out of compassion for beings, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust and much dust, with keen faculties and dull faculties, of good deportment and bad deportment, easy to teach and hard to teach, with some living seeing the danger in misconduct regarding the next world, with some living not seeing the danger in misconduct regarding the next world. Just as if there were blue lotuses, white lotuses, or white lotuses born in the water, grown in the water, gone under the water, nourished from within the water; some blue lotuses, white lotuses, or white lotuses born in the water, grown in the water, gone under the water, standing at water-level; some blue lotuses, white lotuses, or white lotuses born in the water, grown in the water, standing risen above the water, untouched by the water; so too, monks, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust and much dust, with keen faculties and dull faculties, of good deportment and bad deportment, easy to teach and hard to teach, with some living seeing the danger in misconduct regarding the next world, with some living not seeing the danger in misconduct regarding the next world. Then I, monks, replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse: ‘For those whose minds are open, the door to the deathless is open; Let those with ears release faith. I spoke not out of compassion for harm, O Brahmā, among humans the sublime Dhamma.’ Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking ‘I have been given an opportunity by the Blessed One for the teaching of Dhamma,’ paid homage to me, circled me keeping on his right, and vanished right there.
translations.mn26:25: Upaka the Ājīvaka saw me, monks, between Gayā and the Bodhi tree, traveling along the road. Having seen me, he said this to me: ‘Your faculties, friend, are serene, your complexion is pure, bright, and clear. For whom did you go forth, friend? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve?’ When this was said, I, monks, spoke this verse to Upaka the Ājīvaka: ‘I am conqueror of all, all-knower, untainted in all Dhammas; Having relinquished all, freed by the destruction of craving, I have known this myself, whom should I point to? I have no teacher, one like me is not found; In the world with its devas, there is no one equal to me. For I am an arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed teacher; I am the only perfectly enlightened one, cooled and liberated. To set rolling the Wheel of Dhamma, I go to the city of Kāsī; In the blind world, I beat the drum of the deathless.’ ‘Friend, as you declare, you deserve to be a victor without limit.’ ‘Such are victors, who have reached the destruction of the taints; I have conquered evil Dhammas, therefore I am a victor, Upaka.’ When this was said, monks, Upaka the Ājīvaka said ‘May it be so, friend,’ shook his head, took the side-track, and departed.
translations.mn26:26: Then I, monks, gradually wandering by stages, came to Bārāṇasī, Isipatana, the Deer Park, and approached the group of five monks. The group of five monks saw me coming from afar. Seeing me, they made an agreement among themselves: ‘Friends, here comes the ascetic Gotama, devoted to indulgence in luxury, lapsed into indolence, turned to luxury. He is not to be greeted, stood up for, or offered a seat or bowl and robe. But a seat should be set out; if he wishes, he can sit down.’ As I approached, monks, just so the group of five monks were not able to maintain their own agreement. Some came out to greet me and received my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, some set out foot-water. But they still addressed me by name and as ‘friend.’
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, I, monks, said this to the group of five monks: ‘Do you acknowledge that I previously practiced such a practice?’ ‘No indeed, Bhante.’ ‘Monks, the Tathāgata is an arahant, perfectly enlightened. Lend an ear, monks, I have attained the deathless, I will instruct you, I will teach you Dhamma. Practicing as taught, before long—for that for which clansmen rightly go forth from home to homelessness—that unsurpassed end of the holy life you will realize in this very life, enter upon, abide in it, having known it, seen it for yourselves.’
translations.mn26:29: I was not able to persuade, monks, the group of five monks. Twice, monks, I instruct monks, three monks go for alms. With what the three monks bring back on alms round, the group of six lives. Twice, monks, I instruct monks, two monks go for alms. With what the two monks bring back on alms round, the group of six lives.
translations.mn26:30: Then, monks, the group of five monks, thus instructed and advised by me, being subject to birth, seeing the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage, nibbāna, realized the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage, nibbāna; being subject to aging, seeing the danger in what is subject to aging, seeking the unaging, unsurpassed security from bondage, nibbāna, realized the unaging, unsurpassed security from bondage, nibbāna; being subject to sickness … being subject to death … being subject to sorrow … being subject to defilement, seeing the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage, nibbāna, realized the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage, nibbāna. And knowledge and vision arose in them: ‘Our liberation is unshakeable, this is our last birth, there is no more rebirth.’
translations.mn26:31: There are these five strands of sensual pleasure, monks. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, delightful, arousing desire. Sounds cognizable by the ear …pe… odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, delightful, arousing desire. These are the five strands of sensual pleasure, monks.
translations.mn26:34: Just as, monks, a wild deer in the forest, in the thicket, wanders about fearlessly, stands fearlessly, sits fearlessly, lies down fearlessly. Why is that? Because it has gone beyond the range of the hunter, monks. In the same way, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which has directed thought and evaluation, rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He is called, monks, a monk who has struck the blind, eyeless maker of darkness, Māra, lame and gone to the realm of the unseen, the Evil One.
translations.mn26:35: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the stilling of directed thought and evaluation, enters and abides in the second jhāna, which has inner tranquility and unification of mind, without directed thought and evaluation, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. He is called, monks …pe… the Evil One.
translations.mn26:36: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the fading away of rapture, abides equanimous and mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He abides equanimous and mindful, a happy dweller,’ and enters and abides in the third jhāna. He is called, monks …pe… the Evil One.
translations.mn26:37: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, enters and abides in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasurable and purity of equanimity and mindfulness. He is called, monks …pe… the Evil One.
translations.mn26:38: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended perceptions of forms, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, and unmindful of perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ enters and abides in the sphere of infinite space. He is called, monks …pe… the Evil One.
translations.mn26:39: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and abides in the sphere of infinite consciousness. He is called, monks …pe… the Evil One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. At that time several monks were sitting at the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka engaged in discussion on the Dhamma. Then the Blessed One stood at the outer porch waiting for the discussion to conclude. Having known that the discussion had concluded, the Blessed One knocked on the bolt. Those monks opened the door for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka and sat down on the appointed seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘What were you discussing about just now, monks? What was your discussion that was interrupted?’ ‘Our discussion about the Blessed One was interrupted, lord, when the Blessed One arrived.’ ‘Good, monks. It is fitting for you sons of good family who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith that you sit engaged in discussion on the Dhamma. When you have gathered together, monks, there are two things to be done: discussion on the Dhamma or noble silence.
translations.mn26:40: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, enters and abides in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He is called, monks …pe… the Evil One.
translations.mn26:41: Furthermore, monks, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and abides in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He is called, monks …pe… the Evil One.
