translations.mn26:5: There are these two searches, monks: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, someone being subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth; being subject to aging seeks only what is subject to aging; being subject to illness seeks only what is subject to illness; being subject to death seeks only what is subject to death; being subject to sorrow seeks only what is subject to sorrow; being subject to defilement seeks only what is subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what, monks, is said to be subject to birth? Wife and children, monks, are subject to birth; slaves, subject to birth; goats and sheep, subject to birth; fowl and pigs, subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, mares, subject to birth; gold and silver, subject to birth. These are supports, monks, subject to birth. Here, being bound and stupefied, deluded, one being subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth.
translations.mn27:12: He hears that Dhamma from a householder or a householder’s son born in some family. Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Endowed with that gain of faith, he reflects thus: ‘The household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a house, to live the holy life completely perfect, completely pure, like a polished shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?’ Then, after some time, having abandoned a little wealth or much wealth, having abandoned a small circle of relatives or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on ochre robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Thus being one who has gone forth in this way, endowed with the monks' training and livelihood, he has abandoned the taking of life and abstains from taking life; he has laid down weapons and laid down the rod; he is conscientious and merciful, compassionate and sympathetic toward all living beings, he dwells. Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he is a giver, expecting what is given. With a blameless and pure livelihood he dwells. Having abandoned unchastity, he is celibate, restrained, abstaining from sexual intercourse and sensual pleasures. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truth, is devoted to truth, reliable, trustworthy, not a deceiver of the world. Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech; having heard something here, he does not tell it elsewhere for the sake of dividing those people, and having heard something elsewhere, he does not tell it here for the sake of dividing these people. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and an encourager of those who are harmonious; he delights, approves, and rejoices in harmony, and he speaks words that promote harmony. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, courteous, agreeable to many, delightful to many. Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, what is factual, what is beneficial, what is about the Dhamma, what is about discipline; he speaks words that have a reason, timely, specific, connected with the goal. He abstains from engaging in trade in seeds and crops; he eats one meal a day, abstaining from food at night; he abstains from witnessing dancing, singing, music, and shows; he abstains from wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, adornments, and embellishments; he abstains from high and luxurious beds; he abstains from accepting gold and silver; he abstains from accepting raw grain; he abstains from accepting raw meat; he abstains from accepting women and girls; he abstains from accepting male and female slaves; he abstains from accepting goats and sheep; he abstains from accepting fowl and pigs; he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares; he abstains from accepting fields and lands; he abstains from running errands and messages; he abstains from buying and selling; he abstains from cheating with false weights, false measures, and false scales; he abstains from fraud, deception, trickery, and bribery; he abstains from mutilation, murder, imprisonment, robbery, plunder, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with a robe to cover the body and almsfood to sustain the stomach. Whatever way he goes, he goes fully provided. Just as a bird with wings, wherever it flies, flies with both wings; even so, a monk content with a robe to cover the body and almsfood to sustain the stomach, whatever way he goes, goes fully provided. Endowed with this noble moral aggregate, he experiences internal happiness free from blame.
translations.mn27:15: Having seen a form with the eye, he is not one who takes hold of the sign and not one who takes hold of the details. Since cognizable things would flow in with covetousness and displeasure, evil unskillful qualities, if he dwelt with the faculty of sight unrestrained, he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of sight, and applies restraint to the faculty of sight. Having heard a sound with the ear … Having smelled an odor with the nose … Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … Having touched a tangible object with the body … Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not one who takes hold of the sign and not one who takes hold of the details. Since cognizable things would flow in with covetousness and displeasure, evil unskillful qualities, if he dwelt with the faculty of mind unrestrained, he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of mind, and applies restraint to the faculty of mind. Endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences internal happiness free from effervescence.
translations.mn27:16: When walking forward and returning, he acts with clear comprehension; when looking ahead and looking away, he acts with clear comprehension; when bending and extending the limbs, he acts with clear comprehension; when wearing the outer robe, carrying the bowl and robe, he acts with clear comprehension; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, he acts with clear comprehension; when urinating and defecating, he acts with clear comprehension; when walking, standing, sitting, lying down, awake, speaking, and silent, he acts with clear comprehension.
translations.mn27:17: Endowed with this noble moral aggregate, endowed with this noble contentment, endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded dwelling: the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: Having returned from almsround after his meal, he sits down folding his legs crosswise, holding his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness, and he purifies his mind of covetousness. Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate and sympathetic toward all living beings, and he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred. Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful, clearly comprehending, and he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with internal pacification of mind, and he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt, he dwells doubt-free, without hesitation regarding skillful qualities, and he purifies his mind of doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, which defile the mind and weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This too is called, brahmin, the footprint of the Tathāgata, or the resort of the Tathāgata, or the domain of the Tathāgata. But still the noble disciple does not achieve the consummation: ‘The Blessed One is accomplished and fully awakened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of right practice.’
translations.mn27:2: At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was setting out from Sāvatthī in the middle of the day with a full set of horses yoked to his chariot. Jāṇussoṇi the brahmin saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar. Having seen him, he said to the wanderer Pilotika: “Now from where is the gentleman Vacchāyana coming in the middle of the day?” “I am coming from here, sir, from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.” “What does the gentleman Vacchāyana think of the wisdom and erudition of the ascetic Gotama? I suppose he thinks he is wise.” “Who am I, sir, and what is the wisdom and erudition of the ascetic Gotama that I would know it? Surely there is someone like that who would know the wisdom and erudition of the ascetic Gotama.” “The gentleman Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise.” “Who am I, sir, and who is the ascetic Gotama that I would praise him? That gentleman Gotama is the best of devas and humans.” “But on account of what benefit does the gentleman Vacchāyana have such faith in the ascetic Gotama?”
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, a monk, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, attains and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence of mind, unification of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This too is called, brahmin … the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-practiced.
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, a monk, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous and mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He dwells equanimous and mindful, one who dwells happily,’ and attains and dwells in the third jhāna. This too is called, brahmin … the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-practiced.
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, attains and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of equanimity and mindfulness. This too is called, brahmin, the Tathāgata’s footprint, the Tathāgata’s haunt, the Tathāgata’s delight. But still the noble disciple does not reach a conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is fully awakened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-practiced.
translations.mn27:3: “Just as, sir, a skilled elephant tracker would enter an elephant forest. He would see a large elephant footprint, long in length and broad in width. He would reach a conclusion: ‘What a large elephant!’ Just so, sir, when I saw four footprints of the ascetic Gotama, then I reached a conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is fully awakened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-practiced.
translations.mn27:4: What four? Here, sir, I see certain wise, subtle, sharp-witted khattiya pandits, like arrows ready to shoot, who I suppose go around breaking through views and view-holders with wisdom. They hear: ‘The ascetic Gotama, sir, will come down to such and such village or town.’ They prepare a question: ‘We will approach the ascetic Gotama and ask this question. If he answers it in this way, we will set up a dispute against him. Even if he answers it in this way, we will still set up a dispute against him.’ They hear: ‘The ascetic Gotama, sir, has come down to such and such village or town.’ They approach the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, encourages, fires up, and cheers them with a talk on the Dhamma. Instructed, encouraged, fired up, and cheered by the ascetic Gotama with a talk on the Dhamma, they do not even ask the ascetic Gotama the question, let alone set up a dispute against him. On the contrary, disciples of the ascetic Gotama are ordained. When, sir, I saw this first footprint of the ascetic Gotama, then I reached a conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is fully awakened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-practiced.
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi told the Blessed One everything that had been the conversation with the wanderer Pilotika. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: “Brahmin, it is not by that extent that the elephant footprint simile is complete in detail. But brahmin, listen to how the elephant footprint simile is complete in detail. Pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn28:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said:
translations.mn28:10: If, friends, when a monk recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, skillful equanimity based on skill does not settle. He is stirred, he gives rise to urgency: ‘It is a loss for me, it is not a gain for me; it is badly obtained for me, it is not well obtained for me, that when I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way, skillful equanimity based on skill does not settle.’ Just as, friends, a young wife seeing her husband is stirred, gives rise to urgency; even so, friends, if when a monk recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, skillful equanimity based on skill does not settle, he is stirred, he gives rise to urgency: ‘It is a loss for me, it is not a gain for me; it is badly obtained for me, it is not well obtained for me, that when I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way, skillful equanimity based on skill does not settle.’ If, friends, when a monk recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, skillful equanimity based on skill settles, he is gladdened by that. To that extent, friends, the monk has done much.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friends, when the external water element becomes stirred up. It carries away village and town and city and countryside and countryside regions. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean waters a hundred leagues deep go down, waters two hundred leagues deep go down, waters three hundred leagues deep go down, waters four hundred leagues deep go down, waters five hundred leagues deep go down, waters six hundred leagues deep go down, waters seven hundred leagues deep go down. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean seven palm-trees deep of water settles, six palm-trees deep of water settles, five palm-trees deep of water settles, four palm-trees deep of water settles, three palm-trees deep of water settles, two palm-trees deep of water settles, one palm-tree deep of water settles. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean seven fathoms deep of water settles, six fathoms deep of water settles, five fathoms deep of water settles, four fathoms deep of water settles, three fathoms deep of water settles, two fathoms deep of water settles, one fathom deep of water settles. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean half a fathom deep of water settles, waist-deep of water settles, knee-deep of water settles, ankle-deep of water settles. There comes a time, friends, when in the great ocean there is not even a finger-joint depth of water. For that external water element, so vast, its impermanence will become evident, its nature to decay will become evident, its nature to pass away will become evident, its nature to change will become evident.
translations.mn28:13: But for this body of eight fingerbreadths, appropriated by craving, ‘I am’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I’? And for him there is not that here …
translations.mn28:14: if, friends, when a monk recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, skillful equanimity based on skill settles. He is gladdened by that.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friends, when the external fire element becomes stirred up. It burns village and town and city and countryside and countryside regions. Coming to a pleasant stretch of land, whether green or path or rock or water, it goes out without nourishment. There comes a time, friends, when they seek fire even with a cock’s feather or a cow’s hair. For that external fire element, so vast, its impermanence will become evident, its nature to decay will become evident, its nature to pass away will become evident, its nature to change will become evident. But for this body of eight fingerbreadths, appropriated by craving, ‘I am’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I’?
translations.mn28:18-20: And for him there is not that here … if, friends, when a monk recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, skillful equanimity based on skill settles, he is gladdened by that. To that extent, friends, the monk has done much.
translations.mn28:2: “Just as, friends, all the footprints of all quadrupeds come to rest within the footprint of the elephant—it is declared the chief among them because of its size; even so, friends, whatever skillful qualities there are, all of them are included in the four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friends, when the external wind element becomes stirred up. It carries away village and town and city and countryside and countryside regions. There comes a time, friends, when in the last months of summer they seek wind even with a palm-leaf or a fan, and they do not want thatched roofs. For that external wind element, so vast, its impermanence will become evident, its nature to decay will become evident, its nature to pass away will become evident, its nature to change will become evident. But for this body of eight fingerbreadths, appropriated by craving, ‘I am’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I’? And for him there is not that here.
translations.mn28:23: If, friends, others insult and abuse and anger and harass that monk. He understands thus: ‘This painful feeling arisen from ear-contact has arisen in me. But it is dependently arisen, not independently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact.’ He sees that contact too is impermanent, sees that feeling is impermanent, sees that perception is impermanent, sees that formations are impermanent, sees that consciousness is impermanent. His mind enters into the sign of the element, is pacified, stills, and resolves.
translations.mn28:24: And if, friend, that monk is approached by others with what is undesirable, unpleasing, and disagreeable, by contact with hand, contact with clod, contact with stick, contact with knife. He understands thus: ‘This body is of such a nature that when it is struck by contact with hand it feels pain, when struck by contact with clod it feels pain, when struck by contact with stick it feels pain, when struck by contact with knife it feels pain. And it has been said by the Blessed One in the simile of the saw: “Even if bandits or highway robbers were to carve the monk limb from limb with a two-handled saw, bhikkhus, he who harbors ill will in his mind toward them is no follower of my teaching.” My energy shall be aroused, unslackened; mindfulness shall be established, not confused; the body shall be calm, not tense; the mind shall be concentrated, one-pointed. Let them now strike this body with contact with hand, let them strike with contact with clod, let them strike with contact with stick, let them strike with contact with knife. This is how the teaching of the Buddhas is to be practiced.’
translations.mn28:26: Just as, friend, depending on wood, depending on creepers, depending on grass, depending on clay, space surrounded becomes reckoned simply as a house; even so, friend, depending on bones, depending on sinews, depending on flesh, depending on skin, space surrounded becomes reckoned simply as form.
translations.mn28:27: When, friend, the internal eye is not injured and external forms do not come into range, and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no arising of the corresponding portion of consciousness. When, friend, the internal eye is not injured and external forms come into range, but there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no arising of the corresponding portion of consciousness. But when, friend, the internal eye is not injured and external forms come into range, and there is a corresponding engagement, then there is arising of the corresponding portion of consciousness.
translations.mn28:28: That form as it really is is included in the form aggregate with clinging, that feeling as it really is is included in the feeling aggregate with clinging, that perception as it really is is included in the perception aggregate with clinging, those volitional formations as they really are are included in the volitional formations aggregate with clinging, that consciousness as it really is is included in the consciousness aggregate with clinging. He understands thus: ‘So indeed the gathering, assembling, and conglomeration of these five aggregates with clinging is the massing of suffering. And it has been said by the Blessed One: “One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.” And these five aggregates with clinging are dependently arisen. Whatever desire, attachment, inclination, underlying tendency there is with regard to these five aggregates with clinging, that is the origin of suffering. Whatever removal of desire and lust, abandonment of desire and lust there is with regard to these five aggregates with clinging, that is the cessation of suffering.’ In this way, friend, a monk has done much.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friend, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates with clinging are suffering. What are the five aggregates with clinging? They are: the form aggregate with clinging, the feeling aggregate with clinging, the perception aggregate with clinging, the volitional formations aggregate with clinging, the consciousness aggregate with clinging.
translations.mn28:37: The mind is uninjured, external phenomena do not come into range, and there is no corresponding engagement, then there is no arising of the corresponding portion of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There comes a time, friend, when the external water element becomes stirred up. At that time the external earth element disappears. For what reason, friend, with regard to this vast external earth element, its impermanence will become manifest, its nature of passing away will become manifest, its nature of fading away will become manifest, its nature of changing will become manifest. But as for this insignificant body subject to craving, how could ‘I am,’ ‘mine,’ ‘I’ arise here? And for him it does not.
translations.mn29:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One, with reference to Devadatta, addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.mn29:3: Here, bhikkhus, some clansman who has faith goes forth from the household life into homelessness: ‘I have been overwhelmed by birth, by aging, by death, by sorrow, by lamentation, by pain, by displeasure, by despair, overwhelmed by suffering, overcome by suffering; surely there might be some way out of this whole mass of suffering.’ Having gone forth in this way, he generates gain, honor, and fame. He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and fame, nor does he make full resolve with regard to it. He does not exalt himself or disparage others because of that gain, honor, and fame. He does not become intoxicated or infatuated with it, nor does he commit negligence. Being non-negligent, he attains virtue. He is satisfied with that virtue and makes full resolve with regard to it. He exalts himself and disparages others because of that virtue: ‘I am virtuous, of good character, but these other bhikkhus are of bad virtue, evil character.’ He becomes intoxicated and infatuated with that virtue and commits negligence; being negligent, he dwells in suffering. Just as, bhikkhus, a man seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, seeking to wander in search of heartwood, passing over the heartwood of a standing mature tree with heartwood, would pass over the heartwood and take only the outer wood, pass over the outer wood and take only the bark, pass over the bark and take only the sapwood, cut it off and carry it away thinking it was heartwood. A man with vision, seeing him, might say: ‘This good man does not know heartwood, does not know outer wood, does not know bark, does not know sapwood, does not know twigs and leaves. Thus this good man, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, seeking to wander in search of heartwood, passing over the heartwood of a standing mature tree with heartwood, passes over the heartwood and takes only the outer wood, passes over the outer wood and takes only the bark, passes over the bark and takes only the sapwood, cuts it off and carries it away thinking it was heartwood; what is to be done with heartwood he will not experience.’
translations.mn2:10: And which, monks, are the phenomena that are not to be given attention, which one does not give attention to? Those phenomena, monks, with regard to which, when one gives attention to them, if the sensual taint has not arisen, it arises; if arisen, it increases; if the taint of becoming has not arisen, it arises; if arisen, it increases; if the taint of ignorance has not arisen, it arises; if arisen, it increases—these phenomena are not to be given attention, which one does not give attention to. And which, monks, are the phenomena that are to be given attention, which one gives attention to? Those phenomena, monks, with regard to which, when one gives attention to them, if the sensual taint has not arisen, it does not arise; if arisen, it is abandoned; if the taint of becoming has not arisen, it does not arise; if arisen, it is abandoned; if the taint of ignorance has not arisen, it does not arise; if arisen, it is abandoned—these phenomena are to be given attention, which one gives attention to. For him, with non-attention to phenomena that are not to be given attention, with attention to phenomena that are to be given attention, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: He gives wise attention thus: ‘This is suffering’; he gives wise attention thus: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he gives wise attention thus: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he gives wise attention thus: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ For him giving wise attention thus, three fetters are abandoned—identity view, doubt, attachment to precepts and vows. These, monks, are called taints to be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Taints to be abandoned by restraint. And which, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint? Here, monks, a monk dwells with restraint of the eye faculty, having wisely reflected. Whatever taints, burning and torment, would arise for him dwelling without restraint of the eye faculty, for him dwelling with restraint of the eye faculty, those taints, burning and torment, are not. He dwells with restraint of the ear faculty, having wisely reflected …pe… with restraint of the nose faculty …pe… with restraint of the tongue faculty …pe… with restraint of the body faculty …pe… with restraint of the mind faculty. Whatever taints, burning and torment, would arise for him dwelling without restraint of the mind faculty, for him dwelling with restraint of the mind faculty, those taints, burning and torment, are not. Whatever taints, burning and torment, would arise for him dwelling without restraint, for him dwelling with restraint, those taints, burning and torment, are not. These, monks, are called taints to be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: He uses almsfood having wisely reflected: ‘Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, only for the maintenance and support of this body, for stopping harm, for supporting the holy life; thus I shall put an end to old feeling and not produce new feeling, and I shall be blameless and dwell at ease.’
translations.mn2:16: He uses medicines and requisites for curing the sick having wisely reflected: ‘Only for the warding off of arisen afflicting feelings, for the utmost freedom from affliction.’
translations.mn2:17: Whatever taints, burning and torment, would arise for him from not using, from using, those taints, burning and torment, are not. These, monks, are called taints to be abandoned by using.
translations.mn2:3: ‘I say the destruction of the taints, monks, for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and see.’ And what, monks, does one know, what does one see, for the destruction of the taints? Wise attention and unwise attention. Unwise attention, monks, when given, both unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase; but wise attention, monks, when given, unarisen taints do not arise and arisen taints are abandoned.
translations.mn2:6: And which, monks, are the phenomena that are not to be given attention, which one gives attention to? Those phenomena, monks, with regard to which, when one gives attention to them, if the sensual taint has not arisen, it arises; if arisen, it increases; if the taint of becoming has not arisen, it arises; if arisen, it increases; if the taint of ignorance has not arisen, it arises; if arisen, it increases—these phenomena are not to be given attention, which one gives attention to. And which, monks, are the phenomena that are to be given attention, which one does not give attention to? Those phenomena, monks, with regard to which, when one gives attention to them, if the sensual taint has not arisen, it does not arise; if arisen, it is abandoned; if the taint of becoming has not arisen, it does not arise; if arisen, it is abandoned; if the taint of ignorance has not arisen, it does not arise; if arisen, it is abandoned—these phenomena are to be given attention, which one does not give attention to.
translations.mn2:7: For him, with attention to phenomena that are not to be given attention, with non-attention to phenomena that are to be given attention, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase. He gives unwise attention thus: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past? Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I be in the future?’ Or else, with regard to the present moment, there is internal perplexity: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go?’
translations.mn2:8: When he engages in unwise attention in this way, one of six views arises. ‘I have a self’—this view arises in him as true and firm; or ‘I have no self’—this view arises in him as true and firm; or ‘With self I perceive self’—this view arises in him as true and firm; or ‘With self I perceive not-self’—this view arises in him as true and firm; or ‘With not-self I perceive self’—this view arises in him as true and firm; or else he has such a view: ‘My self, which speaks and feels, experiences here and there the results of good and bad deeds; my self is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will stay just like that forever.’ This, monks, is called a view-gone-to, a view-entangled, a view-jungle, a view-vermin, a view-trembling, a view-fetter. Monks, the unlearned ordinary person fettered by a view-fetter is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say he is not freed from suffering.
translations.mn2:9: And, monks, the learned noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the doctrine of the noble ones, well-trained in the doctrine of the noble ones; has seen good men, is skilled in the doctrine of good men, well-trained in the doctrine of good men—knows dhammas that are fit for attention, knows dhammas that are unfit for attention. He, knowing dhammas that are unfit for attention does not attend to them, and knowing dhammas that are fit for attention attends to them.
translations.mn31:10: ‘Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha. But have you, Anuruddha, dwelling diligent, ardent, resolute, attained a superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding beyond human states?’ ‘How could that be, sir? Here, sir, as long as we wish, secluded from pleasures of the senses, secluded from unskillful dhammas, we enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, sir, is the superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones that we, dwelling diligent, ardent, resolute, have attained, a comfortable abiding.’
translations.mn31:11-13: ‘Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha. But with the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding beyond human states?’ ‘How could that be, sir? Here, sir, as long as we wish, with the fading away of applied and sustained thought, with the internal assurance of mind, one-pointedness of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of samādhi, we enter and dwell in the second jhāna. With the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones that we have attained, a comfortable abiding.’
translations.mn31:14: ‘Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha. But with the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding beyond human states?’ ‘How could that be, sir? Here, sir, as long as we wish, with the fading away of rapture we dwell equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, experiencing pleasure with the body, as the noble ones declare: “He dwells equanimous and mindful, one who abides in pleasure”—we enter and dwell in the third jhāna. With the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones that we have attained, a comfortable abiding.’
translations.mn31:15: ‘Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha. But with the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding beyond human states?’ ‘How could that be, sir? Here, sir, as long as we wish, with the giving up of pleasure and the giving up of pain, and with the previous disappearance of both joy and displeasure, we enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-painful-nor-pleasant purification of mindfulness by equanimity. With the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones that we have attained, a comfortable abiding.’
translations.mn31:16: ‘Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha. But with the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding beyond human states?’ ‘How could that be, sir? Here, sir, as long as we wish, completely transcending perceptions of forms, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, ‘space is infinite’—we enter and dwell in the dimension of infinite space. With the surmounting of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this is another superhuman distinction in vision and knowledge worthy of the noble ones that we have attained, a comfortable abiding.’
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One, having instructed, inspired, fired, and delighted the venerables Anuruddha, Nanda, and Kimila with a talk on Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: At that time, the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nanda, and the venerable Kimila were dwelling in the Gosinga Sal Grove.
translations.mn31:3: Then the Blessed One, having emerged from retreat in the evening, went to the Gosinga Sal Grove. The grove-keeper saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: ‘Do not enter this grove, recluse. Three clansmen who are self-willed are dwelling here. Do not disturb them.’
translations.mn31:4: The venerable Anuruddha heard the grove-keeper conversing with the Blessed One. Having heard, he said to the grove-keeper: ‘Do not obstruct the Blessed One, friend grove-keeper. Our Teacher has arrived.’ Then the venerable Anuruddha went to the venerables Nanda and Kimila; having gone, he said to the venerables Nanda and Kimila: ‘Come forward, venerables, come forward, venerables, our Teacher has arrived.’
translations.mn31:5: Then venerables Anuruddha, Nanda, and Kimila, having approached the Blessed One— one received the Blessed One's bowl and robes, one prepared a seat, one set out foot-water. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Those venerables, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. To venerable Anuruddha, seated to one side, the Blessed One said: “I hope you are comfortable, Anuruddha, I hope you are getting by, I hope you are not wearied by almsfood?” “We are comfortable, Blessed One, we are getting by, Blessed One; and we, venerable sir, are not wearied by almsfood.”
translations.mn31:6: “And are you dwelling in concord, Anuruddha, delighting together, without dispute, like milk blended with water, looking upon each other with friendly eyes?” “Indeed we, venerable sir, are dwelling in concord, delighting together, without dispute, like milk blended with water, looking upon each other with friendly eyes.” “But how do you dwell thus, Anuruddha, in concord, delighting together, without dispute, like milk blended with water, looking upon each other with friendly eyes?”
translations.mn31:9: “Indeed we, venerable sir, dwell diligent, ardent, resolute.” “But how do you dwell thus, Anuruddha, diligent, ardent, resolute? “Here, venerable sir, whichever of us returns first from almsround in the village, he prepares the seats, sets out drinking water and food, sets out the spittoon. Whichever returns later from almsround in the village, if there is leftover food and he wants, he eats it; if he does not want, he throws it away where there is no living beings or pours it into water without living beings. He puts away the seats, puts away the drinking water and food, puts away the spittoon, sweeps the dining area. Whichever sees that the water pot, food pot, or milk pot is empty or lacking, he sets it out. If there is something not one's duty, calling a second with a hand gesture, we set it out with a hand signal, but we, venerable sir, do not on that account break silence. But every five days, venerable sir, we sit down for recitation of the Teaching all night. Thus, venerable sir, we dwell diligent, ardent, resolute.”
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Forest in the peaked-roof hall.
translations.mn36:10: “Thus I am confident in the venerable Gotama. For the venerable Gotama has developed body and developed mind.” “Indeed, Aggivessana, this has been brought to you and presented, but I will explain it to you. Aggivessana, since I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ochre robes, and went forth from home to homelessness, it is not possible that arisen pleasant feeling will seize my mind and remain, or arisen painful feeling will seize my mind and remain.”
translations.mn36:12: “What else could there be, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta not yet fully enlightened, this thought arose in me: ‘The householder's life is narrow, the way of renunciation is wide open. It is not easy for one living at home to live the utterly perfect, utterly pure, bright holy life. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from home to homelessness.’
translations.mn36:2: And on that occasion the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, was desirous of entering Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: Then, Aggivessana, this thought arose in me: ‘Suppose I, pressing tooth on tooth, pressing tongue against the palate, should restrain, oppress, and torment my mind with my mind.’ So, Aggivessana, I pressed tooth on tooth, pressed tongue against the palate, and restrained, oppressed, and tormented my mind with my mind. While, Aggivessana, I was restraining, oppressing, and tormenting my mind with my mind, pressing tooth on tooth, pressing tongue against the palate, sweat broke out on my armpits. Just as, Aggivessana, a strong man seizing a weaker man by the head or shoulders would restrain, oppress, and torment him; even so, Aggivessana, while I was restraining, oppressing, and tormenting my mind with my mind, pressing tooth on tooth, pressing tongue against the palate, sweat broke out on my armpits. But my energy was exerted, not sluggish; mindfulness was established, not confused; and my body was ardent, not tranquil, because of the painful striving of one who strives painfully. Even such arisen painful feeling did not seize my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:26: And, Aggivessana, seeing me, some deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is done for.’ Some deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not done for, but he is striving in due season.’ Some deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not done for, nor is he striving in due season; the ascetic Gotama is an arahant, but his way of dwelling is just like that of an arahant.’
translations.mn36:27: Then, Aggivessana, this thought arose in me: ‘Suppose I should undertake complete fasting.’ Then, Aggivessana, deities came to me and said: ‘Do not undertake complete fasting, good sir. If you undertake complete fasting, we will infuse divine nourishment through the pores of your skin, and by that you will sustain yourself.’ Then, Aggivessana, this thought arose in me: ‘If I should declare that I have undertaken complete fasting, and these deities should infuse divine nourishment through the pores of my skin, and I should sustain myself by that, that would be a lie for me.’ So, Aggivessana, I rejected those deities, saying ‘enough.’
translations.mn36:28: Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me: ‘What if I were to eat only a little food, a little at a time, either mung bean broth, or kulattha bean broth, or chickpea broth, or pea broth?’ So, Aggivessana, I ate only a little food, a little at a time, either mung bean broth, or kulattha bean broth, or chickpea broth, or pea broth. While I was eating only a little food, a little at a time, either mung bean broth, or kulattha bean broth, or chickpea broth, or pea broth, my body reached extreme emaciation. Just as it were the śītikā or kāḷapabbā stalks; so too my limbs became like that due to that meager food. Just as it were a pair of bamboo splints; so too my backside became like that due to that meager food. Just as it were a tortoise’s carapace; so too my spine became humped due to that meager food. Just as it were the rafters of a dilapidated house that are slipping and collapsing; so too my ribs were slipping and collapsing due to that meager food. Just as it were the stars visible deep in a deep well, sunken and far down; so too the pupils of my eyes appeared sunken and far down in their sockets due to that meager food. Just as it were a fresh-cut bitter gourd, withered by wind and sun, shriveled up; so too my scalp became shriveled up due to that meager food. When I wanted to touch my belly skin, I only grasped my backbone, Aggivessana; when I wanted to touch my backbone, I only grasped my belly skin, such that my belly skin and backbone were stuck together due to that meager food. When I wanted to defecate or urinate, Aggivessana, I fell on the spot there due to that meager food. When I wanted to relieve this body, Aggivessana, I stroked my limbs with my hand. While I was stroking my limbs with my hand, Aggivessana, the hairs of my body, rotten at the roots, fell out due to that meager food.
translations.mn36:29: And, Aggivessana, people who saw me said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black, he is brown.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black, nor brown, the ascetic Gotama has discolored skin.’ Such was my pure bright skin color, clear and radiant, due to that meager food.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son, walking and wandering for exercise, went to the Great Forest, to the assembly hall. Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son coming from afar. Having seen him, he said to the Blessed One: ‘This Saccaka, sir, the Nigaṇṭha’s son is coming, a speaker of fallacies, considered a sophist by many people. He, sir, wants to disparage the Buddha, wants to disparage the Dhamma, wants to disparage the Saṅgha. May the Blessed One please sit a moment out of compassion.’ The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son went to the Blessed One; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:30: Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have felt painful, sharp, severe, harsh, and bitter feelings by undergoing extreme practices, the utmost is just this much, not more. And whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will feel painful, sharp, severe, harsh, and bitter feelings by undergoing extreme practices, the utmost is just this much, not more. And whatever ascetics or brahmins at present are feeling painful, sharp, severe, harsh, and bitter feelings by undergoing extreme practices, the utmost is just this much, not more. But with this harsh, difficult ascetic practice I do not attain a superhuman state, a noble knowledge and vision beyond human. Could there be another path to awakening?’
translations.mn36:32: Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me: ‘Am I afraid of that pleasure, which is pleasure apart from sensual pleasures and unwholesome dhammas?’ Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me: ‘I am not afraid of that pleasure, which is pleasure apart from sensual pleasures and unwholesome dhammas.’
translations.mn36:34: So, Aggivessana, having eaten substantial food and gained strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome dhammas, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which has thought and applied thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Even such arisen pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, did not take hold of my mind or remain.
translations.mn36:38: With mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, become soft, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives. I recollected many past lives, that is to say—one birth … and so on—thus with details and signs I recollected many past lives.
translations.mn36:39: This, Aggivessana, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose, as I dwelt diligent, ardent, and resolute. Even such arisen pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, did not take hold of my mind or remain.
translations.mn36:4: “There are some ascetics and brahmins, Gotama, who are devoted to the practice of developing the body, but not the mind. For they experience bodily painful feeling. Previously, Gotama, when one was touched by bodily painful feeling, there might be leg cramps, the heart might burst, hot blood might issue from the mouth, one might attain madness and mental distraction. For such a one, Gotama, the mind follows the body, it goes along according to the body. Why is that? Because the mind is undeveloped. But there are some ascetics and brahmins, Gotama, who are devoted to the practice of developing the mind, but not the body. For they experience mental painful feeling. Previously, Gotama, when one was touched by mental painful feeling, there might be leg cramps, the heart might burst, hot blood might issue from the mouth, one might attain madness and mental distraction. For such a one, Gotama, the body follows the mind, it goes along according to the mind. Why is that? Because the body is undeveloped. And for me, Gotama, it is thus: ‘Surely the venerable Gotama’s disciples dwell devoted to the practice of developing the mind, but not the body.’”
translations.mn36:40: With mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, become soft, workable, steady, attained to imperturbability, I directed mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood beings by their karma …pe…
translations.mn36:42: With mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, become soft, workable, steady, attained to imperturbability, I directed mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew as it actually is: ‘These are taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of taints’; I directly knew as it actually is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of taints.’
translations.mn36:43: When I thus knew and thus saw, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensuality, liberated from the taint of existence, liberated from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’
translations.mn36:45: I recall, Aggivessana, teaching Dhamma to numerous assemblies of hundreds. Yet each individual thinks: ‘The ascetic Gotama teaches Dhamma beginning with me.’ But it should not be seen like this, Aggivessana; the Tathāgata teaches Dhamma to others only for the sake of making it clear. And I, Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very discourse, on that same meditation object, settle, make steady, make one-pointed, and concentrate my mind within, by which I regularly abide. “This should be approved of for the venerable Gotama, as it is for an arahant, a fully enlightened Buddha. But does the venerable Gotama sleep by day?”
translations.mn36:46: “I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after the alms round, returning from alms, having spread out a set of three robes on the right side, mindful and aware, I lie down for a siesta.” “Some ascetics and brahmins, Gotama, say this is a confused abiding.” “It is not, Aggivessana, by that much that one is confused or not confused. But, Aggivessana, how one is confused and not confused, listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” Saccaka, the Nigaṇṭha’s son, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn36:47: “Whoever, Aggivessana, has those taints that defile, cause rebirth, are with sorrow, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, and they are unabandoned, him I say is confused. For with the non-abandonment of taints, Aggivessana, one is confused. Whoever, Aggivessana, has those taints that defile, cause rebirth, are with sorrow, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, and they are abandoned, him I say is not confused. For with the abandonment of taints, Aggivessana, one is not confused. For a Tathāgata, Aggivessana, those taints that defile, cause rebirth, are with sorrow, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, are abandoned, their root destroyed, like a palm tree made a stump, made incapable of growing again, a non-arising condition in the future. Just as, Aggivessana, a palm tree whose top has been cut off is incapable of further growth; even so, Aggivessana, for a Tathāgata those taints that defile, cause rebirth, are with sorrow, result in suffering, and lead to future birth, aging, and death, are abandoned, their root destroyed, like a palm tree made a stump, made incapable of growing again, a non-arising condition in the future.”
translations.mn36:5: “But what, Aggivessana, is body development as you have heard?” “Just this—Nanda Vaccha, Kiso Saṅkicca, Makkhali Gosāla—these go naked, unshackled, licking their hands, not using a toothpick after meals, do not accept an invitation, a meal prepared specially, or one announced in advance; they do not receive a kumbhimukha, a kaḷopimukha, between two eating, from a pregnant woman, from one who is suckling, from one who is in a house, from those with spots, where flies are buzzing, where there is a dog, where there are snakes; they do not eat fish, meat, intoxicants, brewed drinks, or buttermilk. They are one-house dwellers or one-morsel eaters, two-house dwellers or two-morsel eaters …pe… seven-house dwellers or seven-morsel eaters. They live on one gift, on two gifts …pe… on seven gifts. They take food once a day, twice a day …pe… seven days. Thus they dwell devoted to the practice of fortnightly complete almsfood.”}
translations.mn36:6: “But do you maintain yourselves just with that much, Aggivessana?” “No, good Gotama. Sometimes, good Gotama, they eat superior solid food, consume superior soft food, drink superior drinks, anoint themselves with superior ointments. Do they thereby sustain this body, strengthen it, support it?” “Whatever you previously discarded and later take up, Aggivessana, that becomes the accumulation and storing up for this body. But have you heard of mind-development, Aggivessana?” Questioned by the Blessed One about mind-development, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son was unable to reply.
translations.mn36:8: “And how, Aggivessana, is the body undeveloped and the mind undeveloped? Here, Aggivessana, for an unlearned ordinary person there arises pleasant feeling. Touched by that pleasant feeling, he becomes attached to pleasure and falls into attachment to pleasure. That pleasant feeling ceases. With the cessation of that pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, he sorrows, grieves, laments, weeps beating his breast, and falls into confusion. For him, Aggivessana, this arisen pleasant feeling persists seizing the mind because the body is undeveloped; this arisen painful feeling persists seizing the mind because the mind is undeveloped. For anyone, Aggivessana, for whom, on both sides, this arisen pleasant feeling persists seizing the mind because the body is undeveloped, this arisen painful feeling persists seizing the mind because the mind is undeveloped, that is how, Aggivessana, the body is undeveloped and the mind undeveloped.
translations.mn36:9: “And how, Aggivessana, is the body developed and the mind developed? Here, Aggivessana, for a learned noble disciple there arises pleasant feeling. Touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not become attached to pleasure, nor does he fall into attachment to pleasure. That pleasant feeling ceases. With the cessation of that pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, he does not sorrow, does not grieve, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, nor does he fall into confusion. For him, Aggivessana, this arisen pleasant feeling does not persist seizing the mind because the body is developed; this arisen painful feeling does not persist seizing the mind because the mind is developed. For anyone, Aggivessana, for whom, on both sides, this arisen pleasant feeling does not persist seizing the mind because the body is developed, this arisen painful feeling does not persist seizing the mind because the mind is developed—that is how, Aggivessana, the body is developed and the mind developed.”
translations.mn38:10: “‘This is real,’ monks, does doubt give rise to uncertainty?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It exists because of food,’ monks, does doubt give rise to uncertainty?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘With the cessation of food, what is real, that is impermanent,’ monks, does doubt give rise to uncertainty?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:11: “‘This is real,’ monks, when one sees it as it really is with right understanding, any uncertainty is abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It exists because of food,’ monks, when one sees it as it really is with right understanding, any uncertainty is abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘With the cessation of food, what is real, that is impermanent,’ monks, when one sees it as it really is with right understanding, any uncertainty is abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:12: “‘This is real,’ monks, are you free from uncertainty about that here?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It exists because of food,’ monks, are you free from uncertainty about that here?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘With the cessation of food, what is real, that is impermanent,’ monks, are you free from uncertainty about that here?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:13: “‘This is real,’ monks, is it well seen as it really is with right understanding?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It exists because of food,’ monks, is it well seen as it really is with right understanding?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘With the cessation of food, what is real, that is impermanent,’ monks, is it well seen as it really is with right understanding?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:14: “If you, monks, were to cling to, adhere to, be attached to, regard as ‘mine’ this view so pure, so purified, would you understand the simile of the raft taught by me as taught for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?” “No, venerable sir.” “If you, monks, do not cling to, adhere to, be attached to, regard as ‘mine’ this view so pure, so purified, would you understand the simile of the raft taught by me as taught for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:15: “There are these four kinds of food, monks, for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, for the assistance of those seeking birth. What four? Material food, coarse or subtle; contact is the second; mental intention is the third; consciousness is the fourth.
translations.mn38:17: Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense fields; with the six sense fields as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, grasping; with grasping as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:19: “Good, monks. Thus you say too, monks, and I say too: When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. That is: With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense fields; with the six sense fields as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, grasping; with grasping as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”}
translations.mn38:2: At that time, a monk named Sāti, son of a fisherman, had this evil view arisen: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, this very consciousness persists, wanders on, not another.”
translations.mn38:20: With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense fields; with the cessation of the six sense fields, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the complete cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: “Good, monks. Thus, monks, you also speak thus, and I also speak thus—when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases, namely: with the cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense fields; with the cessation of the six sense fields, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.mn38:23: “Monks, knowing and seeing thus, would you posit a past [existence]: ‘Were we in the past, were we not in the past, were we something in the past, were we thus in the past, having been what, were we in the past?’” “No, sir.” “Monks, knowing and seeing thus, would you posit a future [existence]: ‘Will we be in the future, will we not be in the future, will we be something in the future, will we be thus in the future, having been what, will we be in the future?’” “No, sir.”
translations.mn38:25: “Good, monks. Monks, you have been brought to this visible, immediate, inviting, direct, personal, to-be-known-by-the-wise Dhamma. Monks, this Dhamma is visible, immediate, inviting, direct, to-be-known-by-the-wise personally—thus was it said, and in reference to this was it said.”
translations.mn38:26: Monks, there are three conjunctions that lead to conception in a womb. Here, the parents come together, but the mother is not in season, and the being-to-be-conceived has not approached—there is no conception then. Here, the parents come together, the mother is in season, and the being-to-be-conceived has not approached—there is no conception then. But, monks, when the parents come together, the mother is in season, and the being-to-be-conceived has approached—thus these three conjunctions lead to conception in a womb.
translations.mn38:27: Monks, the mother carries the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months, with great anxiety, burdened. Monks, after nine or ten months, the mother gives birth to it, with great anxiety, burdened. Once born, it is nurtured with its own blood. And this, monks, in the noble discipline is called maternal blood.
translations.mn38:28: Monks, that boy, growing up, developing his faculties, plays at the toys of boys, such as: stick games, toy-ploughs, tip-cat, hoops, toy-ploughs, carts, bows.
translations.mn38:39: Having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of mind, weakeners of wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with internal assurance of mind, unification of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna …pe… third jhāna …pe… fourth jhāna.
translations.mn38:6: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “What do you think, monks, is this monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, even slightly ordained in this Dhamma and discipline?” “How could it be, sir? No, sir.” When this was said, the monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, sat silent, abashed, with drooping shoulders, downcast eyes, dejected, without response. Then the Blessed One, having seen the monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, sitting silent, abashed, with drooping shoulders, downcast eyes, dejected, without response, said to him: “You will be known, you foolish man, by this own evil view. Here I will question the monks.”
translations.mn38:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, do you also understand the Dhamma I have taught such that this monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, by his own wrong grasp, misrepresents me and digs his own pit, and creates much demerit?” “No, sir. For in many ways, sir, dependent-originated consciousness has been declared by the Blessed One: apart from conditions, there is no arising of consciousness.” “Good, good, monks. Good, monks, you understand the Dhamma I have taught thus. For in many ways, monks, dependent-originated consciousness has been declared by me: apart from conditions, there is no arising of consciousness.” And yet this monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, by his own wrong grasp, misrepresents me and digs his own pit, and creates much demerit. That will be for this foolish man for a long time for his harm and suffering.
translations.mn38:9: “Do you see, monks, ‘This is arisen’?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see, monks, ‘It has arisen from nutriment’?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see, monks, ‘With the cessation of nutriment, what has arisen has the nature to cease’?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn41:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the lands of the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at Sālā, a village of Kosalan brahmins.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous and uneven conduct by mind? Here, householders, a certain person is covetous, coveting the belongings of others: ‘O that what belongs to others would be mine!’ He has a hostile mind, a corrupted thought: ‘May these beings be killed or hurt or destroyed or annihilated or not exist!’ He has wrong view, perverted vision: ‘There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are no in this world ascetics or brahmins who have reached the highest and perfectly practiced, who by themselves know and realize and proclaim this world and the other world.’ Thus, householders, is there threefold unrighteous and uneven conduct by mind. Because of unrighteous and uneven conduct, householders, some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of woe, in a bad destination, in the underworld, in hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous and even conduct by body? Here, householders, a certain person abstains from killing living beings, has given up violence towards living beings, is one who is conscientious, scrupulous, possessed of compassion, sympathetic towards the welfare of all living beings. He abstains from taking what is not given. Whatever belongs to others, whether in a village or in the forest, he does not take it by way of theft. He abstains from sexual misconduct. He does not approach those protected by mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, clan, protected by the Dhamma, those with a master, those provided with a means of livelihood, even those covered by a garland and head-dress. Thus, householders, is there threefold righteous and even conduct by body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is there fourfold righteous and even conduct by speech? Here, householders, a certain person abstains from false speech. When summoned to a meeting, assembly, among relatives, guild, or royal court, and questioned as a witness: ‘Come, good man, say what you know,’ he does not say what he does not know: ‘I do not know’; does not say what he knows: ‘I know’; does not say what he has not seen: ‘I have not seen’; does not say what he has seen: ‘I have seen.’ Thus he does not knowingly speak false speech for his own sake, for another's sake, or for the sake of material gain. He abstains from malicious speech. Having heard here, he does not tell it there for the purpose of division; having heard there, he does not tell it here for the purpose of division. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided, a promoter of friendship among those who are friends; he delights, rejoices, and is glad in concord, and speaks words conducive to concord. He abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such speech as is gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, courteous, agreeable and pleasing to the many. He abstains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, what is factual, what is purposeful, about the Dhamma and the Discipline; he speaks words worth treasuring, with similes, with a definite aim, connected with the goal. Thus, householders, is there fourfold righteous and even conduct by speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous and even conduct by mind? Here, householders, a certain person is not covetous, does not covet the belongings of others: ‘O that what belongs to others would be mine!’ He has a non-hostile mind, an uncorrupted thought: ‘May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, may they look after themselves happily!’ He has right view, unperverted vision: ‘There is giving, there is offering, there is sacrifice; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is another world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are in this world ascetics and brahmins who have reached the highest and perfectly practiced, who by themselves know and realize and proclaim this world and the other world.’ Thus, householders, is there threefold righteous and even conduct by mind. Because of righteous and even conduct, householders, some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If, householders, a righteous and even conductor should wish: ‘O that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might be reborn among noble warrior great clans!’ It is possible that he, on the dissolution of the body, after death, might be reborn among noble warrior great clans. Why is that? Because he is a righteous and even conductor.
translations.mn41:3: Then the Sāleyyaka brahmin householders went to the Blessed One. Some, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging courteous greetings and polite talk, sat down to one side; some, having raised their hands in reverence towards the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some, having announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some sat down to one side silently. Sitting to one side, the Sāleyyaka brahmin householders said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn41:4: “What is the cause, what is the reason, Gotama sir, by which some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of woe, in a bad destination, in the underworld, in hell? And what is the cause, what is the reason, Gotama sir, by which some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world?”
translations.mn41:43: “Suppose, householders, a righteous liver of righteousness should wish: ‘Oh, that by the destruction of the taints I might dwell having realized for myself through direct knowledge here and now the taint-free deliverance of mind, deliverance through wisdom.’ And it is possible that a righteous liver of righteousness might dwell having realized for himself through direct knowledge here and now, by the destruction of the taints, the taint-free deliverance of mind, deliverance through wisdom. Why is that? Because he is a righteous liver of righteousness.”
translations.mn41:5: “Householders, it is because of unrighteous conduct, improper conduct, that some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld. Householders, it is because of righteous conduct, proper conduct, that some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a good destination, the heavenly world.”
translations.mn41:6: “We do not understand in detail the meaning of what the Blessed Gotama has spoken in brief without explaining the meaning in detail. May the Blessed Gotama teach the Dhamma to us in such a way that we may understand in detail the meaning of what he has spoken in brief without explaining the meaning in detail.” “Very well then, householders, listen, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the householder brāhmaṇas of Sāleyya replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn41:8: “And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous and improper conduct by body? Here, householders, a certain person is a killer of living beings, murderous, blood-handed, given to blows and thumps, merciless to living beings. He is a taker of what is not given. He takes what belongs to another—whether in a village or in the forest—and he takes by way of theft what is not given. He is one who engages in sexual misconduct. He engages in sexual intercourse with women who are protected by mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, clan, or who are guarded by the Dhamma, married, covered by a counter-penalty, even those enclosed by a fence. Thus, householders, there is threefold unrighteous and improper conduct by body.
translations.mn41:9: “And how, householders, is there fourfold unrighteous and improper conduct by speech? Here, householders, a certain person is a liar. In an assembly, in a gathering, in the midst of kin, in a guild, or in the king’s court, when summoned as a witness and questioned: ‘Come, good man, tell what you know,’ he says of what he does not know: ‘I know’; of what he knows: ‘I do not know’; of what he has not seen: ‘I have seen’; of what he has seen: ‘I have not seen.’ Thus he speaks falsehood for his own sake, or for another’s sake, or for some material gain. He is a divisive speaker. Having heard something here, he tells it there to cause a rift among these; having heard something there, he tells it here to cause a rift among those. Thus he is a divisive speaker for those who are harmonious, one who encourages discord among those who are in discord, delighted in factions, enjoying factions, exhilarated by factions, one who speaks words that foster factions. He is a harsh speaker. He speaks such speech as is rough, coarse, harsh, cutting, disagreeable to others, abrasive, not leading to concentration. He is a frivolous talker. He speaks untimely, untrue, unbeneficial, against the Dhamma, against discipline. He speaks words that have no substance, untimely, without reason, endless, unbeneficial. Thus, householders, there is fourfold unrighteous and improper conduct by speech.
translations.mn4:20: Then, brāhmaṇa, this thought occurred to me: ‘Why don’t I dwell in those terrifying, hair-raising shrine houses in parks, shrine houses in forests, shrine houses at trees—those nights that are well-known and designated: the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—in such sleeping places, so that perhaps I might see that fear and dread.’ So then, brāhmaṇa, later on, during those nights that are well-known and designated—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—I dwelt in those terrifying, hair-raising shrine houses in parks, shrine houses in forests, shrine houses at trees. And while I was dwelling there, brāhmaṇa, a deer would approach, or a peacock would knock down a twig, or the wind would rustle the leaves; and this thought occurred to me: ‘Surely this is that fear and dread coming.’ Then, brāhmaṇa, this thought occurred to me: ‘Why do I dwell expecting fear and dread from elsewhere? Why don’t I subdue that fear and dread while it has come to me as it really is, right there where it has come to me as it really is?’ While I was walking back and forth, brāhmaṇa, that fear and dread came upon me. I did not stop, nor sit down, nor lie down, but while walking back and forth I subdued that fear and dread. While I was standing, brāhmaṇa, that fear and dread came upon me. I did not walk back and forth, nor sit down, nor lie down, but while standing I subdued that fear and dread. While I was sitting, brāhmaṇa, that fear and dread came upon me. I did not lie down, nor stand up, nor walk back and forth, but while sitting I subdued that fear and dread. While I was lying down, brāhmaṇa, that fear and dread came upon me. I did not sit up, nor stand up, nor walk back and forth, but while lying down I subdued that fear and dread.
