translations.mn4:22-26: Now, brahmin, my energy was exerted, not lazy; mindfulness was established, not confused; the body was tranquil, not tense; the mind was concentrated, one-pointed. With mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past abodes. I recollected many past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so named, of such clan, such appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such lifespan; having died from there, I was reborn elsewhere; there too I was so named, of such clan, such appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such lifespan; having died from there, I have come here.’ Thus I recollected many past abodes with their aspects and particulars.
translations.mn4:27: With mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of men, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood beings by their karma: ‘These beings, possessed of bad conduct by body, bad conduct by speech, bad conduct by mind, abusive of the noble ones, holding wrong view, undertaking wrong-view karma— they, by the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in the plane of misery, a bad destination, the underworld. But these beings, possessed of good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, good conduct by mind, non-abusive of the noble ones, holding right view, undertaking right-view karma— they, by the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of men, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understood beings by their karma.
translations.mn4:28: This, brahmin, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, light arose, as one who is heedful, ardent, and resolute abides.
translations.mn4:29: This, brahmin, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, light arose, as one who is heedful, ardent, and resolute abides.
translations.mn4:3: And before my enlightenment, brahmin, while still a bodhisatta not yet fully enlightened, this thought occurred to me: ‘Dwelling places in remote forest or wilderness are hard to attain, seclusion is hard to practice, solitude is hard to enjoy, and for a monk who does not attain concentration, I think the mind carries him away to the forests.’
translations.mn4:30: This, brahmin, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, light arose, as one who is heedful, ardent, and resolute abides.
translations.mn4:34: Now perhaps, brahmin, you might think: ‘Surely the ascetic Gotama still has lust, hatred, and delusion, therefore he resorts to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness.’ But, brahmin, it should not be seen like this. Seeing two reasons, brahmin, I resort to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness— seeing my own dwelling in happiness in this very life, and having compassion for future generations.
translations.mn4:4: Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness with impure bodily action, on account of impure bodily action they invite unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not resort to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness with impure bodily action; I have pure bodily action. I am one of those among you noble ones with pure bodily action who resort to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness.’ Seeing pure bodily action in myself, brahmin, I had even greater joy in dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn4:5: Then, brahmin, this thought occurred to me: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins resort to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness with impure verbal action … impure mental action … impure livelihood … on account of impure livelihood they invite unwholesome fear and dread.
translations.mn4:6: But I do not resort to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness with impure livelihood; I have pure livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: I am one of those among you noble ones with pure livelihood who resort to dwellings in remote forest or wilderness.’ Seeing pure livelihood in myself, brahmin, I had even greater joy in dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in Beluvagāma. Now on that occasion the householder Dasama, the Aṭṭhakanāgara from Pāṭaliputta, had arrived there on some business.
translations.mn52:12: Again, householder, a monk, having completely surmounted perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, enters upon and abides in the base of infinite space, thinking ‘infinite space’. He reflects thus: ‘This attainment of the base of infinite space is conditioned, volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.’ Remaining there … he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn52:14: Again, householder, a monk, having completely surmounted the base of infinite consciousness, enters upon and abides in the base of nothingness, thinking ‘there is nothing’. He reflects thus: ‘This attainment of the base of nothingness is conditioned, volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.’ He attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then, through passion for that teaching, delight in that teaching, with the destruction of the five lower fetters he is one due to reappear elsewhere, who attains final nibbāna there, without return to this world. This too, householder, is one teaching declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One, whereby for a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet freed, it is freed; if the taints are not yet destroyed, they are destroyed; if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it.”
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to the venerable Ānanda: “Just as, venerable Ānanda, a man searching for one treasure trove should find eleven treasure troves at once; so too I, venerable sir, searching for one door to the deathless, have found eleven doors to the deathless suitable for practice. Just as, venerable sir, a house has eleven doors, and when that house is ablaze, he could escape with his life through any one of those doors; so too I, venerable sir, through any one of these eleven doors to the deathless, will be able to escape with my life. Surely, venerable sir, other sectarians will seek the teacher’s fee from their teacher, how much more then should I make an offering to the venerable Ānanda!”
translations.mn52:2: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka went to Kukkuṭārāma, to that certain monk; having gone, he paid homage to that monk and sat down at one side. Sitting at one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to that monk: “Where now, venerable sir, is the venerable Ānanda dwelling at present? We wish to see the venerable Ānanda.” “The venerable Ānanda, householder, is dwelling at Vesālī in Beluvagāma.”
translations.mn52:3: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka, having settled his affairs in Pāṭaliputta, went to Vesālī, to Beluvagāma, to the venerable Ānanda; having gone, he paid homage to the venerable Ānanda and sat down at one side. Sitting at one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka said to the venerable Ānanda: “Is there, venerable Ānanda, one teaching declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One, whereby for a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet freed, it is freed; if the taints are not yet destroyed, they are destroyed; if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it?” “There is, householder, one teaching declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One, whereby for a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet freed, it is freed; if the taints are not yet destroyed, they are destroyed; if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it.” “What then, venerable Ānanda, is that one teaching declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One, whereby for a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet freed, it is freed; if the taints are not yet destroyed, they are destroyed; if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it?”
translations.mn52:4: “Here, householder, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He reflects thus: ‘This first jhāna is conditioned, volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.’ He attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then, through passion for that teaching, delight in that teaching, with the destruction of the five lower fetters he is one due to reappear elsewhere, who attains final nibbāna there, without return to this world. This too, householder, is one teaching declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One, whereby for a monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, if his mind is not yet freed, it is freed; if the taints are not yet destroyed, they are destroyed; if he has not yet attained the unsurpassed security from bondage, he attains it.
translations.mn52:8: Again, householder, a monk abides pervading one direction with his mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, the third, the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, in every way, he abides pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. He reflects thus: ‘This liberation of mind by loving-kindness is conditioned, volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.’ Remaining there … he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn54:18: Just as, householder, a charcoal pit is a fathom or more in depth, full of glowing coals without flame or smoke. Then a man would come desiring to live, not desiring to die, desiring happiness, and disliking pain. Two strong men would grab him by the arms on both sides and drag him into the charcoal pit. What do you think, householder, would that man thrust his body into it? “Yes, venerable sir.” “Why is that?” “It is known to that man: ‘I will fall into this charcoal pit, and from that cause I will meet death or death-like pain.’ ” In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a charcoal pit, very painful, very dangerous, with much greater danger here.’ Having seen this as it really is with right understanding … he develops equanimity towards it.
translations.mn54:23: Now, householder, that noble disciple, relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness with equanimity, sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … in accordance with their karma, with divine vision purified and transcending that of humans, he knows beings.
translations.mn54:24: Now, householder, that noble disciple, relying on this supreme purity of mindfulness with equanimity, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless freedom of mind, freedom through wisdom.
translations.mn60:10: Here, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who say and hold this view: ‘There is giving … those who declare this having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, both this world and the other world’—for them it is to be expected that, having abandoned bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct—these three unskillful things—they will undertake and practice bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct—these three skillful things. Why is that? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins see danger, detriment, and defilement in unskillful things, and renunciation, benefit, and purity in skillful things.
translations.mn60:12: Here, householders, a wise man reflects: ‘If there is another world, then after the breakup of the body, after death, this good man will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world. Even if there is no other world, this good man, in the present life, will receive praise from the wise: “A virtuous person with right view, who affirms existence.” If there is another world, then for this good man there is gain in both ways—both the praise from the wise in the present life, and rebirth after the breakup of the body, after death, in a good destination, in the heavenly world. Thus this infallible teaching, well-practiced and undertaken, stands covering both sides, abandoning the unskillful position.
translations.mn60:13: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who say and hold this view: ‘In doing, in causing to do, in cutting, in causing to cut, in burning, in causing to burn, in tormenting, in causing to torment, in torturing, in causing to torture, in killing living beings, in taking what is not given, in breaking agreements, in plundering, in making one homeless, in standing on the outskirts, in going to the wife of another, in lying; in doing there is no evil. Even if one were to use a razor-edged wheel to make all the living beings on this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, there is no evil from that cause, there is no coming of evil. Even if one goes to the southern bank of the Ganges killing, slaying, cutting, causing to cut, burning, causing to burn; there is no evil from that cause, there is no coming of evil. Even if one goes to the northern bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, causing to sacrifice; there is no merit from that cause, there is no coming of merit. By giving, restraint, self-control, truthfulness there is no merit, there is no coming of merit.’
translations.mn60:14: Of those very ascetics and brahmins, householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak in direct opposition, and they say: ‘In doing, in causing to do, in cutting, in causing to cut, in burning, in causing to burn, in tormenting, in causing to torment, in torturing, in causing to torture, in killing living beings, in taking what is not given, in breaking agreements, in plundering, in making one homeless, in standing on the outskirts, in going to the wife of another, in lying; in doing there is evil. Even if one were to use a razor-edged wheel to make all the living beings on this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, there is evil from that cause, there is coming of evil. Even if one goes to the southern bank of the Ganges killing, slaying, cutting, causing to cut, burning, causing to burn; there is evil from that cause, there is coming of evil. Even if one goes to the northern bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, causing to sacrifice; there is merit from that cause, there is coming of merit. By giving, restraint, self-control, truthfulness there is merit, there is coming of merit.’ What do you think, householders, are not these ascetics and brahmins speaking in direct opposition to each other? “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn60:16: But there is action, and one holds the view ‘there is no action’; that is wrong view for her. There is action, and one intends ‘there is no action’; that is wrong intention for her. There is action, and one speaks the speech ‘there is no action’; that is wrong speech for her. There is action, and one says ‘there is no action,’ opposing those arahants who speak of action. There is action, and one persuades another ‘there is no action’; that is wrong persuasion for her. And by that wrong persuasion she disparages herself and belittles others. Thus beforehand her good conduct is abandoned, bad conduct is established—this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech opposed to the noble ones, wrong persuasion, self-praise, disparaging others. Thus many evil, unskillful things arise for her because of wrong view.
translations.mn60:17: There, householders, a wise person reflects like this: ‘If there is no action, this person will, with the breakup of the body, attain peace for himself alone; but if there is action, this person will, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, the underworld. Even if there is action, let the word of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; but this person here and now is blameworthy among the wise—a person of immoral conduct, wrong view, an advocate of no-action. If there is action, this person’s position is bad in both ways—what is blameworthy among the wise here and now, and what is reappearance with the breakup of the body, after death, in a plane of deprivation, a bad destination, the underworld. Thus this infallible teaching is badly grasped by him, he stands committed to one side, he abandons the position of the wholesome.
translations.mn60:19: But when there is action, the view ‘there is action’ arises for him; that is his right view. When there is action, he intends ‘there is action’; that is his right intention. When there is action, he speaks the word ‘there is action’; that is his right speech. When there is action, he says ‘there is action’; he does not oppose those arahants who advocate action. When there is action, he convinces another ‘there is action’; that is his teaching of the true Dhamma. And through that teaching of the true Dhamma, he neither praises himself nor disparages others. Thus his immoral conduct is previously abandoned, good conduct is established—and this right view, right intention, right speech, non-opposition to the noble ones, teaching of the true Dhamma, non self-praise, non disparagement of others. Thus many wholesome qualities arise for him because of right view.
translations.mn60:21: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘There is no cause, no reason for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or reason. There is no cause, no reason for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or reason. There is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly persistence; all beings, all persons, all souls, all living beings are without mastery, powerless, without energy, bound to their fate, to their course, to their condition, in the six classes of rebirth, experiencing happiness and suffering.’
translations.mn60:22: Householders, among those very ascetics and brahmins, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak in direct opposition. They say: ‘There is cause, there is reason for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause and reason. There is cause, there is reason for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause and reason. There is power, there is energy, there is manly strength, there is manly persistence; not all beings, all persons, all souls, all living beings are without mastery, powerless, without energy, bound to their fate, to their course, to their condition, in the six classes of rebirth, experiencing happiness and suffering.’ What do you think, householders, don’t these ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition to each other?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn60:29: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘There is absolutely no formless realm.’
translations.mn60:30: Householders, among those very ascetics and brahmins, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak in direct opposition. They say: ‘There is absolutely a formless realm.’ What do you think, householders, don’t these ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition to each other?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn60:32: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘There is absolutely no cessation of existence.’
translations.mn60:35: Householders, there are these four persons existing and found in the world. What four? Here, householders, one person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself. Here, householders, one person torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, one person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, one person neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, nor torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others; he is not self-tormenting, not other-tormenting, content here and now, liberated, cooled, experiencing happiness, dwelling with a mind like Brahma.
translations.mn60:36: And what, householders, is the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself? Here, householders, a certain person is naked, walking about uncovered… and so on… thus devoted to the practice of heating and tormenting the body in various ways. This, householders, is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself.
translations.mn60:37: And what, householders, is the person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, a certain person slaughters sheep… and so on… or whatever other cruel crafts there are. This, householders, is called the person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:38: And what, householders, is the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, a certain person is a king or a noble anointed on the head… and so on… they too, intimidated by punishment, intimidated by fear, with tearful faces, weeping, perform the duties. This, householders, is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:39: And what, householders, is the person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, nor torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others; he is not self-tormenting, not other-tormenting, content here and now, liberated, cooled, experiencing happiness, dwelling with a mind like Brahma?
translations.mn60:4: ‘But do you have, householders, some agreeable teacher in whom you have acquired faith with a reason?’ ‘No, sir, we have no agreeable teacher in whom we have acquired faith with a reason.’ ‘Householders, since you do not obtain an agreeable teacher, this infallible teaching should be undertaken. For an infallible teaching, householders, well grasped, undertaken, will be for your long-term welfare and happiness. And what, householders, is the infallible teaching?
translations.mn60:5: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views: ‘There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are no ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly forth and rightly practiced in the world who, with their own direct knowledge, having realized it, proclaim this world and the other world.’
translations.mn60:6: Of those very ascetics and brahmins, householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak in direct opposition. They say: ‘There is giving, there is offering, there is sacrifice; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is another world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly forth and rightly practiced in the world who, with their own direct knowledge, having realized it, proclaim this world and the other world.’ What do you think, householders: ‘Aren’t these ascetics and brahmins opposing each other point-blank?’ ‘Yes, sir.’
translations.mn63:8: And why, Mālunkyāputta, was this left undeclared by me? Because, Mālunkyāputta, this does not conduce to the purpose, nor to the essentials of the holy life, nor to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to awakening, nor to Nibbāna. Therefore it was left undeclared by me.
translations.mn64:13: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk, having completely transcended perceptions of forms, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, unmindful of perceptions of diversity, having entered upon and dwelt in the sphere of infinite space, thinking ‘space is infinite’—whatever there is there of feeling arisen from that, of perception arisen from that, of formations arisen from that, of consciousness arisen from that … is not liable to return, that is, from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, this is a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, having entered upon and dwelt in the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite’—whatever there is there of feeling arisen from that, of perception arisen from that, of formations arisen from that, of consciousness arisen from that … is not liable to return, that is, from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, this is a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: ‘Do you remember, monks, the five lower fetters taught by me?’ When this was said, the venerable Mālunkyāputta said to the Blessed One: ‘I remember, sir, the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.’ ‘But how do you remember, Mālunkyāputta, the five lower fetters taught by me?’ ‘I remember, sir, identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember attachment to precepts and observances as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. Thus, sir, I remember the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.’
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: ‘This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.’ ‘Then, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.’ ‘Yes, sir,’ the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn64:7: Ānanda, if anyone, by relying upon that path, that practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, would know or see or abandon them—it is possible.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Whatever exists therein that is material, feeling-born, perception-born, formations-born, consciousness-born, he regards those phenomena as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a misfortune, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as not-self. He directs his mind to those phenomena. Having directed his mind to those phenomena, he directs his mind to the deathless element: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Remaining there, he attains the ending of the effluents. If he does not attain the ending of the effluents, then, through passion for that Dhamma, delight in that Dhamma, he is, by the destruction of the five lower fetters, a spontaneously arisen being, one who attains final Nibbāna there, not liable to return, from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, this is a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I wield various kinds of psychic power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I pass through obstacles, whether fences, walls, or mountains, without obstruction, as if in space; may I dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as if on earth; may I travel cross-legged through space as if on solid ground; may I touch and stroke with my hand the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; may I travel with my body even as far as the Brahmā-world’—he should be one who is perfected in morality …pe… he should be one who explains (the teaching) in empty huts.
translations.mn6:15: If a monk should wish: ‘May I, with the divine ear element, purified, surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds, those of deities and those of humans, those that are far and those that are near,’ he should be perfected in virtue …pe… he should frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:16: If a monk should wish: ‘May I, with mind in touch with mind, discern the minds of other beings and other persons: may I discern a mind with lust as “a mind with lust”; or a mind without lust as “a mind without lust”; a mind with hate as “a mind with hate”; or a mind without hate as “a mind without hate”; a deluded mind as “a deluded mind”; or a mind without delusion as “a mind without delusion”; a shrunken mind as “a shrunken mind”; or a distracted mind as “a distracted mind”; an exalted mind as “an exalted mind”; or an unexalted mind as “an unexalted mind”; a supreme mind as “a supreme mind”; or an unsurpassed mind as “an unsurpassed mind”; a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind”; or an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind”; a liberated mind as “a liberated mind”; or an unliberated mind as “an unliberated mind,”’ he should be perfected in virtue …pe… he should frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:2: ‘Dwell perfected in virtue, monks, and perfected in the monastic code. Dwell restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and undertaking training in the training rules you have undertaken.’
translations.mn6:3: If a monk should wish: ‘May my fellow monastics be dear and agreeable to me, and may I be dear and agreeable to my fellow monastics,’ he should be perfected in virtue, devoted to inner serenity of mind, an undistracted meditator, endowed with insight, and he should frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:6: If a monk should wish: ‘When deceased relatives who passed away possessed a mind filled with faith remember me, may that bring great fruit and great benefit to them,’ he should be perfected in virtue, devoted to inner serenity of mind, an undistracted meditator, endowed with insight, and he should frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:7: If a monk should wish: ‘May I be master of disenchantment, and may disenchantment not master me; may I abide conquering arisen disenchantment again and again,’ he should be perfected in virtue …pe… he should frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:8: If a monk should wish: ‘May I be master of fear and dread, and may fear and dread not master me; may I abide conquering arisen fear and dread again and again,’ he should be perfected in virtue …pe… he should frequent empty huts.
translations.mn6:9: If a monk should wish: ‘May I be a gainer of the four absorptions that constitute mental clarity, dwelling happily in this present life,’ he should be perfected in virtue …pe… he should frequent empty huts.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the land of Kāsī with a large Saṅgha of monks. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
translations.mn70:11: “And, monks, this has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by me with wisdom: ‘When someone experiences such a neutral feeling of neither pleasure nor pain, unskillful qualities decline and skillful qualities increase.’ Therefore I say: ‘Dwell experiencing such a neutral feeling of neither pleasure nor pain.’
translations.mn70:12: “Monks, I do not say to all monks: ‘You should make an effort with heedfulness.’ Nor do I say to all monks: ‘You should not make an effort with heedfulness.’ Monks, those monks who are arahants, whose defilements are ended, who have completed what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of rebirth, and are rightly freed through perfect insight—for those monks I say: ‘You should not make an effort with heedfulness.’ Why is that? They have made an effort with heedfulness. They are incapable of being heedless.
translations.mn70:13: “But those monks who are trainees, who desire what has not yet been achieved, who live aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—for those monks I say: ‘You should make an effort with heedfulness.’ Why is that? Perhaps these venerable ones, while making use of suitable dwellings, associating with good friends, and developing their faculties, will realize that for which young men of good families rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, that unsurpassable conclusion to the spiritual life, realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge here and now in this very life. Monks, seeing the fruit of heedfulness for these monks, I say: ‘You should make an effort with heedfulness.’
translations.mn70:14: “There are seven persons existing and found in the world. What seven? One liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated through faith, a follower of Dhamma, a follower of faith.
translations.mn70:15: “And what, monks, is the person who is liberated in both ways? Here, monks, some person dwells having physically experienced with the body those tranquil liberations that are mental and free from material form, and having seen with wisdom, his defilements come to an end. This, monks, is called the person who is liberated in both ways. For this monk I say: ‘You should not make an effort with heedfulness.’ Why is that? He has made an effort with heedfulness. He is incapable of being heedless.
translations.mn70:17: “And what, monks, is the body-witness? Here, monks, some person dwells having physically experienced with the body those tranquil liberations that are mental and free from material form, and having seen with wisdom, some of his defilements come to an end. This, monks, is called the body-witness. For this monk I say: ‘You should make an effort with heedfulness.’ Why is that? Perhaps this venerable one, while making use of suitable dwellings, associating with good friends, and developing his faculties, will realize that for which young men of good families rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, that unsurpassable conclusion to the spiritual life, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge here and now in this very life. Monks, seeing the fruit of heedfulness for this monk, I say: ‘You should make an effort with heedfulness.’
translations.mn70:2: “I, monks, eat only once a day at night. But when I, monks, eat only once a day at night, I experience non-affliction, non-danger, lightness, strength, and comfortable abiding. Come, monks, you too eat only once a day at night. When you too, monks, eat only once a day at night, you will experience non-affliction, non-danger, lightness, strength, and comfortable abiding.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.mn70:20: And what, monks, is the person who follows the Dhamma? Here, monks, some person does not dwell having physically touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form; but by wisdom having seen some taints are destroyed for him, and the Dhammas proclaimed by the Tathāgata are approved by him as penetrable by wisdom to some extent. And these Dhammas exist for him, namely—faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty. This, monks, is called the person who follows the Dhamma. To this monk too, monks, I say ‘One should make an effort with heedfulness.’ Why? Perhaps this venerable one, frequenting suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, developing the faculties—might realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unexcelled culmination of the holy life, for the sake of which the sons of clans rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and dwell having entered upon it. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness for this monk, monks, I say ‘One should make an effort with heedfulness.’
translations.mn70:22: I do not say, monks, that enlightenment is by the first sign; but, monks, by gradual training, gradual action, gradual practice enlightenment comes about.
translations.mn70:23: And how, monks, by gradual training, gradual action, gradual practice does enlightenment come about? Here, monks, one with faith approaches; having approached, he pays respect; having paid respect, he lends an ear; having lent an ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he memorizes the Dhamma; having memorized the Dhammas, he examines their meaning; having examined their meaning, the Dhammas are approved as penetrable; with the approval of penetration of the Dhamma there is birth of desire; with desire born, he makes an effort; having made an effort, he weighs it up; having weighed it up, he makes an exertion; ardent, he realizes with the body the ultimate truth, and sees it by surpassing wisdom.
translations.mn70:24: That faith too, monks, was not; that approaching too, monks, was not; that paying respect too, monks, was not; that lending an ear too, monks, was not; that hearing the Dhamma too, monks, was not; that memorizing the Dhamma too, monks, was not; that examining the meaning too, monks, was not; that approval of penetration of the Dhamma too, monks, was not; that desire too, monks, was not; that effort too, monks, was not; that weighing up too, monks, was not; that exertion too, monks, was not. Wrong grasp of meaning, monks; wrong practice, monks. How far have these foolish men strayed from this Dhamma and Discipline!
translations.mn70:25: There is, monks, a four-footed explanation such that a wise man having heard it would quickly understand the meaning. Shall I teach you that, monks? You should know it.” “How could we know that, venerable sir, who are the knowers of the Dhamma?”
translations.mn70:26: “Even one who is a teacher, monks, greedy for gain, a receiver of gifts, living entangled in gains, even to him such a one does not approach like a trader: ‘May it be thus for us, then we would do it; may it not be thus for us, then we would not do it.’ How much less, monks, one who is the Tathāgata, dwelling completely disentangled from gains.
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages in the Kāsī country, arrived at Kīṭāgiri, a town of the Kāsīs. There the Blessed One dwelt near Kīṭāgiri in the Kāsīs’ town.
translations.mn70:4: At that time the monks Assaji and Punabbasu were residents at Kīṭāgiri. Then several monks approached the monks Assaji and Punabbasu; having approached, they said this to the monks Assaji and Punabbasu: “The Blessed One, friend, eats only once a day at night, and so does the monk community. But when eating only once a day at night, they experience non-affliction, non-danger, lightness, strength, and comfortable abiding. Come, friends, you too eat only once a day at night. When you too, friends, eat only once a day at night, you will experience non-affliction, non-danger, lightness, strength, and comfortable abiding.” When this was said, the monks Assaji and Punabbasu said this to those monks: “We, friends, eat at evening-time, and in the morning, and at the wrong time. And we, eating at evening-time, and in the morning, and at the wrong time, experience non-affliction, non-danger, lightness, strength, and comfortable abiding. Why should we, having abandoned what is visible, run after what is uncertain? We will eat at evening-time, and in the morning, and at the wrong time.”
translations.mn70:7: “Do you not understand that I have taught the Dhamma in such a way that for some person, when experiencing such pleasure, unskillful qualities increase, skillful qualities decline; but for some person, when experiencing such pleasure, unskillful qualities decline, skillful qualities increase; for some person, when experiencing such pain, unskillful qualities increase, skillful qualities decline; but for some person, when experiencing such pain, unskillful qualities decline, skillful qualities increase; for some person, when experiencing such neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unskillful qualities increase, skillful qualities decline; but for some person, when experiencing such neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unskillful qualities decline, skillful qualities increase?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn75:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurūs in a town of the Kurūs called Kammāsadhamma, in the house of the brahmin Bharadvāja, on a couch spread with grass.
translations.mn75:10: “But I, Māgaṇḍiya, when formerly a householder, enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasures, possessed of them and complete, with forms cognizable by eye that are desirable, agreeable, charming, likable, arousing desire, delightful; with sounds cognizable by ear …pe… with odors cognizable by nose … with flavors cognizable by tongue … with tangibles cognizable by body that are desirable, agreeable, charming, likable, arousing desire, delightful. For me, Māgaṇḍiya, there were three pavilions—one for the rainy season, one for the winter, one for the hot season. I, Māgaṇḍiya, during the four months of the rainy season, enjoying myself in the rainy-season pavilion with non-human music, did not come down from the upper pavilion. Then later, having truly understood the origin, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape of sensual pleasures as they really are, having abandoned sensuality-craving, having dispelled the fever of sensuality, dwelling with thirst extinguished, internally pacified in mind, I abide. I see other beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being gnawed by sensuality-craving, burning and scorched by the fever of sensuality, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not pity them, nor do I delight in that. Why is that? There is this delight, Māgaṇḍiya, apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unskillful qualities—even the divine pleasure attained and standing in concentration—I delight in that delight, thus I do not pity the inferior, nor do I delight in that.”
translations.mn75:12: “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, when formerly a householder, I enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasures, possessed of them and complete, with forms cognizable by eye that are desirable, agreeable, charming, likable, arousing desire, delightful, with sounds cognizable by ear …pe… with odors cognizable by nose … with flavors cognizable by tongue … with tangibles cognizable by body that are desirable, agreeable, charming, likable, arousing desire, delightful. Then later, having truly understood the origin, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape of sensual pleasures as they really are, having abandoned sensuality-craving, having dispelled the fever of sensuality, with thirst extinguished, internally pacified in mind, I abide. I see other beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being gnawed by sensuality-craving, burning and scorched by the fever of sensuality, indulging in sensual pleasures, I do not pity them, nor do I delight in that. Why is that? There is this delight, Māgaṇḍiya, apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unskillful qualities—even the divine pleasure attained and standing in concentration—I delight in that delight, thus I do not pity the inferior, nor do I delight in that.”
translations.mn75:13: “Just as, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores on his limbs, full of worms, scratching the openings of his sores with his nails, burning his body over a burning charcoal pit. His friends and companions, relatives and blood relations, would bring a doctor or surgeon for him. That doctor or surgeon would make medicine for him. Taking that medicine, he would be freed from the leprosy, healthy, happy, his own master, able to go wherever he wants. He would see another leper man with sores on his limbs, full of worms, scratching the openings of his sores with his nails, burning his body over a burning charcoal pit. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that man pity this leper man for the charcoal pit or for taking medicine?” “No, sir Gotama. Why is that? When there is disease, sir Gotama, medicine is to be made; when there is no disease, medicine is not to be made.”
translations.mn75:16: “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, sensual pleasures in the past were contacts with painful feelings, great burning, great fever; sensual pleasures in the future will be contacts with painful feelings, great burning, great fever; sensual pleasures even now in the present are contacts with painful feelings, great burning, great fever. And these beings, Māgaṇḍiya, not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being gnawed by sensuality-craving, burning and scorched by the fever of sensuality, with impaired faculties, have inverted perception that there is happiness in sensual pleasures.”
translations.mn75:17: “Just as, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores on his limbs, full of worms, scratching the openings of his sores with his nails, burns his body over a burning charcoal pit. However much, Māgaṇḍiya, that leper with sores on his limbs, full of worms, scratching the openings of his sores with his nails, burns his body over a burning charcoal pit, to that extent those openings of his sores become even more impure, even more foul-smelling, even more putrid, and there is just some slight gratification, some slight pleasure—namely, the itching of the openings of the sores; just so, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being gnawed by sensuality-craving and burning and scorched by the fever of sensuality, indulge in sensual pleasures. However much, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being gnawed by sensuality-craving and burning and scorched by the fever of sensuality, indulge in sensual pleasures, to that extent their sensuality-craving increases, and they burn and scorch with the fever of sensuality, and there is just some slight gratification, some slight pleasure—namely, on account of the five strands of sensual pleasures.”}
translations.mn75:18: “What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, have you seen or heard of a king or a royal minister endowed with, possessing, and enjoying the five strands of sensuality, who without abandoning sensual craving, without allaying the fever of sensuality, dwells or is dwelling or will dwell with thirst extinguished, with mind inwardly peaceful?” “No, good Gotama.” “Good, Māgaṇḍiya. Nor have I, Māgaṇḍiya, seen or heard of a king or a royal minister endowed with, possessing, and enjoying the five strands of sensuality, who without abandoning sensual craving, without allaying the fever of sensuality, dwells or is dwelling or will dwell with thirst extinguished, with mind inwardly peaceful. But, Māgaṇḍiya, any ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt or dwell or will dwell with thirst extinguished, with mind inwardly peaceful—all of them have clearly known, as they really are, the origin, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape from sensual pleasures, and having abandoned sensual craving, allayed the fever of sensuality, they have dwelt or dwell or will dwell with thirst extinguished, with mind inwardly peaceful.”
translations.mn75:2: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having walked for alms in Kammāsadhamma, after his meal, on returning from almsround, he went to a certain forest grove for the day’s abiding. Having entered that forest grove, he sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree.
translations.mn75:22: “I am so confident in the good Gotama. May the good Gotama teach me Dhamma in such a way that I may understand health and see Nibbāna!” “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man born blind; he would not see black and blue forms, he would not see yellow and red forms, he would not see crimson forms, he would not see even or uneven, he would not see star-forms, he would not see the moon and sun. His relatives and friends, his blood relations, would bring a physician to attend on him. That physician would make medicine for him. But coming by that medicine, it would neither cause his eyes to arise nor cleanse his eyes. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would not that doctor be in vain and frustrated to that extent?” “Yes, good Gotama.” “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you Dhamma: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ but you would not understand health or see Nibbāna. That would be my weariness, that my frustration.”
translations.mn75:24: “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you Dhamma: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ and you would understand health and see Nibbāna. With you, with the support of the eyes, sensual desire and attachment in regard to the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned; and you would think: ‘For a long time, alas, I have been tricked, cheated, and deceived by this mind. For when grasping at forms only, I grasped; when grasping at feelings only, I grasped; when grasping at perceptions only, I grasped; when grasping at formations only, I grasped; when grasping at consciousness only, I grasped. With clinging as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be; such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.mn75:25: “I am so confident in the good Gotama. May the good Gotama teach me Dhamma in such a way that I may rise from this seat joyful and exultant!” “Well then, Māgaṇḍiya, associate with good people. When you associate with good people, Māgaṇḍiya, you will hear the true Dhamma; when you hear the true Dhamma, Māgaṇḍiya, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma; when you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, Māgaṇḍiya, you will know and see for yourself: ‘These are diseases, tumors, and darts; here diseases, tumors, and darts come to an end without remainder. With the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease; such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, good Gotama, excellent, good Gotama. As one might set upright what was overthrown, reveal what was hidden, show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the dark: ‘Those with eyes can see visible objects,’ just so the good Gotama has made the Dhamma clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the good Gotama, to Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I receive the going forth in the presence of the good Gotama, may I receive ordination into monkhood!”
translations.mn75:27: “Māgaṇḍiya, when one who was formerly an adherent of another sect desires the going forth here in this Dhamma and discipline, desires ordination, he dwells four months on probation; when four months have passed, with resolute faith the monks give him the going forth, they give him ordination into monkhood. But in this case individual differences are known.” “If, venerable sir, those formerly adherents of another sect desiring the going forth here in this Dhamma and discipline, desiring ordination, dwell four months on probation, and when four months have passed, with resolute faith the monks give them the going forth, give them ordination into monkhood; I will dwell on probation four years, and when four years have passed, with resolute faith may the monks give me the going forth, give me ordination into monkhood.”
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire-hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Māgaṇḍiya the wanderer saw a grass mat spread out in the fire-hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Having seen it, he said to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan: “Whose is this grass mat spread out in the fire-hut of the venerable Bhāradvāja? It seems suitable for an ascetic’s sleeping place.”
translations.mn75:6: The Blessed One heard this conversation between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya with his divine ear-element, purified, surpassing the human. Then the Blessed One, having emerged from retreat at the time of evening, approached the fire-hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan; having approached, the Blessed One sat down on the spread-out grass mat. Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. To the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan sitting to one side, the Blessed One said: “Did you, Bhāradvāja, have some conversation with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya regarding this very grass mat?” When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, alarmed and with hairs standing on end, said to the Blessed One: “It is precisely this that we wanted to report to the venerable Gotama. But the venerable Gotama has declared the undeclared.”
translations.mn75:7: And this private conversation between the Blessed One and the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan had been interrupted. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, walking and wandering for exercise, approached the fire-hut of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. To the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya sitting to one side, the Blessed One said:
translations.mn77:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove at the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground.
translations.mn77:10: There are, Udāyin, these other five qualities by which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and dwell devoted to me. Which five? Here, Udāyin, my disciples speak of me as possessed of virtue: ‘The ascetic Gotama is virtuous, possessed of the complete virtue aggregate.’
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path, by practicing which my disciples develop the four establishments of mindfulness. Here, Udāyin, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … dwells contemplating the mind in the mind … dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path, by practicing which my disciples develop the four right efforts. Here, Udāyin, a monk generates desire, makes effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unskillful phenomena; for the abandoning of arisen evil unskillful phenomena; for the arising of unarisen skillful phenomena; for the continuance, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen skillful phenomena, he generates desire, makes effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path, by practicing which my disciples develop the four bases of psychic power. Here, Udāyin, a monk develops the base of psychic power that has desire to be concentrated, accompanied by mental formations of concentration; develops the base of psychic power that has energy to be concentrated … develops the base of psychic power that has mind to be concentrated … develops the base of psychic power that has investigation to be concentrated, accompanied by mental formations of concentration. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path, by practicing which my disciples develop the five spiritual faculties. Here, Udāyin, a monk develops the faith faculty leading to peace, leading to enlightenment … develops the energy faculty … develops the mindfulness faculty … develops the concentration faculty … develops the wisdom faculty leading to peace, leading to enlightenment. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:2: And on that occasion many well-known wanderers were dwelling in the wanderers’ park at the Moriya copse, such as Annabhāra, Varadhara, Sakuludāyin the wanderer, and other well-known wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path, by practicing which my disciples develop the seven factors of enlightenment. Here, Udāyin, a monk develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor leaning towards seclusion, leaning towards dispassion, leaning towards cessation, resulting in relinquishment; develops the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor … develops the energy enlightenment factor … develops the rapture enlightenment factor … develops the tranquility enlightenment factor … develops the concentration enlightenment factor … develops the equanimity enlightenment factor leaning towards seclusion, leaning towards dispassion, leaning towards cessation, resulting in relinquishment. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path of practice such that my disciples who practice it develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyin, a monk develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, develops right concentration. And there my disciples dwell having attained the superknowledges, the ends, the perfections.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path of practice such that my disciples who practice it develop the eight liberations. He has form and sees forms: this is the first liberation; not percipient of form internally, he sees forms externally: this is the second liberation; he is devoted to beauty: this is the third liberation; having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, understanding ‘space is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space: this is the fourth liberation; having completely transcended the base of infinite space, understanding ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness: this is the fifth liberation; having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, understanding ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness: this is the sixth liberation; having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: this is the seventh liberation; having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling: this is the eighth liberation. And there my disciples dwell having attained the superknowledges, the ends, the perfections.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path of practice such that my disciples who practice it develop the ten kasiṇa bases. One perceives the earth kasiṇa as unlimited above, below, and across; one perceives the water kasiṇa … one perceives the fire kasiṇa … one perceives the air kasiṇa … one perceives the blue kasiṇa … one perceives the yellow kasiṇa … one perceives the red kasiṇa … one perceives the white kasiṇa … one perceives the space kasiṇa … one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa as unlimited above, below, and across. And there my disciples dwell having attained the superknowledges, the ends, the perfections.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the path of practice such that my disciples who practice it develop the four absorptions. Here, Udāyin, a monk, quite secluded from sensuality, secluded from unskillful dharmas, enters and dwells in the first absorption with applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He drenches, pervades, suffuses, and saturates this very body with the pleasure and rapture born of seclusion; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by pleasure and rapture born of seclusion. Just as, Udāyin, a skillful bathman or his apprentice might sprinkle bath powder in a copper basin, and gradually knead it with water so that the ball of bath powder becomes thoroughly soaked with moisture, pervaded inside and out, not dripping; even so, Udāyin, a monk drenches, pervades, suffuses, and saturates this very body with the pleasure and rapture born of seclusion; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by pleasure and rapture born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyin, with the fading away of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second absorption … He drenches, pervades, suffuses, and saturates this very body with the pleasure and rapture born of concentration; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by pleasure and rapture born of concentration. Just as, Udāyin, a deep lake with springs on all sides, with no inlet for water from east, west, north, or south, and with the sky not periodically sending fitting showers; but cool spring-water wells up from within that lake and drenches, pervades, suffuses, and saturates that lake with cool water; there is no part of that lake that is not pervaded by cool water. Even so, Udāyin, a monk drenches, pervades, suffuses, and saturates this very body with the pleasure and rapture born of concentration; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by pleasure and rapture born of concentration.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyin, with the fading away of rapture … a monk enters and dwells in the third absorption. He drenches, pervades, suffuses, and saturates this very body with pleasure free from rapture; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by pleasure free from rapture. Just as, Udāyin, in a blue-, red-, or white-lotus pool, some lotuses or water lilies are born in the water, grow in the water, and are nourished by the water, submerged within it; and those lotuses or water lilies, from the tip down to the root, are pervaded, suffused, filled, and saturated with cool water; there is no part of those lotuses or water lilies that is not pervaded by cool water. Even so, Udāyin, a monk drenches, pervades, suffuses, and saturates this very body with pleasure free from rapture; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by pleasure free from rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyin, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth absorption, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by a pure, bright mind. Just as, Udāyin, a man might sit pervading his body with a white cloth; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by a white cloth. Even so, Udāyin, a monk sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind; there is no part of his whole body that is not pervaded by a pure, bright mind. And there my disciples dwell having attained the superknowledges, the ends, the perfections.
translations.mn77:3: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: “It is too early to go for alms in Rājagaha. Why don’t I go to the wanderers’ park at the Moriya grove, to the wanderer Sakuludāyī?”
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it, with the divine ear-element, purified, surpassing that of humans, hear both sounds—divine and human, those that are far and near. Just as, Udāyin, a strong conch-blower would make himself heard with little effort in all four directions; even so, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it, with the divine ear-element, purified, surpassing that of humans, hear both sounds—divine and human, those that are far and near. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the end of superknowledges.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it recollect many previous abodes, that is to say—one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so-and-so by name, of such-and-such clan, appearance, food, experience of pleasure and pain, lifespan; having passed away from there, I was reborn there; there too I was so-and-so by name, of such-and-such clan, appearance, food, experience of pleasure and pain, lifespan; having passed away from there, I have come here.’ Thus with details and in sequence they recollect many previous abodes. Just as, Udāyin, a man would go from his own village to another village; from that village he would go to yet another village; from that he would return to his own village; he would think: ‘From my own village I went to another village, there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, was silent thus; from that village I went to that village, there too I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, was silent thus; from there I have returned to my own village.’ Even so, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it recollect many previous abodes, that is to say—one birth … thus with details and in sequence they recollect many previous abodes. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the end of superknowledges.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it, with the divine eye, purified, surpassing that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and they understand beings by their karma: ‘These beings, possessed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, denigrators of noble ones, holding wrong view, undertaking wrong-view karma, at the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, the underworld; while these beings, possessed of bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, mental good conduct, non-denigrators of noble ones, holding right view, undertaking right-view karma, at the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, purified, surpassing that of humans, they see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand beings by their karma. Just as, Udāyin, there are two houses with windows. A man with vision standing in between would see people entering the house and leaving it, walking and wandering back and forth; even so, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it, with the divine eye, purified, surpassing that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand beings by their karma … And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the end of superknowledges.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it, by the destruction of the taints, abide having directly known and realized for themselves in this very life the taint-free deliverance of mind, deliverance through wisdom. Just as, Udāyin, in a mountain cleft there is a clear, limpid, undisturbed pool of water; a man with vision standing on the bank would see shells, gravel, and pebbles, moving or still. He would think: ‘This pool of water is clear, limpid, undisturbed; there are these shells, gravel, and pebbles, moving or still.’ Even so, Udāyin, I have declared to my disciples the practice such that my disciples who have practiced it, by the destruction of the taints, abide having directly known and realized for themselves in this very life the taint-free deliverance of mind, deliverance through wisdom. And there many of my disciples dwell having reached the end of superknowledges.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One went to the wanderer Sakuludāyī. Sakuludāyī the wanderer said to the Blessed One: “Come, Blessed One! Welcome, Blessed One! It has been a long time since the Blessed One took the opportunity of coming here. Sit, Blessed One, this seat has been prepared.” The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Sakuludāyī the wanderer, taking a low seat, sat to one side. To Sakuludāyī the wanderer sitting to one side, the Blessed One said: “Now on what discussion were you seated just now, Udāyin? And what was your conversation that got interrupted?”
translations.mn77:7: “But how many qualities do you see in me, Udāyin, by which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me?”}
translations.mn77:9: ‘The ascetic Gotama eats little, and he speaks in praise of eating little,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, yet I have disciples, Udayi, who eat a kosaka-measure, half a kosaka-measure, a beluva-measure, or half a beluva-measure. But occasionally, Udayi, I eat even a full bowlful or more with this bowl. ‘The ascetic Gotama eats little, and he speaks in praise of eating little,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, those of my disciples, Udayi, who eat a kosaka-measure, half a kosaka-measure, a beluva-measure, or half a beluva-measure would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, yet I have disciples, Udayi, who are wearers of rag-robes, bearers of coarse robes—they take cloths from charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, or shops, and make them into patched robes and wear them. But occasionally, Udayi, I wear householder’s robes that are heavy, coarse, and with thick hair. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, those of my disciples, Udayi, who are wearers of rag-robes, bearers of coarse robes—they take cloths from charnel grounds, rubbish heaps, or shops, and make them into patched robes and wear them—would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of almsfood,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, yet I have disciples, Udayi, who are almsfood-eaters, walkers of the alms round, delighting in the going-for-alms ascetic practice, who, when they have entered a village, do not accept an invitation even when seated on a seat. But occasionally, Udayi, even when invited, I eat rice with sauce, with various kinds of curry and condiments. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of almsfood,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, those of my disciples, Udayi, who are almsfood-eaters, walkers of the alms round, delighting in the going-for-alms ascetic practice, who, when they have entered a village, do not accept an invitation even when seated on a seat, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, yet I have disciples, Udayi, who are tree-root-dwellers and open-air-dwellers, who do not resort to shelter for eight months. But occasionally, Udayi, I live in a peaked house with plaster walls, with closeable doors, with windows covered. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, those of my disciples, Udayi, who are tree-root-dwellers and open-air-dwellers, who do not resort to shelter for eight months, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. ‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he speaks in praise of seclusion,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, yet I have disciples, Udayi, who are forest-dwellers with limited lodging, who occupy remote forest sites and jungle thickets as their dwellings, and they descend to the midst of the Sangha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But occasionally, Udayi, I live crowded with monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, and royal ministers, wanderers and their disciples. ‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he speaks in praise of seclusion,’ if, Udayi, my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me for this quality, those of my disciples, Udayi, who are forest-dwellers with limited lodging, who occupy remote forest sites and jungle thickets as their dwellings, and they descend to the midst of the Sangha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this quality, nor live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. Thus, Udayi, my disciples do not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for these five qualities, nor live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me.
translations.mn7:11: ‘Just as my mind has vomited, excreted, rejected, and relinquished that,’ he gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the Dhamma, gains joy connected with the Dhamma. With joy arisen, rapture is born. With a mind full of rapture, the body is pacified. With the body pacified, he experiences pleasure. With pleasureful mind, the mind is concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He abides pervading one direction with his mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, in full, to all extents, with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness that is vast, grown great, boundless, free from enmity and ill will, he abides pervading the entire world;
translations.mn7:17: He understands: ‘There is this, there is the inferior, there is the superior, there is an escape from this perception.’
translations.mn7:18: To him who knows thus, who sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taints of sensuality, his mind is liberated from the taint of becoming, his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. When liberated, there is knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ This, monks, is called ‘a monk bathed internally.’
translations.mn7:19: At that time the brahmin Sundarika-Bharadvaja was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarika-Bharadvaja said to the Blessed One: ‘Does the venerable Gotama go to the river Bahuka to bathe?’ ‘What, brahmin, is the river Bahuka to do?
