What is the river Bahuka going to do?’ ‘The river Bahuka, sir Gotama, is approved of by the world, the river Bahuka, sir Gotama, is considered meritorious by many folk; many folk purify the evil deeds they have done by means of the river Bahuka.’
translations.mn7:2: “Just as, monks, a cloth that is defiled and dirt-stained; if a dyer were to apply it to any dye—whether blue, yellow, red, or crimson—it would appear very dull, not pure in color. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth, monks. So too, monks, when the mind is defiled, a bad destination is expected. Just as, monks, a cloth that is pure and spotless; if a dyer were to apply it to any dye—whether blue, yellow, red, or crimson—it would appear very bright, pure in color. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth, monks. So too, monks, when the mind is undefiled, a good destination is expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarika-Bharadvaja in verses: “Bahuka, Adhikakka, Gaya, Sundarika too; Sarassati, Payaga, and the river Bahumati; A fool constantly resorts to them, but one of evil deeds is not purified. What is Sundarika to do, what Payaga, what the river Bahuka; An enemy of evil deeds done, evil action does not purify him. Of one who is pure it is always pure, the observance of one who is pure is always pure; Of one who is pure, of good deeds, his vow always succeeds; Bathe here, brahmin, make safety toward all beings. If you do not speak lies, if you do not harm living beings; If you do not take what is not given, faithful and without stinginess; Why go to Gaya, your Gaya is even a pond.”
translations.mn7:3: And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind, ill will is a defilement of the mind, anger is a defilement of the mind, resentment is a defilement of the mind, hypocrisy is a defilement of the mind, conceit is a defilement of the mind, envy is a defilement of the mind, stinginess is a defilement of the mind, deceit is a defilement of the mind, craftiness is a defilement of the mind, stubbornness is a defilement of the mind, obstinacy is a defilement of the mind, pride is a defilement of the mind, haughtiness is a defilement of the mind, vanity is a defilement of the mind, heedlessness is a defilement of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: he is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be personally experienced by the wise’;
translations.mn7:7: he is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the straight way, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the true way, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the proper way, that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals; this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the lands of the Kurus with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at a town of the Kurus named Thullakoṭṭhika.
translations.mn82:11: Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to Raṭṭhapāla’s parents; having gone, they said to Raṭṭhapāla’s parents: ‘Dear sirs, this clansman Raṭṭhapāla is lying down right there on the ground between the crops: “Here my death will take place, or the going forth.” If you do not grant the clansman Raṭṭhapāla leave to go forth from the household life into homelessness, his death will take place right there. But if you grant the clansman Raṭṭhapāla leave to go forth from the household life into homelessness, you will see him even when he has gone forth. If the clansman Raṭṭhapāla does not delight in going forth from the household life into homelessness, what other course could there be for him? He will come back right here. Grant the clansman Raṭṭhapāla leave to go forth from the household life into homelessness.’ ‘Sirs, we grant the clansman Raṭṭhapāla leave to go forth from the household life into homelessness. But when one has gone forth, parents should be supported.’ Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla; having gone, they said to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla: ‘Rise up, dear Raṭṭhapāla, your parents have granted you leave to go forth from the household life into homelessness. But when one has gone forth, parents should be supported.’
translations.mn82:12: Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla rose up, took on strength, and went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: ‘I have been granted leave by my parents, sir, to go forth from the household life into homelessness. Let the Blessed One ordain me.’”}
translations.mn82:13: Raṭṭhapāla the clansman obtained ordination in the presence of the Blessed One, he obtained the higher ordination. Then the Blessed One, not long after the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's higher ordination, having stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika for half a month as he pleased, set out on tour for Sāvatthī. Traveling by stages, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One stayed at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.
translations.mn82:14: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, dwelling alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute, in no long time—on that for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life to homelessness, the unexcelled culmination of the spiritual life—realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered upon and dwelled in it. 'My birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being,' he understood. And the venerable Raṭṭhapāla was one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him on his right, put away his lodging, and taking his bowl and robe, set out on tour for Thullakoṭṭhika. Traveling by stages, he eventually arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There the venerable Raṭṭhapāla stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika in King Korabya's deer park. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. Wandering for alms in Thullakoṭṭhika, he went to his father's house.
translations.mn82:17: At that time the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father was having the middle door-chamber swept. The venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father saw the venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar. Seeing him, he said: 'Our only beloved son has gone forth among these shaven-headed little ascetics.' Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla did not receive alms at his father's house, nor a refusal; rather, he received abuse.
translations.mn82:18: At that time the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relative slave-girl wanted to throw away left-over gruel. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to her: 'Sister, if this is something to be thrown away, pour it into my bowl here.' Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relative slave-girl, pouring that left-over gruel into the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's bowl, grabbed hold of his hands and feet and hair. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relative slave-girl went to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother; going to her, she said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother: 'Lady, you should know:
translations.mn82:19: At that time, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was living supported by a certain root of a kuṭṭha tree, eating thrown-away sour gruel. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father went to him, and having gone, he said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “My dear Raṭṭhapāla, would you eat thrown-away sour gruel? Surely, dear Raṭṭhapāla, you should go to your own home.” “How could there be a home for us, householder, who have gone forth from home to homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We did go to your home, householder, but we neither got a gift there nor a refusal; rather, we got only abuse.” “Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go home.” “Enough, householder, I have finished my meal duty today.” “Well then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, accept a meal tomorrow.” Venerable Raṭṭhapāla accepted by silence.
translations.mn82:22: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went to his father’s dwelling. Having gone, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father had that pile of gold and silver uncovered and said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “This wealth, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your mother’s legacy, this is your father’s, this is your grandfather’s. You can enjoy pleasures and make merit, dear Raṭṭhapāla. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, return to the lower life, enjoy pleasures and make merit.” “If you would do as I say, householder, have this pile of gold and silver loaded onto a cart, carried away, and thrown into the middle of the Ganges river. Why? For those things will give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, householder.”
translations.mn82:21: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father, after that night had passed, had fine hard and soft food prepared in his own dwelling and announced the time to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.”
translations.mn82:20: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father, having understood Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s acceptance, went to his own dwelling. Having gone, he had a large pile of gold and silver made, covered it with sacks, and addressed Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s former wife: “Come, daughter-in-law, with whatever ornaments you were formerly adorned with, by which you were dear and pleasing to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla, adorn yourself with those ornaments.”}
translations.mn82:23: Then the former wives of Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, taking him by the feet separately, said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “What kind of celestial nymphs, dear son, are there for whose sake you are living the holy life?” “We are not living the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs, sister.” “The dear son Raṭṭhapāla is addressing us as ‘sister.’” Thereupon they fainted and fell right there.
translations.mn82:24: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his father: “If, householder, food is to be given, give it; do not trouble us.” “Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.” Then Raṭṭhapāla’s father satisfied and gratified Venerable Raṭṭhapāla with his own hand with excellent hard and soft food. When Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had eaten and refused the bowl, he stood and spoke these verses:
translations.mn82:26: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having spoken these verses while standing, went to King Koravya’s deer park; having gone there, he sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Koravya addressed the gamekeeper: “Clear the deer park, dear gamekeeper; we will go to see the pleasant ground.” “Yes, sire,” the gamekeeper replied to King Koravya. While clearing the deer park, he saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree. Seeing him, he went to King Koravya; having gone there, he said to King Koravya: “Your deer park, sire, is clear. There is here a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, son of a leading family in this very Thullakoṭṭhika, of whom you have often spoken highly; he is sitting for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree.” “Well then, dear gamekeeper, there is no need now for the pleasant ground. We will pay homage to that Venerable Raṭṭhapāla.”
translations.mn82:28: Then King Koravya, saying, “Whatever hard and soft food has been prepared there, give it all away,” had fine vehicles harnessed, mounted a fine vehicle, and set out from Thullakoṭṭhika by fine vehicles with a great royal retinue to see Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. He went by vehicle as far as the vehicle could go, descended from the vehicle, and approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla on foot with an enthusiastic company. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Koravya said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “Here, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, sit on the prepared seat.” “Enough, great king, you sit; I am sitting on my own seat.” King Koravya sat down on the prepared seat. When he was seated, King Koravya said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: “There are these four kinds of weariness, Raṭṭhapāla, by which some shave off their hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. Which four? Weariness with aging, weariness with illness, weariness with wealth, weariness with kin.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika went to the Blessed One; some, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, sat down to one side; some, having raised their hands in reverential salutation to the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some, having announced their name and clan in the Blessed One’s presence, sat down to one side; some sat down to one side silently. When the brahmin householders of Thullakoṭṭhika were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, inspired, fired, and delighted them with a talk on the Dhamma.
translations.mn82:34: “These are the four kinds of weariness, Raṭṭhapāla, by which some shave off their hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. You do not have them, Raṭṭhapāla. What knowing, or seeing, or hearing did you have that you went forth from the household life into homelessness?”
translations.mn82:35: “There are, great king, four summaries of Dhamma that were spoken by that Blessed One, the knower, the seer, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, having known and seen which I went forth from the household life into homelessness. Which four?
translations.mn82:4: And on that occasion a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, son of a leading family in that same Thullakoṭṭhika, was sitting in the assembly. Then it occurred to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla: “As far as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy while living in a house to live the perfectly complete, perfectly pure, thoroughly purified holy life like a polished conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, dress in ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?”
translations.mn82:6: Then Raṭṭhapāla, the clansman, soon after the householder donors had left, went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Raṭṭhapāla the clansman said to the Blessed One: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy while living in a house to live the holy life completely perfect, completely pure, like a polished conch shell. I wish, sir, to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. May I receive the going forth and acceptance in the presence of the Blessed One. May the Blessed One give me the going forth.” “But have you been permitted by your mother and father, Raṭṭhapāla, to go forth from the household life into homelessness?” “No, sir, I have not been permitted by my mother and father to go forth from the household life into homelessness.” “The Tathāgatas do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father.” “I will do as you say, sir, so that my mother and father will permit me to go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the lands of the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of monks and arrived at Opāsāda, a village of Kosalan brāhmaṇas. There the Blessed One was staying at Opāsāda in the northern part of the village in the sāla grove of the gods’ garden.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brāhmaṇa Caṅkī, together with a large company of brāhmaṇas, went to the Blessed One; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: At that time the Blessed One was sitting exchanging some polite conversation with the senior brāhmaṇas. At that time a youth named Kāpaṭika, young, with shaven head, about sixteen years old by birth, a master of the three Vedas with their subsidiaries, etymologies, phonetics, and fifth [Veda: history], skilled in philology and grammar, and not unversed in cosmology and the marks of a great man, was sitting in that assembly. He was interrupting the conversation between the Blessed One and the senior brāhmaṇas at intervals. Then the Blessed One quieted the youth Kāpaṭika: “Do not, reverend Bhāradvāja, interrupt the conversation between the senior brāhmaṇas. Reverend Bhāradvāja, bring the conversation to a conclusion.” When this was said, the brāhmaṇa Caṅkī said to the Blessed One: “Do not, Gotama, quiet the youth Kāpaṭika. Kāpaṭika is a clansman youth, Kāpaṭika is learned, Kāpaṭika is wise, Kāpaṭika is eloquent, and Kāpaṭika is capable of holding his own with Gotama in this discussion.”
translations.mn95:2: At that time the brāhmaṇa Caṅkī was living at Opāsāda, which had sevenfold rice, barley, and beans, royal revenue land given by King Pasenadi Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmin donation.
translations.mn95:20: When one sees with purified mind, free from defiling dhammas; then he places faith therein, with faith born he approaches, approaching he sits near, sitting near he lends an ear, with ear lent he hears the Dhamma, having heard the Dhamma he memorizes it, having memorized the dhammas he examines their meaning, examining their meaning the dhammas become clear, with the endurance of clear comprehension of the dhamma desire is born, with desire born he makes an effort, having made an effort he weighs it up, having weighed it up he strives, being strenuous he realizes the supreme truth with the body and sees it with wisdom piercingly. By this much, Bhāradvāja, there is understanding of the truths, by this much one understands the truths, by this much we designate understanding of the truths; but it is not yet attainment of the truths.
translations.mn95:33: “But, good Gotama, what is the profitable dhamma of approaching? We ask the good Gotama about the profitable dhamma of approaching.” “Faith, Bhāradvāja, is profitable for approaching. If faith were not born, one would not approach. Since faith is born, one approaches. Therefore faith is profitable for approaching.”
translations.mn95:5: At that time the brāhmaṇa Caṅkī had gone up to the upper terrace for his siesta. The brāhmaṇa Caṅkī saw the brāhmaṇas and householders of Opāsāda coming out of Opāsāda, in groups, facing north, going to the gods’ garden sāla grove. Seeing this, he addressed the servant: “What is it, good servant, that the brāhmaṇas and householders of Opāsāda, coming out of Opāsāda, in groups, facing north, are going to the gods’ garden sāla grove?”
translations.mn9:11: And what, friends, is food, what is the origin of food, what is the cessation of food, what is the way leading to cessation of food? There are these four, friends, foods for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, for the support of those becoming. Which four? Physical food, coarse or subtle; contact is the second; mental intention is the third; consciousness is the fourth. With the arising of craving there is the arising of food; with the cessation of craving there is the cessation of food; this very noble eightfold path is the way leading to cessation of food, that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
translations.mn9:12: When, friends, a noble disciple understands food thus, understands the origin of food thus, understands the cessation of food thus, understands the way leading to cessation of food thus, he completely abandons the underlying tendency to greed, removes the underlying tendency to aversion, uproots the underlying tendency to the view ‘I am,’ having abandoned ignorance and generated knowledge, he is in this very life one who has ended suffering—by this much, friends, a noble disciple has right view, his view is straight, he has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, he has arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:15: And what, friends, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering—this, friends, is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friends, is the origin of suffering? It is that craving which brings renewal, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, sensual craving, craving for existence, craving for non-existence—this, friends, is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friends, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and ceasing, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go, and rejection of that same craving—this, friends, is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friends, is the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is just this noble eightfold path, namely: right view … right concentration—this, friends, is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: ‘Right view, right view,’ it is said, friends. In what way, friends, does a noble disciple have right view, his view is straight, he has unshakeable confidence in the teaching, he has come to this true Dhamma? “Even if we came from afar, friends, we would come to Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from Venerable Sāriputta, the monks will retain it.” “Well then, friends, listen, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said:
translations.mn9:20: “Very good, friend,” those monks approved and rejoiced in Venerable Sāriputta’s words, then they asked Venerable Sāriputta further: “Could there be, friend, some other aspect by which a noble disciple has right view, his view is straight, he has unshakeable confidence in the teaching, he has come to this true Dhamma?”
translations.mn9:3: “When, friends, a noble disciple understands unwholesome, and understands the root of unwholesome, understands wholesome, and understands the root of wholesome—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple has right view, his view is straight, he has unshakeable confidence in the teaching, he has come to this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:4: And what, friends, is unwholesome, what is the root of unwholesome, what is wholesome, what is the root of wholesome? Killing living beings is unwholesome, taking what is not given is unwholesome, sexual misconduct is unwholesome, false speech is unwholesome, malicious speech is unwholesome, harsh speech is unwholesome, idle chatter is unwholesome, covetousness is unwholesome, ill will is unwholesome, wrong view is unwholesome—this, friends, is called unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friends, is the root of unwholesome? Greed is the root of unwholesome, hatred is the root of unwholesome, delusion is the root of unwholesome—this, friends, is called the root of unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friends, is the root of wholesome? Non-greed is the root of wholesome, non-hatred is the root of wholesome, non-delusion is the root of wholesome—this, friends, is called the root of wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: And what, friends, is outflow, what is the origin of outflows, what is the cessation of outflows, what is the path leading to the cessation of outflows? These three, friends, are outflows: the sensual-outflow, the existence-outflow, the ignorance-outflow. With the arising of ignorance is the arising of outflows, with the cessation of ignorance is the cessation of outflows, this noble eightfold path is the path leading to the cessation of outflows, namely: right view … right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: When, friends, a noble disciple understands unwholesome thus, understands the root of unwholesome thus, understands wholesome thus, understands the root of wholesome thus, he has completely abandoned the underlying tendency to greed, has completely removed the underlying tendency to aversion, has completely uprooted the underlying tendency to the view ‘I am,’ has abandoned ignorance and generated knowledge, he is an end-maker of suffering right in this present life—to this extent, friends, a noble disciple has right view, his view is straight, he has unshakeable confidence in the teaching, he has come to this true Dhamma.
translations.sn1.10:2: ‘For those dwelling in the forest, peaceful celibates; Eating one meal a day, by what does their complexion become bright?’
translations.sn1.10:3: ‘They do not sorrow over the past, nor do they chatter about the future; They live with the present, thereby their complexion becomes bright.
translations.sn1.17:1: ‘It is hard, difficult to endure, and recluseship for the untaught; There are many obstructions there, where the fool would despair.’
translations.sn1.17:2: ‘How could one practice recluseship if one does not restrain the mind; One would despair at every step, following along with resolutions.
translations.sn1.17:3: ‘Like one with bad limbs on his own head, the monk should gather his mental thoughts; Unsupported, without another vehicle, the one who is fully quenched would not reproach anyone.’
translations.sn1.18:1: ‘A man who restrains greed, someone is found in the world; Who awakens from blame, like a fine horse from sleep.’
translations.sn1.18:2: ‘Those who restrain greed with their bodies, who always mindfully go about; Having reached the end of suffering, they go on uneven ground as ascetics.’
translations.sn1.1:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, on that occasion, a certain deity, having approached in the late night, her surpassing beauty illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, went to the Blessed One; having gone to him, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Blessed One: “How, venerable sir, do you cross the flood?” “I cross the flood neither standing nor swimming, friend.” “But how, venerable sir, do you cross the flood neither standing nor swimming?” “When, friend, I stand, then I sink; when, friend, I swim, then I am swept away. Thus, friend, I cross the flood neither standing nor swimming.”
translations.sn1.1:2: ‘For a long time indeed I see a brahmin fully quenched; Neither standing nor swimming, he has crossed the flood, free from clinging in the world.’
translations.sn1.1:3: This the deity spoke. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, thinking “The Teacher has approved of me,” paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him on her right, and vanished right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapodā Grove. Then venerable Samiddhi, rising early in the morning at the end of the night, went to the Tapodā to wash his limbs. Having washed his limbs in the Tapodā and come ashore, he stood in his undergarment rubbing his limbs dry. Then a certain deity, in the far extreme of the night, with surpassing beauty illuminating the entire Tapodā, approached venerable Samiddhi; having approached, standing in the air she addressed venerable Samiddhi with a verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: “Do not beg without having eaten, monk, for one does not beg after having eaten; Having eaten, monk, beg, lest that time pass by.”
translations.sn1.20:20: “Beings with the perception of the declarable, established in the declarable; Not having fully understood the declarable, they are ensnared by the yoke of death.
translations.sn1.20:21: Having fully understood the declarable, one does not misconceive the declarer; For that does not exist for him by which they blame him; If you know, speak, yakkha.”
translations.sn1.20:22: “Indeed, sir, I do not understand the meaning in detail of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand the meaning in detail of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.”
translations.sn1.20:23: “Equal, superior, or inferior, whoever fancies such, quarrels with that one; Unshaken amid the three kinds, equal or superior does not exist for him; If you know, speak, yakkha.”
translations.sn1.20:25: “He gave up the conch, did not reach the celestial chariot, cut off craving here in name-and-form; That one with bonds severed, undying, without outflow, seeking him we did not find; Devas, humans here or beyond, or in all heavenly abodes.
translations.sn1.20:3: “I do not know the time, the time is hidden, not seen; Therefore without having eaten I beg, lest the time pass by for me.”
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity alighting on the ground addressed venerable Samiddhi: “You, monk, are young, recently gone forth, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not wearied of sensual pleasures. Enjoy, monk, human sensual pleasures; do not, giving up the seen, run after the unseen.”
translations.sn1.20:5: “Indeed, friend, I do not run after the unseen, giving up the seen. Indeed, friend, giving up the unseen, I run after the seen. For sensual pleasures, friend, were said by the Blessed One to be very painful, very perilous, with much drawback here. This Dhamma is directly visible, timeless, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be personally known by the wise.”
translations.sn1.20:6: “And how, monk, were sensual pleasures said by the Blessed One to be very painful, very perilous, with much drawback here? And how is this Dhamma directly visible, timeless, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be personally known by the wise?”
translations.sn1.20:7: “Friend, I am new, recently gone forth, only just come to this Dhamma and Discipline. I am not able to explain it in detail. That Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapodā Grove. Approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so you should retain it.”
translations.sn1.20:8: “Monk, it is not easy to approach that Blessed One, surrounded by other very powerful deities. But if you, monk, approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter, we too will come to hear the Dhamma.” “Very well, friend,” venerable Samiddhi replied to that deity and approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, venerable Samiddhi said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.21:2: “Intoxicated as if by liquor, with head as if burning; For the abandoning of sensual lust, mindful the monk should wander.”
translations.sn1.21:3: “Intoxicated as if by liquor, with head as if burning; For the abandoning of identity view, mindful the monk should wander.”
translations.sn1.25:1: “Whoever is a monk who has done what is to be done, with taints destroyed, bearing his last body; He might say ‘I speak,’ or they might say ‘He speaks of me.’”
translations.sn1.25:2: “Whoever is a monk who has done what is to be done, with taints destroyed, bearing his last body; He might say ‘I speak,’ or they might say ‘He speaks of me’; Knowing well the convention in the world, he would speak merely by convention.”
translations.sn1.25:3: “Whoever is a monk who has done what is to be done, with taints destroyed, bearing his last body; Surely that monk does not take up conceit, he might say ‘I speak,’ or they might say ‘He speaks of me.’”
translations.sn1.25:4: “For one who has abandoned conceit there are no bonds, all bonds of conceit are shaken off; That wise one who has transcended conceit-making, he might say ‘I speak.
translations.sn1.25:5: Or they might say ‘He speaks of me,’ knowing well the convention in the world; He would speak merely by convention.”
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain deity, in the far extreme of the night, with surpassing beauty illuminating the entire Jetavana, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.2:5: “With the destruction of delighting in becoming, with the cessation of perception and consciousness; With the cessation of feelings, calming, thus I know, friend; The escape, release, seclusion for beings.”
translations.sn1.36:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then several deities with great bodies, in the far extreme of the night, with surpassing beauty illuminating the entire Jetavana, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity said this verse near the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.36:2: “Faith is the second quality for a man, unless he is established in faithlessness; Fame and glory come to him, and he goes to heaven leaving the body behind.”
translations.sn1.36:4: “He should abandon anger, let go of conceit, overcome all fetters; Not sticking in name-and-form, the one without possessions is not followed by bonds.”
translations.sn1.36:5: “Fools and dim-witted people practice heedlessness; The wise one guards heedfulness as the best treasure.
translations.sn1.38:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi deer park. At that time the Blessed One’s foot had been cut by a splinter. Very severe bodily feelings were assailing the Blessed One—painful, sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable; and yet the Blessed One endured them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being perturbed. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion’s pose, foot resting on foot, mindful and clearly comprehending.
translations.sn1.38:10: Overcome by craving, bound by precepts, practicing harsh asceticism for a hundred years; their minds not rightly freed, such inferior ones do not reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.38:11: There is no restraint for one who desires conceit, no mindfulness for one who is unconcentrated; one who dwells alone in the forest heedlessly would not cross beyond death’s realm.
translations.sn1.38:12: “Abandoning conceit, with mind well-concentrated, with pure heart freed in every way; dwelling alone in the forest heedfully, he would cross beyond death’s realm.”
translations.sn1.38:2: Then seven hundred satullapakāyikā deities, on that night of radiant beauty, illuminating the entire Maddakucchi, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity near the Blessed One uttered this udāna: “The ascetic Gotama is truly a nāga; like a nāga, bodily feelings arisen—painful, sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable—he endures them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being perturbed.”
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity near the Blessed One uttered this udāna: “The ascetic Gotama is truly a lion; like a lion, bodily feelings arisen—painful, sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, disagreeable—he endures them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being perturbed.”
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity near the Blessed One uttered this udāna: “See the well-developed concentration, the mind well-freed, not pressed down, not drawn back, not restrained and suppressed with thinking. Who would think one should transgress such a man-nāga, man-lion, man-thoroughbred, man-bull, man-elephant, man-tooth? Unless it be by not seeing.”
translations.sn1.38:9: “A hundred Vedic experts, practicing asceticism, brahmins wandering; their minds not rightly freed, such inferior ones do not reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.41:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then a certain deity, on that night of radiant beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity near the Blessed One spoke these verses:
translations.sn1.41:4: Giving has a pleasant fruit, not-giving does not have that; thieves take, kings take, fire burns, it is lost.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then with its end he relinquishes it, the body with its possessions; knowing this, the wise one enjoys and gives; having given and enjoyed according to his means, blameless he attains the heavenly state.
translations.sn1.42:1: “What giver is a giver of strength, what giver is a giver of beauty; what giver is a giver of happiness, what giver is a giver of sight; who is the giver of all, tell me that when asked.”
translations.sn1.42:2: “A giver of food is a giver of strength, a giver of cloth is a giver of beauty; a giver of vehicles is a giver of happiness, a giver of lamps is a giver of sight.
translations.sn1.42:3: He is the giver of all, who gives a teaching; he is a giver of deathlessness, who instructs in the Dhamma.
translations.sn1.51:1: “What is good as far as old age, what is good when well-established; what is the jewel of men, what is hard to steal by thieves?”
translations.sn1.51:2: “Virtue is good as far as old age, faith is good when well-established; wisdom is the jewel of men, merit is hard to steal by thieves.
translations.sn1.55:1: “What gives birth to a person, what runs away from him; what enters saṁsāra, what is his great terror?”
translations.sn1.55:2: “Craving gives birth to a person, his mind runs away; a being enters saṁsāra, suffering is his great terror.
translations.sn1.56:1: “What gives birth to a person, what runs away from him; what enters saṁsāra, by what is he not released?”
translations.sn1.56:2: “Craving gives birth to a person, his mind runs away; a being enters saṁsāra, by suffering he is not released.
translations.sn1.57:1: “What gives birth to a person, what runs away from him; what enters saṁsāra, what is his resort?”
translations.sn1.57:2: “Craving gives birth to a person, his mind runs away; a being enters saṁsāra, kamma is his resort.
translations.sn1.59:1: “What is a person’s second, what guides it; in whom delighting, a man is released from all suffering?”
translations.sn1.59:2: “Faith is a person’s second, wisdom guides it; delighting in nibbāna, a man is released from all suffering.
translations.sn1.62:1: “By what is the world led, by what is it drawn; by what single thing, do all follow control?”
translations.sn1.62:2: “By mind the world is led, by mind it is drawn; by that single thing mind, all follow control.
translations.sn1.63:2: “By craving the world is led, by craving it is drawn; by that single thing craving, all follow control.
translations.sn1.64:1: “What fetter is the world, what is its examination; by the relinquishment of what, is nibbāna declared?”
translations.sn1.64:2: “Delight is the world’s fetter, thinking is its examination; by the relinquishment of craving, nibbāna is declared.
translations.sn1.65:1: “What binds the world, what is its examination; by the relinquishment of what, cuts all bonds?”
translations.sn1.65:2: “Delight binds the world, thinking is its examination; by the relinquishment of craving, cuts all bonds.
translations.sn1.69:1: “By what is the world broken, by the removal of what is it released; by the relinquishment of what, cuts all bonds?”
translations.sn1.69:2: “By desire the world is broken, by the removal of desire it is released; by the relinquishment of desire, cuts all bonds.
translations.sn1.71:2: “Having cut what does one sleep happily, having cut what does one not sorrow; of what single thing’s destruction, does Gotama approve?”
translations.sn1.71:3: “Having cut anger one sleeps happily, having cut anger one does not sorrow; of anger with poisonous root, sweet-tipped for the gods; noble ones praise its destruction, for having cut it one does not sorrow.
translations.sn1.73:1: “What here is a man’s best wealth, what well-done brings happiness; what here is the best flavor of flavors, how is living called best?”}
translations.sn1.73:2: “Here faith is the best wealth for a man, virtue well-practiced brings happiness; truth is surely the sweetest of flavors, they call the life of wisdom the best.”
translations.sn1.7:2: “For those whose phenomena are not penetrated, who are led away by others’ views; they sleep and do not wake up, it is time for them to wake up.”
translations.sn1.7:3: “For those whose phenomena are well-penetrated, who are not led away by others’ views; they are awakened, fully knowing, they travel evenly on uneven ground.”
translations.sn1.8:2: “For those whose phenomena are well-emerged, who are led away by others’ views; they sleep and do not wake up, it is time for them to wake up.”
translations.sn1.8:3: “For those whose phenomena are unemerged, who are not led away by others’ views; they are awakened, fully knowing, they travel evenly on uneven ground.”
translations.sn11.14:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks.’ ‘Venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the Thirty-Three: ‘Do not, sirs, disparage this godson. This godson, sirs, formerly as a human being took up faith in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Tathāgata, took up virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom. Having taken up faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Tathāgata, after the breakup of the body, after death, he has arisen in a good destination, the heavenly world, in fellowship with the Thirty-Three gods. He outshines the other gods in beauty and fame.’ Then, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, while comforting the Thirty-Three at that time, spoke these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6: Therefore, the wise one should devote himself to faith and virtue, to serene vision of the teaching; mindful of the Buddha’s instruction.”
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī in Jetavana. Then Sakka, lord of gods, went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of gods, said to the Blessed One: ‘Is it, sir, for the pleasure of humans and contemplatives?’
translations.sn11.15:2: “Pleasure-gardens and forest-gardens, lotus ponds beautifully made; for the pleasure of humans and contemplatives, they are not worth one sixteenth.”
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī in Jetavana. There … he said: ‘Once upon a time, monks, a certain ugly, humpbacked yakkha was sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of gods. There, monks, the Thirty-Three gods were disparaging, complaining, murmuring: “How amazing, sirs, how astonishing, sirs. This ugly, humpbacked yakkha is sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of gods.” As the Thirty-Three gods disparaged, complained, and murmured, so that yakkha became more and more beautiful, more handsome, more serene.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, went to that anger-eating yakkha; having gone, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bent his right knee to the ground, saluted that anger-eating yakkha with joined palms three times by name: “I am Sakka, sir, lord of gods, I am Sakka, sir, lord of gods.” As, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, saluted by name, so that yakkha became more and more ugly and more humpbacked. Having become more ugly and more humpbacked, he vanished right there. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, having sat down on his own seat, while comforting the Thirty-Three at that time, spoke these verses:
translations.sn11.22:4: “I am not one whose mind is badly struck, nor am I swept away by anger; I do not stay angry with you long, anger does not persist in me.
translations.sn11.22:5: When angry I do not speak harshly, nor do I proclaim faults; I restrain myself, seeing my own benefit.”
translations.sn11.24:2: “These two, monks, are fools: one who does not see his offense as an offense, and one who does not properly accept an offense when it is confessed to him according to rule—these two, monks, are fools. These two, monks, are wise: one who sees his offense as an offense, and one who properly accepts an offense when it is confessed to him according to rule—these two, monks, are wise.
translations.sn11.24:3: Once upon a time, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, while comforting the Thirty-Three in the Hall of Justice, at that time spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.24:4: “May anger come under your control, and may you not age among friends; do not blame what is blameless, and do not speak slander; but anger against evil people crushes like a mountain.’”
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks.’ ‘Venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you cannot recollect me, then recollect the teaching: “The teaching is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be personally experienced by the wise.” For those of you, monks, who recollect the teaching, any fear, terror, or horror that arises will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you cannot recollect the teaching, then recollect the Saṅgha: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of straight conduct, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of proper conduct, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is of the four pairs, the eight individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of respectful salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” For those of you, monks, who recollect the Saṅgha, any fear, terror, or horror that arises will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: Why is that? For the Tathāgata, monks, is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, free of lust, free of hate, free of delusion, confident, unshaken, undaunted, not retreating.’” Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said:
translations.sn11.3:13: “In the forest or at the root of a tree, monks, or in an empty house; recollect the awakened one, may there be no fear for you.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you cannot recollect the Buddha, the best of men, chief of the world; then recollect the teaching, onward-leading, well-proclaimed.
translations.sn11.3:15: If you cannot recollect the teaching, onward-leading, well-proclaimed; then recollect the Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: For those monks who thus recollect the Buddha, the teaching and the Saṅgha; there will be no fear, terror, or horror.”
translations.sn11.3:2: “Formerly, monks, there was a battle between the gods and asuras that had broken out. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, addressed the Thirty Gods:
translations.sn11.3:3: ‘If, friends, fear or fright or horripilation should arise in the gods gone to battle, then you should look at my flag-top at that time. For when you look at my flag-top, any fear or fright or horripilation that there is will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you do not look at my flag-top, then you should look at the flag-top of Pajapati, king of gods. For when you look at the flag-top of Pajapati, king of gods, any fear or fright or horripilation that there is will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:8: For what reason? For Sakka, monks, lord of gods, is not free from lust, not free from hate, not free from delusion; he is fearful, frightened, anxious, he flees.’
translations.sn11.3:9: And I, monks, say this: ‘If, monks, when you are gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty house, fear or fright or horripilation should arise, then at that time you should recollect me: “Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.” For when you recollect me, monks, any fear or fright or horripilation that there is will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:12: He fares for the sake of both,  his own and another’s;  Knowing another’s agitation,  he who is mindful calms down.
translations.sn11.5:14: When, monks, verses had been spoken by Sakka, lord of gods, the gods approved, the asuras were silent. Then, monks, the attendants of the gods and asuras said this: ‘Verses have been spoken by Vepacitti, asura-lord. And they are those that resort to punishment and resort to weapons, thus it is strife, thus it is dispute, thus it is quarrel. Verses have been spoken by Sakka, lord of gods. And they are those that do not resort to punishment and do not resort to weapons, thus it is non-strife, thus it is non-dispute, thus it is non-quarrel. Victory to Sakka, lord of gods, by well-spokenness.’ Thus, monks, there was victory to Sakka, lord of gods, by well-spokenness.”
translations.sn11.5:2: ‘Fools would more transgress,  if there were no restrainer;  Therefore with a great stick,  the wise should restrain the fool.’
translations.sn11.5:3: When, monks, a verse had been spoken by Vepacitti, asura-lord, the asuras approved, the gods were silent. Then, monks, Vepacitti, asura-lord, said to Sakka, lord of gods: ‘Speak a verse, lord of gods.’ When this was said, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: ‘This alone I consider  restraint for a fool;  Knowing another’s agitation,  he who is mindful calms down.’
translations.sn11.5:5: When, monks, a verse had been spoken by Sakka, lord of gods, the gods approved, the asuras were silent. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of gods, said to Vepacitti, asura-lord: ‘Speak a verse, Vepacitti.’ When this was said, monks, Vepacitti, asura-lord, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: ‘This alone by forbearance,  I see a taint;  When a fool thinks of it,  out of fear he forbear;  The stupid one mounts up,  like a cow more fleeing.’
translations.sn11.5:8: ‘Let him think so or not,  out of fear he forbear;  The goal supreme for the sake of goals,  nothing greater than patience exists.
translations.sn12.11:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park … “There are these four nourishments, monks, for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, for the support of those becoming. Which four? Physical food, coarse or subtle; contact is the second; mental intention is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These are the four nourishments, monks, for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, for the support of those becoming.
translations.sn12.12:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. “There are these four nourishments, monks, for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, for the support of those becoming. Which four? Physical food, coarse or subtle; contact is the second; mental intention is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These are the four nourishments, monks, for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, for the support of those becoming.”
translations.sn12.15:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Kaccānagotta said to the Blessed One: “‘Right view, right view,’ it is said, sir. In what way, sir, is there right view?”
translations.sn12.15:2: “This world, Kaccāna, for the most part depends upon a duality—upon existence and non-existence. But when one sees with right wisdom, as it really is, the arising of the world, ‘non-existence’ with regard to the world is not found. When one sees with right wisdom, as it really is, the cessation of the world, ‘existence’ with regard to the world is not found. This world, Kaccāna, for the most part is bound by clinging to attachments, clinging to adherence, clinging to underlying tendencies. But one who does not take up clinging to attachments, adherence, underlying tendencies with mind does not adhere, does not take up, does not establish: ‘This is my self.’ He knows: ‘What arises as suffering arises, what ceases as suffering ceases’; he does not doubt, does not waver; herein his knowledge is independent. In this way, Kaccāna, there is right view.
translations.sn12.17:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, Squirrels’ Feeding-ground. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Kassapa the unclothed saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and worldly talk of welcome, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Kassapa the unclothed said to the Blessed One: “We would ask the Venerable Gotama a certain teaching, if the Venerable Gotama would give us leave to question.” “Not now, Kassapa, for questioning; we have entered among houses.”
translations.sn12.17:5: “‘One who acts, that one experiences,’ Kassapa, those who in the beginning recollect thus: ‘suffering is self-made,’ this is eternalism they declare. ‘Another acts, another experiences,’ Kassapa, those who are overwhelmed by feeling recollect thus: ‘suffering is made by another,’ this is annihilationism they declare. Avoiding these two extremes, Kassapa, the Tathāgata teaches Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance there is cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations there is cessation of consciousness …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, sir, excellent, sir. Just as one might set upright what was overturned …pe… ‘those with vision see forms’; even so the Dhamma has been revealed in many ways by the Blessed One. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks, sir. May I receive the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence, may I receive ordination into monkhood.”
translations.sn12.17:7: “Kassapa, when one who was formerly a follower of another sect desires ordination, desires full ordination in this Dhamma and discipline, he dwells under probation for four months. At the end of four months, the monks who are firm in faith give him the going forth, give him full ordination into monkhood. Nevertheless, I recognize individual differences.”
translations.sn12.18:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: “‘That feeling, that one feels,’ Timbaruka, those in the beginning recollect: ‘pleasure and pain are self-made’—thus I do not say. ‘A different feeling, a different one feels,’ Timbaruka, those overwhelmed by feeling recollect: ‘pleasure and pain are made by another’—thus I do not say. Avoiding these two extremes, Timbaruka, the Tathāgata teaches Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance there is cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations there is cessation of consciousness …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.19:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for the fool who is obstructed by ignorance and associated with craving, this body has arisen thus. So this very body and external name-and-form, this duality, contact dependent on this duality touches the six sense fields, by which touched the fool experiences pleasure and pain, or one of them.
translations.sn12.19:2: Bhikkhus, for the wise one who is obstructed by ignorance and associated with craving, this body has arisen thus. So this very body and external name-and-form, this duality, contact dependent on this duality touches the six sense fields, by which touched the wise one experiences pleasure and pain, or one of them.
translations.sn12.19:3: “What is the difference, bhikkhus, what is the point, what is the reason for calling the wise one and the fool different?” “Our Dhammas have the Blessed One as their root, sir, their guide, their refuge. It would be good if the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One were clarified by the Blessed One. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will retain it.”
translations.sn12.19:5: “Bhikkhus, and that ignorance with which the fool is obstructed, and that craving with which he is associated—this body has arisen. That ignorance of the fool is not abandoned, that craving is not extinguished. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the fool has not properly practiced the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body the fool is reborn in a body, and being reborn in a body he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. ‘He is not freed from suffering,’ I say.
translations.sn12.23:5: And what, bhikkhus, is the basis for craving? ‘Feeling’ should be said …pe… ‘contact’ should be said … ‘six sense fields’ should be said … ‘name-and-form’ should be said … ‘consciousness’ should be said … ‘formations’ should be said. Bhikkhus, I say formations have a basis, not without a basis. And what, bhikkhus, is the basis for formations? ‘Ignorance’ should be said.
translations.sn12.23:6: Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as basis formations, with formations as basis consciousness, with consciousness as basis name-and-form, with name-and-form as basis six sense fields, with six sense fields as basis contact, with contact as basis feeling, with feeling as basis craving, with craving as basis clinging, with clinging as basis existence, with existence as basis birth, with birth as basis suffering, with suffering as basis faith, with faith as basis joy, with joy as basis rapture, with rapture as basis tranquility, with tranquility as basis pleasure, with pleasure as basis concentration, with concentration as basis knowledge and vision of things as they really are, with knowledge and vision of things as they really are as basis disenchantment, with disenchantment as basis dispassion, with dispassion as basis liberation, with liberation as basis knowledge of destruction.
translations.sn12.23:7: Just as, bhikkhus, when it rains heavily on the upper mountain and the water flows down the slope filling the mountain clefts, gullies, ravines. The mountain clefts, gullies, ravines being filled fill the little pools. The little pools being filled fill the great pools. The great pools being filled fill the little rivers. The little rivers being filled fill the great rivers. The great rivers being filled fill the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Bhūmija, having emerged from retreat at the time of evening, approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhūmija said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: Ānanda, when there is body-consciousness, pleasure and pain arise internally due to bodily volition. Ānanda, when there is speech-consciousness, pleasure and pain arise internally due to verbal volition. Ānanda, when there is mind-consciousness, pleasure and pain arise internally due to mental volition and ignorance as condition.
translations.sn12.25:11: Or he himself forms that bodily formation, Ānanda, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arise internally. Others form that bodily formation for him, Ānanda, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arise internally. He forms that bodily formation mindfully, Ānanda, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arise internally. He forms that bodily formation unmindfully, Ānanda, conditioned by which that pleasure and pain arise internally.
translations.sn12.25:2: “There are some ascetics and brahmins, friend Sāriputta, who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be created by oneself. There are some ascetics and brahmins, friend Sāriputta, who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be created by another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, friend Sāriputta, who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be both created by oneself and created by another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, friend Sāriputta, who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be neither created by oneself nor created by another, but arisen by chance. Here, friend Sāriputta, what is the Blessed One’s position? How should we answer so that we are speakers of what has been spoken by the Blessed One, not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one who follows the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma will find grounds for blame?”
translations.sn12.25:3: “Pleasure and pain, friend, have been declared by the Blessed One as dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Speaking thus, one would be a speaker of what has been spoken by the Blessed One, not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one who follows the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma will find grounds for blame.
translations.sn12.25:4: Here, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be created by oneself—that too is conditioned by contact. Those who … those who … those ascetics and brahmins who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be neither created by oneself nor created by another, but arisen by chance—that too is conditioned by contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: Here, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be created by oneself—could they feel it apart from contact? That is not possible. Those who … those who … those ascetics and brahmins who are advocates of action who declare pleasure and pain to be neither created by oneself nor created by another, but arisen by chance—could they feel it apart from contact? That is not possible.”
translations.sn12.25:6: Then Venerable Ānanda heard this discussion between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija. Then Venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. When he was seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire discussion that had taken place between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija.
translations.sn12.25:7: “Good, good, Ānanda! Sāriputta has answered correctly. Pleasure and pain, Ānanda, have been declared by me as dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Speaking thus, one would be a speaker of what has been spoken by me, not misrepresent me with what is untrue, explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one who follows the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma will find grounds for blame.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, monks, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention—this is called name. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—this is called form. Thus this is name, and this is form. This, monks, is called name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, monks, is consciousness? These six, monks, are classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This, monks, is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, monks, are formations? These three, monks, are formations: body-formation, speech-formation, mind-formation. These, monks, are called formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, monks, is ignorance? It is ignorance with regard to suffering, ignorance with regard to the origin of suffering, ignorance with regard to the cessation of suffering, ignorance with regard to the path leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, monks, is existence? These three, monks, are existences: sensuous existence, form existence, formless existence. This, monks, is called existence.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, monks, is clinging? These four, monks, are types of clinging: sensuous clinging, view clinging, precept-and-rite clinging, self-doctrine clinging. This, monks, is called clinging.
translations.sn12.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed Venerable Sāriputta: “It has been said in the Pārāyana, Sāriputta, in the Ajita questions:
translations.sn12.31:2: ‘Those who know the Dhamma, and the many trainees here; Of them, my wise one, declare the conduct, when asked, good sir.’
translations.sn12.31:3: How, Sāriputta, should the meaning of this briefly stated statement be understood in detail?” When this was said, Venerable Sāriputta was silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: “Do you see it as ‘This is actually true,’ Sāriputta?” “One sees it as ‘This is actually true,’ venerable sir, sees it with right understanding as it really is. Having seen it as ‘This is actually true’ with right understanding as it really is, one practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is actually true. One sees it as ‘Arisen from food’ with right understanding as it really is. Having seen it as ‘Arisen from food’ with right understanding as it really is, one practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is arisen from food. With the cessation of food, what is actually true is a cessation-Dhamma—this one sees with right understanding as it really is. Having seen with right understanding as it really is that with the cessation of food, what is actually true is a cessation-Dhamma, one practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is a cessation-Dhamma. Thus, venerable sir, one is a trainee.”}
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, venerable sir, is there a conditioned phenomenon? ‘This exists,’ venerable sir: he sees it as it really is with right view. Having seen ‘This exists’ as it really is with right view, he is freed without clinging through disgust, dispassion, and cessation regarding what exists. ‘It exists due to food,’ he sees as it really is with right view. Having seen ‘It exists due to food’ as it really is with right view, he is freed without clinging through disgust, dispassion, and cessation regarding what exists due to food. ‘Due to the cessation of food, what exists is a cessation phenomenon,’ he sees as it really is with right view. Having seen ‘Due to the cessation of food, what exists is a cessation phenomenon’ as it really is with right view, he is freed without clinging through disgust, dispassion, and cessation regarding the cessation phenomenon. Thus, venerable sir, there is a conditioned phenomenon. Thus, venerable sir, that which was stated in the Pārāyana, to Ajita:
translations.sn12.35:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. ‘With ignorance as condition, monks, there are formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering,’ he said. When this was said, a certain monk said this to the Blessed One: ‘But what, venerable sir, is aging-and-death, and whose is this aging-and-death?’ ‘That is not a proper question,’ the Blessed One said. ‘Whether one should say “What is aging-and-death, and whose is this aging-and-death?” or, monk, one should say “Another aging-and-death, and another’s is this aging-and-death,” or, monk, one should say “The same being is the same body,” or, monk, with the view “Another being, another body,” there is no living of the holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: “With birth as condition, aging-and-death.”’
translations.sn12.35:2: ‘But what, venerable sir, is birth, and whose is this birth?’ ‘That is not a proper question,’ the Blessed One said. ‘Whether one should say “What is birth, and whose is this birth?” or, monk, one should say “Another birth, and another’s is this birth,” both these are the same in meaning, the difference is merely one of grammar. Or, monk, with the view “The same being is the same body,” there is no living of the holy life. Or, monk, with the view “Another being, another body,” there is no living of the holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: “With existence as condition, birth.”’
translations.sn12.35:3: ‘But what, venerable sir, is existence, and whose is this existence?’ ‘That is not a proper question,’ the Blessed One said. ‘Whether one should say “What is existence, and whose is this existence?” or, monk, one should say “Another existence, and another’s is this existence,” both these are the same in meaning, the difference is merely one of grammar. Or, monk, with the view “The same being is the same body,” there is no living of the holy life; or, monk, with the view “Another being, another body,” there is no living of the holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: “With clinging as condition, existence” …pe… “with craving as condition, clinging … with feeling as condition, craving … with contact as condition, feeling … with the six sense fields as condition, contact … with name-and-form as condition, the six sense fields … with consciousness as condition, name-and-form … with formations as condition, consciousness.”
translations.sn12.35:4: ‘But what, venerable sir, are formations, and whose are these formations?’ ‘That is not a proper question,’ the Blessed One said. ‘Whether one should say “What are formations, and whose are these formations?” or, monk, one should say “Other formations, and another’s are these formations,” both these are the same in meaning, the difference is merely one of grammar. Or, monk, with the view “The same being is the same body,” there is no living of the holy life; or, monk, with the view “Another being, another body,” there is no living of the holy life. Avoiding these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: “With ignorance as condition, formations.”’
translations.sn12.35:5: But with the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, monk, any of those subtle designations, pursued, proliferated that there are for him: ‘What is aging-and-death, and whose is this aging-and-death?’ or ‘Another aging-and-death, and another’s is this aging-and-death,’ or ‘The same being is the same body,’ or ‘Another being, another body’—all these are abandoned by him, their root destroyed, like a palm tree made into a stump, deprived of the conditions of existence, not destined to re-arise in the future.
translations.sn12.35:7: But with the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, monk, any of those subtle designations, pursued, proliferated that there are for him. What is existence …pe… what is clinging … what is craving … what is feeling … what is contact … what are the six sense fields … what is name-and-form … what is consciousness …pe….
translations.sn12.38:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. ‘Whatever, monks, one thinks, plans, and mentally proliferates, that becomes a basis for the establishing of consciousness. With a basis, there is a footing for consciousness. When consciousness is established and grown, there is future rebirth into existence. With future rebirth into existence, there is future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.38:2: But if, monks, one does not think, does not plan, but does mentally proliferate, that becomes a basis for the establishing of consciousness. With a basis, there is a footing for consciousness. When consciousness is established and grown, there is future rebirth into existence. With future rebirth into existence, there is future birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.44:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. ‘Monks, I will teach the arising and passing away of the world. Listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak,’ he said. ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: “And what, monks, is the arising of the world? Dependent on eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, monks, is the arising of the world.”
translations.sn12.44:3: “Dependent on ear and sounds …pe… dependent on nose and odors … dependent on tongue and flavors … dependent on body and tangibles … dependent on mind and ideas, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling …pe… with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, monks, is the arising of the world.”
translations.sn12.44:4: “And what, monks, is the disappearance of the world? Dependent on eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving. With the complete fading away and cessation of that same craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is the disappearance of the world.”
translations.sn12.46:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin went to the Blessed One, and on arrival, having exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, after concluding the courteous talk, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.46:2: “Does one make, does one experience?” “ ‘One makes, one experiences,’ brahmin, this is one extreme.”
translations.sn12.46:3: “But does another make, does another experience?” “ ‘Another makes, another experiences,’ brahmin, this is the second extreme. Avoiding these two extremes, brahmin, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. But with the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.51:10: When he experiences a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not clung to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ When he experiences a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not clung to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ When he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not clung to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ When he experiences a pleasant feeling, he experiences it dissociated. When he experiences a painful feeling, he experiences it dissociated. When he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he experiences it dissociated.
translations.sn12.51:11: While experiencing a feeling limited by the body, he understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited by the body.’ While experiencing a feeling limited by life, he understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited by life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, beyond the ending of life, all that is felt, not delighted in, will cool here; only the body will remain.’
translations.sn12.51:12: “Suppose, monks, a man were to take a hot potter’s wheel and place it on level ground. The heat there would subside right there, and the shards would remain. In the same way, monks, while experiencing a feeling limited by the body, a monk understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited by the body.’ While experiencing a feeling limited by life, he understands: ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited by life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, beyond the ending of life, all that is felt, not delighted in, will cool here; only the body will remain.’”
translations.sn12.51:13: “What do you think, monks, would an arahant monk generate a meritorious volitional formation, or an unmeritorious volitional formation, or a neutral volitional formation?” “No, lord.”
translations.sn12.51:14: “And if there were absolutely no volitional formations, with the cessation of volitional formations, would consciousness appear?” “No, lord.”
translations.sn12.51:2: “Monks, by what investigating should a monk investigate so as to investigate entirely for the complete ending of suffering?” “The Dhammas are rooted in the Blessed One, lord, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, lord, if the Blessed One would make known the meaning of what has been said. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it in mind.” “Very well then, monks, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, lord,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn12.51:3: “Here, monks, a monk investigating considers: ‘This suffering that arises in the world in various ways and kinds, aging-and-death: what is its origin, what its arising, what its coming-into-existence, what its source?
