When what exists is there aging-and-death, when what does not exist is there no aging-and-death?’ Investigating, he understands: ‘This suffering that arises in the world in various ways and kinds, aging-and-death, this suffering has birth as its origin, birth as its arising, birth as its coming-into-existence, birth as its source. When birth exists, there is aging-and-death; when birth does not exist, there is no aging-and-death.’”
translations.sn12.51:4: “He understands aging-and-death, understands the arising of aging-and-death, understands the cessation of aging-and-death, and understands the path leading to the cessation of aging-and-death, and he practices in accordance with the Dhamma; this, monks, is called a monk who has entirely practiced for the complete ending of suffering, for the cessation of aging-and-death.”
translations.sn12.51:5: “Further, investigating he investigates: ‘But this birth, what is its origin, what its arising, what its coming-into-existence, what its source? When what exists is there birth, when what does not exist is there no birth?’ Investigating, he understands: ‘Birth has becoming as its origin, becoming as its arising, becoming as its coming-into-existence, becoming as its source. When becoming exists, there is birth; when becoming does not exist, there is no birth.’”}
translations.sn12.51:6: He understands birth, understands the origin of birth, understands the cessation of birth, understands the path leading to the cessation of birth, and he practices in that way, walking in accordance with the Dhamma; this, monks, is called a monk who has entirely practiced for the complete destruction of suffering for the cessation of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, further reflecting, he reflects: ‘But what is the condition for this becoming? …pe… What is the condition for this clinging? … What is the condition for this craving? … Feeling … contact … What is the condition for this six sense fields? … Name-and-form … What is the condition for this consciousness? … What is the condition for these formations, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their source; when what exists are formations present, when what is absent are formations not present?’ Reflecting thus, he understands: ‘Formations have ignorance as their condition, have ignorance as their origin, are born of ignorance, arisen from ignorance; when ignorance exists, formations come to be; when ignorance is absent, formations do not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:8: He understands formations, understands the origin of formations, understands the cessation of formations, understands the path leading to the cessation of formations, and he practices in that way, walking in accordance with the Dhamma; this, monks, is called a monk who has entirely practiced for the complete destruction of suffering for the cessation of formations.
translations.sn12.51:9: Monks, when a person makes a meritorious formation from ignorance, consciousness becomes headed for merit. When he makes a demeritorious formation, consciousness becomes headed for demerit. When he makes an imperturbable formation, consciousness becomes headed for the imperturbable. But when a monk’s ignorance is abandoned and knowledge arisen, he does not make a meritorious formation, nor a demeritorious formation, nor an imperturbable formation out of the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge. Not making, not intending, he does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, he does not tremble; untrembling, he personally attains nibbāna. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further here.’
translations.sn12.52:2: Monks, just as if a great mass of fire were burning with ten, twenty, thirty, or forty bundles of faggots, and a man from time to time would throw on dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry sticks, that great mass of fire, being thus sustained, thus nourished, would burn for a long time. So too, monks, when one dwells seeing delight in things that can be clung to, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging …pe… this is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.52:3: Monks, when one dwells seeing danger in things that can be clung to, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. This is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. “Monks, when one dwells seeing delight in things that can be clung to, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, becoming …pe… this is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:2: Monks, suppose there were a great tree. Its roots growing downwards, its roots growing sideways, all would bring up sap upwards. That great tree, being thus sustained, thus nourished, would stand for a long time. So too, monks, when one dwells seeing delight in things that can be clung to, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging …pe… this is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:3: Monks, when one dwells seeing danger in things that can be clung to, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming …pe… this is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.61:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park … “Monks, even an unlearned ordinary person should become disenchanted, dispassionate, and freed regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because, monks, the buildup and breakdown, the taking up and laying down of this body composed of the four great elements is seen. Therefore, an unlearned ordinary person should become disenchanted, dispassionate, and freed regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:2: But regarding what is called mind, or mentality, or consciousness, an unlearned ordinary person is not able to become disenchanted, dispassionate, and freed. Why is that? Because for a long time, monks, this has been clung to, taken as ‘I’, ‘mine’, and held to by an unlearned ordinary person: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ Therefore, an unlearned ordinary person is not able to become disenchanted, dispassionate, and freed regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:3: Monks, better for an unlearned ordinary person to regard this body composed of the four great elements as self than to regard mind. Why is that? Because this body composed of the four great elements is seen to stand for one year, two years, three years, four years, five years, ten years, twenty years, thirty years, forty years, fifty years, a hundred years, even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: Here, monks, the learned noble disciple carefully and properly reflects on dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases—that is, with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering. With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness …pe… thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’
translations.sn12.62:3: Here, monks, the learned noble disciple carefully and properly reflects on dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.’ With contact as condition, pleasant feeling arises, monks. With the cessation of that very contact that is pleasant feeling, the pleasant feeling arisen dependent on that very contact that is pleasant feeling ceases, it calms. With contact as condition, painful feeling arises, monks. With the cessation of that very contact that is painful feeling, the painful feeling arisen dependent on that very contact that is painful feeling ceases, it calms. With contact as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises, monks. With the cessation of that very contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen dependent on that very contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling ceases, it calms.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, monks, with the striking together and rubbing of two sticks, heat is produced, fire is generated. With the separation and disjoining of those very two sticks, that heat ceases, it calms; even so, monks, with contact as condition, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact that is pleasant feeling, the pleasant feeling arisen dependent on that very contact that is pleasant feeling ceases, it calms …pe… with contact as condition … painful feeling … with contact as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen dependent on that very contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling ceases, it calms.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, monks, would those people carry food for the sake of a jungle fire, or for the sake of intoxication, or for the sake of adornment, or for the sake of beautification?” “No, sir.” “But would they not carry food just for the sake of crossing the desert?” “Yes, sir.” “‘In the same way, monks, I say that physical food should be seen.’ With physical food fully understood, monks, lust for the five strands of sensual pleasures is fully understood. With lust for the five strands of sensual pleasures fully understood, there is no fetter by which the noble disciple who is bound by that fetter would again come to this world.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, monks, should contact as food be seen? Just as, monks, a cow is wanderer-born and stands relying on a stump. Those creatures that rely on a stump would eat it. If it stands relying on a tree, those creatures that rely on a tree would eat it. If it stands relying on water, those creatures that rely on water would eat it. If it stands relying on air, those creatures that rely on air would eat it. Whatever it stands relying on, monks, that wanderer-born cow, those creatures that rely on that would eat it. In the same way, monks, I say ‘contact as food should be seen.’ With contact as food fully understood, monks, the three feelings are fully understood. With the three feelings fully understood, I say of the noble disciple there is nothing further needed.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, monks, should mental intention as food be seen? Just as, monks, a brazier of live coals sufficient for one man, full of glowing coals, without smoke, without dust. Then a man would come desiring to live, not desiring to die, desiring happiness, averse to suffering. Two strong men would grab him by the arms on both sides and drag him to the brazier of live coals. There, monks, that man’s intention, aspiration, and resolution would be far away. Why is that? Because this is his thought: ‘I will fall into this brazier of live coals and on account of that I will meet death or death-like suffering.’ In the same way, monks, I say ‘mental intention as food should be seen.’ With mental intention as food fully understood, monks, the three cravings are fully understood. With the three cravings fully understood, I say of the noble disciple there is nothing further needed.
translations.sn12.64:2: If there is lust, delight, and craving for physical food, monks, then consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is descent of name-and-form. Where there is descent of name-and-form, there is growth of formations. Where there is growth of formations, there is future rebirth into existence. Where there is future rebirth into existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, monks, I say there is sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:4: Just as, monks, a dyer or painter would take a well-dyed canvas or wall or cloth and draw a figure of a woman or a man complete in all its limbs and parts; even so, monks, if there is attachment, delight, and craving for nutriment of chunks, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is descent of name-and-form. Where there is descent of name-and-form, there is growth of formations. Where there is growth of formations, there is future rebirth into existence. Where there is future rebirth into existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, that is sorrowful, monks, I say: with anguish, with despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: Monks, if there is no attachment, no delight, no craving for nutriment of chunks, consciousness does not become established there, does not grow. Where consciousness does not become established, does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of formations. Where there is no growth of formations, there is no future rebirth into existence. Where there is no future rebirth into existence, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, that is sorrowless, monks, I say: without anguish, without despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Just as, monks, if there were a peaked house or a peaked hall with a window to the north or south or east, when the sun rises it would shine through the window: where would it land? ‘On the western wall, venerable sir.’ ‘Monks, if there were no western wall, where would it land?’ ‘On the ground, venerable sir.’ ‘Monks, if there were no ground, where would it land?’ ‘In water, venerable sir.’ ‘Monks, if there were no water, where would it land?’ ‘Not landed, venerable sir.’ ‘Even so, monks, if there is no attachment, no delight, no craving for nutriment of chunks …pe….’
translations.sn12.65:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. ‘Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta not yet fully enlightened, this thought arose in me: “Alas, this world has fallen into trouble: it is subject to birth, to aging, to death, to passing away, to rebirth; yet it does not understand an escape from this suffering, from aging-and-death. When will an escape from this suffering, from aging-and-death, become clear?” Then, monks, this thought arose in me: “When what exists is there aging-and-death, aging-and-death is dependent on what?” Then, monks, through careful attention with wisdom there arose in me the insight: “When there is birth there is aging-and-death; aging-and-death is dependent on birth.”
translations.sn12.65:3: Then, monks, this thought arose in me: ‘This consciousness turns back; it does not go on beyond name-and-form.’ To this extent then one is born, ages, dies, passes away, or is reborn: that is, consciousness is dependent on name-and-form; name-and-form is dependent on consciousness; the six sense fields are dependent on name-and-form; contact is dependent on the six sense fields …pe… thus is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. ‘Arising, arising’—in regard to things never heard of before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then, monks, this thought arose in me: ‘When what does not exist is there no consciousness; with the cessation of what does consciousness cease?’ Then, monks, through careful attention with wisdom there arose in me the insight: ‘When name-and-form does not exist, consciousness does not exist; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness.’
translations.sn12.65:6: Then, monks, this thought arose in me: ‘This is the path to enlightenment that I have discovered: with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense fields; with the cessation of the six sense fields comes the cessation of contact …pe… thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. ‘Cessation, cessation’—in regard to things never heard of before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light.
translations.sn12.65:7: Just as, monks, a man wandering through a forest would see an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of former times. He would follow it. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, inhabited long ago by people of former times, with parks, with woods, with lotus ponds, delightful. Then, monks, that man would inform a king or a royal minister: ‘Sire, know this: while wandering in the forest I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of former times. I followed it. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient royal capital … delightful. Sire, have that city built.’ Then, monks, the king or royal minister would have that city built. And in due course that city would become prosperous and flourishing, populous and crowded, with growth and development. Even so, monks, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by former rightly self-awakened ones.
translations.sn12.66:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a town of the Kurus called Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Monks!’ ‘Venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: ‘Monks, I will give you a teaching on betweenness; listen and pay close attention; I will speak.’ When this was said, one monk said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, I understand betweenness.’ ‘But how do you understand betweenness, monk?’ Then that monk explained it. But that monk did not satisfy the Blessed One’s mind with his explanation.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “This is the time, Blessed One; this is the time, Well-Gone One; may the Blessed One teach the intermediate. Having heard from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it.” “Then, Ānanda, listen, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn12.66:5: Then, investigating further, he investigates the intermediate with right investigation: ‘But where does this craving arise that arises, where does it establish itself that establishes itself?’ Investigating with right investigation, he knows: whatever in the world is agreeable and alluring, here this craving arises that arises, here it establishes itself that establishes itself. And what in the world is agreeable and alluring? The eye is agreeable and alluring in the world, here this craving arises that arises, here it establishes itself that establishes itself. The ear is agreeable and alluring in the world … the nose is agreeable and alluring in the world … the tongue is agreeable and alluring in the world … the body is agreeable and alluring in the world … the mind is agreeable and alluring in the world, here this craving arises that arises, here it establishes itself that establishes itself.
translations.sn12.66:6: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, in the past regarded whatever in the world is agreeable and alluring as permanent, failed to see it as happiness, failed to see it as self, failed to see it as health, failed to see it as security. They increased craving. Those who increased craving increased fuel. Those who increased fuel increased suffering. Those who increased suffering were not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they were not freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:7: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, in the future will regard whatever in the world is agreeable and alluring as permanent, will see it as happiness, will see it as self, will see it as health, will see it as security. They will increase craving. Those who increase craving will increase fuel. Those who increase fuel will increase suffering. Those who increase suffering will not be freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they will not be freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:8: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, even now regard whatever in the world is agreeable and alluring as permanent, see it as happiness, see it as self, see it as health, see it as security. They increase craving. Those who increase craving increase fuel. Those who increase fuel increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they are not freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.67:1: On one occasion Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were staying near Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita emerged from retreat and went to Venerable Sāriputta; having gone, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat to one side. Having sat to one side, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said to Venerable Sāriputta: “Friend Sāriputta, is aging-and-death made by oneself, made by another, made by both oneself and another, or does it arise by chance, without cause or condition?” “Friend Koṭṭhika, aging-and-death is not made by oneself, not made by another, not made by both oneself and another, nor does it arise by chance, without cause or condition. Rather, aging-and-death has birth as its condition.”
translations.sn12.67:2: “Friend Sāriputta, is birth made by oneself, made by another, made by both oneself and another, or does it arise by chance, without cause or condition?” “Friend Koṭṭhika, birth is not made by oneself, not made by another, not made by both oneself and another, nor does it arise by chance, without cause or condition. Rather, birth has existence as its condition.”
translations.sn12.67:4: “Friend Sāriputta, is consciousness made by oneself, made by another, made by both oneself and another, or does it arise by chance, without cause or condition?” “Friend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is not made by oneself, not made by another, not made by both oneself and another, nor does it arise by chance, without cause or condition. Rather, consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.”
translations.sn12.67:5: “Just now we understood Venerable Sāriputta’s statement like this: ‘Friend Koṭṭhika, name-and-form is not made by oneself, not made by another, not made by both oneself and another, nor does it arise by chance, without cause or condition. Rather, name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.’”}
translations.sn12.67:7: 'But how, friend Sāriputta, should the meaning of this statement be understood?' 'Then, friend, I will give you a simile. For by a simile some wise people understand the meaning of what is spoken. Suppose, friend, two bundles of reeds were to stand leaning on each other. Just so, friend, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense fields; with the six sense fields as condition, contact …pe… thus is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. If, friend, one of those bundles of reeds were to be pulled away, the other would fall; if the other were pulled away, the first would fall. Just so, friend, with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense fields; with the cessation of the six sense fields comes the cessation of contact …pe… thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.67:8: 'Amazing, friend Sāriputta; marvelous, friend Sāriputta. So well-spoken by Venerable Sāriputta. And we approve of this statement by Venerable Sāriputta with these thirty-six topics:
translations.sn12.68:13: 'Then is Venerable Nārada an arahant with taints destroyed?' 'Friends, I have truly seen with right understanding as it really is that "the cessation of becoming is nirvāna," but I am not an arahant with taints destroyed. Suppose, friends, there was a pond in a desert track, and there was neither a rope nor a water-dip there. Then a man were to come along, oppressed and afflicted by heat, weary and thirsty. He would look at that pond. His knowledge would be "there is water," but he would not dwell having physically touched it with the body. Just so, friends, I have truly seen with right understanding as it really is that "the cessation of becoming is nirvāna," but I am not an arahant with taints destroyed.'
translations.sn12.68:6: 'Then is Venerable Musila an arahant with taints destroyed?' When this was said, Venerable Musila was silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There the Blessed One …pe… 'Bhikkhus, the great ocean slopes and inclines to the great rivers, the great rivers slope and incline to the small rivers, the small rivers slope and incline to the great lakes, the great lakes slope and incline to the small lakes. Just so, bhikkhus, ignorance slopes and inclines to formations, formations slope and incline to consciousness, consciousness slopes and inclines to name-and-form, name-and-form slopes and inclines to the six sense fields, the six sense fields slope and incline to contact, contact slopes and inclines to feeling, feeling slopes and inclines to craving, craving slopes and inclines to clinging, clinging slopes and inclines to becoming, becoming slopes and inclines to birth, birth slopes and inclines to aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Sanctuary. Now on that occasion the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, esteemed, and received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick in abundance. The Saṅgha of bhikkhus too was honored, respected, revered, venerated, esteemed, and received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick in abundance. But the wanderers of other sects were dishonored, not respected, not revered, not venerated, not esteemed, and did not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
translations.sn12.70:10: 'But now, venerables, knowing and seeing thus, do you dwell having physically touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:11: 'Then, venerables, this explanation and non-attainment of these dhammas is our problem, friend.' 'We are liberated by wisdom, friend Susima.'
translations.sn12.70:12: 'I do not understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement by the venerables. May the venerables speak in such a way that I may understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement by the venerables.' 'Whether you understand or not, friend Susima, we are liberated by wisdom.'
translations.sn12.70:13: Then Venerable Susima rose from his seat and went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Susima told the Blessed One everything that had been the conversation with those bhikkhus. 'First comes knowledge of the stability of the dhammas, afterwards knowledge of nirvāṇa.'
translations.sn12.70:14: 'Venerable sir, I do not understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement by the Blessed One. May the Blessed One speak in such a way that I may understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement by the Blessed One.' 'Whether you understand or not, Susima, first comes knowledge of the stability of the dhammas, afterwards knowledge of nirvāṇa.
translations.sn12.70:16: 'Therefore, Susima, any form whatsoever—past, future, present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." Any feeling whatsoever … Any perception whatsoever …pe… Any formations whatsoever—past, future, present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all formations should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." Any consciousness whatsoever—past, future, present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing in this way, Susima, the learned noble disciple is disillusioned with form too, disillusioned with feeling too, disillusioned with perception too, disillusioned with formations too, disillusioned with consciousness too. Being disillusioned, he becomes dispassionate; from dispassion, he is freed. When freed, for him there comes the knowledge: ‘I am freed.’ He understands: ‘My birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing more here for this state.’
translations.sn12.70:18: ‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death’—Susima, do you see that?” “Yes, sir.” “‘With existence as condition, birth’—Susima, do you see that?” “Yes, sir.” “‘With clinging as condition, existence’—Susima, do you see that?” “Yes, sir.” “‘With craving as condition, clinging’—Susima, do you see that?” “Yes, sir.” “With feeling as condition, craving … with contact as condition, feeling … with the six sense fields as condition, contact … with name-and-form as condition, the six sense fields … with consciousness as condition, name-and-form … with formations as condition, consciousness … with ignorance as condition, formations—Susima, do you see that?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn12.70:2: At that time the wanderer Susima was staying in Rājagaha with a large company of wanderers. Then the company said to the wanderer Susima: “Go, friend Susima, and live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. Having learned the teaching, you can teach us. We’ll learn the teaching from you and teach it to laypeople. In this way we too will be honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, and given gifts of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.” “Yes, friends,” replied the wanderer Susima to his company. Then he went to the Venerable Ānanda, exchanged greetings with him, and after the greetings and polite talk, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Susima said to the Venerable Ānanda: “I wish, friend Ānanda, to live the holy life in this teaching and training.”
translations.sn12.70:21: “But, Susima, with this understanding and vision, do you hear with the divine ear-element, purified, surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn12.70:25: “But, Susima, with this understanding and vision, do you dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn12.70:27: Then the Venerable Susima bowed with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said to the Blessed One: “I have done wrong, sir, in acting so foolishly, so confusedly, so unskillfully, in going forth as a homeless one in this well-proclaimed teaching and training. May the Blessed One please forgive me my wrongdoing so that I may restrain myself in future.”
translations.sn12.70:3: Then the Venerable Ānanda took the wanderer Susima to the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “This wanderer Susima, sir, said to me: ‘I wish, friend Ānanda, to live the holy life in this teaching and training.’” “Then, Ānanda, ordain Susima.” And the wanderer Susima received the going forth near the Blessed One, he received the full ordination.
translations.sn12.70:5: “But, reverends, with this understanding and vision, do you experience various kinds of psychic power: having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one; you appear and vanish; you pass through obstacles, walls, and mountains as if through space; you dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; you walk on water as if it were earth; you sit cross-legged in space as if it were a solid object; you fly through the air like a bird with wings; with your hand you touch and stroke the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; you exercise mastery with your body even as far as the Brahmā world?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:6: “But, reverends, with this understanding and vision, do you hear with the divine ear-element, purified, surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:7: “But, reverends, with this understanding and vision, do you know the minds of other beings and other persons with your mind, penetrating their minds with your mind: ‘This one’s mind has passion; this one’s mind is without passion; this one’s mind has anger; this one’s mind is without anger; this one’s mind has delusion; this one’s mind is without delusion; this one’s mind is constricted; this one’s mind is distracted; this one’s mind is expansive; this one’s mind is not expansive; this one’s mind is supreme; this one’s mind is not supreme; this one’s mind is concentrated; this one’s mind is unconcentrated; this one’s mind is freed; this one’s mind is unfreed’?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:8: “But, reverends, with this understanding and vision, do you recollect many past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world contraction, many eons of world expansion, many eons of world contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so-and-so by name, of such-and-such a clan, with such-and-such an appearance, such-and-such food, such-and-such experience of pleasure and pain, such-and-such a lifespan. Having passed away there, I was reborn elsewhere, where I was so-and-so by name, of such-and-such a clan, with such-and-such an appearance, such-and-such food, such-and-such experience of pleasure and pain, such-and-such a lifespan. Having passed away there, I was reborn here.’ Thus you recollect many past lives with details and features?” “No, friend.”}
translations.sn12.70:9: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus, seeing thus, with the divine eye purified, transcending that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations, knowing beings according to their karma: ‘These beings, who were endowed with body misconduct, endowed with speech misconduct, endowed with mind misconduct, disparagers of the noble ones, holding wrong view, undertaking wrong view karma, after the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in the plane of misery, bad destination, the underworld; but these beings, who were endowed with good bodily conduct, endowed with good speech conduct, endowed with good mental conduct, non-disparagers of the noble ones, holding right view, undertaking right view karma, after the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, the heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye purified, transcending that of humans, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations, know beings according to their karma”?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn16.11:1: On one occasion the venerable Mahākassapa was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, Kalandakanivāpa. At that time the venerable Ānanda was wandering in the Southern Hills with a large Saṅgha of monks.
translations.sn16.11:10: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘My intense shame and moral dread will be established regarding elders, juniors, and middles.’ That’s how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘Whatever Dhamma I hear that is conducive to skillfulness, I will make it a bone, make it a consideration, bring it to mind with all my mind, and listen to the Dhamma with attentive ear.’ That’s how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mindfulness of the body accompanied by application will not be abandoned.’ That’s how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friend, the Blessed One advised me with this advice, then rose from his seat and departed. For seven days, friend, I subsisted on almsfood; on the eighth day another realization arose.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friend, the Blessed One, stepping off the path, went to a certain tree root. Then I, friend, having folded in four a robe of cast-off rags, said to the Blessed One: ‘Here, Blessed One, please sit, so that it may be for my long-term welfare and happiness.’ The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to me: ‘This robe of cast-off rags is soft, Kassapa.’ ‘Out of compassion, Blessed One, please accept my robe of cast-off rags.’ ‘But will you wear rag-robes for me, Kassapa, coarse, cast-off, fit for subsisting on?’ ‘I will wear, Blessed One, your coarse rag-robes, cast-off, fit for subsisting on.’ Then I, friend, gave the Blessed One the robe of cast-off rags. But I took up the Blessed One’s coarse rag-robes, cast-off, fit for subsisting on.
translations.sn16.11:17: I, friend, dwelling having personally realized in this very life the undefiled freedom of mind, freedom through wisdom, due to the destruction of the taints; or if one should regard a seven-ratna nāga or an eight-ratna nāga as coverable by a palm-leaf, one might regard my six direct knowledges as coverable.
translations.sn16.11:2: At that time about thirty monks who were companions of the venerable Ānanda had given up the training and returned to the lower life, mostly as youths. Then the venerable Ānanda, having wandered in the Southern Hills as he pleased, approached the venerable Mahākassapa at Rājagaha, the Bamboo Grove, Kalandakanivāpa; having approached, he paid homage to the venerable Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. The venerable Mahākassapa said to the venerable Ānanda sitting to one side: “For what purpose, friend Ānanda, did the Blessed One prescribe three almsmeals in families?”
translations.sn16.11:3: “Three purposes, venerable Kassapa, for which the Blessed One prescribed three almsmeals in families—for the restraint of unskillful persons, for the comfortable abiding of skillful monks, so that those of evil desires would not split the Saṅgha by taking sides, and for the prosperity of families. These are the three purposes, venerable Kassapa, for which the Blessed One prescribed three almsmeals in families.”
translations.sn16.11:4: “But why, friend Ānanda, do you wander around with these new monks who have unguarded sense doors, who do not know moderation in eating, who are uncommitted to wakefulness? I think you are wandering for the destruction of the crop, I think you are wandering for the destruction of families. Your assembly is withering away, friend Ānanda; your new disciples are rotting away, friend. Surely this youth does not know moderation.”
translations.sn16.11:6: The nun Thullanandā heard: “It seems the venerable Mahākassapa disparaged the venerable Ānanda, the white-clad ascetic, with talk of a youth.”
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the nun Thullanandā, displeased and speaking displeased words, said: “But why does the venerable Mahākassapa, being formerly of another sect, think that the venerable Ānanda, the white-clad ascetic, should be disparaged with talk of a youth?” The venerable Mahākassapa heard the nun Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “Indeed, friend Ānanda, that nun Thullanandā spoke rashly without reflection. From the time I shaved off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, friend, I do not acknowledge any other teacher worthy of recitation apart from that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Previously, friend, while I was a householder, this thought occurred to me: ‘The home life is narrow, the homeless life is wide open. It is not easy for one living at home to live the utterly perfect, utterly pure, stainless holy life. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’ Then, friend, after some time, having had a set of robes made from cast-off rags, I went forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of those arahants in the world, shaving off my hair and beard, putting on ochre robes.
translations.sn16.13:2: Kassapa, just as gold does not disappear as long as no counterfeit gold arises in the world. But when counterfeit gold arises in the world, then gold disappears. In the same way, Kassapa, the true Dhamma does not disappear as long as no counterfeit of the true Dhamma arises in the world. But when a counterfeit of the true Dhamma arises in the world, then the true Dhamma disappears.
translations.sn16.13:4: There are these five things, Kassapa, that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma. Which five? Here, Kassapa, monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers dwell without respect and without reverence toward the Teacher, dwell without respect and without reverence toward the Dhamma, dwell without respect and without reverence toward the Saṅgha, dwell without respect and without reverence toward training, dwell without respect and without reverence toward concentration—these are the five things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Mahākassapa and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having exchanged greetings and courtesies, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘It is said here, friend Kassapa, that one without remorse and without dread is incapable of awakening, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme security from bondage; but one with remorse and with dread is capable of awakening, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the supreme security from bondage.’
translations.sn16.2:3: ‘And how, friend, is one without dread? Here, friend, a monk does not dread: “Unarisen evil unwholesome states might arise, leading to harm,” does not dread: “Arisen evil unwholesome states, not abandoned, might lead to harm,” does not dread: “Unarisen wholesome states might not arise, leading to harm,” does not dread: “Arisen wholesome states might cease, leading to harm.” This is how, friend, one is without dread. This is how, friend, one without remorse and without dread is incapable of awakening, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme security from bondage.
translations.sn16.2:4: ‘And how, friend, is one with remorse? Here, friend, a monk has remorse: “Unarisen evil unwholesome states might arise, leading to harm,” has remorse: “Arisen evil unwholesome states, not abandoned, might lead to harm,” … has remorse regarding unarisen wholesome states … . This is how, friend, one is with remorse.
translations.sn16.5:1: Thus have I heard … at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘You are now old, Kassapa, and these rag-robes of yours are heavy. So, Kassapa, wear laypeople’s robes, eat on invitations, and dwell near me.’
translations.sn21.10:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, Kalandakanivāpa. At that time a certain monk named Elder was a solitary dweller and a speaker in praise of solitary dwelling. He enters a village for alms alone, returns alone, sits in seclusion alone, and paces back and forth alone. Then several monks went to the Blessed One; having gone, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: ‘Here, Bhante, a certain monk named Elder is a solitary dweller and a speaker in praise of solitary dwelling.’
translations.sn21.10:3: ‘Elder, this solitary dwelling does not exist, I say. But, Elder, listen to how solitary dwelling is fully developed in detail, pay close attention, I will speak.’ ‘Yes, Bhante,’ … ‘And how, Elder, is solitary dwelling fully developed in detail? Here, Elder, what is past is abandoned, what is future is released, and in regard to present acquisitions of personality, sensual desire is well subdued. This is how, Elder, solitary dwelling is fully developed in detail.’
translations.sn21.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the monks: ‘Friends, monks.’ ‘Friend,’ those monks replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: “Here, friend, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘Noble silence, noble silence, they say. What is noble silence?’ Then, friend, this occurred to me: ‘Here a monk, with the subsiding of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal clarity and unification of mind, without thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called noble silence.’ And I, friend, with the subsiding of thought and examination, entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal clarity and unification of mind, without thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. While I was dwelling in this way, friend, perceptions and intentions accompanied by thought arose in me.”
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: “Friends, monks.” “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said:
translations.sn21.2:2: “Here, friend, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘Is there anything in the world such that grief, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would arise in me due to its change and alteration?’ Then, friend, this occurred to me: ‘There is nothing in the world such that grief, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would arise in me due to its change and alteration.’”
translations.sn21.3:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Now on that occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling at Rājagaha in Veḷuvana, at the Kalandakanivāpa, in one dwelling. Then the Venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.3:2: “Your faculties, friend Moggallāna, are serene; your complexion is pure, bright. Surely the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna has dwelt today with a serene abiding.” “I dwelt today with a coarse abiding, friend. But I had a talk on the Dhamma.” “With whom did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a talk on the Dhamma?” “I had a talk on the Dhamma with the Blessed One, friend.” “The Blessed One, friend, is now far away dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approach the Blessed One by supernormal power, or did the Blessed One approach the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by supernormal power?” “I did not approach the Blessed One by supernormal power, friend, nor did the Blessed One approach me by supernormal power. But as far as the Blessed One has developed the divine eye and the divine ear, to that extent I have developed the divine eye and the divine ear. And as far as I have developed the divine eye and the divine ear, to that extent the Blessed One has developed the divine eye and the divine ear.” “How, then, did the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a talk on the Dhamma with the Blessed One?”
translations.sn21.3:3: “Here, friend, I said this to the Blessed One: ‘One with aroused energy, one with aroused energy, Bhante, it is said. How, Bhante, is one with aroused energy?’ When this was said, friend, the Blessed One said this to me: ‘Here, Moggallāna, a monk dwells with aroused energy—“May my skin, sinews, and bones remain, may my flesh and blood dry up, but I will not give up the energy until I have attained what can be reached by manly strength, manly energy, manly exertion.” This, Moggallāna, is one with aroused energy.’ That, friend, is how I had a talk on the Dhamma with the Blessed One.”
translations.sn21.3:6: ‘Sāriputta with wisdom,  and with virtue and calm;  Even a monk who has gone to the far shore,  would be no more than that.’”
translations.sn21.6:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya coming from afar. Seeing him, he addressed the monks: “Do you see, monks, this monk coming—ugly, unsightly, crook-backed, the monks’ laughingstock?” “Yes, Bhante.” “This monk, monks, is one of great power, great majesty, and that attainment is not easy, which this monk had not previously attained. For the sake of which sons of clans rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, that unexcelled end of the holy life he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, and dwells having entered upon it.” This the Blessed One said …pe… the Teacher:
translations.sn21.6:2: “Swans, herons, peacocks,  elephants, stately deer;  All fear the lion,  there is no equal in body.
translations.sn21.8:1: Dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Nanda, the stepson of the Blessed One’s mother, having dressed in patchwork robes, having anointed his eyes, taking a clean almsbowl, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Nanda: “It is not fitting for you, Nanda, a clansman of faith who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, that you should wear patchwork robes, anoint your eyes, and carry a clean almsbowl. This is fitting for you, Nanda, a clansman of faith who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, that you should be a forest-dweller, an almsfood-eater, a rag-robe wearer, and dwell without attachment to sensual pleasures.” This the Blessed One said …pe… the Teacher:
translations.sn21.8:2: “When will I see Nanda,  a forest-dweller, rag-robe wearer;  Living with empty awareness,  without attachment to sensual pleasures.”}
translations.sn21.9:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Tissa, son of the Blessed One’s paternal uncle, went to the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat to one side, sorrowful, depressed, with tears streaming. Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Tissa: ‘Why now, Tissa, do you sit to one side sorrowful, depressed, with tears streaming?’ ‘It’s just so, Bhante, the monks have surrounded me and abused me with harsh speech.’ ‘Well then, Tissa, you spoke, but you were not able to speak fittingly; it is not fitting for you, Tissa, as a clansman of faith who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, that you spoke but were not able to speak fittingly. This is fitting for you, Tissa, as a clansman of faith who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness: “May you speak and be able to speak fittingly.”’
translations.sn22.100:2: ‘Bhikkhus, have you seen what is called “conduct”?’ ‘Yes, Bhante.’ ‘That conduct, bhikkhus, is called mind; for conduct is just mind-made. Even by that conduct, bhikkhus, mind is even more mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should constantly review your own mind: “This mind has long been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.” Bhikkhus, beings are defiled by the defilement of mind; beings are purified by the purification of mind.
translations.sn22.100:3: Bhikkhus, I do not see any other single class so mind-made as, bhikkhus, these animals. Those animals, bhikkhus, are just mind-made; even by those animals, bhikkhus, mind is even more mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should constantly review your own mind: “This mind has long been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.” Bhikkhus, beings are defiled by the defilement of mind; beings are purified by the purification of mind.
translations.sn22.101:1: Sāvatthī. ‘Bhikkhus, I say the destruction of the āsavas comes about for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and see. And what, bhikkhus, does one know and see for the destruction of the āsavas to occur? “Thus form, thus the arising of form, thus the passing away of form; thus feeling … thus perception … thus volitional formations … thus consciousness, thus the arising of consciousness, thus the passing away of consciousness”—bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, the destruction of the āsavas occurs.
translations.sn22.101:2: Bhikkhus, for a monk dwelling without devotion to development, even if the wish were to arise: “Oh, that my mind might be freed from the āsavas without clinging,” yet his mind is not freed from the āsavas without clinging. Why is that? “Because it is undeveloped,” it should be said. Undeveloped in what? Undeveloped in the four establishments of mindfulness, undeveloped in the four right efforts, undeveloped in the four bases of psychic power, undeveloped in the five faculties, undeveloped in the five powers, undeveloped in the seven awakening factors, undeveloped in the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:3: Bhikkhus, just as if there were eight, ten, or twelve eggs laid by a hen, and that hen had not properly sat on them, not properly incubated them, not properly developed them. Even if that hen were to have the wish: “Oh, that my chicks might break out of the eggshell with their talons or beak and hatch out safely,” yet those chicks are incapable of breaking out of the eggshell with their talons or beak and hatching out safely. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the hen’s eggs are eight, ten, or twelve; those eggs have not been properly sat on, properly incubated, or properly developed by the hen. In the same way, bhikkhus, for a monk dwelling without devotion to development, even if the wish were to arise: “Oh, that my mind might be freed from the āsavas without clinging,” yet his mind is not freed from the āsavas without clinging. Why is that? “Because it is undeveloped,” it should be said. Undeveloped in what? Undeveloped in the four establishments of mindfulness … the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Bhagga at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove in the deer park. Then the householder Nakulapitā went to the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Nakulapitā said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.1:10: He regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling; or feeling in self, or self in feeling. He adopts the abiding position: “I am feeling, this is my feeling.” For him who adopts the abiding position ‘I am feeling, this is my feeling,’ that feeling alters and changes. Due to the alteration and change of that feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.1:11: He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception; or perception in self, or self in perception. He adopts the abiding position: “I am perception, this is my perception.” For him who adopts the abiding position ‘I am perception, this is my perception,’ that perception alters and changes. Due to the alteration and change of that perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.1:12: He regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations; or volitional formations in self, or self in volitional formations. He adopts the abiding position: “I am volitional formations, these are my volitional formations.” For him who adopts the abiding position ‘I am volitional formations, these are my volitional formations,’ those volitional formations alter and change. Due to the alteration and change of those volitional formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.1:13: He perceives consciousness as self, or self as endowed with consciousness; or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. He is obsessed and obsessed with the view: ‘I am consciousness, this is my consciousness.’ When that consciousness changes and becomes otherwise for him who is obsessed and obsessed with the view ‘I am consciousness, this is my consciousness,’ sorrow and lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise. In this way, householder, one has a sick body and a sick mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is there a sick body but not a sick mind? Here, householder, a learned noble disciple who has seen the ariyans, is skilled in the ariyans’ doctrine, well-trained in the ariyans’ doctrine, has seen noble ones, is skilled in the noble ones’ doctrine, well-trained in the noble ones’ doctrine, does not perceive form as self, or self as endowed with form; or form in self, or self in form. He is not obsessed and obsessed with the view: ‘I am form, this is my form.’ When that form changes and becomes otherwise for him who is not obsessed and obsessed with the view ‘I am form, this is my form,’ no sorrow and lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.1:2: ‘I am old, venerable sir, aged, advanced in years, having reached the age of eighty years, with a sick body, constantly ill.’ ‘But I, venerable sir, have seen the impermanent as impermanent in the Blessed One and the bhikkhus worthy of mental development. May the Blessed One advise me, venerable sir; may the Blessed One instruct me, for my long-term welfare and happiness.’
translations.sn22.1:3: ‘That is so, householder, that is so. This body, householder, is sick, like an overgrown and enveloped boil. For what reason, householder, would one who bears this body expect even a moment’s health, unless he is childish? Therefore, householder, you should train like this: “Mindful of this sick body, my mind will be not sick.” That is how you should train, householder.’
translations.sn22.1:4: Then the householder Nakulapitar went to the Blessed One, delighted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and went to the Venerable Sāriputta. Having gone, he paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. When the householder Nakulapitar had sat down to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said to him: ‘Your faculties, householder, are serene; your complexion is pure, bright. Did you approach the Blessed One today and hear a talk on Dhamma?’
translations.sn22.1:7: ‘It did not occur to us to question the Blessed One further: “How, venerable sir, is one both with a sick body and sick mind, and how is one with a sick body but not sick mind?”’ ‘We would come from afar, venerable sir, to the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the Venerable Sāriputta would explain the meaning of this statement.’
translations.sn22.1:8: ‘Well then, householder, listen, pay close attention, I will speak.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ the householder Nakulapitar replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said:
translations.sn22.1:9: ‘And how, householder, is one both with a sick body and sick mind? Here, householder, an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen the ariyans, is unskilled in the ariyans’ doctrine, untrained in the ariyans’ doctrine, has not seen noble ones, is unskilled in the noble ones’ doctrine, untrained in the noble ones’ doctrine, perceives form as self, or self as endowed with form; or form in self, or self in form. He is obsessed and obsessed with the view: “I am form, this is my form.” When that form changes and becomes otherwise for him who is obsessed and obsessed with the view “I am form, this is my form,” sorrow and lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.22:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the bearer of the burden? The person is what is spoken of. This venerable one of such name, such clan; he is called, bhikkhus, the bearer of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? That craving which is rebirth-leading, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there, namely, sensuality-craving, existence-craving, annihilation-craving. This is called, bhikkhus, the taking up of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? The complete fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving up, relinquishment, release, non-clinging. This is called, bhikkhus, the laying down of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:6: ‘The five aggregates are the burden,  And the person the bearer of the burden;  Taking up the burden is suffering in the world,  Laying down the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakkans at Devadaha, a town of the Sakyans. Then several bhikkhus who were latecomers went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. When those bhikkhus had sat down to one side, they said to the Blessed One: “We wish, venerable sir, to go to the border region, to set up dwelling in the border region.”
translations.sn22.2:10: Friends, if dwelling having entered upon unwholesome dhammas there would be happy abiding in the seen dhamma, untroubled, un-distressed, un-agitated, and with the breakup of the body, after death, a good destination would be expected, the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome dhammas. But because, friends, dwelling having entered upon unwholesome dhammas there is unhappy abiding in the seen dhamma, troubled, distressed, agitated, and with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is expected, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome dhammas.
translations.sn22.2:2: ‘But did you look to Sāriputta?’ ‘No, venerable sir, we did not overlook the Venerable Sāriputta.’ ‘Look to Sāriputta, bhikkhus. Sāriputta, bhikkhus, is wise, a helper to the bhikkhus, a co-farer.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.2:3: At that time the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One in a certain Eḷagala cave. Then those monks, delighting in and approving of the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and went to the Venerable Sāriputta. Having gone to him, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Venerable Sāriputta: ‘We wish, friend Sāriputta, to go to the hinterland, to dwell in the hinterland. Our Teacher has not been consulted.’
translations.sn22.2:5: ‘Even if we had to come from afar, friend, we would come to the Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. May the Venerable Sāriputta himself explain the meaning of this statement.’ ‘Then, friends, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.’ ‘Yes, friend,’ those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk went to the Blessed One …pe… and, sitting to one side, said to the Blessed One: ‘May the Blessed One teach me Dhamma in brief, sir, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might live alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute.’ ‘Whatever, monk, one investigates, that one infers; whatever one infers, that one comes to a conclusion about. Whatever one does not investigate, one does not infer; whatever one does not infer, that one does not come to a conclusion about.’ ‘It is known, Blessed One! It is known, Well-Farer!’
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantis at Kuraraghara on Mount Papāta. Then the householder Hāliddikāni went to the Venerable Mahākaccāna, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: ‘This has been said by the Blessed One in the Aṭṭhaka Vagga concerning Māgaṇḍiya’s questions:
translations.sn22.3:10: ‘And how, householder, is one not empty of lust for sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, not abandoned desire, not abandoned affection, not abandoned thirst, not abandoned burning, not abandoned craving. That is how, householder, one is not empty of lust for sensual pleasures.’
translations.sn22.3:11: ‘And how, householder, is one empty of lust for sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, abandoned desire, abandoned affection, abandoned thirst, abandoned burning, abandoned craving. That is how, householder, one is empty of lust for sensual pleasures.’
translations.sn22.3:12: ‘And how, householder, is one one who drives ahead? Here, householder, someone thinks: “May I be of such form in the future, may I be of such feeling in the future, may I be of such perception in the future, may I be of such formations in the future, may I be of such consciousness in the future.” That is how, householder, one is one who drives ahead.’
translations.sn22.3:14: ‘And how, householder, is one a maker of strife-talk among people? Here, householder, someone is a maker of such strife-talk: “You don’t understand this Dhamma and Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma and Vinaya. What do you understand of this Dhamma and Vinaya? You have a wrong view; I have the right view. What should have been said later is said first; what should have been said first is said later. What was well said by me is not well received by you; what was not well said by me is well received by you. Your position has been refuted; you’re defeated. Come now, abandon your position and come over to mine!” That is how, householder, one is a maker of strife-talk among people.’
translations.sn22.3:17: ‘Having abandoned a home, a homeless wanderer,  Not doing wrong in the village, like a sage among mendicants;  Empty of lust for sensual pleasures, not driving ahead,  How could one make strife-talk among people?’
translations.sn22.3:6: ‘And how, householder, is one a homeless wanderer? Bound by the attachment and clinging to the sign of form is called a “homeless wanderer.” The sign of sound …pe… the sign of odor … the sign of flavor … the sign of tangibles … bound by the attachment and clinging to the sign of dhammas is called a “homeless wanderer.” That is how, householder, one is a homeless wanderer.’
translations.sn22.3:8: ‘And how, householder, is one sociable in the village? Here, householder, someone dwells associated with laypeople, sharing their joys and sorrows, happy when they are happy, suffering when they suffer, personally undertaking work that arises. That is how, householder, one is sociable in the village.’
translations.sn22.3:9: ‘And how, householder, is one not sociable in the village? Here, householder, a monk dwells not associated with laypeople, not sharing their joys and sorrows, not happy when they are happy, not suffering when they suffer, not personally undertaking work that arises. That is how, householder, one is not sociable in the village.’
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. ‘Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins perceive the self in various ways, all of them perceive it as the five aggregates subject to clinging, or a certain one of these. Which five? Here, bhikkhus, an unlearned ordinary person, who has not seen noble ones, is not skilled and disciplined in the noble Dhamma, has not seen good persons, is not skilled and disciplined in the Dhamma of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. Feeling … perception … formations … he regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: Thus this perception of his remains as ‘I am.’ But with regard to ‘I am,’ bhikkhus, there is an influx into the five faculties that have not subsided—the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty. There is, bhikkhus, a mind; there are dhammas; there is the element of ignorance. When an unlearned ordinary person is touched by a feeling born of ignorance-contact, for him there arises: “I am”; “I am this”; “I will be”; “I will not be”; “I will be with form”; “I will be formless”; “I will be with perception”; “I will be without perception”; “I will be neither with perception nor without perception.”}
translations.sn22.48:1: At Sāvatthī. ‘I will teach you the five aggregates, monks, and the five clinging-aggregates. Listen to that. What are the five aggregates, monks? Any kind of form whatever, monks—past, future, present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the form aggregate. Any kind of feeling whatever … any kind of perception … those formations whatever—past, future, present; internal or external; gross or subtle …: this is called the formations aggregate. Any kind of consciousness whatever—past, future, present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the consciousness aggregate. These are called the five aggregates, monks.’
translations.sn22.53:1: At Sāvatthī. ‘When consciousness is unobstructed, monks, it proceeds; when unobstructed, it arrives. If consciousness were to stand still based on form, taking form as its object, supported by form, sustained by delight, it would grow, increase, expand. Or if consciousness were to stand still based on feeling … or if consciousness were to stand still based on perception … Or if consciousness were to stand still based on formations, monks, taking formations as its object, supported by formations, sustained by delight, it would grow, increase, expand.’
translations.sn22.53:2: Monks, whoever should say: “Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will explain the coming, going, passing away, rebirth, growth, increase, or expansion of consciousness”: this is not possible.
translations.sn22.54:2: If consciousness were to stand still based on form, monks, taking form as its object, supported by form, sustained by delight, it would grow, increase, expand. Or if consciousness were to stand still based on feeling, monks … or if consciousness were to stand still based on perception, monks … Or if consciousness were to stand still based on formations, monks, taking formations as its object, supported by formations, sustained by delight, it would grow, increase, expand.
translations.sn22.55:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One spontaneously uttered this exclamation: “‘It was not mine; it will not be mine; it has not been; it will not be’: a monk who is assured thus would cut off the lower fetters.” When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: “But how, sir, does a monk who is assured ‘It was not mine; it will not be mine; it has not been; it will not be’ cut off the lower fetters?”
translations.sn22.55:10: But how, sir, knowing and seeing does the destruction of the āsavas occur right then?” “Here, monk, an unlearned ordinary person falls into what should not be fallen into. This is for that unlearned ordinary person: ‘It was not mine; it will not be mine; it has not been; it will not be.’
translations.sn22.55:4: He does not truly understand form as ‘form is suffering,’ feeling as ‘feeling is suffering,’ perception as ‘perception is suffering,’ formations as ‘formations are suffering,’ consciousness as ‘consciousness is suffering.’
translations.sn22.55:5: He does not truly understand form as ‘form is not-self,’ feeling as ‘feeling is not-self,’ perception as ‘perception is not-self,’ formations as ‘formations are not-self,’ consciousness as ‘consciousness is not-self.’
translations.sn22.55:6: He does not truly understand form as ‘form is conditioned,’ feeling as ‘feeling is conditioned,’ perception as ‘perception is conditioned,’ formations as ‘formations are conditioned,’ consciousness as ‘consciousness is conditioned.’ He does not truly understand ‘form will pass away,’ ‘feeling will pass away,’ ‘perception will pass away,’ ‘formations will pass away,’ ‘consciousness will pass away.’
translations.sn22.55:8: He truly understands form as ‘form is impermanent,’ feeling as ‘feeling is impermanent,’ perception as ‘perception is impermanent,’ formations as ‘formations are impermanent,’ consciousness as ‘consciousness is impermanent.’ Form as suffering … consciousness as suffering … form as not-self … consciousness as not-self … form as conditioned … consciousness as conditioned … He truly understands ‘form will pass away,’ ‘feeling will pass away,’ ‘perception will pass away,’ ‘formations will pass away,’ ‘consciousness will pass away.’
translations.sn22.55:9: With the passing away of form, the passing away of feeling, the passing away of perception, the passing away of formations, the passing away of consciousness: thus, monk, a monk who is assured ‘It was not mine; it will not be mine; it has not been; it will not be’ cuts off the lower fetters.” “‘A monk who is assured thus cuts off the lower fetters,’ sir.
translations.sn22.56:13: And what is consciousness, monks? These six are classes of consciousness, monks: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called consciousness, monks. With the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of consciousness; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness. This very noble eightfold path is the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.56:14: Whatever monks or brahmins, monks, have directly known consciousness thus, have directly known the origin of consciousness thus, have directly known the cessation of consciousness thus, have directly known the practice that leads to the cessation of consciousness thus, and have undertaken the practice for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, they are well-practicing. Those who are well-practicing are grounded in this teaching and discipline.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it fourfold? I have directly known form, I have directly known the origin of form, I have directly known the cessation of form, I have directly known the practice that leads to the cessation of form; feeling … perception … volitional formations … I have directly known consciousness, I have directly known the origin of consciousness, I have directly known the cessation of consciousness, I have directly known the practice that leads to the cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn22.56:5: And whatever monks or brahmins, monks, have directly known form thus … have directly known the practice that leads to the cessation of form thus, and are liberated by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation without clinging regarding form, they are supremely liberated. Those who are supremely liberated are omniscient. For those who are omniscient, there is no designation of rebirth.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Sāvatthī. ‘A monk skilled in the seven positions, monks, who has examined the triple aspect in this teaching and discipline is called an omniscient one who has lived the holy life and is a supreme person.’ And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the seven positions? Here, monks, a monk understands form, understands the origin of form, understands the cessation of form, understands the practice that leads to the cessation of form; he understands the gratification in form, understands the danger in form, understands the escape from form; he understands feeling … perception … volitional formations … he understands consciousness, understands the origin of consciousness, understands the cessation of consciousness, understands the practice that leads to the cessation of consciousness; he understands the gratification in consciousness, understands the danger in consciousness, understands the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, monks, are volitional formations? These six classes of intention, monks—intention regarding forms … intention regarding mental phenomena. These are called volitional formations, monks. With the arising of contact comes the arising of volitional formations; with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of volitional formations. This very noble eightfold path is the practice that leads to the cessation of volitional formations, that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:15: The happiness and joy that arise in dependence on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal of desire and lust for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: And whatever monks or brahmins, monks, have directly known consciousness thus, have directly known the origin of consciousness thus, have directly known the cessation of consciousness thus, have directly known the practice that leads to the cessation of consciousness thus; have directly known the gratification in consciousness thus, have directly known the danger in consciousness thus, have directly known the escape from consciousness thus, and are liberated by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation without clinging regarding consciousness, they are supremely liberated.
