Those who are supremely liberated are omniscient. For those who are omniscient, there is no designation of rebirth. Thus, monks, a monk is skilled in the seven positions.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, monks, is form? The four great elements and form derived from the four great elements. This is called form, monks. With the arising of nutriment comes the arising of form; with the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form. This very noble eightfold path is the practice that leads to the cessation of form, that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:5: And whatever monks or brahmins, monks, have directly known form thus, have directly known the origin of form thus, have directly known the cessation of form thus, have directly known the practice that leads to the cessation of form thus; have directly known the gratification in form thus, have directly known the danger in form thus, have directly known the escape from form thus, and are liberated by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation without clinging regarding form, they are supremely liberated. Those who are supremely liberated are omniscient. For those who are omniscient, there is no designation of rebirth.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what, monks, is feeling? These six classes of feeling, monks—feeling born of eye-contact … feeling born of mind-contact. This is called feeling, monks. With the arising of contact comes the arising of feeling; with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling. This very noble eightfold path is the practice that leads to the cessation of feeling, that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:7: The happiness and joy that arise in dependence on feeling—this is the gratification in feeling. Those feelings that are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feeling. The removal of desire and lust for feeling, the abandoning of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: At Sāvatthī. ‘The Tathāgata, monks, the perfected one, the perfectly awakened one, is called perfectly awakened because of liberation by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation without clinging regarding form. A monk, monks, who is liberated by wisdom is called liberated by wisdom because of liberation by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation without clinging regarding form.
translations.sn22.58:3: The Tathāgata, monks, the perfected one, the perfectly awakened one, is called perfectly awakened because of liberation by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation without clinging regarding perception … volitional formations … consciousness. A monk, monks, who is liberated by wisdom is called liberated by wisdom because of liberation by disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation without clinging regarding consciousness.
translations.sn22.59:10: Any kind of consciousness—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.59:7: “Therefore, monks, any form whatsoever—past, future, present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one should see all form as it really is with right understanding: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.5:11: Consciousness does not delight in, does not welcome, does not adhere to. With consciousness not delighting, not welcoming, not adhering, the delight in consciousness ceases. With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of clinging … and so there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what, monks, is the origin of form, the origin of feeling, the origin of perception, the origin of formations, the origin of consciousness? Here, monks, a monk delights in, welcomes, and adheres to.
translations.sn22.5:3: And what does he delight in, welcome, and adhere to? He delights in, welcomes, and adheres to form. With his delighting, welcoming, and adhering to form, delight arises. That delight in form is clinging. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:4: He delights in feeling … He delights in perception … He delights in formations … He delights in, welcomes, and adheres to consciousness. With his delighting, welcoming, and adhering to consciousness, delight arises. That delight in consciousness is clinging. With clinging as condition, becoming … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:8: And what does he not delight in, not welcome, not adhere to? He does not delight in, welcome, or adhere to form. With his not delighting, not welcoming, not adhering to form, the delight in form ceases. With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.60:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Forest, in the hall with the peaked roof. Then Mahāli the Licchavin approached the Blessed One … and, sitting to one side, Mahāli the Licchavin said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.60:2: “The ancient Pūraṇa Kassapa, sir, said this: ‘There is no cause or condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition. There is no cause or condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition.’ What does the Blessed One say about this?”
translations.sn22.60:3: “Mahāli, there is cause and condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause and condition. Mahāli, there is cause and condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause and condition.”
translations.sn22.60:4: “But what, sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the defilement of beings; how are beings defiled with cause and condition?”
translations.sn22.60:5: “Mahāli, if form were entirely painful, followed by pain, infested by pain, pervaded by pain, not pervaded by pleasure, then beings would not be infatuated with form. But because form is pleasurable, followed by pleasure, infested by pleasure, pervaded by pleasure, not pervaded by pain, beings are infatuated with form; with infatuation they become bound; with bondage they are defiled. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings; thus beings are defiled with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.60:8: And if consciousness, Mahāli, were entirely painful … beings would not be infatuated with consciousness. But because consciousness is pleasurable … beings are infatuated with consciousness; with infatuation they become bound; with bondage they are defiled. This too, Mahāli, is a cause, this is a condition for the defilement of beings. Thus beings are defiled with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.60:9: “But what, sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings; how are beings purified with cause and condition?” “Mahāli, if form were entirely pleasurable … beings would not become dispassionate toward form. But because form is painful … beings become dispassionate toward form; with dispassion they become detached; with detachment they are purified. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings. Thus beings are purified with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing thus, monks, the instructed noble disciple is dispassionate toward form, toward feeling … toward perception … toward formations … toward consciousness. With dispassion he becomes detached; with detachment he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further here.’ Monks, as far as there are beings, as far as the crest of existence, these are supreme, these are most excellent in the world, namely the arahants.
translations.sn22.76:4: “How happy are the arahants, No craving can be found in them; Their conceit is cut down completely, The net of delusion torn apart.
translations.sn22.76:6: Having fully understood the five aggregates, They dwell in the range of the true Dhamma; Worthy of praise, good men, True sons of the Buddha.
translations.sn22.76:7: Endowed with the seven treasures, Trained in the three trainings; Great heroes, they reflect wisely, Free from fear and dread.
translations.sn22.76:8: Endowed with the ten powers, Great elephants, concentrated; These are supreme in the world, No craving can be found in them.
translations.sn22.76:9: With the arising of unlearning knowledge, This is the final body; The essence of the holy life, With no further condition.
translations.sn22.79:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins remember past abodes in various ways, all of them remember the five aggregates subject to clinging or one of them. Which five? ‘I was such-and-such in the past period’—thus, bhikkhus, in remembering, one remembers form itself. ‘I was such-and-such feeling in the past period’—thus, bhikkhus, in remembering, one remembers feeling itself. ‘I was such-and-such with perception in the past period’ … ‘such-and-such with formations in the past period’ … ‘I was such-and-such with consciousness in the past period’—thus, bhikkhus, in remembering, one remembers consciousness itself.
translations.sn22.79:10: ‘Just now I am worn out by consciousness. In the past time too I was worn out by consciousness just like now by present consciousness. But if I were to delight in future consciousness, in the future time too I would be worn out by consciousness just like now by present consciousness.’ Having reflected thus, he is not attached to past consciousness; he does not delight in future consciousness; he practices for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:7: There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Just now I am worn out by form. In the past time too I was worn out by form just like now by present form. But if I were to delight in future form, in the future time too I would be worn out by form just like now by present form.’ Having reflected thus, he is not attached to past form; he does not delight in future form; he practices for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.
translations.sn22.80:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Grove. Then the Blessed One, having robed up in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu, on returning from the alms-round after the meal, he approached the Great Forest for the day’s abiding. Having entered the Great Forest, he sat down for the day’s abiding at the foot of a beluvalaṭṭhika tree.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Blessed One consented with silence. Then Brahmā Sahampati, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to the right, and vanished right there.
translations.sn22.80:5: Then the Blessed One, having risen from retreat at the time of evening, approached the Nigrodha Grove; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One created a miraculous display such that those bhikkhus, with a single mind and one-pointedness, would come to where he was. Those bhikkhus too, with a single mind and one-pointedness, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus:
translations.sn22.80:6: “This, bhikkhus, is the extreme of livelihoods, namely, alms round. Bhikkhus, in the world they revile an almsman: ‘A bowl-in-hand wanderer.’ And yet, bhikkhus, clansmen resort to this out of need, due to need; not sent by king or thief, not in debt, not in fear, not because they have made their living; but rather: ‘We are overwhelmed by birth, aging, and death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs, overcome by suffering, overpowered by suffering—perhaps the ending of this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’
translations.sn22.80:7: Thus, bhikkhus, this clansman has gone forth. But he becomes lustful for sensual pleasures, with strong passion for them, with a hostile mind, with corrupted thought and volition, forgetful, not fully aware, unconcentrated, with distracted mind, with uncontrolled faculties. Bhikkhus, just as a piece of cotton wool that is lit at both ends and stuffed with dung in the middle is of no use for burning in a village or in the forest, even so, bhikkhus, I declare this person to be deprived of householder’s pleasures and not fulfilling the goal of the monastic life.
translations.sn22.80:9: These two views, bhikkhus—existence-view and non-existence-view. There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Is there any clinging in the world such that when I cling to it I would not be blameworthy?’ He understands thus: ‘There is no clinging in the world such that when I cling to it I would not be blameworthy. For if I were to cling to form itself I would be clinging; to feeling itself … to perception itself … to formations themselves … to consciousness itself I would be clinging. For me that would be the condition for becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would come to be. Such would be the origin of this whole mass of suffering.’
translations.sn22.81:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then the Blessed One, having robed up in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms. Having walked for alms in Kosambī, on returning from the alms-round after the meal, he himself packed away his resting place, took his bowl and robe, and set out on tour without informing or taking leave of his attendants, alone, without a companion.
translations.sn22.81:10: He does not regard form as self … nor feeling as self … nor perception … nor formations … nor consciousness as self; nevertheless he has such a view: ‘That self, that world; after death I shall be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, that is my self.’ Bhikkhus, that eternalist view is a formation. And what is the cause of that formation … Thus, bhikkhus, for one who knows and sees thus, the destruction of the taints occurs without delay.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering in stages, arrived at Pālileyyaka. There the Blessed One dwelt at the root of a bhaddasāla tree. Then several monks went to Venerable Ānanda; having gone, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. Having exchanged greetings and polite talk, they sat down to one side. Those monks sitting to one side said to Venerable Ānanda: “For a long time, friend Ānanda, we have not heard Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One; we wish, friend Ānanda, to hear Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.”
translations.sn22.82:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park at Migāramātū’s mansion together with a large Saṅgha of monks. And on that occasion, on that Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the night of the full moon, the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, was sitting in the open air.
translations.sn22.82:10: “What, Bhante, is the gratification in form, what the danger, what the escape; what in feeling … what in perception … what in formations … what is the gratification in consciousness, what the danger, what the escape?” “Whatever happiness and pleasure arises dependent on form—that is the gratification in form. That form is impermanent, suffering, a dharma subject to change—that is the danger in form. The giving up, dispassion, cessation of desire and lust for form—that is the escape from form. Whatever happiness and pleasure arises dependent on feeling … dependent on perception … dependent on formations … dependent on consciousness—that is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, a dharma subject to change—that is the danger in consciousness. The giving up, dispassion, cessation of desire and lust for consciousness—that is the escape from consciousness.” “Excellent, Bhante,” that monk approved and rejoiced in what the Blessed One said, and asked the Blessed One a further question:
translations.sn22.82:11: “How, Bhante, does one know, how does one see so that with regard to this body with consciousness and all external signs, tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit do not exist?” “Whatever form, monk, past, future, present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus it is seen as it really is with right understanding. Whatever feeling … whatever perception … whatever formations … whatever consciousness, past, future, present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all consciousness: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus it is seen as it really is with right understanding. Thus, monk, one who knows thus, one who sees thus, with regard to this body with consciousness and all external signs, tendencies to I-making, mine-making, and conceit do not exist.”
translations.sn22.82:12: At that time, a certain monk had this thought in his mind: “It seems form is not-self, feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is not-self; when actions are not-self, how will they touch the self?” Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in that monk’s mind, addressed the monks:
translations.sn22.82:13: “Monks, it is possible that some foolish man here, unlearned, without vision, with a mind dominated by craving, might overpass the Teacher’s instruction, thinking: ‘It seems form is not-self, feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is not-self. When actions are not-self, how will they touch the self?’ You, monks, have been trained in cross-questioning in this and that regard in those and these dhammas.
translations.sn22.82:4: “And these five aggregates of clinging, Bhante, what is their root?” “These five aggregates of clinging, monk, have desire as their root.” …pe… “Is that very clinging these five aggregates of clinging, Bhante, or is there clinging apart from the five aggregates of clinging?” “Monk, it is not that very clinging that these five aggregates of clinging are, nor is there clinging apart from the five aggregates of clinging, but rather, whatever desire and lust there is therein, that is clinging therein.” “Excellent, Bhante,” that monk …pe… asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:5: “Might there be, Bhante, desire and lust regarding the five aggregates of clinging?” “There might, monk,” the Blessed One said: “Here, monk, for some it occurs thus: ‘May I be such a form in the future, may I be such a feeling in the future, may I be such a perception in the future, may I be such a formation in the future, may I be such a consciousness in the future.’ Thus, monk, there might be desire and lust regarding the five aggregates of clinging.” “Excellent, Bhante,” that monk …pe… asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:7: “What, Bhante, is the cause, what the condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate; what the cause, what the condition for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate; what the cause, what the condition for the manifestation of the perception aggregate; what the cause, what the condition for the manifestation of the formations aggregate; what the cause, what the condition for the manifestation of the consciousness aggregate?” “The four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the formations aggregate. Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the manifestation of the consciousness aggregate.” “Excellent, Bhante,” that monk …pe… asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: “But how, sir, does identity view arise?” “Here, monk, an unlearned ordinary person who has not seen noble ones, is not skilled and disciplined in the noble teaching, who has not seen good men, is not skilled and disciplined in the good man’s teaching, regards form as self, or self as possessed of form; or form as in self, or self as in form; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness; or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. This is how, monk, identity view arises.” “Excellent, sir,” that monk … asked:
translations.sn22.82:9: “But how, sir, does identity view not arise?” “Here, monk, a learned noble disciple who has seen noble ones, is skilled and disciplined in the noble teaching, who has seen good men, is skilled and disciplined in the good man’s teaching, does not regard form as self, or self as possessed of form; or form as in self, or self as in form; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessed of consciousness; or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. This is how, monk, identity view does not arise.” “Excellent, sir,” that monk … asked:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks.” “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said:
translations.sn22.83:3: “Just as, friend Ānanda, a woman or man, young, youthful, with a full head of hair, looking into a mirror or a clear, bright, clean bowl of water, might examine the image of their own face by applying, not by not applying; even so, friend Ānanda, through applying to form there is ‘I am,’ not through not applying. Through applying to feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness there is ‘I am,’ not through not applying.
translations.sn22.84:10: “This simile, Tissa, was made by me for the purpose of making known the meaning. And this is the meaning here: ‘A man unskilled in the path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for the ordinary person. ‘A man skilled in the path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘A forked path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for doubt. ‘The left path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, namely: wrong view …pe… wrong concentration. ‘The right path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for the noble eightfold path, namely: right view …pe… right concentration. ‘A steep forest thicket’—this, Tissa, is a designation for ignorance. ‘A great abyss, a swamp’—this, Tissa, is a designation for sensual pleasures. ‘A steep cliff’—this, Tissa, is a designation for anger and resentment. ‘An even, delightful terrain’—this, Tissa, is a designation for Nibbāna. Delight, Tissa, delight, Tissa. By my instruction, by my guidance, by my instruction.”
translations.sn22.84:5: “Excellent, excellent, Tissa. It is just so, Tissa. Just as in the case of one without attachment to volitional formations, without attachment to consciousness, without desire, without affection, without thirst, without burning, without craving, for that consciousness, due to its change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn22.84:6: “Excellent, excellent, Tissa. It is just so, Tissa. Just as in the case of one without attachment to consciousness. What do you think, Tissa, in the case of one without attachment to form, without desire, without affection, without thirst, without burning, without craving, for that form, due to its change and alteration, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.85:1: On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Now on that occasion the monk Yamaka had taken up such an evil view: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk with destroyed taints, at the breakup of the body, perishes, is annihilated, does not exist after death.’
translations.sn22.85:10: “What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard form … feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn22.85:11: “What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard this formless … feelingless … perceptionless … formationless … conscienceless as the Tathāgata?” “No, friend.” “But, friend Yamaka, with the Tathāgata not found in the present life as a truth of the ordinary way, is it proper for you to explain it like this: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk with destroyed taints, at the breakup of the body, perishes, is annihilated, does not exist after death’?”
translations.sn22.85:12: “I had that evil view in the past, friend Sāriputta, because I did not see, but now, having heard the Venerable Sāriputta’s exposition of Dhamma, that evil view is abandoned, and the Dhamma is realized by me.”
translations.sn22.85:16: He does not truly understand impermanent form as ‘impermanent form.’ He does not truly understand impermanent feeling as ‘impermanent feeling.’ He does not truly understand impermanent perception as ‘impermanent perception.’ He does not truly understand impermanent volitional formations as ‘impermanent volitional formations.’ He does not truly understand impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness.’
translations.sn22.85:19: He does not truly understand conditioned form as ‘conditioned form.’ Conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned volitional formations … conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness.’
translations.sn22.85:20: He does not truly understand destructive form as ‘destructive form’. Destructive feeling as ‘destructive feeling’ … destructive perception as ‘destructive perception’ … destructive volitional formations as ‘destructive volitional formations’ he does not truly understand. Destructive consciousness as ‘destructive consciousness’ he does not truly understand.
translations.sn22.85:21: He takes up form, he clings to it, he determines it: ‘This is my self’. Feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness he takes up, he clings to it, he determines it: ‘This is my self’. These five aggregates of clinging that he has taken up and clung to lead to his long-term harm and suffering.
translations.sn22.85:23: He truly understands impermanent form as ‘impermanent form’. Impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent volitional formations … impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness’ he truly understands.
translations.sn22.85:25: He truly understands not-self form as ‘not-self form’. Not-self feeling … not-self perception … not-self volitional formations … not-self consciousness as ‘not-self consciousness’ he truly understands.
translations.sn22.85:5: When those monks were unable to separate the venerable Yamaka from that evil view, then those monks rose from their seats and went to the venerable Sāriputta. After going to him, they said to the venerable Sāriputta: ‘The monk Yamaka, friend Sāriputta, has this kind of evil view arisen: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk with destroyed taints, at the breaking up of the body, perishes and is annihilated, and does not exist after death.” May the venerable Sāriputta go to the monk Yamaka out of compassion.’ The venerable Sāriputta assented with silence. Then the venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from retreat in the evening, went to the venerable Yamaka. After going to him, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Yamaka …pe… and, sitting to one side, the venerable Sāriputta said to the venerable Yamaka:
translations.sn22.85:6: ‘Is it true, friend Yamaka, that this evil view has arisen in you: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk with destroyed taints, at the breaking up of the body, perishes and is annihilated, and does not exist after death”?’ ‘Yes, friend, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk with destroyed taints, at the breaking up of the body, perishes and is annihilated, and does not exist after death.’
translations.sn22.85:9: ‘What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata as present in form?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘Do you regard the Tathāgata as present apart from form?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘In feeling … apart from feeling …pe… in perception … apart from perception … in volitional formations … apart from volitional formations … in consciousness do you regard the Tathāgata as present?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘Do you regard the Tathāgata as present apart from consciousness?’ ‘No, friend.’
translations.sn22.86:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying near Vesālī in the Great Wood in the peaked-roof hall. At that time the venerable Anurādha was staying not far from the Blessed One in a wilderness hut. Then several wanderers of other sects went to the venerable Anurādha. After going to him, they exchanged greetings with the venerable Anurādha. After exchanging greetings and polite conversation, they sat to one side. Sitting to one side those wanderers of other sects said to the venerable Anurādha: ‘With regard to that Tathāgata, friend Anurādha, supreme man, highest man, who has attained the highest attainment, does the Tathāgata make a declaration in these four positions: “The Tathāgata exists after death,” or “The Tathāgata does not exist after death,” or “The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” or “The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death”?’
translations.sn22.86:10: ‘What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form … feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?’ ‘No, sir.’
translations.sn22.86:11: ‘What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard this formless … feelingless … perceptionless … formationless … consciousnessless one as the Tathāgata?’ ‘No, sir.’
translations.sn22.86:12: ‘And since, Anurādha, the Tathāgata is not found in truth in the here-and-now, is it proper for you to declare: “With regard to that Tathāgata, friend, supreme man, highest man, who has attained the highest attainment, the Tathāgata makes a declaration apart from these four positions— ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘does not exist … both exists and does not exist … neither exists nor does not exist after death”?’ ‘No, sir.’
translations.sn22.86:2: When this was said, the venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers of other sects: ‘With regard to that Tathāgata, friends, supreme man, highest man, who has attained the highest attainment, the Tathāgata makes a declaration apart from these four positions: “The Tathāgata exists after death,” or “The Tathāgata does not exist after death,” or “The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” or “The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.”’ When this was said, the wanderers of other sects said to the venerable Anurādha: ‘This monk is new, recently gone forth, or perhaps an elder who is foolish and inexperienced.’ Then the wanderers of other sects, having disparaged the venerable Anurādha with disparagement of a new monk and disparagement of a foolish one, rose from their seats and departed.
translations.sn22.86:3: Then it occurred to the venerable Anurādha soon after those wanderers of other sects had left: ‘If those wanderers of other sects were to ask me a further question, how should I answer so that I would be true to the Blessed One’s teaching, not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, explain Dhamma in accordance with Dhamma, and so that no legitimate debater would find grounds for blame?’
translations.sn22.86:8: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form as the Tathāgata?” “No, sir.” “Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.86:9: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?” “No, sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?” “No, sir.” “In feeling … apart from feeling … in perception … apart from perception … in formations … apart from formations … in consciousness … apart from consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.89:10: “Just as, friends, the fragrance of a blue-, red-, or white lotus. Would one who spoke thus speak rightly: ‘The fragrance of the petals,’ or ‘the fragrance of the color,’ or ‘the fragrance of the filament’?” “No, sir.” “And how, friends, would one speak rightly?” “‘The fragrance of the flower,’ friends, is how one would speak rightly.” “Just so, friends, I do not say ‘I am form,’ nor do I say ‘I am apart from form.’ I do not say ‘I am feeling … perception … formations … consciousness,’ nor do I say ‘I am apart from consciousness.’ But, friends, regarding ‘I am’ obtained with respect to the five aggregates of clinging, I do not regard ‘This I am.’
translations.sn22.89:11: “And while, friends, a noble disciple’s five lower fetters are abandoned, still there remains for him: the conceit ‘I am’ following along with the five aggregates of clinging, the desire ‘I am,’ the underlying tendency to ‘I am,’ uneradicated. In due course, abiding in contemplation of rise and fall with respect to the five aggregates of clinging—‘Thus form, thus the arising of form, thus the passing away of form; thus feeling … thus perception … thus formations … thus consciousness, thus the arising of consciousness, thus the passing away of consciousness’—as he abides in contemplation of rise and fall with respect to these five aggregates of clinging, whatever there is of the conceit ‘I am,’ the desire ‘I am,’ the underlying tendency to ‘I am’ following along with the five aggregates of clinging, uneradicated, that too goes to destruction.
translations.sn22.89:12: “Just as, friends, a cloth that is soiled and stained. Its owners take it to a laundryman. The laundryman kneads it with lye or cow dung or beans in clean water. And while the cloth becomes pure and spotless, still there remains for it the lingering smell of lye or cow dung or beans, uneradicated. The laundryman gives it back to the owners. The owners put it away in a box scented with incense. Whatever lingering smell of lye or cow dung or beans there was, uneradicated, that too goes to destruction. Just so, friends, while a noble disciple’s five lower fetters are abandoned, still there remains for him the conceit ‘I am,’ the desire ‘I am,’ the underlying tendency to ‘I am’ following along with the five aggregates of clinging, uneradicated. In due course, he abides in contemplation of rise and fall with respect to the five aggregates of clinging. ‘Thus form, thus the arising of form, thus the passing away of form; thus feeling … thus perception … thus formations … thus consciousness, thus the arising of consciousness, thus the passing away of consciousness.’ As he abides in contemplation of rise and fall with respect to these five aggregates of clinging, whatever there is of the conceit ‘I am,’ the desire ‘I am,’ the underlying tendency to ‘I am’ following along with the five aggregates of clinging, uneradicated, that too goes to destruction.”
translations.sn22.89:13: When this was said, the elder monks said to venerable Khemaka: “We did not question venerable Khemaka out of desire to harass, but venerable Khemaka has explained, taught, declared, established, revealed, analyzed, and elucidated the Blessed One’s teaching in detail.”
translations.sn22.90:1: On one occasion many elder monks were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, having emerged from retreat, venerable Channa took up his outer robe and bowl, went to the dwelling of the elder monks, and said to them: “May the venerable elders instruct me, may the venerable elders teach me, may the venerable elders give me a talk on the Dhamma so that I may see the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.90:2: When this was said, the elder monks said to venerable Channa: “Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self.”
translations.sn22.90:3: Then it occurred to venerable Channa: “I also have this same thought: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent, all phenomena are not-self.’ Yet my mind does not enter, settle, become still, or attain confidence in the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nibbāna. Anxiety arises, clinging arises; the mind reverts: ‘Then who is now my self?’ But it is not by seeing thus that one sees the Dhamma. Who might teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I may see the Dhamma?”
translations.sn22.90:4: Then this occurred to Venerable Channa: “This Venerable Ānanda is dwelling in Kosambī at Ghosita’s park, praised and approved by the Teacher and by wise co-dwellers in the holy life, and Venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching the Dhamma such that I would see the Dhamma; and I have sixty years’ association with Venerable Ānanda. What if I were to go to Venerable Ānanda?” Then Venerable Channa, having arranged his lodging and taking his bowl and robe, went to Venerable Ānanda at Ghosita’s park in Kosambī; having gone, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda …pe… and, sitting to one side, Venerable Channa said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn22.90:8: “Even with this much we are delighted with Venerable Channa; perhaps Venerable Channa will make the stake splinter. Lend an ear, friend Channa; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma.” Then with just that, sublime joy and rapture arose in Venerable Channa: ‘I am capable of understanding the Dhamma!’
translations.sn22.94:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I do not quarrel with the world; it is the world that quarrels with me. Bhikkhus, a speaker of Dhamma does not quarrel with anyone in the world. Whatever, bhikkhus, is not approved of in the world by the wise, that I also say ‘it does not exist.’ Whatever, bhikkhus, is approved of in the world by the wise, that I also say ‘it exists.’
translations.sn22.94:3: And what, bhikkhus, is approved of in the world by the wise, which I say ‘it exists’? Form, bhikkhus, is impermanent, suffering, a dharma subject to change; this is approved of in the world by the wise; I also say ‘it exists.’ Feeling is impermanent …pe… consciousness is impermanent, suffering, a dharma subject to change; this is approved of in the world by the wise; I also say ‘it exists.’ This, bhikkhus, is approved of in the world by the wise; I also say ‘it exists.’
translations.sn22.94:4: There exists, bhikkhus, in the world a world-dhamma; that the Tathāgata fully awakens to, fully comprehends; having fully awakened to it, fully comprehended it, he declares it, teaches it, makes it clear, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it plain.
translations.sn22.94:7: Bhikkhus, one who, when it is declared, taught, made clear, established, revealed, analyzed, and made plain in this way by the Tathāgata, does not know, does not see it—for that one, bhikkhus, a foolish ordinary person, blind, eyeless, not knowing, not seeing, what can I do?
translations.sn22.95:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Ayujjhā on the bank of the Ganges River. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.sn22.95:10: As one reflects, investigates thoroughly; What is seen thoroughly becomes empty, hollow, Who sees it thoroughly.
translations.sn22.95:11: Having regard for this body, Taught by one of broad wisdom; The abandoning of three dhammas, See form as discarded.
translations.sn22.95:12: Life, heat, and consciousness, When this body is abandoned; Then it lies cast off, After-meal, inanimate.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuum, A magic trick, a babbler of fools; This is called a butcher, No core is found here.
translations.sn22.95:2: “Bhikkhus, suppose this Ganges River were carrying along a great lump of foam. A person with vision would see it, reflect on it, investigate it thoroughly. To him—seeing it, reflecting, investigating it thoroughly—it would appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. What substance could there be in a lump of foam, bhikkhus? Just so, bhikkhus, whatever form …pe… whether past, future, or present … far or near, a bhikkhu sees it, reflects, investigates it thoroughly. To him—seeing it, reflecting, investigating it thoroughly—it appears empty, hollow, insubstantial. What substance could there be in form, bhikkhus?
translations.sn22.95:3: “Bhikkhus, suppose in the autumn, when the sky teems with thunderclouds, a water bubble arises and ceases on the water. A person with vision would see it, reflect on it, investigate it thoroughly. To him—seeing it, reflecting, investigating it thoroughly—it would appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. What substance could there be in a water bubble, bhikkhus? Just so, bhikkhus, whatever feeling …pe… whether past, future, or present … far or near, a bhikkhu sees it, reflects, investigates it thoroughly. To him—seeing it, reflecting, investigating it thoroughly—it appears empty, hollow, insubstantial. What substance could there be in feeling, bhikkhus?
translations.sn22.95:4: “Bhikkhus, suppose in the last month of the hot season, at midday, a mirage shimmers. A person with vision would see it, reflect on it, investigate it thoroughly. To him—seeing it, reflecting, investigating it thoroughly—it would appear empty, hollow …pe… What substance could there be in a mirage, bhikkhus? Just so, bhikkhus, whatever perception …pe….
translations.sn22.95:5: “Bhikkhus, suppose a person needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to enter a forest with an axe. There he would see a standing, new, straight banana tree without shoots. He would cut it at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut off the top; having cut off the top, he would peel away the leaves. While peeling away the leaves, he would not find even the core, how much less the heartwood. A person with vision would see it, reflect on it, investigate it thoroughly. To him—seeing it, reflecting, investigating it thoroughly—it would appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. What substance could there be in a banana tree, bhikkhus? Just so, bhikkhus, whatever formations …pe… whether past, future, or present … far or near, a bhikkhu sees them, reflects, investigates them thoroughly. To him—seeing them, reflecting, investigating them thoroughly—they appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. What substance could there be in formations, bhikkhus?”
translations.sn22.95:6: Just as, monks, a magician or a magician’s apprentice would produce an illusion on a crossroads. A man with eyes would see it, reflect on it, and wisely investigate it. When he sees it, reflects on it, and wisely investigates it, it would appear to him as empty, as void, as insubstantial. What substance could there be, monks, in an illusion? In the same way, monks, whatever consciousness—past, future, or present … far or near—a monk sees it, reflects on it, and wisely investigates it. When he sees it, reflects on it, and wisely investigates it, it appears to him as empty, as void, as insubstantial. What substance could there be, monks, in consciousness?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing thus, monks, the instructed noble disciple is disillusioned with form, with feeling … with perception … with choices … with consciousness. Being disillusioned, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is freed. When freed, there comes the knowledge ‘I’m freed’ … ‘There is no more rebirth’—he understands.
translations.sn22.95:9: “Form is like a lump of foam,  feeling like a water bubble;  Perception is like a mirage,  choices like a plantain trunk;  Consciousness like an illusion,  so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.
translations.sn22.96:1: At Sāvatthī. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: ‘Is there, sir, any form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same forever and eternal? Is there, sir, any feeling that is permanent … any perception … any choices that are permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same forever and eternal? Is there, sir, any consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same forever and eternal?’ ‘There is not, monk, any form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same forever and eternal. There is not, monk, any feeling … any perception … any choices … any consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same forever and eternal.’
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Blessed One, taking up a little ball of dung with his hand, said to the monk: ‘Even this much, monk, attainment of self-existence is not permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same forever and eternal. If there had been even this much attainment of self-existence that was permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, this holy life would not have been made known for the complete ending of suffering. But since, monk, even this much attainment of self-existence is not permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, the holy life is made known for the complete ending of suffering.
translations.sn22.96:3: Once upon a time, monk, I was a king, a noble, a consecrated one. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand cities headed by Kusāvatī as capital. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand palaces headed by the palace of righteousness. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand peaked roof houses headed by the Great Ornamented Peaked Roof House. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand couches made of ivory, wood, gold, with woollen spreads, spreads with long hair fringes, counterpanes, with coverings of plantain fibre, red on both sides, with red cushions. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with gold, with gold banners, covered with nets of gold, headed by Uposatha Elephant King. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand horses adorned with gold, with gold banners, covered with nets of gold, headed by Valāhaka Horse King. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand chariots adorned with gold, with gold banners, covered with nets of gold, headed by Victory Chariot. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one, there were eighty-four thousand gems headed by the gem jewel. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one … there were eighty-four thousand women headed by Subhaddā. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one … there were eighty-four thousand noblemen attendants headed by the jewel of attendants. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one … there were eighty-four thousand cows with fine hides, wearing bronze bells. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one … there were eighty-four thousand koṭis of robes of finest wool, finest silk, finest woollen cloth, finest linen. When I was that king, noble, consecrated one … there were eighty-four thousand pots of cooked rice; in the evening and morning the meal was brought.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Blessed One, putting a little dust of the nail point on the tip of his fingernail, said to the monk: ‘Even this much, monk, form is not permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, remaining the same forever and eternal. If there had been even this much form that was permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, this holy life would not have been made known for the complete ending of suffering. But since, monk, even this much form is not permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, the holy life is made known for the complete ending of suffering.
translations.sn35.101:4: Suppose, monks, people were to take the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta’s Grove, or burn them, or do with them as they wish. Would you think: “People are taking us, or burning us, or doing with us as they wish”?’
translations.sn35.116:2: Then those monks thought: “This venerable Ānanda has been praised by the Teacher and is respected by wise co-practitioners. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of what has been stated in brief and summarized by the Blessed One. What if we were to go to venerable Ānanda; having gone, we would ask venerable Ānanda about this matter.”
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those monks went to venerable Ānanda; having gone, they exchanged greetings with venerable Ānanda. Having exchanged greetings and courtesies, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn35.116:5: “Just as, friend, a person seeking core wood, searching for core wood, looking for core wood, passing by a standing great tree with core wood, passing by the root, passing by the trunk, would think to search for core wood in the branches and foliage; so too, friend, with the Teacher right in front of you, you think to ask us about this matter. For the Blessed One, friend, knowing knows, seeing sees—he is the eye, the knowledge, the Dhamma, the Brahmā, the speaker, the proclaimer, the leader to benefit, the giver of immortality, the lord of Dhamma, the Realized One. And this was the right time for you to ask the Blessed One himself about this matter. You should hold it just as the Blessed One would explain it to you.”
translations.sn35.116:6: “Indeed, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One, knowing knows, seeing sees—he is the eye, the knowledge, the Dhamma, the Brahmā, the speaker, the proclaimer, the leader to benefit, the giver of immortality, the lord of Dhamma, the Realized One. And this was the right time for us to ask the Blessed One himself about this matter. We will hold it just as the Blessed One explains it to us. But venerable Ānanda has been praised by the Teacher and is respected by wise co-practitioners. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of what has been stated in brief and summarized by the Blessed One. Please explain it, venerable sir, without making it difficult.”
translations.sn35.116:7: “Then, friends, listen, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda said:
translations.sn35.116:9: “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to venerable Ānanda. Then they rose from their seats and went to the Blessed One; having gone, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn35.117:1: “Before my enlightenment, monks, when I was still a bodhisatta not yet awakened, this thought arose in me: ‘These five strands of sensual pleasures, which have previously touched my mind, have passed away, ceased, changed: if my mind were to go repeatedly to them, either a little in the present or in the future.’ Then, monks, this thought arose in me: ‘These five strands of sensual pleasures, which have previously touched my mind, have passed away, ceased, changed: heedfulness, mindfulness, and guarding of the mind should be practiced by me in regard to them.’ Therefore, monks, for you too, these five strands of sensual pleasures, which have previously touched your mind, have passed away, ceased, changed: if your mind were to go repeatedly to them, either a little in the present or in the future. Therefore, monks, for you too, these five strands of sensual pleasures, which have previously touched your mind, have passed away, ceased, changed: heedfulness, mindfulness, and guarding of the mind should be practiced by you in regard to them. Therefore, monks, that sense field should be understood where the eye stops, and perception of forms stops …pe… where the tongue stops, and perception of tastes stops …pe… where the mind stops, and perception of dhammas stops.” Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.sn35.118:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then Sakka, lord of gods, went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of gods, said to the Blessed One: “What is the cause, Bhante, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain nibbāna in this very life? And what is the cause, Bhante, what is the reason why some beings here do attain nibbāna in this very life?”
translations.sn35.118:2: “There are, lord of gods, visible forms cognizable by eye that are likable, agreeable, pleasing, attractive, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk approves of them, welcomes them, persists in attachment, then consciousness becomes dependent on them, clinging takes hold. When there is clinging, lord of gods, a monk does not attain nibbāna …pe….
translations.sn35.118:3: There are, lord of gods, tastes cognizable by tongue …pe… there are, lord of gods, mental phenomena cognizable by mind that are likable, agreeable, pleasing, attractive, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk approves of them, welcomes them, persists in attachment, then consciousness becomes dependent on them, clinging takes hold. When there is clinging, lord of gods, a monk does not attain nibbāna. This, lord of gods, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here do not attain nibbāna in this very life.
translations.sn35.118:4: There are, lord of gods, visible forms cognizable by eye that are likable, agreeable, pleasing, attractive, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not approve of them, does not welcome them, does not persist in attachment, then consciousness does not become dependent on them, no clinging takes hold. When there is no clinging, lord of gods, a monk attains nibbāna …pe….
translations.sn35.127:1: On one occasion the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita's Park. Then King Udena approached the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja. Having exchanged greetings and courtesies that were to be exchanged, he sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, King Udena said this to the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja: 'What is the cause, what is the reason, Bhāradvāja, by which these young monks—tender, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not having dallied with sensual pleasures—live the complete and pure holy life for their entire lives, and fulfill it?' 'It has been said by the Blessed One, great king, the knower, the seer, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one: "Here, monks, establish the thought of a mother towards those of the stature of a mother, the thought of a sister towards those of the stature of a sister, the thought of a daughter towards those of the stature of a daughter." This, great king, is the cause, this is the reason by which these young monks—tender, with black hair... live the complete and pure holy life for their entire lives, and fulfill it.'
translations.sn35.127:2: 'The mind, Bhāradvāja, is unsteady. Sometimes even towards those of the stature of a mother, things of lust arise, towards those of the stature of a sister, things of lust arise, towards those of the stature of a daughter, things of lust arise. Is there, Bhāradvāja, another cause, another reason by which these young monks—tender, with black hair... live the complete and pure holy life for their entire lives, and fulfill it?'
translations.sn35.127:3: 'It has been said by the Blessed One, great king, the knower, the seer, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one: "Here, monks, reflect on this very body from the soles of the feet upwards and from the tips of the hairs downwards, enclosed by skin, full of many kinds of impurity: In this body there are hairs of the head, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, contents of the stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, fat, grease, spittle, mucus, oil of the joints, urine." This too, great king, is a cause, this is a reason by which these young monks—tender, with black hair... live the complete and pure holy life for their entire lives, and fulfill it.' 'For those monks, Bhāradvāja, who have developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, developed wisdom, it is easy. But for those monks, Bhāradvāja, who have undeveloped body, undeveloped virtue, undeveloped mind, undeveloped wisdom, it is difficult. Sometimes, Bhāradvāja, when one intends to consider the repulsive, the attractive comes instead. Is there, Bhāradvāja, another cause, another reason by which these young monks—tender, with black hair... live the complete and pure holy life for their entire lives, and fulfill it?'
translations.sn35.127:4: 'It has been said by the Blessed One, great king, the knower, the seer, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one: "Here, monks, dwell with sense faculties guarded. Having seen a form with the eye, do not seize at signs, do not seize at secondary characteristics. For one dwelling with the eye faculty unguarded, with that as basis, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might flow in; practice restraint there. Guard the eye faculty; undertake restraint regarding the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... Having smelled an odor with the nose... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having felt a tangible object with the body... Having cognized a mental object with the mind, do not seize at signs, do not seize at secondary characteristics. For one dwelling with the mind faculty unguarded, with that as basis, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might flow in; practice restraint there. Guard the mind faculty; undertake restraint regarding the mind faculty." This too, great king, is a cause, this is a reason by which these young monks—tender, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not having dallied with sensual pleasures—live the complete and pure holy life for their entire lives, and fulfill it.'
translations.sn35.136:2: "Forms, sounds, flavors, odors,  contacts, and mental objects as a whole;  Pleasurable, delightful, agreeable,  are said to be to that extent."
translations.sn35.136:3: "In the world with its devas,  these are approved as pleasures by you;  Where these cease,  that is approved as suffering by them."
translations.sn35.136:4: "Pleasure seen by the noble ones,  the cessation of self-identification;  This is contrary,  for one seeing with the whole world."
translations.sn35.136:5: "What others call pleasure,  the noble ones say is suffering;  What others call suffering,  the noble ones know as pleasure."
translations.sn35.136:6: "See the Dhamma hard to understand,  deluded here, the ignorant;  Darkness is closed up,  for one not seeing, in darkness."
translations.sn35.136:7: "And for the awakened it is open,  like light for those who see;  They do not know what is near,  the path of Dhamma, inexpert."
translations.sn35.136:8: "By those sunk in becoming and lust,  following along with becoming and lust;  Having arisen in Māra's realm,  this Dhamma is not well-awakened."
translations.sn35.63:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One... Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Migajāla said this to the Blessed One: '"One who dwells alone, one who dwells alone," it is said, venerable sir. How far, venerable sir, is one a one who dwells alone, and how far a one who dwells with a companion?'
translations.sn35.69:1: On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Upasena were dwelling at Rājagaha in the Cool Grove, in the Squirrel Sanctuary. At that time the Venerable Upasena had been struck by a snake. Then the Venerable Upasena addressed the monks: 'Come, friends, lift this body of mine onto a couch and carry it outside. Formerly this body used to rot right here, like a log of rotten wood.'
translations.sn35.74:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One... Having sat down to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One: 'In such-and-such dwelling, venerable sir, there is a certain newly ordained monk, inexperienced, afflicted, suffering, seriously ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach that monk out of compassion.'
translations.sn35.74:12: 'Good, good, monk. Well done, monk, you understand the Dhamma taught by me for the sake of dispassion from lust. For dispassion from lust, monk, I have taught the Dhamma. What do you think, monk, is the eye permanent or impermanent?'
translations.sn35.74:18: 'But that which is impermanent, suffering, a phenomenon subject to change—is it fit to regard it thus: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"?'
translations.sn35.74:2: Then the Blessed One, having heard both the new talk and the sick talk, and knowing “the monks have little wisdom,” went to that monk. That monk saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he made room on the couch. Then the Blessed One said to that monk: “Enough, monk, don’t make room for me on the couch. There are these seats laid out; I will sit there.” The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to that monk: “I hope you’re getting better, monk. I hope you’re comfortable. I hope your painful feelings are decreasing and not increasing, and that the decrease is evident and not the increase.”
translations.sn35.74:3: “It’s not going well for me, sir, it’s not comfortable. My painful feelings are increasing and not decreasing, and the increase is evident and not the decrease.”
translations.sn35.75:7: “I understand the teaching taught by the Blessed One for the sake of final extinguishing with no clinging.”
translations.sn35.75:8: “Excellent, excellent, monk. Excellent, monk, you understand the teaching I taught for the sake of final extinguishing with no clinging. For it is for the sake of final extinguishing with no clinging, monk, that I taught the teaching.
translations.sn35.88:1: Then venerable Puṇṇa went to the Blessed One. He went, paid homage … and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, venerable Puṇṇa said to the Blessed One: “May the Blessed One please teach me Dhamma in brief. May I hear the Blessed One’s teaching and live alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.sn35.88:12: “If, sir, people from Sunāparanta hit me with clods, then this thought will occur to me: ‘Excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are truly excellent, in that they hit me with clods rather than with a stick.’ That’s how it will be for me, Blessed One. That’s how it will be for me, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:14: “If, sir, people from Sunāparanta hit me with a knife, then this thought will occur to me: ‘Excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are truly excellent, in that they hit me, depriving me of life, with a sharp knife.’ That’s how it will be for me, Blessed One. That’s how it will be for me, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:16: “If, sir, people from Sunāparanta deprive me of life with a sharp knife, then this thought will occur to me: ‘There are disciples of that Blessed One who are disgusted, repelled, and repulsed by body and life, and they seek a knife-wielder. I have got this knife-wielder without searching for it.’ That’s how it will be for me, Blessed One. That’s how it will be for me, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:17: “Excellent, Puṇṇa. With this subduing and calming, Puṇṇa, you will be able to live in the Sunāparanta district. Now then, Puṇṇa, you may go whenever you think it’s time.”
translations.sn35.88:18: Then venerable Puṇṇa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, got up from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping his right side toward him, and packed away his dwelling and taking his bowl and robes, set out on a tour for the Sunāparanta district. Traveling by stages, he arrived at the Sunāparanta district. There venerable Puṇṇa stayed in the Sunāparanta district. Then in due course venerable Puṇṇa guided about five hundred laymen in Sunāparanta. In due course he guided about five hundred laywomen. In due course he realized the three knowledges. In due course he attained nirvana.
translations.sn35.88:19: Then several monks went to the Blessed One … and sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: “That clansman named Puṇṇa, sir, who was given brief advice by the Blessed One, has passed away. What is his destination and future rebirth?”
translations.sn35.88:4: “In which district will you stay, Puṇṇa, now that I have given you this brief advice?” “There is, sir, a district called Sunāparanta. I will stay there.”
translations.sn35.88:5: “The people of Sunāparanta are fierce, Puṇṇa. The people of Sunāparanta are rough. If the people of Sunāparanta abuse and insult you, Puṇṇa, what will you think?”
translations.sn35.88:6: “If, sir, people from Sunāparanta abuse and insult me, then this thought will occur to me: ‘Excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are truly excellent, in that they abuse and insult me with their hand rather than hitting me.’ That’s how it will be for me, Blessed One. That’s how it will be for me, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.88:8: “If, sir, people from Sunāparanta hit me with their hand, then this thought will occur to me: ‘Excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are excellent, these people from Sunāparanta are truly excellent, in that they hit me with their hand rather than with a clod.’ That’s how it will be for me, Blessed One. That’s how it will be for me, Holy One.”
translations.sn35.95:1: Then venerable Mālukyaputta went to the Blessed One … and sitting to one side, venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: “May the Blessed One please teach me Dhamma in brief. May I hear the Blessed One’s teaching and live alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.sn35.95:10: “And for you, Mālukyaputta, in what can be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will just be the seen, in the heard just the heard, in the sensed just the sensed, in the cognized just the cognized. When for you, Mālukyaputta, in what can be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will just be the seen, in the heard just the heard, in the sensed just the sensed, in the cognized just the cognized; then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be by that. When, Mālukyaputta, you will not be by that; then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be in that. When, Mālukyaputta, you will not be in that; then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be here, hereafter, or between the two. This is the end of suffering.”
translations.sn35.95:12: ‘With mindfulness lost on seeing a form,  Making a dear sign in mind;  With mind attached he feels,  And clings to it and stands.
translations.sn35.95:13: His feelings grow,  Many born from forms;  Envy and guarding too,  His mind gets overwhelmed;  Thus accumulating suffering,  Far away nirvana is called.
translations.sn35.95:14: With mindfulness lost on hearing a sound,  Making a dear sign in mind;  With mind attached he feels,  And clings to it and stands.
translations.sn35.95:16: With mindfulness lost on smelling an odor,  Making a dear sign in mind;  With mind attached he feels,  And clings to it and stands.
translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted the flavor, with mindfulness lost,  making a dear sign in the mind;  With a mind full of passion he feels it,  and he dwells dwelling upon that.
translations.sn35.95:2: “Now then, Mālunkyaputta, what shall we say to the young monks. For you, monk, old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the age of decrepitude, to ask for brief instruction.”
translations.sn35.95:20: Having contacted the contact, with mindfulness lost,  making a dear sign in the mind;  With a mind full of passion he feels it,  and he dwells dwelling upon that.
translations.sn35.95:22: Having known the dhamma, with mindfulness lost,  making a dear sign in the mind;  With a mind full of passion he feels it,  and he dwells dwelling upon that.
translations.sn35.95:24: He is not delighted in forms,  seeing a form, mindful;  With a dispassionate mind he feels it,  and he does not dwell dwelling upon that.
translations.sn35.95:25: Just as when seeing a form for him,  and experiencing feeling when attending to it;  It diminishes, does not increase,  thus he conducts himself mindful;  Thus diminishing suffering,  nearness is called nibbāna.
translations.sn35.95:26: He is not delighted in sounds,  having heard a sound, mindful;  With a dispassionate mind he feels it,  and he does not dwell dwelling upon that.
translations.sn35.95:27: Just as when hearing a sound for him,  and experiencing feeling when attending to it;  It diminishes, does not increase,  thus he conducts himself mindful;  Thus diminishing suffering,  nearness is called nibbāna.
translations.sn35.95:28: He is not delighted in smells,  having smelled a smell, mindful;  With a dispassionate mind he feels it,  and he does not dwell dwelling upon that.
translations.sn35.95:3: “Indeed, venerable sir, I am old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the age of decrepitude. May the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma briefly, may the Well-Gone One teach the Dhamma briefly, so that I might understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said. So that I might be an heir to what the Blessed One has said.”
translations.sn35.95:30: He is not delighted in flavors,  having tasted a flavor, mindful;  With a dispassionate mind he feels it,  and he does not dwell dwelling upon that.
translations.sn35.95:35: Just as when knowing the dhamma for him,  and experiencing feeling when attending to it;  It diminishes, does not increase,  thus he conducts himself mindful;  Thus diminishing suffering,  nearness is called nibbāna.
translations.sn35.95:36: “I understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement of the Blessed One in this way.” “Good, good, Mālunkyaputta. Good, Mālunkyaputta, you understand the detailed meaning of what I said briefly:
translations.sn35.95:4: “What do you think, Mālunkyaputta, those forms cognizable by eye that you have not seen, have never seen before, you do not see, and it is not that you will see? Is there desire, lust, or affection for them there?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn35.95:9: “Those dhammas cognizable by mind that you have not known, have never known before, you do not know, and it is not that you will know? Is there desire, lust, or affection for them there?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn36.19:12: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined? Here, Ānanda, a monk, having completely transcended the dimension of infinite space, enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness, perceiving ‘infinite consciousness.’ This, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than that pleasure, more sublime and refined. Those who might say: ‘Experiencing this as the utmost peace, happiness, and pleasure’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined.
translations.sn36.19:15: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined? Here, Ānanda, a monk, having completely transcended the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than that pleasure, more sublime and refined.
translations.sn36.19:7: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined? Here, Ānanda, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful dhammas, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than that pleasure, more sublime and refined. Those who might say: ‘Experiencing this as the utmost peace, happiness, and pleasure’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined.
translations.sn36.19:8: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, with internal clarity and confidence of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of samādhi. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than that pleasure, more sublime and refined. Those who might say: ‘Experiencing this as the utmost peace, happiness, and pleasure’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined.
translations.sn36.19:9: And what, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous and mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body, of which the nobles declare: ‘He dwells equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily,’ and enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This, Ānanda, is a pleasure other than that pleasure, more sublime and refined. Those who might say: ‘Experiencing this as the utmost peace, happiness, and pleasure’—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is a pleasure other than this pleasure, more sublime and refined.
translations.sn36.21:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “There are some ascetics and brahmins, sir Gotama, who say and hold this view: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is due to past karma.’ What does the venerable Gotama say about this?”
translations.sn36.21:2: “Even feelings arisen from bile, Sīvaka, arise here in some cases. This, Sīvaka, should be understood for oneself, that even feelings arisen from bile arise here in some cases. This, Sīvaka, is agreed upon as true in the world, that even feelings arisen from bile arise here in some cases. There, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is due to past actions.’ They overstep what is known for oneself, and they overstep what is agreed upon as true in the world. Therefore, I say of those ascetics and brahmins that they are mistaken.”
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, sir Gotama, excellent, sir Gotama …pe… From today let the Blessed One regard me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain monk went to the Blessed One, approached him, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “What, sir, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the way leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the way leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger? What is the escape?”
translations.sn36.31:2: And what, monks, is immaterial joy? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal clarity of mind, unification of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration. This is called, monks, immaterial joy.
translations.sn36.31:3: And what, monks, is immaterial, more immaterial joy? The joy that arises when a monk with taints destroyed reflects upon his mind freed from lust, reflects upon his mind freed from hatred, reflects upon his mind freed from delusion—this is called, monks, immaterial, more immaterial joy.
translations.sn36.31:5: And what, monks, is immaterial pleasure? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied thought and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal clarity of mind, unification of mind, without applied thought, without sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of joy, he dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, experiencing pleasure with the body, and the noble ones declare of him: ‘He dwells equanimous and mindful, a pleasant abiding,’ entering and dwelling in the third jhāna. This is called, monks, immaterial pleasure.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, monks, is immaterial, more immaterial pleasure? The pleasure and joy that arises when a monk with taints destroyed reflects upon his mind freed from lust, reflects upon his mind freed from hatred, reflects upon his mind freed from delusion—this is called, monks, immaterial, more immaterial pleasure.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, monks, is immaterial equanimity? Here, monks, a monk, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is called, monks, immaterial equanimity.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, monks, is immaterial, more immaterial equanimity? The equanimity that arises when a monk with taints destroyed reflects upon his mind freed from lust, reflects upon his mind freed from hatred, reflects upon his mind freed from delusion—this is called, monks, immaterial, more immaterial equanimity.
