translations.sn36.4:2: One who does not endure these, painful arisen feelings; Bodily, life-ending, by which one touched is overwhelmed.
translations.sn36.4:3: He cries out and weeps, weak and unaroused; He does not rise from hell, nor does he reach even the depth.
translations.sn36.6:2: And, monks, when a learned noble disciple is touched by a painful feeling, he does not sorrow, does not lament, does not grieve, does not beat his breast, does not fall into bewilderment. He feels one feeling—a bodily one, not a mental one.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise one does not feel feeling, even pleasure or pain, though learned; This is a great distinction of the steadfast one from an ordinary person, of the skillful one.
translations.sn36.6:5: Of one learned in the Dhamma, who sees this world and the beyond; Desirable qualities do not agitate the mind, undesirable ones do not provoke aversion.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, monks, is a monk mindful? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Thus, monks, a monk is mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how, monks, is a monk clearly comprehending? Here, monks, a monk is one who acts in clearly knowing when going forward and returning; he is one who acts in clearly knowing when looking ahead and looking away; he is one who acts in clearly knowing when flexing and extending; he is one who acts in clearly knowing when wearing the outer robe, carrying the bowl and robe; he is one who acts in clearly knowing when eating, drinking, consuming, and tasting; he is one who acts in clearly knowing when urinating and defecating; he is one who acts in clearly knowing when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and keeping silent. Thus, monks, a monk is clearly comprehending. Monks, a monk should be mindful and clearly comprehending at the right time. This is my instruction to you.”
translations.sn36.7:5: If, monks, while a monk dwells with mindfulness, clearly knowing, heedful, ardent, and resolute, a pleasant feeling arises, he understands thus: ‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. But it is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this body. Now this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. When a pleasant feeling has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, how could it be permanent?’ He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and pleasant feeling, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. While he dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and pleasant feeling, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment, the underlying tendency to lust regarding the body and pleasant feeling is abandoned.
translations.sn36.7:8: When he feels a pleasant feeling, he knows ‘It is impermanent’; he knows ‘It is not clung to’; he knows ‘It is not delighted in’; when he feels a painful feeling … when he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows ‘It is impermanent’; he knows ‘It is not clung to’; he knows ‘It is not delighted in.’ When he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached; when he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached; when he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. While experiencing a feeling limited to the body, he knows ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited to the body’; while experiencing a feeling limited to life, he knows ‘I am experiencing a feeling limited to life.’ He knows: ‘With the breakup of the body, after the end of life, all feelings, not delighted in, will become cool right here.’
translations.sn4.13:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi Deer Park. On that occasion the Blessed One’s foot had been cut by a splinter, and severe pains, sharp, piercing, sharp, disagreeable, unpleasant, were assailing the Blessed One’s body. But the Blessed One endured them, mindful and clearly knowing, without complaining. Then the Blessed One, having arranged his outer robe in four layers, lay down on his right side in the lion’s pose, foot upon foot, mindful and clearly knowing. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; and having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.13:2: “Are you drowsy, or drunk on poetry? Your thoughts are confused, not present; Alone in a secluded lodging, why do you sleep with mouth open?”
translations.sn4.13:3: “I am not drowsy, nor drunk on poetry; Having understood the goal, I am free from sorrow; Alone in a secluded lodging, I lie down compassionately for all beings.
translations.sn4.13:4: “Even if a dart enters the chest, piercing the heart again and again; Here those with darts would find sleep, but I lie down without darts.
translations.sn4.13:5: “I do not fear waking, nor do I fear hearing; Night and day they do not regret me; I see no loss anywhere in the world, therefore I sleep compassionately for all beings.”
translations.sn4.18:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Pañcasālā, a brahmin village. On that occasion young girls at Pañcasālā brahmin village were having a festival. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and outer robe, entered Pañcasālā brahmin village for alms. On that occasion the brahmin householders of Pañcasāla had been possessed by Māra the Evil One: ‘Do not let the ascetic Gotama get almsfood.’
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Blessed One entered Pañcasālā brahmin village for alms with his bowl just as clean as it was when he set out, and he returned with his bowl just as clean as it was. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; and having approached, he said to the Blessed One: ‘Did you not, ascetic, get almsfood?’ ‘Indeed, Evil One, you arranged it just so that I would not get almsfood.’ ‘Well then, venerable sir, let the Blessed One enter Pañcasālā brahmin village for alms a second time. I will arrange it so that the Blessed One gets almsfood.’
translations.sn4.19:4: “What they say is mine, and those who say ‘it is mine’; If you have a mind for that, ascetic, you will not escape me.”
translations.sn4.19:5: “What they say is not mine, and those who say it are not me; Know thus, Evil One, you will not even see the path.”
translations.sn4.1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the foot of the Ajapāla Nigrodha Tree, just recently fully awakened. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in retreat, this thought arose in his mind: ‘I am free from that practice with painful exertion. Well freed from that futile practice with painful exertion. Well freed, having attained enlightenment.’
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Evil One, having known with his mind the thought in the Blessed One’s mind, approached the Blessed One; and having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: “Having deviated from the practice of austerities by which men are purified; Unpurified, you consider yourself purified, you have deviated from the path to purity.”
translations.sn4.1:6: “Morality, concentration, and wisdom, developing the path to awakening; I have attained the supreme purity, you are struck down, End-maker.”
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Evil One thought: ‘The Blessed One knows me, the Fortunate One knows me,’ and he vanished right there, dejected and disappointed.
translations.sn4.20:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling in the Kosalans’ territory in a forest hut in the Himavant region. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in retreat, this thought arose in his mind: ‘Could I rule by righteousness, without killing, without causing to kill, without imprisoning, without causing to imprison?’
translations.sn4.20:3: “A whole mountain of gold, solid gold; Not even two lotuses would suffice for it, so act wisely, ascetic.
translations.sn4.20:4: “He who has seen suffering, with its origin, how could that being bow to sensual pleasures? Having understood the formations in the world, let him train for the taming of that being.”
translations.sn4.21:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Silavati. And on that occasion several monks were dwelling not far from the Blessed One, heedful, ardent, resolute. Then Māra the Evil One, having created the appearance of a brahmin, with a large matted dreadlock, clothed in antelope hide, old, with a goatherd’s staff, wheezing and coughing, taking up an udumbara staff, approached those monks; having approached, he said to those monks: “Sirs, you are young, gone forth, with soft skin, black hair, endowed with beauty and youth, first in age, not delighting in sensual pleasures. Sirs, enjoy human sensual pleasures. Do not, having abandoned what is visible, pursue what is produced later.” “We, brahmin, do not pursue what is produced later, having abandoned what is visible. Rather, brahmin, we pursue what is visible, having abandoned what is produced later. For sensual pleasures, brahmin, have been declared by the Blessed One as very painful, very perilous, with much drawback therein. This Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be personally known by the wise.” When this was said, Māra the Evil One shook his head, stuck out his tongue, raised a threefold frown on his forehead, and departed, grasping his staff.
translations.sn4.24:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the Ajapāla Nigrodha. And on that occasion Māra the Evil One had been a companion of the Blessed One for seven years, seeking entry but not obtaining entry. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: Not having found satisfaction there, the wind-shaken one departs; like a crow rubbing against a rock, we will shake Gotama off.
translations.sn4.24:2: “Overcome by sorrow, do you meditate in the forest? Old and withered, do you still hope for gain? Did you go to the village and get nothing? Why do you not make proof with people? No one attains proof with you.”
translations.sn4.24:3: “Having dug up the root of sorrow entirely, without coming, I meditate unsorrowing; having cut off all the muttering of becoming-desire, taint-free I meditate, kin of the heedless.”
translations.sn4.24:6: “If you have awakened to the path, secure, leading to the deathless; go away alone, why do you instruct others?”
translations.sn4.24:7: “Those people who are stream-crossers ask about the deathless; asked by them, I declare what is true, without anxiety.”
translations.sn4.24:8: “Just as, sir, not far from a village or town there is a pond. There is a water-crow there. Then, sir, several boys or girls from that village or town might go out and approach that pond; having approached, they might draw out that water-crow from the water and place it on dry land. Whatever limb that water-crow, sir, should stretch out or contract, those boys or girls would cut it off, break it, shatter it with a stick or piece of wood. Thus, sir, that water-crow, with all its limbs cut off, broken, shattered, would be incapable of entering that pond. Even so, sir, whatever outflows are bodily, cultivated, developed, all those have been cut off, broken, shattered by the Blessed One. I am now incapable, sir, of approaching the Blessed One again, that is, seeking entry.” Then Māra the Evil One, right there in the presence of the Blessed One, spoke these insulting verses:
translations.sn4.24:9: “A stone with the color of fat, the crow circled around; not finding anything soft here, perhaps there might be satisfaction.
translations.sn4.25:10: ‘An arahant, a well-farer in the world, not led by lust; having overcome Māra’s realm, therefore I greatly sorrow.’
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra’s daughters, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, Craving Māra’s daughter addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: “Having attained the goal, calm of heart, having conquered the army of dear and lovely form; alone I meditate, having realized bliss, therefore I do not make proof with people; no one attains proof with me.”
translations.sn4.25:16: “How does a monk dwell much, overcome by talk, having crossed the five floods, here avoiding a sixth; how meditating much, with sensual perceptions, external, not finding that one?”
translations.sn4.25:17: “Relaxed in body, well-freed in mind, unentangled, mindful, without son; knowing the Dhamma, meditation without applied thought, he does not waver, does not remember, does not tire.
translations.sn4.25:2: “Why are you distressed, dear? Whom among men do you sorrow for? We will bind that one with the bond of lust, like an elephant in the wilderness; having bound him, we will bring him, he will be your slave.”
translations.sn4.25:20: “Cut off Craving, the wanderer with the company; surely many faithful ones will fare along. This leader of people, without son, if cut off, will lead beyond the King of Death.”
translations.sn4.25:23: “Fools, rub the mountain with lotus stalks; scratch the cliff with a nail, eat iron with teeth.
translations.sn4.25:24: “Like a mountain, pile up your head; make a pit in the underworld; like rubbing a pig’s shoulder, shake Gotama off.”
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra’s daughters, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said to the Blessed One: “We will attend to your feet, ascetic.” Then the Blessed One paid them no attention, as he was freed in the supreme ending of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra’s daughters, having gone aside, thought thus: “The intentions of men are of various kinds. What if we were to create a hundred hundred youths of princely appearance each?” Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra’s daughters, created a hundred hundred youths of princely appearance each and approached the Blessed One; having approached, they said to the Blessed One: “We will attend to your feet, ascetic.” The Blessed One paid them no attention either, as he was freed in the supreme ending of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.8:1: Thus have I heard— on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, right there in the presence of the Blessed One, he spoke this verse:
translations.sn4.8:3: “She grieves for her children, the one with children,  The cowherd likewise grieves for his cows;  Grieving for his attachments is a man’s sorrow,  But he who is without attachments does not grieve.”
translations.sn44.1:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Now on that occasion the nun Khemā, while wandering on tour in the Kosalan lands, had arrived at Toranavatthu, between Sāvatthī and Sāketa. Then king Pasenadi Kosala, while going from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, arrived at Toranavatthu for a single night’s lodging, between Sāketa and Sāvatthī. Then king Pasenadi Kosala addressed a certain man: ‘Come, good man, find such a monk or brahmin at Toranavatthu whom I might pay respects to today.’
translations.sn44.1:2: ‘Yes, sire,’ the man replied to king Pasenadi Kosala. Then he roamed around the whole of Toranavatthu but did not see such a monk or brahmin whom king Pasenadi Kosala would pay respects to. He saw the nun Khemā who had arrived at Toranavatthu for lodging. Having seen her, he went to king Pasenadi Kosala, and having gone to him, he said to king Pasenadi Kosala:
translations.sn44.1:3: ‘There is no such monk or brahmin at Toranavatthu, sire, whom the lord would pay respects to. But there is, sire, a nun named Khemā, a disciple of that Blessed One, the Arahant, Perfectly Enlightened One. And of that lady a fine reputation has spread: “She is wise, experienced, intelligent, learned, a speaker of good words, an eloquent speaker.” May the lord pay respects to her.’
translations.sn44.1:6: ‘Well then, great king, I will ask you a counter-question. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, great king: is there any accountant or calculator or enumerator who can count the sand in the Ganges—either “So much sand,” or “So many hundreds of sands,” or “So many thousands of sands,” or “So many hundred thousands of sands”?’ ‘No, lady.’ ‘Is there any accountant or calculator or enumerator who can count the water in the great ocean—either “So many measures of water,” or “So many hundreds of measures of water,” or “So many thousands of measures of water,” or “So many hundred thousands of measures of water”?’ ‘No, lady.’ ‘Why not?’ ‘Lady, the ocean is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom.’ ‘Just so, great king, whatever form one tries to show the Tathāgata by, that form is abandoned by the Tathāgata, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of existence, not destined for future arising. Freed from reckoning by form, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—like the great ocean. He does not think, “The Tathāgata exists after death,” nor “The Tathāgata does not exist after death,” nor “The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” nor “The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.”
translations.sn44.1:9: Whatever consciousness one tries to show the Tathāgata by, that consciousness is abandoned by the Tathāgata, its root destroyed, made like a palmyra stump, deprived of the conditions of existence, not destined for future arising. Freed from reckoning by consciousness, great king, the Tathāgata is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom—like the great ocean. He does not think, “The Tathāgata exists after death,” nor “The Tathāgata does not exist after death,” nor “The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” nor “The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.” Then king Pasenadi Kosala, having rejoiced in and approved of what was said by the nun Khemā, rose from his seat, paid homage to the nun Khemā, circumambulated her keeping her to his right, and departed.
translations.sn45.1:2: “Ignorance, monks, is the forerunner in the attainment of unskillful qualities, followed by shamelessness and recklessness. With ignorance as condition, monks, there is false view; with false view as condition, there is wrong intention; with wrong intention as condition, there is wrong speech; with wrong speech as condition, there is wrong action; with wrong action as condition, there is wrong livelihood; with wrong livelihood as condition, there is wrong effort; with wrong effort as condition, there is wrong mindfulness; with wrong mindfulness as condition, there is wrong concentration.
translations.sn45.2:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at a town of theirs called Nagaraka. Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “This is half of the spiritual life, lord, that is, good friendship, good companionship, good camaraderie.”
translations.sn45.2:2: “Do not say that, Ānanda, do not say that. The whole of the spiritual life is good friendship, good companionship, good camaraderie. When a bhikkhu has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, it may be expected that he will develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.2:3: “And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, maturing in relinquishment; he develops right intention … right speech … right action … right livelihood … right effort … right mindfulness … right concentration supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, maturing in relinquishment. It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, develops and cultivates the noble eightfold path.”}
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi going out of Sāvatthī with a complete set of white oxen-drawn chariots. The oxen were yoked with white ornaments, the chariot was white, the entourage was white, the reins were white, the whip-handle was white, the parasol was white, the turban was white, the clothes were white, the sandals were white, and it was drawn by a white thoroughbred. Seeing him, people said: “What a divine chariot, sir. It is just like a divine chariot.”
translations.sn45.4:10: Non-ill will is non-harming, detachment whose weapon it is; Forbearance is leather armor, it is practiced for yoga-security.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having gone for alms in Sāvatthī, returned from almsround after his meal and went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: “Ānanda,” the Blessed One said: “This very thing, Ānanda, is a designation of this noble eightfold path: ‘divine chariot,’ also ‘dhamma chariot,’ also ‘unrivaled victory in battle.’”
translations.sn45.4:8: One who has faith and wisdom, the factors yoked to the yoke; Shame and moral dread, mind yoked, mindfulness the charioteer.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot equipped with virtue, jhāna-wheel the wheel-power; Equanimity yoke-concentration, renunciation the enclosure.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach and analyze for you the noble eightfold path. Listen, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, Bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this is called, bhikkhus, right view.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, intention of non-harming—this is called, bhikkhus, right intention.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this is called, bhikkhus, right speech.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct—this is called, bhikkhus, right action.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns his living by right livelihood—this is called, bhikkhus, right livelihood.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right effort? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome factors; he generates desire … for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome factors … for the arising of unarisen wholesome factors … for the continuance, non-disappearance, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome factors: makes effort, arouses energy, exerts the mind, and strives—this is called, bhikkhus, right effort.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what, bhikkhus, is right mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body—ardent, fully aware, mindful—having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena—ardent, fully aware, mindful—having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world—this is called, bhikkhus, right mindfulness.
translations.sn46.11:1: Bhikkhus, just as all those creatures that resort to the four postures—walking at times, standing at times, sitting at times, lying down at times—do so depending on the earth, established on the earth; even so, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu depending on virtue, established in virtue, develops the seven awakening-factors, makes much of the seven awakening-factors.
translations.sn46.14:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Now on that occasion the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at the Pippali Cave, sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then the Blessed One, having emerged from retreat in the evening, went to the Venerable Mahākassapa; having gone, he sat on the prepared seat. Sitting down, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: “Kassapa, is there any relief for you, any comfort? Are painful feelings subsiding, not increasing? Is their subsiding evident, not their increase?” “Venerable sir, there is no relief for me, no comfort. My painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding. Their increase is evident, not their subsiding.”
translations.sn46.29:2: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness awakening-factor supported by seclusion …pe… develops the equanimity awakening-factor supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, maturing in relinquishment. When the seven awakening-factors are developed and made much in this way, bhikkhus, they lead to the abandoning of the fettering factors.
translations.sn46.30:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas, in a Sumbhan town named Setaka. Then the Venerable Udāyī went to the Blessed One …pe… sitting to one side, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: “It’s astounding, sir, it’s astounding, sir. I had such great love and respect and shame and moral dread for the Blessed One. For when I was a layperson before, I had little faith in the Dhamma and little faith in the Saṅgha. Seeing my love and respect and shame and moral dread for the Blessed One, I went forth from the lay life to homelessness. The Blessed One taught me Dhamma: ‘This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the passing away of form; this is feeling … this is perception … this is formation … this is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the passing away of consciousness.’
translations.sn46.30:3: Then, sir, while I was withdrawn to an empty hut, I truly understood these five clinging-aggregates as they really are: ‘This is suffering’; ‘This is the origin of suffering’; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ My Dhamma had been penetrated, the path had been attained. When developed and cultivated in this way, it will lead me on to suchness as I abide in this way: ‘My birth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing more to come in this way of life.’
translations.sn46.38:1: Mendicants, when a noble disciple has focused on the skeleton, has focused the mind, has properly attended with all their mind, and listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, at that time their five hindrances are not present. At that time their seven awakening factors go to fulfillment through development.
translations.sn46.3:1: “Mendicants, I say there is great fruit in seeing those mendicants who are perfected in ethics, perfected in immersion, perfected in wisdom, perfected in freedom, perfected in the knowledge and vision of freedom. I say there is great fruit in hearing those mendicants. I say there is great fruit in approaching those mendicants. I say there is great fruit in attending those mendicants. I say there is great fruit in recollecting those mendicants. I say there is great fruit in going forth in their presence. Why is that? Having heard the Dhamma from such mendicants, you live withdrawn in two ways of seclusion—bodily seclusion and mental seclusion. While living withdrawn in this way, you recollect and reflect on that Dhamma.
translations.sn46.3:2: Mendicants, when a mendicant lives withdrawn in this way, recollecting and reflecting on that Dhamma, at that time the mindfulness awakening factor is initiated in them; at that time they develop the mindfulness awakening factor; at that time the mindfulness awakening factor goes to fulfillment in them through development. Abiding mindful in this way, they investigate that Dhamma with wisdom, scrutinize it, and carefully examine it.
translations.sn46.51:20: And what is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen energy awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen energy awakening factor? There is the element of initiative, the element of effort, the element of exertion. Frequent consideration of them: this is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen energy awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen energy awakening factor.
translations.sn46.51:21: And what is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen rapture awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen rapture awakening factor? There are things that are grounds for rapture awakening factor. Frequent consideration of them: this is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen rapture awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen rapture awakening factor.
translations.sn46.51:22: And what is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen tranquility awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen tranquility awakening factor? There is bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Frequent consideration of them: this is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen tranquility awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen tranquility awakening factor.
translations.sn46.51:23: And what is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen immersion awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen immersion awakening factor? There is a sign of serenity and a sign of non-distraction. Frequent consideration of them: this is the food for the arising of yet-unarisen immersion awakening factor, or for the fulfillment by development of the arisen immersion awakening factor.
translations.sn46.52:1: Then, on that occasion several mendicants put on their robes in the morning, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those mendicants: ‘It’s too late now to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. Why don’t we go to the monastery of the wandering ascetics of other sects?’
translations.sn46.52:10: And what is the method by which the seven awakening factors become fourteen? Mindfulness of phenomena internally is mindfulness awakening factor, and mindfulness of phenomena externally is mindfulness awakening factor. This is called ‘mindfulness awakening factor’ in the recitation. In this method it becomes two.
translations.sn46.52:11: Investigation of phenomena internally with wisdom, scrutinizing and carefully examining is investigation-of-principles awakening factor, and investigation of phenomena externally with wisdom, scrutinizing and carefully examining is investigation-of-principles awakening factor. This is called ‘investigation-of-principles awakening factor’ in the recitation. In this method it becomes two.
translations.sn46.52:12: Bodily energy is energy awakening factor, and mental energy is energy awakening factor. This is called ‘energy awakening factor’ in the recitation. In this method it becomes two.
translations.sn46.52:13: Rapture with applied thought and sustained thought is rapture awakening factor, and rapture without applied thought and sustained thought is rapture awakening factor. This is called ‘rapture awakening factor’ in the recitation. In this method it becomes two.
translations.sn46.52:14: Bodily tranquility is tranquility awakening factor, and mental tranquility is tranquility awakening factor. This is called ‘tranquility awakening factor’ in the recitation. In this method it becomes two.
translations.sn46.52:15: Even the concentration with applied thought and sustained thought is a factor of enlightenment of concentration, even the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought is a factor of enlightenment of concentration. ‘Factor of enlightenment of concentration’—thus this is how it is recited. And this too, by this method, is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those monks went to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects; having gone, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. Having exchanged greetings and courtesies, they sat down to one side. When those monks had sat down to one side, the wanderers of other sects said this to them:
translations.sn46.52:3: “Friend, the ascetic Gotama teaches his disciples thus: ‘Here, monks, abandoning the five hindrances, defilements of mind, weakeners of wisdom, develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.’ We too, friend, teach our disciples thus: ‘Here, friends, abandoning the five hindrances, defilements of mind, weakeners of wisdom, develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.’ So what is the difference, what is the preference, what is the reason for distinction between the ascetic Gotama and us, namely—concerning teaching the Dhamma or instruction?”
translations.sn46.52:4: Then those monks neither approved nor rejected what had been said by those wanderers of other sects; without approving or rejecting, they got up from their seats and left: ‘We will understand the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.’ Then those monks, having gone for alms in Sāvatthī, and having returned from the alms round after the meal, went to the Blessed One; having gone, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. When those monks had sat down to one side, they said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.52:8: “When wanderers of other sects say thus, monks, they should be told thus: ‘Is there, friend, a method by relying on which method the five hindrances become ten, the seven factors of enlightenment fourteen?’ When thus questioned, monks, wanderers of other sects would not be able to reply, and they would moreover meet with vexation. Why is that? Because it is outside their domain, monks. I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with ascetics, brahmins, devas, humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one who has heard it from this one.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what, monks, is the method by relying on which method the five hindrances become ten? Internal sensuous desire, monks, is a hindrance, external sensuous desire is a hindrance. ‘Hindrance of sensuous desire’—thus this is how it is recited. And this too, by this method, is twofold. Internal ill will, monks, is a hindrance, external ill will is a hindrance. ‘Hindrance of ill will’—thus this is how it is recited. And this too, by this method, is twofold. Sloth, monks, is a hindrance, torpor is a hindrance. ‘Hindrance of sloth and torpor’—thus this is how it is recited. And this too, by this method, is twofold. Restlessness, monks, is a hindrance, remorse is a hindrance. ‘Hindrance of restlessness and remorse’—thus this is how it is recited. And this too, by this method, is twofold. Internal doubt about phenomena, monks, is a hindrance, external doubt about phenomena is a hindrance. ‘Hindrance of doubt’—thus this is how it is recited. And this too, by this method, is twofold. This, monks, is the method by relying on which method the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:10: Monks, when the mind is restless, at that time it is not the time for developing the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, not the time for developing the energy factor of enlightenment, not the time for developing the rapture factor of enlightenment. Why is that? Monks, a restless mind is hard to calm with those dhammas.
translations.sn46.53:11: Monks, suppose a man wanting to extinguish a great mass of flames would throw on dry grass, dry cow dung, dry sticks, and fan it with a windbag, but not cover it with sand; could that man extinguish the great mass of flames?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn46.53:13: And when, monks, the mind is restless, at that time it is the time for developing the tranquillity factor of enlightenment, the time for developing the concentration factor of enlightenment, the time for developing the equanimity factor of enlightenment. Why is that? Monks, a restless mind is easy to calm with those dhammas.
translations.sn46.53:14: Monks, suppose a man wanting to extinguish a great mass of flames would throw on wet grass, wet cow dung, wet sticks, and sprinkle it with water, and cover it with sand; could that man extinguish the great mass of flames?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn46.53:2: “When wanderers of other sects say thus, monks, they should be told thus: ‘Friend, when the mind is sluggish, which factors of enlightenment at that time are not the time for development, which factors of enlightenment at that time are the time for development? But friend, when the mind is restless, which factors of enlightenment at that time are not the time for development, which factors of enlightenment at that time are the time for development?’ When thus questioned, monks, wanderers of other sects would not be able to reply, and they would moreover meet with vexation. Why is that? Because it is outside their domain, monks.
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this generation with ascetics, brahmins, devas, humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one who has heard it from this one.
translations.sn46.53:4: Monks, when the mind is sluggish, it is not the time for developing the tranquillity enlightenment factor, not the time for developing the concentration enlightenment factor, not the time for developing the equanimity enlightenment factor. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is hard to arouse by these qualities, monks.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose, monks, a man wanted to brighten a small fire. He would throw on damp grass, damp cow dung, damp sticks, he would sprinkle it with water, and cover it with dust. Could that man brighten the small fire?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn46.53:7: And when, monks, the mind is sluggish, it is the time for developing the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, the time for developing the energy enlightenment factor, the time for developing the rapture enlightenment factor. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is easily aroused by these qualities, monks.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose, monks, a man wanted to brighten a small fire. He would throw on dry grass, dry cow dung, dry sticks, he would fan it with a breeze from his mouth, and not cover it with dust. Could that man brighten the small fire?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn46.54:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Koliyans in a Koliyan town named Haliddavasana. Then several monks, having dressed in the morning, taking their bowls and robes, entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then those monks thought: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Haliddavasana. Why don’t we go to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.54:11: Monks, those wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed as follows: ‘Friends, when loving-kindness mind-deliverance is developed, what is its characteristic, what is its excellence, what is its fruit, what is its final goal? Friends, when compassion mind-deliverance is developed, what is its characteristic, what is its excellence, what is its fruit, what is its final goal? … When sympathetic joy mind-deliverance is developed, what is its characteristic …? When equanimity mind-deliverance is developed, what is its characteristic, what is its excellence, what is its fruit, what is its final goal?’ When thus questioned, monks, the wanderers of other sects would be unable to reply and would meet with vexation. Why is that? Because it is outside their domain, monks. Monks, I do not see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.54:12: And how, monks, when loving-kindness mind-deliverance is developed, what is its characteristic, what is its excellence, what is its fruit, what is its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by loving-kindness … he develops the equanimity enlightenment factor accompanied by loving-kindness, grounded in seclusion, grounded in dispassion, grounded in cessation, maturing in relinquishment. If he wishes ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in what is not repulsive,’ he dwells perceiving the repulsive there. If he wishes ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in what is repulsive,’ he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive there. If he wishes ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in what is not repulsive and in what is repulsive,’ he dwells perceiving the repulsive there. If he wishes ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in what is repulsive and in what is not repulsive,’ he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive there. If he wishes ‘Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and aware,’ he dwells equanimous there, mindful and aware, or else he enters and dwells in the beautiful liberation. Monks, I say that loving-kindness mind-deliverance has the beautiful as its excellence for a monk of my instruction who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: And how, monks, when compassion mind-deliverance is developed, what is its characteristic, what is its excellence, what is its fruit, what is its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by compassion … he develops the equanimity enlightenment factor accompanied by compassion, grounded in seclusion, grounded in dispassion, grounded in cessation, maturing in relinquishment. If he wishes ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in what is not repulsive,’ he dwells perceiving the repulsive there … If he wishes ‘Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and aware,’ he dwells equanimous there, mindful and aware. Or else, having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory reaction, unmindful of perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. Monks, I say that compassion mind-deliverance has the base of infinite space as its excellence for a monk of my instruction who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: And how, monks, when sympathetic joy mind-deliverance is developed, what is its characteristic, what is its excellence, what is its fruit, what is its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by sympathetic joy … he develops the equanimity enlightenment factor accompanied by sympathetic joy, grounded in seclusion, grounded in dispassion, grounded in cessation, maturing in relinquishment. If he wishes ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in what is not repulsive,’ he dwells perceiving the repulsive there … If he wishes ‘Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and aware,’ he dwells equanimous there, mindful and aware. Or else, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. Monks, I say that sympathetic joy mind-deliverance has the base of infinite consciousness as its excellence for a monk of my instruction who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.8:1: On one occasion the Venerable Upavāna and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to the Venerable Upavāna. Having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Upavāna. Having exchanged greetings and courtesies, he sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Upavāna:
translations.sn46.8:2: “Could a monk know, friend Upavāna, ‘Through my own wise attention these seven awakening factors are well developed for me, leading to ease of dwelling’?” “He could know, friend Sāriputta, ‘Through my own wise attention these seven awakening factors are well developed for me, leading to ease of dwelling’.”
translations.sn47.10:1: Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to a certain dwelling place for monks. Having gone, he sat down on a prepared seat. Then several nuns went to the Venerable Ānanda. Having gone, they paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, those nuns said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn47.10:2: “Here, Venerable Ānanda, several nuns dwelling with minds well established in the four establishments of mindfulness are realizing a superior distinction of immediate effect.” “That’s so, sisters, that’s so, sisters. For one, sisters, who is a monk or nun dwelling with mind well established in the four establishments of mindfulness, it is to be expected that they will realize a superior distinction of immediate effect.”
translations.sn47.10:7: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk is a mindful observer of phenomena… ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While a mindful observer of phenomena is dwelling, either bodily fever arises with phenomena as object, or mental sloth and torpor, or the mind is externally distracted. Then, Ānanda, the monk should fix his mind on some inspiring sign. When he fixes his mind on some inspiring sign, joy is born. With joy born, rapture is born. With rapture-born body is pacified. With pacified body he experiences pleasure. With pleasured mind becomes concentrated. He reflects thus: ‘For the sake of that for which I fixed my mind, that has been accomplished for me. Come now, let me withdraw.’ He withdraws but does not think or examine. ‘I am without applied thought and sustained thought, mindful internally, I am happy’ he understands. Thus, Ānanda, there is development by fixing,
translations.sn47.10:9: Thus, Ānanda, I have taught development by fixing, taught development without fixing. Ānanda, whatever a teacher should do out of sympathy for his disciples, compassionate, pitying, that I have done for you. These roots of trees, Ānanda, these empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda, do not be negligent, lest you regret it later. This is our instruction to you.”
translations.sn47.13:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Now on that occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans at Nālaka village, sick, suffering, gravely ill. And Cunda the novice was the Venerable Sāriputta’s attendant.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then the Venerable Sāriputta passed away due to that very illness. Then Cunda the novice, taking the Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and robe, went to Sāvatthī, Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, to the Venerable Ānanda. Having gone, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, Cunda the novice said this to the Venerable Ānanda: ‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has passed away. This is his bowl and robe.’
translations.sn47.13:3: “Friend Cunda, this matter has come up that needs to be presented to the Blessed One. Come, friend Cunda, let us go to the Blessed One and report this matter to him.” “Yes, sir,” Cunda the novice replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then the Venerable Ānanda and Cunda the novice went to the Blessed One. Having gone, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “This Cunda the novice, sir, said thus: ‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has passed away; this is his bowl and robe.’ And, sir, on hearing that ‘the Venerable Sāriputta has passed away,’ my body became as if drugged, I could not see the directions, the teachings did not appear to me.”
translations.sn46.54:3: “The ascetic Gotama, friend, teaches his disciples thus: ‘Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of mind that weaken wisdom, live pervading one direction with a mind coupled with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, with a mind coupled with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will, pervading the all-encompassing world. Live pervading one direction with a mind coupled with compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, with a mind coupled with compassion, vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will, pervading the all-encompassing world. Live pervading one direction with a mind coupled with sympathetic joy, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, with a mind coupled with sympathetic joy, vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will, pervading the all-encompassing world. Live pervading one direction with a mind coupled with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, with a mind coupled with equanimity, vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will, pervading the all-encompassing world.’”
translations.sn47.19:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sedaka, a town of the Sumbhas. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Once upon a time, monks, a bamboo-worker had climbed up a bamboo wagon and addressed his apprentice basket-weaver: ‘Come, dear basket-weaver, climb up the bamboo wagon and stand at the end of my yoke.’ ‘Yes, teacher,’ replied the apprentice basket-weaver to the bamboo-worker. Having climbed up the bamboo wagon, he stood at the end of his teacher’s yoke. Then, monks, the bamboo-worker said this to his apprentice basket-weaver: ‘You protect me, dear basket-weaver, and I will protect you. Thus protected and guarding one another, we will teach skills, earn a living, and descend safely from the bamboo wagon.’ When this was said, monks, the apprentice basket-weaver said this to the bamboo-worker: ‘No, teacher, it will not be like that. You, teacher, protect yourself, and I will protect myself. Thus self-protected and self-guarding, we will teach skills, earn a living, and descend safely from the bamboo wagon.’
translations.sn47.19:2: “That is the correct way,” the Blessed One said. “As the apprentice basket-weaver said to his teacher. The foundations of mindfulness are to be practiced for the sake of protecting oneself; the foundations of mindfulness are to be practiced for the sake of protecting others. Protecting oneself, one protects others; protecting others, one protects oneself.
translations.sn47.20:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sedaka, a town of the Sumbhas. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.sn47.20:2: “Monks, suppose a large crowd of people were to assemble, saying, ‘Come, behold the country beauty, the country beauty!’ A great crowd of people would assemble, excited, saying, ‘The country beauty is supremely skilled in dancing, supremely skilled in singing. The country beauty is dancing and singing!’ Then a man would come desiring life, not desiring death, desiring happiness, and disliking pain. To him it would be said: ‘Here, man, is an oil lamp to be held between the great assembly and the country beauty. A man with a raised sword behind you will follow close behind. Wherever he strikes you even a little, there he will cut off your head.’ What do you think, monks, would that man disregard that oil lamp and heedlessly look elsewhere?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn47.25:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then a certain brahmin went to the Blessed One, exchanged greetings with him, and after the greetings and polite talk had been concluded, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: “What is the cause and condition, Gotama, by which the true Dhamma does not last long after the Tathāgata’s parinibbāna? And what is the cause and condition, Gotama, by which the true Dhamma lasts long after the Tathāgata’s parinibbāna?”
translations.sn47.25:2: “Brahmin, when the four foundations of mindfulness are undeveloped and uncultivated, the true Dhamma does not last long after the Tathāgata’s parinibbāna. And when the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, the true Dhamma lasts long after the Tathāgata’s parinibbāna.
translations.sn47.29:2: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went to the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha. Having gone, he sat down on the prepared seat. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Sirivaḍḍha: “I hope you are tolerating it, householder, I hope you are getting by, I hope your painful feelings are abating and not increasing, and that their abatement is evident, not their increase?” “No, sir, I am not tolerating it, I am not getting by. My painful feelings are increasing and not abating, and their increase is evident, not their abatement.”
translations.sn47.29:3: “Then, householder, you should train like this: ‘I will dwell contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; feeling in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.’ That’s how you should train, householder.”
translations.sn47.33:1: “For some, monks, the four foundations of mindfulness are neglected; for them the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering is neglected. For some, monks, the four foundations of mindfulness are undertaken; for them the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering is undertaken.
translations.sn47.37:1: “There are four foundations of mindfulness, monks. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating the body in the body, desire for the body is abandoned. With the abandonment of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, desire for feelings is abandoned. With the abandonment of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: He dwells contemplating mind in mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating mind in mind, desire for mind is abandoned. With the abandonment of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: “There are four foundations of mindfulness, monks. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. With the full understanding of the body, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. While he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. With the full understanding of feelings, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: He lives contemplating mind [as] mind-observer, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having overcome covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For him dwelling contemplating mind [as] mind-observer, mind is fully understood. With the full understanding of mind, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: “I will teach you the establishments of mindfulness, monks, and the development of the establishments of mindfulness, and the path leading to the development of the establishments of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, monks, are the establishments of mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk lives contemplating the body [as] body-observer, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having overcome covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; lives contemplating feelings [as] feelings-observer … lives contemplating mind [as] mind-observer … lives contemplating dhammas [as] dhammas-observer, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having overcome covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, monks, is called the establishments of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.40:2: And what, monks, is the development of the establishments of mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk lives contemplating phenomena of arising in the body, lives contemplating phenomena of passing away in the body, lives contemplating phenomena of arising and passing away in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having overcome covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Contemplating phenomena of arising in feelings … contemplating phenomena of arising in mind … contemplating phenomena of arising in dhammas, lives contemplating phenomena of passing away in dhammas, lives contemplating phenomena of arising and passing away in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having overcome covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, monks, is called the development of the establishments of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.4:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans in Sālā, a brahmin village. There the Blessed One addressed the monks …pe… and said:
translations.sn47.4:2: “Those monks of yours, monks, who are new, recently gone forth, who have come to this Dhamma and discipline, those monks should be encouraged, settled, and established in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Come, friends, dwell contemplating the body [as] body-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the knowledge and vision of the body as it really is; dwell contemplating feelings [as] feelings-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the knowledge and vision of feelings as they really are; dwell contemplating mind [as] mind-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the knowledge and vision of mind as it really is; dwell contemplating dhammas [as] dhammas-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the knowledge and vision of dhammas as they really are.
translations.sn47.4:3: Those monks, monks, who are learners, who have not attained, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage, even they dwell contemplating the body [as] body-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of the body; dwell contemplating feelings [as] feelings-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of feelings; dwell contemplating mind [as] mind-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of mind; dwell contemplating dhammas [as] dhammas-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of dhammas.
translations.sn47.4:4: Those monks, monks, who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of being, and are rightly freed by perfect gnosis, even they dwell contemplating the body [as] body-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, released from body; dwell contemplating feelings [as] feelings-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, released from feelings; dwell contemplating mind [as] mind-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, released from mind; dwell contemplating dhammas [as] dhammas-observers, ardent, clearly comprehending, with one-pointed, lucid, concentrated, one-pointed minds, released from dhammas.
translations.sn47.6:1: “Once upon a time, monks, an osprey suddenly swooped down on a quail and seized it. Then, monks, the quail, being carried off by the osprey, lamented: ‘We were unlucky, we were without merit, in that we wandered in an unsuitable range, in a foreign territory. If only we had wandered in our own suitable range, in our own ancestral territory, this osprey would not have been a match for me, that is, in battle.’ ‘But what is your own suitable range, your own ancestral territory, quail?’ ‘It is that—ploughshare-shaft turning place, mud-pit spot.’ Then, monks, the osprey, relying on its own strength, not lacking in its own strength, not flattering, released the quail: ‘Go, quail, even there, if you go, you won’t escape me.’
translations.sn47.6:2: Then, monks, the quail went to the ploughshare-shaft turning place, the mud-pit spot, climbed onto a large clod of mud, and stood taunting the osprey: ‘Come and get me now, osprey, come and get me now, osprey!’ Then, monks, that osprey, relying on its own strength, not lacking in its own strength, not flattering, folding its wings on both sides, suddenly swooped down on the quail. When, monks, the quail knew ‘This osprey has come with great speed for me,’ then right there in that clod of mud it made an opening. Then, monks, the osprey right there smashed its chest. So it is, monks, for one who wanders in an unsuitable range, in a foreign territory.
translations.sn47.6:3: Therefore, monks, do not wander in an unsuitable range, in a foreign territory. For those who wander in an unsuitable range, in a foreign territory, Māra gets a foothold, Māra gets an opportunity. And what, monks, is a monk’s unsuitable range, a foreign territory? It is the five strands of sensual pleasures. Which five? Forms cognizable by eye that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, beautiful, connected with sensual desire, alluring; sounds cognizable by ear …pe… odors cognizable by nose …pe… flavors cognizable by tongue …pe… tangibles cognizable by body that are agreeable, pleasing, charming, beautiful, connected with sensual desire, alluring—these, monks, are a monk’s unsuitable range, a foreign territory.
translations.sn47.7:1: “There are, monks, rugged, uneven places in the Himavat, the king of mountains, where neither monkeys wander nor humans. There are, monks, rugged, uneven places in the Himavat, the king of mountains, where monkeys wander, but not humans. There are, monks, even, delightful tracts of land in the Himavat, the king of mountains, where both monkeys and humans wander. There, monks, hunters plaster sticky lime on the monkeys’ paths for the affliction of monkeys.
translations.sn47.8:2: Indeed, bhikkhus, that foolish, unlearned, unskilled cook does not take up a sign of his master’s taste: ‘Today this sour dish of mine pleases the master, he brings it, he takes much of it, he speaks praise of it. Today this sour cream dish of mine pleases the master, he brings the sour cream, he takes much of the sour cream, he speaks praise of the sour cream. Today this bitter cream dish of mine … this pungent cream dish … this sweet cream dish … this salty dish … this unsalty dish … this salty cream dish of mine … this unsalty cream dish pleases the master, he brings the unsalty cream, he takes much of the unsalty cream, he speaks praise of the unsalty cream.’
translations.sn47.8:4: Indeed, bhikkhus, that foolish, unlearned, unskilled monk is not one who obtains happiness in the present life, nor one who obtains mindfulness and clear comprehension. Why is that? Because that foolish, unlearned, unskilled monk does not take up a sign of his own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Just as, bhikkhus, a wise, learned, skilled cook who is attending on a king or a royal minister with various kinds of dishes—with sour creams, bitter creams, pungent creams, sweet creams, salty dishes, unsalty dishes, salty creams, unsalty creams.
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Vajirā, having dressed in the morning, taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from almsround, she went to the Andhavana to spend the day. Having entered the Andhavana, she sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the nun Vajirā, desiring to make her fall away from samādhi, approached the nun Vajirā; having approached, he addressed the nun Vajirā in verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: “By what is this being created, what is the creator of the being; The being is created by what, by what does the being cease?”
translations.sn5.10:3: Then the nun Vajirā thought: “Who is this—human or non-human—speaking a verse?” Then the nun Vajirā thought: “This is Māra the Evil One desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, desiring to make me fall away from samādhi, speaking a verse.” Then the nun Vajirā, having understood “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verse:
translations.sn5.10:4: “Why do you assume ‘a being’? Māra, is that your view? Only a heap of formations here, no being is found.
translations.sn5.10:5: Just as the combination of parts is called ‘chariot,’ so too, when the aggregates are present, ‘being’ is the convention.
translations.sn5.10:6: Suffering alone arises, suffering stands and passes away; Nothing apart from suffering arises, nothing apart from suffering passes away.”
translations.sn5.1:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the nun Āḷavikā, having dressed in the morning, taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from almsround, she went to the Andhavana desiring seclusion. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the nun Āḷavikā, desiring to make her fall away from seclusion, approached the nun Āḷavikā; having approached, he addressed the nun Āḷavikā in verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: “There is no escape in the world, what’s the use of your seclusion; Enjoy sensual pleasures, don’t later regret it.”
translations.sn5.1:3: Then the nun Āḷavikā thought: “Who is this—human or non-human—speaking a verse?” Then the nun Āḷavikā thought: “This is Māra the Evil One desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, desiring to make me fall away from seclusion, speaking a verse.” Then the nun Āḷavikā, having understood “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verse:
translations.sn5.1:4: “There is an escape in the world, touched by my wisdom; O Evil One with heedlessness as kin, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sensual pleasures like spears with sixty tips, heaps of bones gnawed by dogs; What you call sensual pleasure, that was no pleasure for me.”
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking “The nun Āḷavikā knows me,” afflicted and dejected, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: “What is attained by seers, that state so hard to attain; That is not possible to reach by a woman with two-finger wisdom.”
translations.sn5.2:4: “What does womanhood matter when the mind is well-concentrated, when knowledge is present, rightly discerning the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.2:5: Whoever should think like this: ‘I am woman’ or ‘I am man,’ or anything else, Māra would have no chance to say that.”
translations.sn5.3:2: “Why are you like a daughter grieving for her mother, tearful-faced; Gone alone to the forest, are you searching for a man?”
translations.sn5.3:3: Then the nun Kisāgotamī thought: “Who is this—human or non-human—speaking a verse?” Then the nun Kisāgotamī thought: “This is Māra the Evil One desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, desiring to make me fall away from samādhi, speaking a verse.”
translations.sn5.3:5: “Completely like a daughter grieving for her mother, men are just that close to me; I neither grieve nor weep, nor do I fear that, friend.
translations.sn5.3:6: Delight is destroyed everywhere, the mass of darkness is split; Having conquered Māra’s army, I dwell with taints destroyed.”
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking “The nun Kisāgotamī knows me,” afflicted and dejected, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Vijayā, having dressed in the morning …pe… sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the nun Vijayā, desiring to make her fall away from samādhi, approached the nun Vijayā; having approached, he addressed the nun Vijayā in verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: “You are young and beautiful, and I am young and handsome; With a five-stringed lute, come, let us take delight.”
translations.sn5.4:4: “Forms, sounds, flavors, smells, and delightful tangibles; I renounce them all for you, Māra, I have no desire for them.
translations.sn5.4:5: With this putrid body, breaking and crumbling; I am disgusted, I am repelled, sensual craving is eradicated.
translations.sn5.4:6: Those beings who resort to form, and those who abide in the formless; and that attainment of cessation, darkness is dispelled everywhere.
translations.sn5.5:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, having dressed in the morning time …pe… stood at the root of a fully blooming sāla tree. Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, and desiring to make her fall away from samādhi, approached her; having approached, he addressed the nun Uppalavaṇṇā with a verse:
translations.sn5.5:2: “Nun, having approached the fully blooming top, you stand alone at the root of the sāla tree; You have no second of lovely form, fool, don’t you fear the wild forest?”
translations.sn5.5:4: “Even a hundred thousand wild ones, if such ones should come here; My hair doesn’t stand on end, I’m not afraid, I don’t fear even one Māra.
translations.sn5.5:6: With mind well subdued, the bases of psychic power well developed; Freed from all bonds, I don’t fear you, friend.
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking “The nun Uppalavaṇṇā knows me,” miserable and dejected, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: “Why don’t you delight in birth, one born enjoys sensual pleasures; Who urged you to this, nun, don’t delight in birth.”
translations.sn5.6:3: “For one born there is death, one born touches sufferings; Bondage, slaughter, defilement, therefore I don’t delight in birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha taught the Dhamma, the transcending of birth; For the relinquishment of all suffering, he placed me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: Those beings who resort to form, and those who abide in the formless; Not knowing cessation, they go to future becoming.
translations.sn5.7:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Upacālā, having dressed in the morning time …pe… sat at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding. Then Māra the Evil One approached the nun Upacālā; having approached, he said to the nun Upacālā: “Nun, for rebirth where do you wish to be reborn?” “Friend, I don’t wish to be reborn anywhere.”
translations.sn5.7:2: “The Thirty-three, the Yāma realm, and the Tusita gods; The gods who delight in creation, the gods who have control over what is created; Direct your mind there, you will experience delight.
translations.sn5.7:3: “The Thirty-three, the Yāma realm, and the Tusita gods; The gods who delight in creation, the gods who have control over what is created; Bound by the bond of sensuality, they come under Māra’s control again.
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is ablaze, the whole world is burning; The whole world is blazing, the whole world is quaking.
translations.sn5.7:5: The unquaking, unblazing, not frequented by common people; The path where Māra has no access, there my mind delights.
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking “The nun Upacālā knows me,” miserable and dejected, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Sīsupacālā, having dressed in the morning time …pe… sat at the root of a tree for the day’s abiding. Then Māra the Evil One approached the nun Sīsupacālā; having approached, he said to the nun Sīsupacālā: “Nun, whose doctrine do you approve?” “Friend, I don’t approve anyone’s doctrine.”
translations.sn5.8:2: “For whom did you shave your head, you look like an ascetic; You don’t approve any doctrine, why do you wander deluded?”
translations.sn5.8:3: “Outside here are the heretics, they are pleased with their views; I don’t approve their Dhamma, they are not expert in the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: Freed and untorn everywhere, the eye-witness sees everything; Having reached the destruction of all deeds, freed in the destruction of clinging; The Blessed One is my teacher, I approve his dispensation.
translations.sn5.9:2: “By whom was this image made, who is the maker of the image; Where does the image arise, where does the image cease?”
translations.sn5.9:4: “This image was not made by self, this evil was not made by another; Arisen dependent on a cause, it ceases with the cessation of the cause.
translations.sn5.9:6: Thus the aggregates and elements, and these six sense bases; Arisen dependent on a cause, they cease with the cessation of the cause.
translations.sn56.11:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
translations.sn56.11:10: And when, monks, this knowledge and vision of things as they really are in regard to these four noble truths with its three turnings and twelve aspects was thoroughly purified, then, monks, I claimed: ‘I have awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people.’ And insight arose in me: ‘My liberation is unshakeable; this is my last birth; there is no more rebirth.’ This is what the Blessed One said. Satisfied, the group of five monks delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this discourse was being spoken, there arose in the venerable Koṇḍañña the dust-free, stainless eye of the Dhamma: ‘Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.’
translations.sn56.11:13: At that moment, at that instant, at that second, the cry reached as far as the Brahmā-world. And this ten-thousandfold world-system quaked, shook, and trembled, and an immeasurable, magnificent radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the divine splendor of the gods.
translations.sn56.11:2: “Monks, these two extremes should not be followed by one who has gone forth. Which two? There is devotion to sensual pleasures, which is low, coarse, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And there is devotion to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless. Monks, by not approaching these two extremes, the Tathāgata has awakened to the middle way, which gives vision, which gives knowledge, and which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:3: “And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives vision, which gives knowledge, and which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to nibbāna? It is just this noble eightfold path, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives vision, which gives knowledge, and which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to nibbāna.”}
translations.sn56.11:4: And this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wants is also suffering—in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. And this, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: that craving which gives rise to further becoming, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there, namely sensual craving, craving for becoming, craving for non-becoming. And this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: the remainderless fading away and ceasing, giving up, relinquishing, letting go, and non-clinging of that very craving. And this, monks, is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering: this very noble eightfold path, that is, right view …pe… right concentration.
translations.sn56.11:5: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light. ‘This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me …pe… light. ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light.
