translations.sn56.11:6: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me …pe… light. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light.
translations.sn56.11:7: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me …pe… light. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light.
translations.sn56.11:8: ‘This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light. ‘This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me …pe… light. ‘This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed,’ monks—with reference to things never heard before there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, light.
translations.sn56.11:9: And so long as I did not truly understand, monks, the threefold revolution, twelve aspects of these four noble truths with the knowledge and vision that accords with reality, so pure and clear, for that long I did not declare, monks, in this world with its devas, Mara, and Brahma, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and people: ‘I have become a fully enlightened Buddha.’
translations.sn56.20:1: “These four, monks, are actual, not otherwise, not different. Which four? ‘This is suffering,’ monks, it is actual, it is not otherwise, it is not different; ‘this is the origin of suffering,’ it is actual, it is not otherwise, it is not different; ‘this is the cessation of suffering,’ it is actual, it is not otherwise, it is not different; ‘this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,’ it is actual, it is not otherwise, it is not different—these four, monks, are actual, not otherwise, not different.
translations.sn56.26:1: “Whichever beings, monks, you might have compassion for, and whichever you might think should be heard—whether friends or companions or relatives or kin—those, monks, you should exhort, direct, and establish in the true understanding of the four noble truths.
translations.sn56.26:2: Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Whichever beings, monks, you might have compassion for, and whichever you might think should be heard—whether friends or companions or relatives or kin—those, monks, you should exhort, direct, and establish in the true understanding of these four noble truths.
translations.sn56.27:1: “These four, monks, are noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering—these four noble truths, monks, are actual, not otherwise, not different; therefore they are called ‘noble truths.’
translations.sn56.28:1: “These four, monks, are noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. In this world with its devas, Mara, and Brahma, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, princes and people, the Tathagata is noble; therefore they are called ‘noble truths.’
translations.sn56.30:1: On one occasion many elder monks were staying at Cetiya. Then, after their meal on return from almsround, while seated together in the pavilion, this discussion arose among them: ‘Does one who sees suffering also see the origin of suffering, see the cessation of suffering, see the path leading to the cessation of suffering?’
translations.sn56.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in the siṁsapā grove. Then the Blessed One, having taken some siṁsapā leaves in his hand, addressed the monks: “What do you think, monks, which are more numerous—the few siṁsapā leaves that I have taken in my hand, or those above in the siṁsapā grove?” “Very few, Bhante, are the siṁsapā leaves taken by the Blessed One in his hand; but those above in the siṁsapā grove are far more numerous.” “So too, monks, far more numerous is what I have known with direct knowledge but have not declared to you. And why, monks, has that not been declared by me? It is not connected with the goal, not fundamental to the holy life, does not flow towards disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, awakening, or Nibbāna; therefore it has not been declared by me.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what, monks, has been declared by me? ‘This is suffering’—I have declared that, monks; ‘This is the origin of suffering’—I have declared that; ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—I have declared that; ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—I have declared that.
translations.sn56.31:3: And why, monks, has that been declared by me? Because it is connected with the goal, it is fundamental to the holy life, it flows towards disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and Nibbāna; therefore it has been declared by me.
translations.sn56.35:1: “Monks, suppose a man were to say: ‘My good man, early in the morning they will spear you with seven hundred spears, at midday they will spear you with seven hundred spears, in the evening they will spear you with seven hundred spears. Thus, my good man, pierced day after day with three times seven hundred spears, you who have a lifespan of a hundred years, who live a hundred years, at the end of a hundred years will realize the four noble truths that you have not yet realized.’
translations.sn56.35:2: It would be enough, monks, for a clansman who has faith to go forth. Why is that? For this wandering-on is without discoverable beginning. Its beginning is not discerned—of beings roaming and wandering on, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving. Even so, monks, I do not say that realization of the four noble truths is accompanied by suffering and grief; but I do say that realization of the four noble truths is accompanied by ease and joy. Which four? The noble truth of suffering … the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.36:1: “Monks, suppose a man were to cut up all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jambudīpa into one pile and make stakes from them. Having made stakes, he were to impale on large stakes those large creatures in the great ocean, on medium stakes those medium creatures in the great ocean, on small stakes those small creatures in the great ocean. And there would still remain, monks, coarse creatures in the great ocean that had not been impaled.
translations.sn56.36:2: Then all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jambudīpa would come to depletion and exhaustion. Far more numerous, monks, are the small creatures in the great ocean that are not easy to impale on stakes. Why is that? Because of the subtlety of their bodies. So great, monks, is the lower shore. Therefore, monks, a person who is freed from the lower shore, who possesses right view, understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’ as it really is.
translations.sn56.42:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: ‘Come, monks, let us go to the Paṭibhāna Cliff for the day’s abiding.’ ‘Yes, Bhante,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, together with a number of monks, went to the Paṭibhāna Cliff. A certain monk saw a great chasm at the Paṭibhāna Cliff. Seeing it, he said to the Blessed One: ‘This chasm is vast, Bhante, a terrifying chasm, Bhante. Is there, Bhante, any chasm greater and more terrifying than this chasm?’ ‘There is, monk, a chasm greater and more terrifying than this chasm.’
translations.sn56.42:2: “But what, Bhante, is the chasm greater and more terrifying than this chasm?” “Whatever monks or brahmins do not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ do not understand as it really is: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—they delight in formations leading to birth, they delight in formations leading to aging, they delight in formations leading to death, they delight in formations leading to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Delighting in formations leading to birth, delighting in formations leading to aging, delighting in formations leading to death, delighting in formations leading to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, they fabricate formations leading to birth, fabricate formations leading to aging, fabricate formations leading to death, fabricate formations leading to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Having fabricated formations leading to birth, having fabricated formations leading to aging, having fabricated formations leading to death, having fabricated formations leading to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, they fall into the chasm of birth, fall into the chasm of aging, fall into the chasm of death, fall into the chasm of sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. They are not freed from birth, from aging, from death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs. ‘They are not freed from suffering,’ I say.
translations.sn56.45:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Forest at the peaked-roofed hall. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw many Licchavi youths practicing archery in the assembly hall, shooting arrows from afar with fine palm-leaf arrows, unerring one after another. Seeing this, it occurred to him: “The Licchavi youths are well-trained, indeed very well-trained; that they should shoot arrows from afar with fine palm-leaf arrows, unerring one after another.”
translations.sn56.45:3: “What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult to do or harder to achieve—shooting an arrow from afar with a fine palm-leaf arrow unerringly one after another, or threading the tip of a split hair seven times? ” “This is harder to do and harder to achieve, venerable sir, threading the tip of a split hair seven times.” “Even harder to penetrate, Ānanda, is what those penetrate who penetrate ‘this is suffering’ as it really is …pe… ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’ as it really is.
translations.sn56.46:1: “There are, bhikkhus, inter-worldly realms that are perilous, unprotected, and shrouded in darkness, where the light of the moon and sun—no matter how powerful, no matter how mighty—does not reach.”
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, one bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Great indeed, venerable sir, is that darkness, exceedingly great indeed, venerable sir, is that darkness. Is there, venerable sir, darkness greater and more frightful than this darkness?” “There is, bhikkhu, darkness greater and more frightful than this darkness.”
translations.sn56.48:1: “Bhikkhus, suppose this great earth were all water. And a man were to toss a single yoke-pin into it. Then the east wind would carry it to the west, the west wind to the east, the north wind to the south, the south wind to the north. And there is a blind turtle that comes up once every hundred years. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that blind turtle, coming up once every hundred years, put its neck into that single yoke-pin?” “It would be an extraordinary thing, venerable sir, if that blind turtle, coming up once every hundred years, were to put its neck into that single yoke-pin.”
translations.sn56.48:2: “Even more extraordinary, bhikkhus, is obtaining human birth. Even more extraordinary, bhikkhus, is a Tathāgata arising in the world, an Arahant, perfectly enlightened. Even more extraordinary, bhikkhus, is the teaching and discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shining in the world. Bhikkhus, human birth has been obtained, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, perfectly enlightened, and the teaching and discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world.”}
